## D71. Real wall-clock budget for `search/architecture`'s escalation cascade — the third port of
D69's own pattern, this time reaching all the way to the real agent-facing `flux_search`
CHIA node/MCP tool, with a real, structural constraint (screening's own batch dispatch isn't
interruptible) found and designed around rather than glossed over

**Decision.** `search/architecture`'s `run_architecture_dse` gains `wall_clock_budget_s`: real,
measured elapsed time, checked before each **escalation** rung's own evaluator call — not before
screening, which is a real, deliberate scope limit (see below). `ArchitectureDSEReport` gains
`stopped_early: bool` and `wall_clock_s: float`. Unlike D69/D70, this decision also threads the
new parameter all the way through the real agent-facing surface this strategy already has:
`flows/chia_nodes/src/flux_chia_nodes/search.py`'s `flux_search` CHIA node/MCP tool gains the same
`wall_clock_budget_s` parameter, passed straight through to `run_architecture_dse` — `search/
annealing`/`search/exhaustive` (D69/D70) have no CHIA node at all, so this is the first time this
whole D69-started line of work reaches an agent, not just a library caller.

**Why.** A bare "continue" after D70. D70's own Implications named the two remaining real targets
(`search/architecture`, `search/agentic`) without picking one, so, following D70's own precedent
of picking the more concrete/tractable option, I chose `search/architecture` over `search/
agentic`: it doesn't share D57's own consolidated engine (a five-strategy-wide surface, a riskier
place for a still-only-twice-proven pattern), and — unlike `search/annealing`/`search/exhaustive`
— it already has a real CHIA node/MCP tool (`flux_search`), so this port closes a real gap in the
*agent-facing* surface, not just the library, a genuinely higher-value target than a third
library-only port would have been.

**A real, structural design question, resolved by recognizing what's actually interruptible
here, not forcing the same shape D69/D70 already used:** `search/architecture`'s screening step
calls `evaluate_batch()` once, on every candidate at once — deliberately, so a real, parallel
evaluator (`ChiaParallelEvaluator`, D34's own real concurrent-Ray-task dispatch) can screen every
candidate simultaneously rather than one at a time. Unlike D70's own exhaustive-search port (where
switching a batched call to one-at-a-time was a real, safe, zero-behavior-change fix), doing the
same here would mean either abandoning real batch/parallel dispatch entirely or trying to
half-consume an in-flight parallel batch with no clean way to know which candidates actually
finished — a real regression, not a neutral implementation detail. Escalation, by contrast, is
already a real, naturally sequential rung-by-rung cascade (screen once, then confirm the winner
through coarse SystemC, then cycle-accurate RTL, in order) — a real, pre-existing per-rung
checkpoint to check a budget at, and, in practice, exactly where a real budget matters most: the
escalation rungs are the slow, real-compile-and-simulate steps; screening (one real ZigZag call)
is comparatively fast.

**What was verified — real ZigZag/SystemC/RTL timing, checked before any code was trusted, the
same discipline D69/D70 both used:**
- **No behavioral change for the unbudgeted case**: the full pre-existing
  `tests/unit/test_search_architecture_dse.py` (12 tests) and
  `tests/integration/test_architecture_dse_live.py` (the real, pinned width-4/8/16 sweep with
  real SystemC+RTL escalation agreeing exactly at 265.0 cycles) both pass unchanged.
- **A real baseline measured first**: the known real `mlp-gemm0.yaml`/`simple-npu-1d-v1.yaml`
  width-4/8/16 sweep, screened through real ZigZag then escalated through real SystemC and real
  RTL, takes 21.055s total — SystemC and RTL each contributing roughly half (~10.5s), confirmed
  directly, not assumed proportional.
- **A real budgeted run against the identical sweep**: `wall_clock_budget_s=12.0` lets the real
  SystemC rung complete (12.594s total) and stops before the real RTL rung —
  `stopped_early=True`, `escalation == ["systemc"]` — while `winner`/`winner_screening_result`
  are still the real, complete screening result (screening itself was never interrupted).
- **A real, direct proof the budget is a genuine stopping condition**: `wall_clock_budget_s=0.0`
  against a fake evaluator skips every escalation rung before the first one is ever called
  (checked against the fake's own real call count), while screening still completes fully and a
  real winner is still reported — the exact intended split between "interruptible" and "not."
- **The real CHIA node path verified directly, not assumed safe from the diff's own shape**:
  `flux_search("zigzag", ..., escalation_backends=["systemc", "rtl"], wall_clock_budget_s=12.0)`
  reproduces the identical real 12s cutoff through the full CHIA-node call path (including real
  Ray initialization) — confirmed the apparent crash-looking traceback on exit was Ray's own
  known, harmless worker-shutdown noise printed *after* the real, correct result, not a real
  failure (checked by re-running with output ordering examined directly, not assumed benign).
  The full pre-existing `tests/integration/test_chia_flux_search_live.py` suite (12 tests) also
  confirmed passing unchanged.
- **3 new unit tests** (`tests/unit/test_search_architecture_dse.py` — no-budget default,
  zero-budget skips every rung while screening still completes, a synthetic-timing partial-
  escalation case) and **1 new integration test**
  (`tests/integration/test_architecture_dse_live.py`, real ZigZag+SystemC+RTL: the real 12s
  SystemC-completes/RTL-cut-off comparison above, now a permanent regression check).
- **Full regression**: the complete unit suite plus conformance suite — 696 passed / 22 skipped
  (up from D70's 693), 0 failed.

**Implications.**
- gap-analysis.md G16's real wall-clock-budget capability now covers three of this repo's four
  non-agentic search strategies (`search/annealing`, `search/exhaustive`, `search/architecture`'s
  escalation phase) — and, for the first time in this line of work, reaches an actual agent-facing
  tool (`flux_search`), not just a library function a Python caller would need to import directly.
- The real, structural "screening isn't interruptible, escalation is" split this decision
  documented is itself a template for the one remaining target, `search/agentic`: its own five
  strategies each run a harness-driven propose/observe loop (D57's shared engine) that's already
  sequential, closer in shape to `search/annealing`'s own per-iteration checkpoint than to
  `search/architecture`'s batched screening — suggesting that port, when it happens, will look
  more like D69's than D71's, a real, useful prediction for whoever picks it up next.
- Only one of gap-analysis.md G16's four search-strategy families remains without any real
  wall-clock budget enforcement: `search/agentic`. Named explicitly here again, not implied
  covered by this decision's own real but partial reach.

## D72. Closing a real gap in the "three surfaces, all verified" discipline: `evaluators/thermal`
and `evaluators/booksim`'s chiplet D2D path had never actually been called over the real MCP wire

**Decision.** Two new integration tests in `tests/integration/test_flux_mcp_tool_live.py`:
`test_evaluate_tool_call_runs_the_real_thermal_backend_over_mcp` and
`test_evaluate_tool_call_runs_the_real_chiplet_d2d_interconnect_over_mcp` — both call the generic
`flux_evaluate` MCP tool with `backend="thermal"`/`backend="booksim"` (a chiplet-topology
architecture) respectively, over the real wire protocol (`mcp.ClientSession` +
`streamable_http_client`), pinned against the exact same real numbers their own in-process tests
already established (D64/D65 for thermal, D66/D67 for the chiplet path).

**Why.** The user opened `docs/agent-surface.md` in their IDE alongside a bare "continue" —
not an instruction, but a real, concrete prompt to actually look at that file rather than start a
new, unrelated capability. Doing so surfaced a real, previously-unnoticed staleness: its own
"verified end to end with a real MCP client... against real ZigZag, real Verilator-RTL, real
Timeloop, real Booksim2, real Noxim, real CACTI, real gem5" claim (last touched when D63 added the
26th tool) never mentioned 3D-ICE at all, and grepping `test_flux_mcp_tool_live.py` directly
(not trusting the doc's own claim) confirmed *why*: every real `evaluate` tool call in that whole
file uses `backend="zigzag"` — `evaluators/thermal` (D64/D65) and `evaluators/booksim`'s own
chiplet `anynet` path (D66/D67) had each been verified in-process (a direct adapter call, then the
`flux_evaluate` CHIA node) but never once actually sent over the real MCP wire, the third of this
repo's own "one definition, three surfaces" discipline.

**What was verified — both real backends, over the real wire, pinned against already-established
real numbers, not new ones invented for this test:**
- `backend="thermal"` against `simple-npu-1d-thermal-v1.yaml` reproduces D64's own exact pinned
  numbers (`peak_temp_c=29.673000000000002`, `avg_temp_c=29.135000000000048`,
  `provenance.evaluator="3d-ice@real"`) through the real MCP round trip.
- `backend="booksim"` against `chiplet-2die-noc-v1.yaml` reproduces a real, positive
  `latency_cycles` and the exact real topology label D67 introduced
  (`"anynet-chiplet-2die-1link"`), `provenance.evaluator="booksim2@real"`, confirming the
  D2D-specific `anynet` dispatch path (not the KNCube one) is what actually ran over the wire.
- **Full regression**: the complete unit suite plus conformance suite — 696 passed / 22 skipped,
  unchanged from D71 (these are integration-only tests, added to a file outside that suite) —
  and the two new tests themselves confirmed passing directly.
- `docs/agent-surface.md`'s own stale claim corrected to name both real backends explicitly,
  cross-referenced to the decisions that built them.

**Implications.**
- The "three surfaces, all verified" discipline this repo has followed since its own early
  decisions is now actually true for `evaluators/thermal` and the chiplet D2D path, not merely
  claimed — a real, previously-silent gap between what agent-surface.md said and what was actually
  tested, found only by checking the test file directly rather than trusting its own prose.
- A real, generalizable process lesson: a doc's own "verified against X, Y, Z" list is a real
  claim that can quietly drift out of sync with what's actually tested as new backends are added
  without a dedicated MCP-level test of their own (both `evaluators/thermal` and the chiplet path
  have no dedicated tool — they're only reachable through the generic `flux_evaluate`, which is
  easy to forget to exercise with a new `backend` value specifically). Worth a similar direct
  check — grep the actual test file, don't just re-read the doc's own claim — the next time a new
  backend is added without its own dedicated tool.

## D73. Real wall-clock budget for all five `search/agentic` axes at once — the fourth and final
port of D69's pattern, closing gap-analysis.md G16's real wall-clock-budgeting capability across
every search-strategy family this repo has, plus threading it to every real CHIA node/MCP tool
this time, not just the library

**Decision.** `search/agentic/_engine.py`'s shared `drive_propose_observe_loop` (D57's own
consolidated driver, called by all five `run_agentic_X_search` functions) gains
`wall_clock_budget_s`, checked against real, measured elapsed time before every real
LLM-proposal-plus-evaluation round — and now returns `(stopped_early, wall_clock_s)` instead of
nothing, so all five callers can report both real facts without duplicating the timing logic.
Every one of the five `AgenticXSearchReport` dataclasses (mapping, architecture, NoC, memory,
joint) gains `stopped_early`/`wall_clock_s`, and every one of the five `run_agentic_X_search`
functions gains the same `wall_clock_budget_s` parameter. Unlike D69/D70 (library-only) and
matching D71's own reach, this decision also threads the new parameter all the way through the
real agent-facing surface: all five `flux_agentic_X_search` CHIA nodes
(`flows/chia_nodes/src/flux_chia_nodes/agentic.py`) and all five of their MCP tool methods
(`flows/mcp/src/flux_mcp/tool.py`) gain `wall_clock_budget_s` too.

**Why.** A bare "continue" after D72. D72 itself was a real, if smaller, detour prompted by the
user having `docs/agent-surface.md` open — with that closed, D71's own Implications (echoed again
in D70's) pointed at exactly one remaining real target for this whole D69-started line of work:
`search/agentic`. D71 itself had already predicted the *shape* this port would need — closer to
D69's per-iteration checkpoint than to D71's own batch-vs-sequential split — because all five
agentic strategies already run a genuinely sequential, one-candidate-at-a-time propose/observe
loop (unlike `search/architecture`'s own batched screening). That prediction held exactly: this
port needed no new structural design question the way D71's own batch-interruptibility question
did — the interesting real design question here was scope (one shared engine vs. five separate
implementations), and D57 had already answered it.

**A real, structural reason to do this at the shared-engine level rather than five separate
copies, verified as real leverage, not assumed:** every one of the five `run_agentic_X_search`
functions already called the identical `drive_propose_observe_loop(strategy, state, evaluator,
metric)` line — a single, one-line signature change plus one field addition to each of the five
already-near-identical `AgenticXSearchReport` dataclasses closed this gap for all five axes at
once, the exact "shared logic lives once" value proposition D57 itself was built to deliver,
confirmed real here rather than theoretical.

**What was verified — real Ollama + real ZigZag, checked before any code was trusted, the same
discipline D69–D71 all used:**
- **No behavioral change for the unbudgeted case across all five axes**: the full pre-existing
  unit suite for all five strategy files (85 tests) passes unchanged, and the real, live
  mapping-axis integration test (`test_search_agentic_live.py`, real Ollama + real ZigZag,
  converging to the same proven 1554-cycle optimum `test_search_exhaustive_live.py` established)
  passes unchanged too.
- **A real budgeted run through the full CHIA node stack** (real Ray init, real
  `chia.models.ollama.OllamaLLM`, real ZigZag): `flux_agentic_mapping_search(..., max_iterations=18,
  wall_clock_budget_s=3.0)` stops after exactly 1 real iteration — confirming a real local LLM
  round trip (measured here at over 12 real seconds for one proposal) dominates each iteration's
  own cost far more than the fast underlying ZigZag evaluation, the real reason a wall-clock
  budget matters most for this axis family specifically.
- **A real, direct proof the budget is a genuine stopping condition** (unit-level, all five axes):
  `wall_clock_budget_s=0.0` stops every axis before its own fake LLM proposer is ever called
  (`proposer.calls == 0`), confirmed per-axis, not assumed to generalize from the mapping axis
  alone.
- **7 new unit tests in the mapping-axis file** (`tests/unit/test_search_agentic_strategy.py` —
  the core timing logic: no-budget default, zero-budget immediate stop, a synthetic-timing
  partial-run case) **and 1 thin confirmation test in each of the other four axes' own files**
  (avoiding duplicating the core logic five times over, while still proving each axis genuinely
  reaches the shared engine's new parameter) **and 1 new real integration test**
  (`tests/integration/test_search_agentic_live.py`, real Ollama + real ZigZag: the 3s/1-iteration
  case above, now a permanent regression check).
- **Full regression**: the complete unit suite plus conformance suite — 703 passed / 22 skipped
  (up from D72's 696), 0 failed.

**Implications.**
- gap-analysis.md G16 ("cost is now a design parameter") now has real, checked, enforced
  wall-clock-budget support across **every one of this repo's four search-strategy families** —
  `search/annealing` (D69), `search/exhaustive` (D70), `search/architecture`'s escalation cascade
  (D71), and all five `search/agentic` axes (D73) — the real closure of a line of work D69 opened.
  The one real piece of G16 left open is dollar-cost budgeting, which has no non-zero real figure
  anywhere in this repo yet to build against honestly (the same honest gap named at every step of
  this line of work, not newly discovered here).
- The four real design questions this line of work actually answered, each different, each
  worth remembering as a template for the next repo that builds this kind of feature: (1) real
  signal over fabricated one (wall-clock, not a fake dollar figure, D69); (2) name the real
  consequence when a guarantee breaks, don't just report a number (`stopped_early` on
  `search/exhaustive`, D70); (3) recognize what's structurally interruptible before forcing a
  shape (`search/architecture`'s escalation-only scope, D71); (4) find and use real shared
  leverage instead of five separate copies when the infrastructure to do so already exists (D73).
- Every one of the four ports reached the real agent-facing tool surface except D69/D70
  (`search/annealing`/`search/exhaustive`), which simply have none — named explicitly here again,
  not a gap this decision could have closed.

## D74. Real DRAM bank/refresh-timing simulation via DRAMsim3 — closing the last named-open item
of gap-analysis.md G6, and by far the simplest external-tool build this repo has done

**Decision.** A new package, `evaluators/dramsim3/`, adapts real DRAMsim3 (University of Maryland
Memory-Systems Research, MIT — Li et al., "DRAMsim3: a Cycle-accurate, Thermal-Capable DRAM
Simulator," IEEE Computer Architecture Letters) as this repo's first DRAM bank/refresh-timing
evaluator. `build.py` clones and builds it on first use, pinned to a fixed commit
(`29817593b3389f1337235d63cac515024ab8fd6e`), the same "fetch an external resource once, cache it"
pattern `evaluators/booksim`/`noxim`/`cacti`/`gem5`/`thermal` already use.
`architecture_translator.py` scans `Candidate.arch`'s hierarchy for the first `class=="memory"`
entry declaring `attrs.dramsim3_config` (naming one of DRAMsim3's own real, bundled `.ini` timing
configs by filename, e.g. `"DDR4_8Gb_x8_3200"`), with optional `attrs.dramsim3_cycles`/
`attrs.dramsim3_stream` overrides (defaults: 100,000 cycles, DRAMsim3's own `"random"` synthetic
stream). `adapter.py`'s `DramSim3Evaluator` runs the real `dramsim3main <config> --stream <stream>
-c <cycles>` binary and parses its real `dramsim3.txt` output into `latency_cycles`
(`average_read_latency`), `energy_pj` (`total_energy`), `power_w` (`average_power / 1000`, DRAMsim3
reports mW), plus real per-command bank-activate/refresh counts (`num_act_cmds`/`num_ref_cmds`) in
`Bottleneck.per_level_utilisation`. `"dramsim3"` is registered in `flows/cli/src/flux_cli/
registry.py`'s evaluator registry — no new CHIA node/MCP tool, reachable through the existing
generic `flux_evaluate`, the same shape D64 already established for `evaluators/thermal`. New
example `ir/architecture/examples/simple-npu-1d-dram-v1.yaml`.

**Why.** A bare "continue" after D73. With D69–D73's wall-clock-budget line of work now closed
across every search-strategy family, I returned to gap-analysis.md's remaining open items (the
same scope-proportionality judgment used after D68: not a sixth consecutive decision in the same
vein, but a deliberate return to external-tool integration after diversifying through D69–D73) and
picked G6's one remaining named-open item, "DRAM bank/refresh detail" — the same gap category
D64/D65 (thermal) and D66/D67 (chiplet D2D) already closed the other pieces of. DRAMsim3 was
chosen over a hypothetical analytical DRAM-timing model specifically because it's real,
MIT-licensed, actively used in real published research, and ships real, datasheet-sourced DDR/
LPDDR/GDDR/HBM/HMC timing configs — enabling the same "anchor to the tool's own real reference
values, never fabricate" posture D26/D35/D64 already established, this time for DRAM timing
parameters this repo's IR has no honest way to source itself.

**What was verified — real DRAMsim3, checked by hand before any Flux-side translator code was
trusted, the same discipline every external-tool integration here has used:**
- **By far the simplest external-tool build in this repo's whole adapter set**: one real,
  empirically-found fix — DRAMsim3's own bundled `CMakeLists.txt` declares
  `cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 2.8)`, which modern CMake refuses outright ("Compatibility with
  CMake < 3.5 has been removed"); fixed with CMake's own suggested `-DCMAKE_POLICY_VERSION_MINIMUM=
  3.5` flag, no source file edited — versus 3D-ICE's four-fix saga (D64) or gem5's five (D38).
  Needed **zero** `flake.nix` changes at all: `cmake` was already on `.#default`'s `PATH` (added
  for `evaluators/noxim`'s own build, D32).
- **Reproduces DRAMsim3's own bundled reference config run exactly** before any Flux-side
  translator code was trusted: `configs/DDR4_8Gb_x8_3200.ini` at `-c 100000 --stream random` gives
  `average_read_latency=774.856`, `total_energy=3.18535e+08` (pJ), `average_power=3185.35` (mW),
  `average_bandwidth=18.8373` (GB/s), and real per-command counts (`num_act_cmds=18581`,
  `num_ref_cmds=16`) confirming real bank/refresh-level detail — the same "prove the tool works
  standalone first" discipline D25's Booksim2 torus88 reproduction already established.
- **The real Flux adapter, run end to end** against `simple-npu-1d-dram-v1.yaml` +
  `mlp-gemm0.yaml`, reproduces this exact same run through the translator:
  `latency_cycles=774.856`, `energy_pj=318535000.0`, `power_w=3.18535`.
- **A real, physically-meaningful cross-config sanity check**, three real bundled configs, same
  workload/arch otherwise: `DDR4_8Gb_x8_3200` → 774.856 cycles / 3.18535W; `LPDDR4_8Gb_x16_2400` →
  1014.83 cycles / 2.32168W; `DDR3_8Gb_x8_1866` → 637.37 cycles / 3.78597W. LPDDR4 ("Low Power
  DDR4," designed specifically for lower power) genuinely shows the lowest power of the three — the
  physically correct direction, not assumed.
- **A real error-path confirmation**: requesting a nonexistent config name correctly raised
  `NotExpressibleError` with a clear message, not a silent fallback or crash.
- **11 new unit tests** (`test_dramsim3_architecture_translator.py`, 7; `test_dramsim3_output_
  parser.py`, 4 — including a two-channel-output rejection, since v0.1 is deliberately
  single-channel only) **and 6 new integration tests**
  (`test_dramsim3_adapter_live.py`: DRAMsim3's own reference reproduction, real bank/refresh
  activity, the LPDDR4-vs-DDR4/DDR3 physical sanity check, two `NotExpressibleError` paths, and a
  real `flux_evaluate` CHIA-node round trip).
- **Full regression**: the complete unit suite plus conformance suite — **714 passed / 22 skipped,
  0 failed** (up from D73's 703), exactly the 11 new unit tests added, with the 6 new integration
  tests confirmed passing separately (integration tests aren't part of this suite, the same
  convention every prior decision here has followed).

**Implications.**
- gap-analysis.md G6 ("System-level effects absent (NoC, chiplets, DRAM detail, thermal)") is now
  **fully closed** — NoC (D6/D32), chiplet thermal stacking (D64/D65), chiplet D2D interconnect
  (D66/D67), and DRAM bank/refresh detail (D74) are all real, checked models now, each honestly
  scoped rather than claiming more than it verified.
- The same "same metric name, different underlying quantity" trap D37 (CACTI) and D38 (gem5)
  already named is true here too, and is documented explicitly rather than left implicit:
  DRAMsim3's own `latency_cycles` are real DRAM clock cycles at the configured DDR speed grade, not
  the same abstract quantity ZigZag/Timeloop report for a whole accelerator's execution — no
  automatic conversion exists (or should exist) between them without a real, currently-absent
  clock-frequency concept in Architecture IR.
- Deliberately did not build a `.ini`-config-from-IR-fields path — reusing DRAMsim3's own real,
  published configs by name is the honest choice given this repo's IR has no way to source dozens
  of precise DDR timing parameters legitimately; a future decision could revisit this if a real
  need to synthesize novel DRAM configs (rather than select among real, existing ones) arises.
- v0.1's single-channel-only scope is a deliberate, checked limitation (`NotExpressibleError` on
  any config reporting more than one channel), not an oversight — no tested bundled config
  currently exercises the multi-channel case, so it's named rather than silently mishandled.

## D75. A first real native, in-repo cost model — `core/`'s `flux-core` Rust crate — and an
honest, measured finding about when a native core actually helps

**Decision.** A new capability in `core/` (previously skeleton-only): `src/roofline.rs`, pure
Rust, implements the same compute-bound roofline lower-bound formula (`total_macs / lanes`)
`validity/src/flux_validity/roofline.py` already independently checks every other evaluator's own
`latency_cycles` against — computed here as a real metric in its own right, not merely checked,
the first evaluator in this repo whose cost model never shells out to or imports an external
tool. Zero `pyo3` dependency, tested with plain `cargo test` (10 tests, no Python or libpython
link needed). A `python` Cargo feature (`dep:pyo3`, off by default) adds a thin PyO3
extension-module edge in `src/lib.rs`, exposing three call shapes: `roofline_latency_cycles`
(single candidate, full Workload/Architecture IR JSON in), `roofline_latency_cycles_batch` (many
full Architecture IR documents against one workload, batched across the FFI boundary in one
call), and `roofline_latency_cycles_for_lane_sweep` (the genuine numeric hot-loop shape —
`Vec<i64>` lanes in, `Vec<f64>` cycles out, no per-candidate JSON parsing, matching
docs/architecture.md's own "SoA layouts", "no allocation per candidate" language). A new package,
`evaluators/native/` (`flux-evaluator-native`), wraps the compiled extension as a real
Evaluator-ABI-conformant `NativeEvaluator`, registered as `"native"` in `flux_cli.registry` —
same shape as every prior evaluator (D64/D74), no new CHIA node needed.

**Why.** The user, asked directly "what next" (not a bare "continue" this time — a genuine
question, answered with the real, ranked options `docs/roadmap.md`'s own "Immediate next actions"
and the remaining open `docs/gap-analysis.md` gaps named), chose G9 ("Performance and scaling")
over three other real options (a synthesis-fidelity rung blocked on a missing PDK; a from-scratch
torus-capable NoC evaluator with no existing open-source alternative found; a general
breadth-vs-depth call). `core/README.md`'s own standing note (from D33) was explicit about what
building this would actually require: "a native core only pays off for a genuinely native,
in-repo cost model that doesn't shell out to or import an external tool, which doesn't exist
anywhere in this repo yet. Building *that* is new capability work, not a port of what's here." The
already-validated `validity/roofline.py` formula was the obvious, honest choice for that first
in-repo cost model — reusing a formula this repo had already checked for correctness (real
Timeloop's own mapper hits it exactly for `mlp-gemm0.yaml`) rather than inventing a new one, the
same "anchor to already-validated numbers" posture this whole session has used for every external
tool integration, applied here to Flux's own prior work instead.

**What was verified — real `cargo`/`rustc`, real PyO3, real measured throughput, checked before
any claim was written down:**
- **PyO3 works in this environment without `maturin`**, confirmed directly before committing to
  the design: a scratch crate (`cargo build --release`, `cdylib` crate-type) produces a real
  `.so`; loading it via `importlib.util.spec_from_file_location` (bypassing Python's normal
  extension-suffix-tagged import machinery entirely) works with no extra tooling. `cargo` has real
  network access to crates.io (confirmed: `pyo3 0.22.6` and its full dependency tree downloaded
  and compiled cleanly) — no `flake.nix` change was needed; `cargo`/`rustc` were already on
  `.#default`'s `PATH`.
- **10/10 pure-Rust unit tests pass** (`cargo test`, no `python` feature, no libpython link),
  including an exact reproduction of the already-established real 512.0-cycle bound for
  `mlp-gemm0.yaml` (4×32×32=4096 MACs) against `simple-npu-1d-v1.yaml`'s 8-lane array, and a
  real inverse-scaling check (256.0 at 16 lanes, 1024.0 at 4 lanes).
- **The compiled Python extension reproduces the identical numbers** through the real
  `flux_core.so` loaded manually: `512.0` for the single-call shape, `[1024.0, 512.0, 256.0,
  128.0, 64.0]` for a batched 5-architecture-width sweep.
- **A real, honestly-measured throughput comparison — the actual point of this decision, not an
  assumed "Rust is faster"**: the batched-JSON-document shape measured ~7.2×10⁵ evals/s — clears
  docs/architecture.md's own stated `≥10⁵ dense-layer mapping evaluations/second/core` target by
  ~7x, but is *slower* than the equivalent pure-Python loop over already-parsed dicts
  (~1.6×10⁶ evals/s), since each call re-parses a full JSON document per candidate — real,
  non-trivial IR-translation work, not a hot-loop primitive. The numeric hot-loop shape (macs
  precomputed once, `Vec<i64>` lanes in) measured ~1.8×10⁷ evals/s — clears the target by ~180x —
  but lands within noise of the equivalent pure-Python list comprehension (~1.9×10⁷ evals/s):
  for a computation this cheap (one division), the cost of marshaling a Python list into a Rust
  `Vec` and back dominates over the arithmetic itself, so native Rust brings no measurable
  speedup here.
- **The real Python adapter, end to end**: `NativeEvaluator` reproduces the exact same 512.0/
  256.0/1024.0 cycle numbers through the full ABI (`Candidate` → `Result`), rejects an
  unexpressible multi-op workload with `NotExpressibleError`, and is reachable through the
  generic `flux_evaluate` CHIA node with no dedicated tool, verified over a real Ray dispatch.
- **4 new unit tests** (`test_native_evaluator_validation.py` — the ABI-level pre-checks that run
  before the extension is ever built, so no compiled artifact is needed for them) **and 6 new
  integration tests** (`test_native_evaluator_live.py`: the real 512.0-cycle reproduction, the
  real lane-count sensitivity check, an unexpressible-workload rejection, the real native-vs-
  Python throughput regression check for the numeric hot loop, a JSON-batch-reproduces-single-call
  check, and a real `flux_evaluate` CHIA-node round trip).
- **Full regression**: the complete unit suite plus conformance suite — **718 passed / 22
  skipped, 0 failed** (up from D74's 714), exactly the 4 new unit tests added, with the 6 new
  integration tests and the 10 Rust `cargo test` tests confirmed passing separately.

**Implications.**
- docs/gap-analysis.md G9 ("Performance and scaling") moves from **Open** to **Partial**: a real
  native core exists for the first time, and the raw `≥10⁵ evals/s/core` numeric target from
  docs/architecture.md/docs/roadmap.md's Phase 3 exit criterion is genuinely cleared — but the
  more important, more honest finding is that native Rust brought *no measurable speedup* over
  pure Python for a cost model this cheap. Content-addressed memoization and batched evaluation
  (both already real since D19/Phase 1) were never actually blocked on a native core; the one real
  piece of G9 still open is dependency-tracked incremental re-evaluation, untouched by this
  decision.
- **The real, generalizable finding this decision produced, worth remembering for the next native-
  core decision**: FFI/marshaling cost, not raw arithmetic speed, is the actual bottleneck for a
  sufficiently cheap per-candidate computation — a native core only pays for itself once a real
  cost model is expensive enough per candidate (genuine loop-nest reuse/tiling counting, for
  instance) that crossing the language boundary stops dominating. This isn't a reason to abandon
  the native-core line of work; it's a real, checked scoping fact for whoever picks it up next,
  replacing D33's own "doesn't exist yet, so untested" with an actual measured data point.
- `NativeEvaluator`'s own reported quantity is a theoretical lower bound, not a latency
  prediction — documented loudly (adapter docstring, package README) specifically so it's never
  mistaken for a competitive alternative to ZigZag/Timeloop/RTL's own real, calibrated numbers;
  its real value is as a fast, free, always-available sanity floor for search strategies, and as
  proof this repo's long-stated native/PyO3 boundary (docs/architecture.md's "Performance
  engineering" section, unbuilt since Phase 0) actually works end to end.
- The next real native-core step, if picked up, has a concrete, no-longer-hypothetical target: a
  genuinely more expensive in-repo cost model (e.g. a real loop-nest tiling/reuse counter over
  Mapping IR, doing actual iteration-counting work per candidate rather than one division) is the
  first place a native/Python speedup would plausibly show up, per this decision's own measured
  finding.

## D76. Confirming D75's own hypothesis for real: a genuinely branchier per-candidate
computation shows a real, measured native speedup, where D75's single division didn't

**Decision.** A new module, `core/src/flat_mapping.rs`: a faithful, behavior-verified port of
`search/exhaustive/src/flux_search_exhaustive/candidates.py`'s own `_largest_divisor_at_most` (a
real, branchy modulo-search loop — "the largest whole divisor of `bound` that is `<= limit`") and
its flat-mapping candidate enumeration (every spatial-split-dim × temporal-loop-order-permutation
combination for a workload/architecture pair). Deliberately a *port* of an already-validated
Python algorithm, not a new invented cost model — this crate builds no Mapping IR document itself
(that real IR-construction work stays in `search/exhaustive`'s own Python
`build_flat_mapping_candidate`); only the combinatorial generation logic worth benchmarking
natively was ported. Two new PyO3 functions on the existing `flux_core` extension:
`largest_divisor_at_most` and `generate_flat_mapping_candidates`.

**Why.** A bare "continue" after D75. D75's own Implications named this exact next step
explicitly: "a genuinely more expensive in-repo cost model... is the first place a native/Python
speedup would plausibly show up." `search/exhaustive/candidates.py`'s own
`_largest_divisor_at_most` was the obvious, honest choice for that next test — a real,
already-validated, already-tested algorithm (not a new formula needing its own validation), with
genuinely branchy per-call work (a modulo-search loop, unlike D75's single division), directly
answering the open question D75's own record raised rather than leaving it as a hypothesis.

**What was verified — real `cargo test`, real compiled extension, real measured throughput,
correctness checked before any speed claim:**
- **Real Python ground truth captured first, not assumed**: `list(itertools.permutations(["B",
  "C", "K"]))` and `_largest_divisor_at_most(32, 5)` were run for real before writing the Rust
  port's own test fixtures, confirming the recursive permutation algorithm this port uses matches
  Python's own documented "lexicographic in input position" ordering exactly, not just by
  reasoning about it.
- **14/14 `cargo test` pass** (10 from D75's `roofline.rs`, 4 new in `flat_mapping.rs`), including
  an exact reproduction of the real, already-established 18-candidate space for `mlp-gemm0.yaml`/
  `simple-npu-1d-v1.yaml` (docs/phase1-exit-criterion-report.md's Finding 4) and a permutation-
  order check against real captured `itertools.permutations` output.
- **The compiled extension's own output is byte-identical to the real Python algorithm** — not
  just "looks similar" — checked field-by-field (`spatial_dim`, `spatial_size`,
  `temporal_order`) against `search/exhaustive`'s own real `_largest_divisor_at_most` plus real
  `itertools.permutations`, both for the real 18-candidate fixture and a larger synthetic
  8-loop-dim space (322,560 candidates).
- **A real, measured, honest counter-finding to D75 — native genuinely wins this time**:
  `largest_divisor_at_most` called in a tight loop measured **~3.1x faster** in Rust than the
  identical real Python function (7.57M vs 2.44M calls/s) — real per-call branchy work, not
  marshaling-dominated. Full batched candidate enumeration at the larger synthetic scale measured
  **~1.37x faster** (472K vs 346K candidates/s) — a smaller margin than the raw per-call case,
  since marshaling the full 322,560-item output list back across the FFI boundary still costs
  something, but still a real, positive speedup, unlike D75's single-division formula which showed
  none.
- **2 new integration tests** (added to `test_native_core_flat_mapping_live.py`, 4 total): exact
  correctness for `largest_divisor_at_most` across six real cases, byte-identical enumeration
  reproduction for the real 18-candidate fixture, and two real, direction-only (not fixed-ratio,
  given real timing noise) speedup regression checks — both passing with the real measured
  margins well above noise.
- **Full regression**: the complete unit suite plus conformance suite — unchanged at **718
  passed / 22 skipped, 0 failed** (no new Python package/unit tests this time — this decision
  added pure-Rust code plus integration tests only), with the 14 Rust tests and 4 new integration
  tests confirmed passing separately.

**Implications.**
- D75's own open question is now answered with real data, not left as an untested hypothesis: a
  native core's real value is gated on per-candidate computational cost, confirmed on both sides —
  D75's single division showed no speedup, D76's branchy divisor search showed a real ~3x one.
  This is the concrete, reusable scoping rule for any future native-core work in this repo:
  benchmark before assuming, and expect the win to scale with how much real branchy/iterative
  work happens per candidate versus how much data crosses the FFI boundary.
- **Deliberately not wired into `search/exhaustive`'s actual `ExhaustiveMappingStrategy`** — this
  decision proves the native primitive is real and faster, not that swapping it in is a drop-in
  change (the existing strategy also builds a real Mapping IR document per candidate, real Python
  work this crate deliberately doesn't duplicate). Left as real, explicitly named future work,
  the same "prove the capability, name the integration gap honestly" split D64/D74 already used
  for their own evaluators before any dedicated CHIA node was considered.
- docs/gap-analysis.md G9 gains a second, confirming data point rather than a new open item: the
  "native core" sub-item's honest scope is now sharper — it helps for real per-candidate
  computation, not for cheap analytic formulas — rather than a blanket "native core exists/doesn't
  exist" claim either way.

## D77. Closing a real doc-staleness gap D75/D76 themselves created: three "no native core exists"
claims left uncorrected in `docs/architecture.md`/`docs/roadmap.md`

**Decision.** Fixed four stale claims, found by direct `grep` for "no native core exists" and
"premature optimization" (not by re-reading either doc's own prose and trusting it): `docs/
architecture.md`'s design-principle #7 and its "Performance engineering" section header both
still said "no native core exists yet"; that section's own seven-row capability table still had
no status column at all, describing every row as unbuilt; `docs/roadmap.md`'s KPI table and Risks
table each still had a "no native core exists" / "premature optimization, correctly deferred"
claim, both written before D75/D76 existed. All four corrected in place — the Performance
engineering table gained a `Status` column, row by row, rather than a single blanket sentence,
since the real state is now genuinely mixed (hot loop and language boundary partially real;
memoization real but never actually blocked on a native core; enumeration partially real per D76;
incrementality/within-node parallelism/native-specific determinism still fully open) — a single
"partially done" sentence would have hidden which specific claims are now true.

**Why.** D76's own Implications didn't name this gap directly, so this isn't a directly-flagged
continuation — it's the same kind of detour D72 was: a bare "continue" led to checking whether the
two just-completed decisions (D75/D76) had left any of their own claims stale elsewhere in the
docs, the same "check the actual file directly, don't just trust a doc's own prior prose" lesson
D72 named as generalizable. It held again here: `docs/architecture.md`'s own "Performance
engineering" section is the exact place D33's original "no native core exists" judgment call was
first written down (referenced directly in D33's own record and in `core/README.md`'s standing
note), so it was the first place to check once that judgment call was superseded by real data —
and it hadn't been touched by either D75 or D76's own edits, which both focused on `docs/
decisions.md`/`docs/gap-analysis.md`/`flux/README.md` instead.

**What was verified.** A direct `grep -rn "no native core exists\|premature optimization"` across
`docs/*.md` and every package README, confirming exactly four hits, all now corrected (two in
`docs/architecture.md`, two in `docs/roadmap.md`) — not assumed complete from memory of what D75/
D76 already touched. No code change; no regression run needed (docs-only).

**Implications.**
- The same generalizable lesson D72 already named applies again, now confirmed a second time
  across two unrelated decisions (D64/D66/D67's own MCP-wire gap, and now D75/D76's own
  cross-doc staleness): whenever a decision supersedes an earlier decision's own explicit
  judgment call (D33's "no native core exists, deferred"), grep for that judgment call's own
  wording across the whole docs tree before considering the superseding decision fully closed —
  don't assume the decision's own record and the one doc it was written against are the only
  places that claim lived.
- `docs/architecture.md`'s "Performance engineering" table now carries a real `Status` column,

## D78. Real sparsity-aware evaluation — `evaluators/timeloop` gains Timeloop's own real
`sparse_optimizations`/`densities` mechanism, closing Phase 5's sparsity item without a
separate Sparseloop adapter

**Decision.** `op["sparsity"]` — a Workload IR schema field the schema already declared
(`$defs.op.properties.sparsity`, unused until now) — names a real, caller-declared density for
one of an einsum op's own operand tensors: `{<flux_tensor_name>: {"distribution":
"hypergeometric", "density": <0.0-1.0>}}`. A memory hierarchy entry's `attrs.sparse_optimizations`
(a free-form extension under the already-unconstrained `attrs` object, no schema change — the
same pattern D74 used for `dramsim3_config`) declares a real hardware gating optimization that
exploits it: `[{"type": "gating", "target": <flux_tensor_name>, "condition_on":
[<flux_tensor_name>, ...]}]`. `evaluators/timeloop/workload_translator.py` gains
`flux_tensor_to_timeloop_dataspace`/`op_sparsity_to_timeloop_densities`, translating Flux tensor
names to Timeloop's own real `Inputs`/`Weights`/`Outputs` dataspace names (by matching each
tensor's declared `rank` against the op's own batch/reduction/output dim sets) and `op.sparsity`
into Timeloop's real `problem.instance.densities` block. `architecture_translator.py` gains a new
`tensor_name_map` parameter and emits a real `sparse_optimizations.action_optimization` YAML
block on any memory component that declares one. `adapter.py` wires both in, restricted to
single-op workloads (tensor-role resolution needs one unambiguous op, the same scope explicit
Mapping IR already has). New real examples: `ir/workload/examples/mlp-gemm0-sparse-v1.yaml`,
`ir/architecture/examples/simple-npu-1d-sparse-v1.yaml`.

**Why.** The user, asked directly "what next," chose G9 (native core); after D75/D76/D77 closed
that thread, the next bare "continue" prompted a fresh look at `docs/roadmap.md`'s ranked list
and remaining gaps. With G6 (system effects) and G9 (native core) both substantially addressed,
Phase 5's own status line still named "multi-core and sparsity" as fully open. Multi-core needs a
genuinely new adapter (Stream/COALA) with no existing groundwork here; sparsity, by contrast, had
a real, tractable, already-cached path: `evaluators/timeloop` already runs the exact Docker image
(`timeloopaccelergy/accelergy-timeloop-infrastructure`) that bundles Sparseloop's own real
capability, merged into mainline Timeloop as `sparse_optimizations`/`densities` rather than a
separate binary — confirmed directly (`docker images` showed the image already pulled from prior
work, and `docker run ... grep -rl sparse_optimizations` found real, bundled Sparseloop example
configs inside it) before committing to the design, the same "verify the tool is real and
tractable first" discipline every external-tool decision here has used.

**What was verified — extensive real, hands-on experimentation against the real bundled Docker
image before any translator code was written, not assumed from documentation:**
- **Web documentation was actively misleading, caught by testing, not trusted**: a fetched page
  described `sparse_optimizations` as a top-level key with a `representation-format`/`targets`
  structure; the real, bundled, actually-runnable example configs inside the pinned Docker image
  (`/usr/local/src/timeloop-python/arch_spec_examples/sparseloop/`) use a simpler,
  component-inline `sparse_optimizations.action_optimization` structure instead — confirmed by
  reading the real files, not the web page.
- **A real, non-obvious build/compatibility trail**, found by direct experimentation: Accelergy's
  bundled `intmac`/`register` primitive classes in this pinned image's version need `width` (not
  just `datawidth`) and the literal subclass name `reg` (not `register`) to resolve to a real,
  nonzero-cost energy estimator — found via real Accelergy error logs, not guessed.
- **`fixed_structured` distribution was tested and found unsuitable, not assumed**: a real density
  sweep (0.0/0.25/0.5/0.75/1.0) against a hand-built two-component test showed a non-monotonic
  gated fraction (100%/25%/0%/0%/0%) — not a physically sensible relationship for this scope
  (later web research confirmed why: `fixed_structured` models genuinely *structured* sparsity,
  e.g. NVIDIA-style N:M patterns, needing parameters beyond a bare density scalar). A second real
  sweep using `hypergeometric` instead showed a clean, monotonically-decreasing gated fraction
  (100%/37.5%/6.25%/0%/0%) — the real, verified basis for this decision's `hypergeometric`-only
  scope.
- **A real, hand-built, nonzero-cost energy test** (before any Flux-side translator existed):
  gating a real `SRAM`/`reg`-class storage component (not the zero-cost custom register class
  `evaluators/timeloop`'s own reference architecture uses for its innermost register) at 0.25
  hypergeometric density showed real cycles 16→4 and real total energy ~18065fJ→~7054fJ — both
  physically correct directions (fewer cycles, less energy, from a hardware feature designed to
  skip zero-valued work).
- **The real Flux translator, run end to end through the actual adapter** (real `tl.call_mapper`
  search, not just `tl.call_model`): `mlp-gemm0.yaml`/`simple-npu-1d-v1.yaml` (no sparsity)
  reproduces the exact, already-established real numbers this repo has cited since Phase 1
  (512.0 cycles / 620000.0 pJ); `mlp-gemm0-sparse-v1.yaml`/`simple-npu-1d-sparse-v1.yaml` (0.25
  hypergeometric density on the input tensor, gated at `gbuf`) gives 128.0 cycles / 250000.0 pJ —
  a real ~4x cycle and ~2.5x energy reduction relative to the identical dense pair, the physically
  correct direction, and consistent with the earlier hand-built probe's own ~4x cycle ratio.
- **A real, hand-verified edge case, confirmed before claiming it's safe**: declaring `op.sparsity`
  with no matching `attrs.sparse_optimizations` anywhere produces byte-identical results to the
  fully-dense baseline (512.0/620000.0 exactly) — unconsumed density metadata is genuinely inert
  in real Timeloop, not an error and not a silent, wrong cost reduction; verified directly rather
  than assumed either way.
- **15 new unit tests** (10 in `test_timeloop_workload_translator.py`: tensor-dataspace mapping,
  densities translation, unknown-tensor/unsupported-distribution/out-of-range-density rejections;
  5 in `test_timeloop_architecture_translator.py`: sparse_optimizations YAML emission,
  missing-tensor-name-map/unknown-tensor/unsupported-action-type rejections, and a check that the
  common no-sparsity case is completely unaffected) **and 4 new integration tests**
  (`test_timeloop_sparsity_live.py`: the real dense-baseline cross-check, the real sparse
  reduction pinned exactly, a multi-op-with-sparsity rejection, and the real inert-no-op case) —
  plus the pre-existing 16 `evaluators/timeloop` integration tests confirmed passing unchanged.
- **Full regression**: the complete unit suite plus conformance suite — **733 passed / 22
  skipped, 0 failed** (up from D77's 718), exactly the 15 new unit tests added.

**Implications.**
- docs/roadmap.md's Phase 5 status line and Build-vs-reuse table both updated: sparsity is real
  now (this decision), multi-core/layer-fusion (Stream/COALA) and in-memory compute (CiMLoop)
  remain the only fully-open items in that row — named honestly, not folded together as if all
  were still equally unstarted.
- No separate `evaluators/sparseloop` package was needed — a real, useful finding in its own
  right, worth remembering the next time a "the field has tool X" gap is picked up: Sparseloop's
  real capability was already reachable through `evaluators/timeloop`'s own existing Docker
  dependency, since Sparseloop's real contribution was merged into mainline Timeloop rather than
  shipped as a separate binary. Checking whether an existing adapter's own bundled tooling already
  covers a "new" gap, before building a new adapter from scratch, is a real, generalizable step —
  this decision is the first time in this whole session that step paid off.
- `type: "skipping"`/`"spatial-skipping"` and `distribution: "fixed_structured"` are named
  explicitly as untested/unsuitable rather than silently unsupported — a caller who needs
  structured (N:M) sparsity or a skip-based (not gate-based) optimization has a real, honest
  starting point (this decision's own real density-sweep methodology) rather than an
  undocumented gap to rediscover from scratch.

## D79. Real incremental, dependency-tracked re-evaluation — `flux_characterize_memory_level`'s
own pre-existing dependency reduction turns out to already be the real thing docs/gap-analysis.md
G9 asked for

**Decision.** `flux_characterize_memory_level` (D37) gains an optional `store: ResultStore |
None = None` parameter. When given, the evaluator it dispatches to is wrapped in `flux_store.
CachingEvaluator` (D19) — but around `minimal_arch`, the single-memory-level document this
function already built (before this decision, for an unrelated reason: giving `evaluators/cacti`
a document it can accept, since CACTI needs exactly one `class=='memory'` node, not the caller's
full multi-level architecture). No new dependency-tracking machinery was written — `minimal_arch`
already *was* the real, narrowed set of inputs this node's own computation depends on; wrapping
the existing cache around it, instead of around the caller's full `arch`, is the entire change.

**Why.** The user, asked directly "what next" after D78 closed the sparsity thread, was offered a
menu of the current real, tractable, open items (refreshed from a genuinely stale `docs/
roadmap.md` "Immediate next actions" list — its own "scope-proportionality" item had been
substantially answered by D74–D78's own breadth work without the list being updated to say so,
fixed as part of answering the question) and chose "incremental re-evaluation," docs/
gap-analysis.md G9's one remaining named piece. The real design question this raised: every
evaluator here (D33's own finding) is a monolithic external-tool call — ZigZag/Timeloop/CACTI/
DRAMsim3/3D-ICE/Booksim2 can't be *partially* re-run for a changed input, so "recompute only what
depends on it" can't mean decomposing an external tool's own internal computation. The honest,
tractable place it *can* mean something real: a node whose own real dependency on the caller's
full input is *provably narrower* than the full input itself. `flux_characterize_memory_level`
turned out to be exactly that, and had already done the narrowing work for an unrelated reason —
found by inspecting its own source rather than designing new infrastructure from scratch first.

**What was verified — a stub-evaluator unit suite proving the mechanism, then real CACTI proving
it end to end, the same two-tier discipline `test_caching.py`/`test_caching_live.py` already
established for `CachingEvaluator` itself:**
- **5 new unit tests** (`test_memory_characterize_caching.py`, a `_CountingEvaluator` stub
  matching `test_caching.py`'s own pattern): no `store` given still calls the real evaluator every
  time (zero behavior change for D37's existing callers); a second call whose full architecture
  differs only in an unrelated hierarchy level (`dram`, untouched by a `"gbuf"` characterization)
  is a real cache hit (1 call, not 2); a second call that changes the *characterized* level's own
  `size_kb` is correctly still a real cache miss (2 calls) — not over-broad; a different
  `word_width_bits` for the same level is correctly a cache miss too (it's baked into
  `minimal_arch`, a real physical input CACTI actually uses); an exact-repeat request is a real
  cache hit.
- **2 new real integration tests** (`test_chia_flux_characterize_memory_level_live.py`, monkey-
  patching `flux_evaluator_cacti.adapter.run_cacti` with a call-counting wrapper around the real
  function — proof by counting, not by wall-clock time, the same rigor D75/D76's own throughput
  claims used): two full architectures differing only in `dram` size give exactly **one** real
  `run_cacti` invocation across both calls, with both results matching the exact already-pinned
  real number (`area_mm2=0.527745648101`); the real D26/D27 memory_size-axis winner (gbuf at 1.25
  KiB) still forces a real second `run_cacti` call and gives the real, physically smaller area —
  confirming the cache is neither too broad nor too narrow, against the actual binary, not a stub.
- **Full regression**: the complete unit suite plus conformance suite — **738 passed / 22
  skipped, 0 failed** (up from D78's 733), exactly the 5 new unit tests added; the 2 new
  integration tests and the pre-existing 5 `flux_characterize_memory_level` integration tests
  confirmed passing separately (7/7).

**Implications.**
- docs/gap-analysis.md G9 moves to **Mostly closed** — both of its named pieces (native core,
  incremental re-evaluation) now have real, if narrow, evidence behind them, replacing "not
  started" for the second piece the same way D75 replaced it for the first.
- **Deliberately not generalized into reusable dependency-tracking infrastructure.** This
  decision proves the pattern works for one real node whose own dependency was already an
  explicit, separately-motivated reduction — it does not build a general "declare an evaluator's
  own read-set, get automatic narrowed caching" framework. That would be real, valuable future
  work, but building it speculatively, before a second real consumer exists to validate the
  design against, would risk the same "contract without capability" trap docs/gap-analysis.md's
  own ArchGym cautionary note names — named honestly as the boundary here, not silently implied
  as solved for every evaluator.
- A real, generalizable lesson worth remembering the next time a "not started" gap is picked up:
  check whether an existing function already did the narrowing work for an unrelated reason
  before assuming new infrastructure is required — the same step D78 used when it found
  Sparseloop's real capability already reachable through `evaluators/timeloop`'s own existing
  Docker dependency, now confirmed a second time in a completely different part of the codebase.

## D80. Real Stream (multi-core/layer-fusion DSE) plumbing proven end to end — real nix
packaging, a real diagnosed-and-fixed native SIGSEGV, and a real, deterministic solve; Flux IR
translation deliberately deferred

**Decision.** `flake.nix` gains real nix derivations for Stream's own dependency chain: `xdsl`
(0.29.1, pure-Python PyPI wheel), `ortools` (9.15.6755, a real prebuilt manylinux PyPI wheel —
nixpkgs' own `python312Packages.ortools` was tried first and rejected, see below), and
`streamDse` (1.13.11, KU Leuven MICAS, MIT, built directly on the `zigzag-dse==3.8.5` this repo
already vendors). A fourth derivation, `onnxNew`, **replaces** (not adds to) the shell's existing
`python312Packages.onnx` — a real, load-bearing fix, not new capability, for a genuine native
crash found and diagnosed in the course of this decision (see below). No Flux IR translation
code was written: this decision proves Stream's own real plumbing works in this repo's nix
environment, end to end, using 100% of Stream's own real reference inputs (its own bundled
hardware YAML, its own real GitHub test workload — vendored unmodified at
`tests/fixtures/stream/`, see `PROVENANCE.md` there) — a new integration test,
`tests/integration/test_stream_plumbing_live.py`, is the only new test-facing artifact.

**Why.** A bare "continue" after D79 ran into a real dead end: every remaining item on
`docs/roadmap.md`'s "Immediate next actions" list was either genuinely blocked (Hammer, no PDK),
already investigated and found intractable (a torus NoC evaluator, D32), or low-value busywork
(wiring D76's native speedup into `search/exhaustive`, whose real candidate spaces are too small
to ever benefit). Reported this honestly rather than picking a weak default; the user chose to
research Stream (KU Leuven MICAS's multi-core/layer-fusion extension of ZigZag) as the one
remaining item with real, substantial value — closing `docs/roadmap.md`'s last-named-untouched
Phase 5 item, multi-core/layer-fusion. Real due diligence (the same discipline D78 used for
Sparseloop) found genuine complexity across four independent dimensions — a new Flux-IR-to-ONNX
export direction, a new multi-core Architecture IR concept, a real `pydantic` version conflict,
and a heavy new `ortools` dependency — reported back before writing any adapter code, per explicit
instruction. The user chose the narrowest real first step: prove the plumbing works before
building any Flux-side translation.

**What was verified — real nix builds, a real native crash fully diagnosed via `gdb`, and a real,
deterministic Stream solve, in that order:**
- **A real nixpkgs build failure found and worked around**, not assumed: nixpkgs' own
  `python312Packages.ortools` transitively depends on `scipy`, whose own bundled test suite fails
  a real, hypothesis-based floating-point property test (`test_support_moments_sample`) in this
  nixpkgs snapshot — confirmed by actually starting that build and reading its own failure log,
  not assumed from a search result. Fixed the same way `zigzagDse` already handles a niche
  academic package: build from the tool's own real, prebuilt PyPI wheel instead of fighting
  nixpkgs' from-source derivation.
- **Three real version-pin conflicts found and resolved via `pythonRelaxDeps`** (the same
  escape hatch `chia`'s own derivation already established for its pydantic/ray/fastapi pins):
  `xdsl`'s own `immutabledict<4.2.2`/`typing-extensions<4.13` ceilings are both below what this
  shell's nixpkgs snapshot actually has (4.3.1/4.13.2); `stream-dse`'s own `pydantic<2.12` ceiling
  is below this shell's 2.13.4. All three relaxed and then verified against real, working Stream
  calls, not assumed safe from the relaxation alone.
- **A real, reproducible native SIGSEGV, fully diagnosed via `gdb`, not guessed at**: the first
  full nix build succeeded and every import (`stream`, `stream.api`, `ortools`, `xdsl`) worked
  cleanly, but a real end-to-end Stream call (Stream's own bundled `tpu_like_quad_core.yaml`
  hardware + its own real GitHub-hosted `2conv_1_8_32_32_16_32_3.onnx` test workload) crashed
  with `SIGSEGV` the instant `ConstraintOptimizationAllocationStage` started — confirmed
  independent of solver backend first (both `ortools_gscip`, Stream's own default, and
  `ortools_highs` crash identically; `GSCIP` itself turned out not even to be registered in this
  ortools wheel — `CreateSolver("GSCIP")` returns `None` cleanly, not a crash, ruling out "wrong
  backend" as the cause). `gdb -batch -ex run -ex "bt full"` against a minimal repro script gave
  the real, definitive answer: two *different, ABI-incompatible* copies of `libprotobuf.so`
  loaded in the same process — nixpkgs' own pre-built `onnx` (linked at nixpkgs' own build time
  against `libprotobuf.so.35.1.0`) and OR-Tools' own separately-vendored, wheel-bundled copy
  (`ortools/.libs/libprotobuf.so.33.1.0`) — both registering message descriptors into protobuf's
  shared global registry, corrupting memory when the ABIs don't match. The same "read the real
  stack trace, don't guess" discipline D64's own OpenBLAS ILP64/LP64 segfault diagnosis already
  used.
- **A real, empirically-tested fix, not the first guess**: a dedicated pinned-version `protobuf`
  derivation was tried first (matching ortools' own stated `<6.34,>=6.33.1` requirement) and
  rejected — nix's own `pythonCatchConflictsPhase` correctly refused it outright, since nixpkgs'
  `onnx` already pulls a different, incompatible protobuf into the same closure, and Nix's
  `python.withPackages` mechanism requires exactly one consistent version across a whole shared
  environment. The real, working fix was replacing nixpkgs' own compiled `onnx` with ONNX's own
  official PyPI wheel (`onnxNew`) — a professionally-built manylinux wheel from the ONNX project
  itself, not nixpkgs' own rebuild — verified directly to resolve the crash, not assumed from the
  theory alone.
- **A real, deterministic, non-trivial solve, reproduced twice independently**: with `onnxNew` in
  place, the identical Stream call completes cleanly (`backend="ortools_highs"`, since the
  ortools wheel's own missing GSCIP registration rules out Stream's own default backend value),
  running three real HiGHS MIP solves (`transfer_tensor_alloc`, objectives 14350/2019328/10, all
  reported `Status: Optimal`) and reporting `total_latency=14344.0` — reproduced exactly on a
  second, fully independent run.
- **No regression to existing ONNX-dependent code**, checked directly: `test_onnx_frontend_live.py`
  (2/2) and `test_zigzag_adapter_live.py` (5/5) both pass unchanged against the swapped `onnxNew`.
- **Full regression**: the complete unit suite plus conformance suite — unchanged at **738
  passed / 22 skipped, 0 failed** (this decision is nix-infrastructure- and integration-test-only,
  no unit-testable Flux code was written). The new `test_stream_plumbing_live.py` (2 tests)
  confirmed passing separately, in ~16s.

**Implications.**
- `docs/roadmap.md`'s multi-core/layer-fusion Phase 5 item moves from "no real groundwork at all"
  to "real, working plumbing — Flux IR translation is the one remaining real piece." The next
  decision that picks this up has a genuinely lower-risk starting point: the nix environment, the
  Python API shape (`stream.api.optimize_allocation_co_generic`), and the real solver-backend
  gotcha (`ortools_highs`, not the default `ortools_gscip`) are all now known and proven, not
  open questions.
- The real remaining work, named honestly rather than implied solved: a Flux-Workload-IR-to-ONNX
  exporter (the reverse direction of `frontends/onnx`, which only goes ONNX→Flux IR today) and a
  real multi-core Architecture IR concept (every existing example here models exactly one compute
  array) — both genuinely new IR-level capabilities, not just adapter plumbing, and each likely
  deserves its own decision given the depth already found in this one.
- A real, generalizable lesson from the segfault diagnosis, worth remembering for any future
  decision that mixes a nixpkgs-prebuilt package with a PyPI-wheel-vendored native dependency:
  when two different sources (nixpkgs' own build, a PyPI wheel's own bundled copy) both link the
  *same* named C++ library into one process, version-metadata compatibility checks (what
  `pythonRelaxDeps`/PyPI's own `Requires-Dist` check) are necessary but not sufficient — the real
  question is whether the *native* `.so` files are ABI-compatible, which only `gdb`/a real crash
  reproduction can answer definitively.
- `stream-dse`'s own default `backend="ortools_gscip"` is real, working guidance for this repo's
  specific pinned `ortools` wheel: it silently has no GSCIP solver registered at all. Any future
  caller of `stream.api.*` from this repo must pass `backend="ortools_highs"` explicitly — named
  here so the next decision doesn't have to rediscover it via another crash.

## D81. A real Flux-Workload-IR-to-ONNX exporter — closing D80's own first-named remaining piece,
proven end to end through real Stream

**Decision.** `frontends/onnx` gains `workload_ir_to_onnx_model` (`exporter.py`) — the exact
reverse of the package's own existing `onnx_model_to_workload_ir`, same v0.1 scope for symmetry:
a chained sequence of two-operand `einsum` ops, each a plain 2D GEMM, fully static bounds. Each op
becomes one real ONNX `Gemm` node with a deterministic all-zero weight initializer (a real DSE
cost-model consumer reads only shapes/dtypes, never actual weight values, so a fixed fill is
honest — it doesn't pretend to represent a trained model this exporter has no access to).
`onnx.checker.check_model` validates every exported model before it's returned. New package
dependency: `numpy` (weight-array construction).

**Why.** A bare "continue" after D80 went straight to the concrete next step D80's own record
named first: "a Flux-Workload-IR-to-ONNX exporter... deliberately deferred out of D80's own
narrow 'prove the plumbing' scope." Before designing it, one real, unverified assumption was
checked first, matching this whole session's "verify before building" discipline: Stream's own
real test workload uses `Conv` nodes exclusively, raising a real question of whether Stream's own
ONNX parser accepts the `Gemm`/`MatMul` shape every existing Flux workload example already uses.
Checked directly (not assumed) by listing Stream's own installed package's `parser/onnx/`
directory: real, dedicated `gemm.py` and `matmul.py` handler modules exist alongside `conv.py` —
confirming the natural, faithful translation (einsum → `Gemm`, not an awkward 1×1-kernel `Conv`
workaround) was viable before any exporter code was written.

**What was verified — a real round trip through the forward frontend, then a real, decisive round
trip through actual Stream:**
- **11 new unit tests** (`test_onnx_exporter.py`, mirroring `test_onnx_frontend.py`'s own
  structure): single-op and two-op-chain export, `onnx.checker` validation, round-trips back
  through `onnx_model_to_workload_ir` reproducing the exact original bounds (including the real
  `mlp-gemm0.yaml` example: 4×32×32 survives the full export→reimport cycle exactly), and
  rejections for non-`einsum` ops, non-2D-GEMM expressions, transposed output, a broken
  chain (mismatched reduction size between consecutive ops), a dynamic bound, and an empty
  workload — mirroring every rejection case the forward direction already covers.
- **A real, decisive end-to-end proof through actual Stream, not just `onnx.checker`**: the real
  `mlp-gemm0.yaml` workload, exported and fed through real `stream.api.
  optimize_allocation_co_generic` (Stream's own real, bundled single-core hardware config,
  `eyeriss_like_single_core.yaml` — deliberately sidestepping the still-open multi-core
  Architecture IR question, since this decision is about the *workload* translation direction
  only) — Stream's own log output confirms it parsed a real `Gemm node mlp.gemm0` (not silently
  falling back to something else), ran real HiGHS MIP solves, and reported
  `total_latency=871.0`, a real, deterministic, non-trivial number. A second real check, a
  genuinely different two-layer chain (not just the single-op case), also runs through real
  Stream successfully. Both pinned in a new integration test,
  `tests/integration/test_stream_flux_export_live.py` (2/2 passing).
- **A real, unrelated flaky test found and fixed along the way**, during this decision's own
  full-suite regression check (not part of this decision's own scope, but caught and not silently
  ignored, the same "grep the whole tree" discipline D72/D77 already established for doc
  staleness, applied here to test flakiness instead): `test_search_annealing_strategy.py`'s own
  `test_a_real_wall_clock_budget_stops_measurably_earlier_than_an_unbounded_run` (D69) failed
  reproducibly (not randomly — every time) when run as part of the full 748-test suite, but passed
  reliably in isolation. Root cause, found by reading the test's own real logic, not guessed: it
  measures a first "unbounded" `run_simulated_annealing` call's own wall-clock time, then derives
  a budget from it for a *second*, separately-timed call — but the first of two back-to-back calls
  in one process measurably pays a real, one-time warm-up cost (attribute/import caching) the
  second doesn't, so a budget derived from the first call's own (inflated) time was too generous
  once the second, genuinely-timed "budgeted" run ran faster per-iteration than that estimate
  assumed. Fixed with a real, discarded warm-up call before the timed comparison begins — the
  exact same "import-time costs shouldn't count against steady-state per-candidate cost"
  discipline `core/benches/profile_exhaustive_search.py`'s own module docstring already
  established elsewhere in this repo, applied here for the first time to a *test's* own timing
  logic rather than a benchmark script's. Verified fixed, not just patched-and-hoped: 3/3 clean
  runs in isolation (already reliable) and, more importantly, 2/2 clean full-suite runs
  (previously failing reproducibly every time).
- **Full regression**: the complete unit suite plus conformance suite — **749 passed / 22
  skipped, 0 failed** (up from D80's 738: 11 new exporter unit tests, 0 net change from the
  flaky-test fix itself since it corrected an existing test rather than adding one), confirmed
  stable across two independent full-suite runs. The new integration test
  (`test_stream_flux_export_live.py`, 2 tests) confirmed passing separately.

**Implications.**
- D80's own two named remaining pieces for multi-core/layer-fusion are now down to one: the
  Flux-Workload-IR-to-ONNX direction is real and proven end to end through actual Stream; a real
  multi-core Architecture IR concept (every existing example here still models exactly one
  compute array) is the sole remaining piece, deliberately not attempted here — this decision
  used Stream's own real single-core reference hardware specifically to keep that boundary clean.
- The exporter's own scope is deliberately identical to the forward frontend's — same class of
  workload, same rejections, checked by literal symmetry rather than redesigning independently.
  A future decision that widens `onnx_frontend.py`'s own scope (multi-input graphs, Conv,
  non-static shapes, ...) would need to widen this exporter to match, or explicitly document why
  the two directions diverge.
- The real flaky-test fix is a small, generalizable addition to this repo's own established
  "warm-up run before timing" discipline: previously only applied to a benchmark script
  (`core/benches/profile_exhaustive_search.py`), now shown to matter for a test's own timing
  assertions too — worth applying the same pattern proactively to any other wall-clock-comparison
  test this repo adds in the future (D69's sibling ports for `search/exhaustive`/`search/
  architecture`/`search/agentic` were checked directly: none of their own tests compare two
  separately-timed runs against each other the way this one uniquely did, so none share this
  exact risk).
