## D96. Review-driven fix sweep: a four-stream Fable review of the whole D85–D95 arc, then closing every high-priority finding it produced

**Decision.** Run a structured review of the current code and project state — one real full
regression run plus three parallel read-only review agents (code correctness over the D85–D95
packages; repository/project state; documentation integrity) — then fix everything high-priority
the review surfaced, in one arc, with a real test for every behavioral change.

**Why.** The D85–D95 arc added two whole packages and ~1,800 staged lines; nothing had
adversarially reviewed that code as a body of work (each decision verified its own claims, but
nobody had hunted for cross-cutting failure modes: late crashes, contract violations, silent
misreporting). The review found 20 real code findings — none caught by the 832-test suite,
because every one lives on a path the tests never exercised (unknown-metric names, timeouts,
malformed-but-schema-valid inputs, backends without usage metadata).

**What was found and fixed (each verified by a new or updated real test).**
- *Confidentiality enforcement was one opt-in call site, not the claimed "structural refusal"*:
  `require_not_confidential` guarded only the CHIA node; importing
  `flux_codegen_rtl_harness.asap7.synthesize_with_asap7` directly returned real absolute areas
  for a confidential-flagged PDK unchecked. Enforcement moved into the engine's public entry
  point itself (`rtl_harness` gained a real `flux-redaction` dependency — acyclic, the policy
  package has zero runtime deps); `_synthesize_with_asap7_unchecked` (underscore-private) is the
  one sanctioned bypass, used solely by the redacted node, which must keep working precisely
  when the PDK *is* confidential. `policy.py`'s docstring now states the honest boundary: "the
  public raw path refuses", not "no Python code could ever obtain the number".
- *The redacted delta is invertible via a caller-chosen baseline* (`candidate = baseline × (1 +
  delta)` for anyone who knows the baseline's own area — ASAP7 cell areas are public).
  Deliberately NOT "fixed" in code: a caller-opaque baseline is a deployment/policy property no
  data type can provide. `core.py`'s docstring now states precisely what the structural
  guarantee does and does not cover, so it gets used for what it actually is.
- *Late crashes after all real work was done*: an `objective_metric`/`metric` the backend never
  emits (ZigZag ignores the requested-metrics set) crashed with a raw `KeyError` at the replay/
  aggregation step, after LLM spend, calibration, validity, conformance, and the store write.
  Both `generation/architecture.py` and `workload_dynamism/sweep.py` now fail fast with a typed
  error after at most one real evaluation. `GenerationError` — previously exported, documented,
  and never raised anywhere — is now genuinely raised for exactly the caller errors its
  docstring always claimed (schema-invalid `base_arch`, unknown objective metric).
- *A typo'd `reference_backend` was misreported as an honest "not expressible" conformance
  outcome* (`make_evaluator` sat inside `except ValueError`). Hoisted to the top of the
  function: a bad name is now a loud error before any LLM call.
- *Both synthesis paths leaked their work dirs* (~4.1 MB decompressed liberty per ASAP7 call; a
  50-variant sweep left ~205 MB of orphan temp dirs) and let `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` escape
  the documented `SynthesisError` contract, aborting whole DSE reports. try/finally rmtree +
  timeout→`SynthesisError` in both, unit-tested with a monkeypatched subprocess (no Yosys needed
  — the point is the behavior holds regardless of the tool).
- *`CostTrackingProposer` silently accumulated $0.00 for a backend whose usage metadata it
  couldn't read* — the exact outcome `UnknownModelPricingError` exists to block, through a
  different door. New `MissingUsageMetadataError`, raised loudly. **One existing D88 test
  (`test_missing_metadata_is_treated_as_zero_tokens_not_an_error`) encoded the buggy behavior
  as its contract and was deliberately inverted** — recorded here explicitly since changing an
  existing test's asserted behavior is exactly the kind of thing this log exists to make
  visible.
- *Validation gaps behind schema-valid inputs*: malformed `{dyn: ...}` declarations (one
  element, bare int, inverted lo>hi — all schema-valid, `bounds` is unconstrained) escaped as
  bare unpacking errors or silently collapsed quantile sampling to `hi`; a `leaf_sources` key
  mismatch escaped as a bare `KeyError` instead of `InvalidSpecError`; composite top-level port
  names were never identifier-checked (`"2bad"` reached Verilator as a syntax error in a file
  the caller never wrote); a non-`empirical` distribution scheme was parsed and discarded; a
  sparse percentile table crashed with a bare `KeyError`. All now typed, early errors.
- *Mirror drift*: `generation`'s YAML fence regex was strictly weaker than the `generate_rtl`
  sibling it claims to mirror (an uppercase ```` ```YAML ```` tag leaked into the payload and
  wasted a real repair attempt) — now the identical `\w*` pattern. `rtl_dse`'s
  `synthesis_cache_db_path` renamed to `cache_db_path`, matching every sibling node. The MCP
  `sweep_dynamic_shape` tool gained the `corpus_root` parameter the underlying node already
  accepted. Stale docstrings fixed: `sweep.py`'s module docstring still said distribution refs
  were "never resolved to real data" (the opposite of what D87 built); `generate_systemc`'s
  "harness_result is None only if every attempt failed to compile" was simply false (it is the
  *last* attempt's result, discarding an earlier partial pass).
- *Repo/doc hygiene*: untracked the stale `result` nix-build symlink and the shellHook-generated
  `.nix-bin/flux` (both now root-gitignored, along with `.pytest_cache/`); deleted 15 MB of
  stray gem5 `build/` output and two leftover pytest-collection logs; fixed `flake.nix`'s two
  stale package-count comments (18/20 → 24); fixed the six stale tool counts D95's sweep missed
  (`flux/flows/mcp/README.md` said "seventeen" in four places — its hand-copied 17-name method
  list is now a pointer to `tool.py`'s own always-current enumeration instead of a second copy
  that can go stale; `flux/README.md` said "seventeen" and "twenty-seven", and its MCP-row
  ordinal narrative now runs through the thirtieth tool); added the missing G15 closure note to
  `docs/gap-analysis.md`'s Tier-4 bullet.

**What was verified.** Every fix has a real test asserting the new behavior (five test files
extended, one new `test_rtl_synth_robustness.py`, one D88 test deliberately inverted with the
reasoning in its own docstring); targeted run green, then the full regression suite re-run
green. The review's own four highest-severity findings were independently re-verified in source
before any fix was written — grep for the single `require_not_confidential` call site, the
missing `rmtree` in both synthesis paths, the raw `KeyError` at the replay step, and
`make_evaluator` inside the `except` — not taken on the reviewing agent's word.

**Implications.**
- The reward-hacking-adjacent lesson: two of the twenty findings were *overclaiming docstrings*
  on security-relevant properties ("structural refusal" that was one opt-in call; "cannot
  recover the absolute value" that inverts given a known baseline). The fix for an overclaim is
  sometimes enforcement (the engine guard) and sometimes honest scoping (the invertibility
  caveat) — choosing which requires understanding what the mechanism can actually guarantee,
  not just making the docstring match the code.
- A 832-test suite catching none of twenty real findings is not evidence the suite is bad — all
  twenty live on paths the suite deliberately never exercised (error paths, malformed inputs,
  timeouts). It is evidence that adversarial review and regression testing find disjoint bug
  populations, worth both doing.
- D95's own "sweep the docs after a multi-decision arc" lesson recurred immediately: D95's
  sweep covered eight files and missed a ninth (`flux/flows/mcp/README.md`, 13 tools behind).
  The structural fix applied here — replace hand-copied enumerations with pointers to the one
  authoritative list — is better than sweeping more carefully next time.
- Deliberately NOT changed: frozen dataclasses with dict fields still raise `TypeError` on
  `hash()` (no caller hashes them today; `field(hash=False)` would silently change equality/hash
  semantics for a hypothetical); the quantile grid's banker's rounding (the review's asymmetry
  claim was checked and found wrong — pairs sum to 100, the grid is symmetric); `extra_sources`
  cache keys still hash pre-normalization text (a guaranteed-safe cache *miss*, not a wrong
  answer — fixing it invalidates every existing cache entry for a marginal hit-rate gain).

## D97. Comment rationalization: duplicated decision-narratives become pointers to this log

**Decision.** Establish and apply a comment/docstring convention: code comments keep *what a
thing is* and the *load-bearing why* (the constraint, gotcha, or invariant a future editor must
not break), and point to this log's D-numbers for the *story* (what was tried, what failed, what
was verified) instead of re-narrating it inline. Applied now to the worst duplicated-narrative
offenders; governs future writing everywhere. Also close the last small review leftovers D96
didn't reach.

**Why.** Three separate staleness bugs (D95's sweep, D96's six leftover counts, and the two
stale `flake.nix` counts) shared one root cause: the same fact hand-copied into multiple prose
homes, each aging independently. The fix that worked in D96 — replace `flows/mcp/README.md`'s
hand-copied 17-name list with a pointer to the one authoritative enumeration — generalizes: a
pointer cannot go stale; a copy always eventually does. The verbose narrate-everything style
stays exactly right for *this log* (append-only, dated, never edited); it was never the right
format for code comments, which sit next to code that changes.

**What was done.**
- `flux/flake.nix`'s header docstring: ~7.4k characters of re-narrated build sagas (gem5's
  GCC/zlib/Ray environment story, 3D-ICE's ILP64/gnu89/`ar`-race story, booksim/noxim/cacti
  provisioning) compressed to a per-adapter bullet list — every operational fact kept (what's
  provided, what's excluded and why in one line, where each workaround lives), every story
  pointered to its D-number. Its enumerated package list — stale twice — is now a pointer to
  `localSrcDirs` itself. The seven `localSrcDirs`-excluded adapters are now all named with
  reasons (`native`/`dramsim3`/`thermal` were previously undocumented omissions, a D96 review
  leftover).
- `flux/README.md`: the `flux-mcp` row's ordinal-by-ordinal tool narrative ("the fifteenth …
  the thirtieth", ~3.4k characters, stale twice) replaced by a pointer to `tool.py`'s own
  docstring enumeration, with a note saying why it is deliberately not maintained a third time.
  The package-count sentence now states the honest split — 31 local packages, 24 wired onto the
  dev shell's PYTHONPATH automatically, seven added explicitly by their callers — replacing the
  ambiguous "24 (`evaluators/*` …)" glob that implied all evaluators were wired.
- Module headers with the heaviest duplicated history compressed the same way (facts +
  invariants kept, stories pointered): `flows/chia_nodes/agentic.py`, `flows/chia_nodes/cost.py`
  (its pricing-source URLs, fetch date, and named simplifications all kept — those are facts,
  not narrative), `workload_dynamism/distributions.py`.
- Deliberately NOT touched: technical docstrings whose length is load-bearing detail rather
  than history (`synth.py`'s honest generic-cell-vs-area naming, `policy.py`'s just-rewritten
  enforcement boundary, `driver_gen.py`'s clocking contract), and this log itself.
- Remaining review leftovers closed: root `.gitignore` now ignores only
  `.claude/settings.local.json` + `.claude/worktrees/` rather than relying on any blanket
  ignore, so a future shared `.claude/settings.json` would be tracked.

**What was verified.** Full regression suite re-run green after the sweep (docstring/comment
changes plus the README/flake edits — the suite guards against a "comment-only" change that
actually clipped code, which is exactly how a hand-edited 7k-character deletion goes wrong).
The `native` exclusion reason was checked against that adapter's own README before being
asserted in `flake.nix` — the first phrasing ("can't import without a build") was checked,
found wrong (import works; first *use* builds), and corrected before landing.

**Implications.**
- The convention, stated once for future work: if a comment tells a story with a D-number's
  worth of history, write the D-number. If it states a constraint the adjacent code depends on,
  keep it inline — a pointer is not a substitute for the invariant itself.
- This was a worst-offenders pass, not a whole-repo retrofit — remaining long-form module
  docstrings get the convention applied opportunistically as their files are next touched, not
  in one bulk edit whose diff would swamp real changes.

## D98. The calibration flywheel: conformance runs feed the calibration store

**Decision.** Add `flux_calibration.record_conformance_residuals(report, store, *,
workload_hash, arch_hash, caveat)` — every conformance check already computes exactly the
(predicted, reference) pair `CalibrationStore.add_record` needs; this records it, closing the
loop between the two halves of the calibration package that had never been connected in
production code. Wired, opt-in (`record_residuals: bool = False`), into `flux_conformance_check`
and `generate_architecture_candidate` (function, CHIA node, and MCP tool surfaces for both).

**Why.** Before this, `add_record` had zero production callers — the store was filled only by
offline tooling and tests (a D96-review finding, drawn as a dashed "idea" edge in the overview
artifact). Conformance checks computed real ground-truth comparisons and then dropped them:
running a hundred real conformance checks left future calibrated CIs exactly as uninformed as
before the first one. The mechanism to fix this needed no new machinery at all — only the
connection.

**Design points, each deliberate:**
- *Idempotent per exact candidate*: an (evaluator, metric, workload_hash, arch_hash) tuple with
  an existing exact-match record is skipped (`has_exact_match`, already built for D8's domain
  tiering). Re-running one check never multiply-weights one observation — without this, a
  caller polling the same conformance check would concentrate the residual distribution onto
  one candidate's error.
- *`predicted_value` comes from the report's own `declared_value`* — safe even though the
  declared side is calibrated before checking, because `calibrate_estimate()` widens only the
  CI and never shifts `value` (checked against its source before relying on it), so the
  recorded prediction is the raw model output, not a calibrated echo.
- *Zero reference values are skipped, not recorded* — a relative residual against zero is
  undefined; `add_record` would raise.
- *Opt-in, not default-on*: recording makes the next identical call return a different
  (better-informed) CI and flip the candidate's domain to exact-match — a real before/after
  difference between two identical invocations. That is the flywheel working, but it should be
  chosen, not stumbled into; a caller experimenting against a scratch reference backend must
  not silently pollute a shared store.

**What was verified.** New `tests/unit/test_calibration_flywheel.py` (4 tests, green first
run): the recorded residual matches `(predicted - reference) / reference` exactly; idempotence
(second identical call inserts nothing, a different workload_hash does); zero-reference skip;
and the decisive end-to-end effect — an empty store yields a bare point estimate and
out-of-domain, one recorded conformance run makes the *next* `calibrate_result` call return a
genuinely widened CI that now contains the reference value the model missed, with
`domain.distance == 0.0` (exact match). Full regression suite green.

**Implications.**
- The overview artifact's dashed "auto-ingest residuals (idea)" edge is now a solid, real edge
  labeled opt-in — the first of the review-era idea-edges to become real.
- With the flywheel on, `flux_agentic_dse_loop`-style loops that conformance-check winners
  now leave the store better calibrated than they found it — the "calibration data is expensive
  to obtain" risk in docs/roadmap.md's risk table shrinks a little with every real run that
  opts in.
- Still open, unchanged: nothing automatically decides *when* to opt in (an active-learning
  escalation policy that spends reference-evaluator budget where it most improves calibration
  remains the roadmap's own named, unbuilt piece).

---

## D99. Actionable escalation: the advisory becomes a budget-disciplined buy

**Decision.** `flux_calibrate(escalate_if_recommended=True, reference_backend="rtl")` — when,
and only when, the calibrated result's own escalation policy recommends it, buy one real
reference measurement, record its residual through the D98 flywheel, and re-calibrate against
the now-better-informed store before returning. No new node (the CHIA-node and MCP-tool counts
stay at thirty); two new parameters on the existing `flux_calibrate` surface, default-off.

**Why.** D98's own Implications named this as the open piece: the flywheel existed but nothing
decided *when* to spend reference-evaluator budget on it. The escalation policy (D8) has always
encoded exactly that decision — "spend high-fidelity budget where it changes the answer": CI too
wide, or out of validated domain — but was advisory-only; the D96-review artifact literally
annotates it "recommends, never re-runs". This connects the two: the policy that knows *when*
now drives the flywheel that knows *how*, making `flux_calibrate` self-improving in one call.

**Budget discipline, each gate real and tested:**
- *No recommendation → no spend*: the reference backend is never even constructed on the
  default path or when the calibrated CI is already trusted.
- *Already bought → not bought again*: if every declared metric already has an exact-match
  calibration record for this (workload, arch), the reference is skipped even when escalation
  is still recommended (one record < the trusted-n threshold keeps the recommendation alive —
  re-buying the identical measurement would add zero information, D98's idempotent recorder
  would insert nothing, and the real simulator time would be pure waste).
- *NotExpressible → honest no-op*: a reference translator that rejects the candidate returns
  the calibrated result unchanged — "couldn't buy ground truth here", the same precedent
  `flux_conformance_check` and the generation loop already set, not a crash.
- *The recorded prediction is the raw model output*: the re-calibration runs against the
  original uncalibrated `Result`, and D98 already established `declared_value` survives
  calibration unshifted.

**What was verified.** New `tests/unit/test_calibrate_escalation.py` (4 tests, green first
run, stub evaluators counting real calls): default path never touches the reference; the
escalated call buys exactly one measurement and returns a genuinely re-calibrated result (CI
contains the reference value the model missed, `domain.distance == 0.0`); an identical second
call spends nothing further; a NotExpressible reference is attempted once and returns the
calibrated result unchanged. Full regression suite re-run green.

**Implications.**
- The overview artifact's "advisory: escalate" annotation becomes "escalate (opt-in auto-buy)"
  — the second review-era gap on that diagram to turn real, after D98's flywheel edge.
- A search loop that calls `flux_calibrate(escalate_if_recommended=True)` per candidate now
  implements a real, if greedy, active-learning calibration policy for free: budget flows
  exactly to the candidates whose estimates are least trusted, once each.
- Still open: the policy triggers on CI width and domain only — Pareto-front relevance (the
  third trigger docs/calibration.md names) still needs a search-level (L5) view no single
  Result carries, unchanged since D8.

---

## D100. The architecture→RTL bridge: from an accepted candidate to verified RTL, no caller-authored spec

**Decision.** `flux_generation.derive_design_spec(workload, arch)` mechanically derives a real
`DesignSpec` from an accepted Architecture IR + Workload IR pair — ports from the candidate's
own compute width (`architecture_ir_to_lanes`, reused from `evaluators/rtl`, not reimplemented),
golden test vectors computed by a deterministic Python dot product over data seeded from the
(workload, arch) content hashes — and `flux_generate_rtl_for_architecture` (the thirty-first
node/tool, all three surfaces) feeds it straight into the existing D44 generate-verify-repair
loop. From candidate architecture to real, harness-verified Verilog in one call.

**Why.** The user's own question started this thread ("Can AI generate a behavioral spec, so we
can go from ref arch IR to RTL?"), and the D96-review artifact carried it as a dashed idea-edge
since: the RTL-generation loop was real but demanded a caller-authored spec, and the
architecture-generation loop produced candidates nothing could implement. The division of labor
is the same one D39/D43 established and every real finding since has reinforced: *the LLM never
invents its own ground truth*. Ports and expected outputs are computed here, deterministically,
before any LLM sees anything; only the RTL implementation is generated.

**Scope, named:** exactly one einsum op and one single-dim compute node (mirroring
`evaluators/rtl`'s own v0.1 scope), the derived module is the LANES-wide combinational
dot product — the compute primitive `mac_array.sv` instantiates LANES of — and a
`_MAX_LANES = 64` port-count sanity cap. Deriving full multi-level designs (memory hierarchy,
control) is the open remainder. The round trip's *upward* half — using composed, verified RTL
as a candidate-specific conformance reference in place of the fixed template — stays a dashed
idea: it additionally needs cycle measurement on generated designs, which the pass/fail harness
doesn't do.

**What was verified.**
- Unit (4 tests, pure derivation): ports match the architecture's own width; every golden
  vector's expected output equals the real dot product of its inputs at the workload's own
  int8 precision; the same candidate pair derives byte-identical specs (content-hash-seeded,
  no wall-clock/process state) while a different width derives a different spec; every
  out-of-scope pair (no compute node, two ops, lanes past the cap, zero vectors) fails as
  `DerivationError` before any LLM spend.
- Live (1 test, real Ollama + real Verilator, passed first attempt, ~60s): a real 4-lane
  candidate architecture → derived spec → `qwen2.5-coder:7b` wrote the module → Verilator
  verified 4/4 golden vectors. A real end-to-end path from Architecture IR to verified RTL
  that did not exist before this decision.
- Full regression suite green; the 30→31 count swept across every live doc claim
  (`tool.py` docstring + enumeration, agent-surface heading + table row, gap-analysis G12,
  roadmap, both READMEs) — historical decisions-log entries left untouched, per this log's own
  append-only rule.

**Implications.**
- The overview artifact's downward derive edge flips from dashed idea to solid real — the
  third review-era gap on that diagram to turn real (after D98's flywheel and D99's actionable
  escalation), and the workload→architecture→RTL story is now half a real cycle rather than
  two disconnected loops.
- `GenerationResult.final_arch` from D91's loop is now directly consumable: generate a
  candidate, then generate its RTL, in two calls — worth composing into one node if a real use
  case wants it (not built speculatively now).
- The upward half (candidate-specific conformance reference) is the remaining dashed edge, and
  its real blocker is now precisely named: cycle measurement on generated RTL, not spec
  derivation.

## D101. Adversarial validation, first real attempt: no hackable direction found, one sharp negative result

**Decision.** Actually run the experiment docs/roadmap.md's calibration-strategy list has
demanded since it was written ("find a design the model loves and RTL hates, before release —
not attempted yet at scale"): the complete RTL-expressible candidate family for a real GEMM
workload — every lanes value dividing K (6 widths) × two gbuf sizes, 12 candidates — real
ZigZag vs. real Verilator ground truth, plus a measured before/after of the D98/D99 calibration
defense. Full numbers: `flux/docs/adversarial-validation-report.md`. The robust findings are
encoded as a permanent live regression (`tests/integration/test_adversarial_validation_live.py`,
green in ~20s against both real backends).

**What was found, all real:**
- *No reward-hackable direction exists on this grid.* ZigZag over-estimates latency for every
  candidate (+193% for lanes ≤ 16, +93% at 32) — uniformly conservative, never optimistic. A
  latency-minimizing search cannot be lured toward a candidate ground truth rejects.
- *Ranking concordance is perfect* — ordering by ZigZag latency equals ordering by real RTL
  latency across all 12 candidates. The metric misleads on magnitude, never on choice.
- *The sharp negative result:* the residual is NOT family-constant (~2.93× for lanes ≤ 16,
  1.93× at 32). Measured consequence: one bought residual at the most-adversarial point yields
  family-widened CIs covering only 2/12 candidates — lanes-8's true 529 cycles misses the
  widened floor of 540.4 by 2%. Single-point calibration produces confidently-wrong intervals
  for the rest of the family. This is direct empirical support for D99's per-candidate buy
  design and for `_MIN_TRUSTED_N`'s humility (escalation correctly stayed recommended for all
  12 candidates after the first record, n=1 < 3).
- *The real residual attack surface is named precisely:* metrics ground truth cannot measure at
  all. RTL structurally ignores gbuf sizing (D27); ZigZag's latency happens not to
  differentiate it either on this workload, but its energy metrics do — and nothing can
  falsify those. Reward-hacking risk here is a ground-truth-coverage gap (G7's remainder), not
  evaluator optimism. Roofline validity correctly flagged nothing — its lower bound catches
  impossible under-estimates, a different attack than the one probed.

**What was verified.** Every number in the report from one real 12-candidate run; the live
property test re-derives the conservative direction, the ranking concordance, and the
single-point non-generalization (asserting its own-point coverage AND the cross-width
non-coverage — with a comment saying that if the non-coverage ever flips green, that is a real
residual-structure change deserving a fresh decision record, not a silent pass). Full
regression suite green. Honest scope: 12 candidates is the *complete* expressible family for
this workload, but "at scale" (larger workloads, energy, LLM-driven seam-probing) is explicitly
not claimed — roadmap item 5 and G14 updated to "first real attempt done", not "closed."

**Implications.**
- The defense-in-depth story now has its first offensive data point: the layers (independent
  validity, conformance, calibration humility) were built against an attack that — on the one
  family fully checkable today — turns out not to exist, while the check exposed a *different*
  weakness (single-point calibration generalization) the defensive layers' own design had
  already, correctly, guarded against. Attack-testing validated the architecture from a
  direction construction-testing never could.
- The experiment doubles as the first real multi-candidate exercise of the D98 flywheel + D99
  budget gates working together against real backends.
- A future "at scale" pass has a concrete recipe to extend: swap the exhaustive grid for
  `flux_agentic_dse_loop` with an objective deliberately rewarding evaluator-vs-reference
  disagreement, and widen past the RTL-expressible family once a second ground-truth backend
  (e.g. the D100 bridge's upward half) exists to check the currently-unfalsifiable axes.

## D102. Roadmap refresh: the D96–D101 arc's own outcomes folded back into the plan

**Decision.** Update docs/roadmap.md's three now-stale planning surfaces against what D96–D101
actually established: the risk row still claiming active-learning escalation "not yet built"
(D99 built the greedy per-candidate version), the calibrated-CI-coverage KPI row still claiming
"every calibrated CI checked has covered the true value" (D101 measured 2/12 coverage for
family-extrapolated CIs — the old blanket claim is now contradicted by this repo's own data and
had to be scoped to the per-candidate-bought mode where it genuinely holds), and the
Immediate-next-actions list, which gains the arc's three precisely-named remainders as a ranked
item: the upward conformance half (blocked on cycle measurement for generated designs), at-scale
adversarial validation (with D101's concrete recipe), and the Pareto-front escalation trigger
(needs a search-level view, unchanged since D8).

**Why.** The same D95/D97 pattern, applied promptly this time instead of being found by a later
review: a multi-decision arc changes what is true, and the planning docs age silently unless
swept right after. The KPI row is the sharpest case — it wasn't merely stale, it was *actively
wrong* per D101's own measurement, and a KPI table that keeps a claim the repo's own adversarial
data contradicts is exactly the kind of self-flattery the decision log exists to prevent. The
refreshed row now states precisely where ≥90% coverage is honest (a candidate's own bought
residual) and where it measurably fails (single-point family extrapolation).

**What was verified.** All three replacements anchored on exact current text (a failed anchor
aborts the edit, the same discipline every decisions.md insertion uses); full regression suite
re-run green after the edits — docs-only changes, but the suite runs regardless, per this
repo's own standing practice for every decision, D90/D95 precedent.

**Implications.**
- The Immediate-next-actions list is now an honest queue again: hammer/P&R (item 1, partially
  unblocked), torus NoC (item 2, blocked on a simulator), and the D98–D101 remainders (item 3,
  each with its blocker named) — nothing in it is secretly done, nothing done is secretly
  missing from it.
- The KPI scoping is the durable lesson: a coverage target is only meaningful relative to a
  named calibration *mode*. Future KPI rows should bind their claim to the mechanism that
  produces it, not to "calibration" in the abstract.

## D103. Real layer fusion through Stream — and the Mapping IR's `fusion` block gets its first consumer

**Decision.** Wire Stream's own `intra_core_tiling` (its second headline capability, named as
not-attempted future work by D80–D82's own README and roadmap rows ever since) through a
fusion-only Flux Mapping IR document. `evaluators/stream` gains `fusion_translator.py`:
`mapping.fusion` (`{group: [op ids], tile: {<row dim>: <tile size>}}`) → Stream's real tiling
entries, with `Candidate.mapping` no longer unconditionally rejected.

**Why this, now.** It was the last *unblocked* named-open item — the remaining ones need external
tools (torus simulator, hammer-shell) or a design session (cycle measurement for D100's upward
half). It also closes a subtler gap: the Mapping IR has carried a `fusion` block since day one
(docs/ir.md, "this is Stream's contribution"), and no adapter had ever consumed it — a schema
field that exists but nothing reads is a claim the repo hadn't earned.

**Two facts pinned empirically, both of which would have made a docs-only implementation
silently wrong:**
- *Stream filters tiling entries by `entry["dim"].split(".")[0] in group_node_names` — a FIRST-dot
  split.* Flux op ids are conventionally dotted (`ffn.down`) and the ONNX exporter names nodes by
  op id, so entries built from raw op ids match nothing and are **silently dropped**: measured
  1080.0 with and without them, byte-identical. Found by testing the obvious implementation and
  not believing the null result. The adapter now renames ONNX nodes dot→underscore before Stream
  parses them (metadata only — graph edges are value names), and rejects post-sanitization
  collisions rather than letting two ops share a name.
- *`tile` is a tile SIZE, not a split count.* Tiling at the full bound (B=4) reproduces the
  unfused latency exactly (1080.0), size 2 gives 1040.0, size 1 gives 976.0 — a real pipelining
  win, the second layer starting on tile 0's output while the first works on tile 1. Both the
  full-tile identity and the fused number are pinned as tests; if Stream's semantics ever change,
  they fail loudly rather than drifting.

**Contract: every violation is a loud `NotExpressibleError`, nothing silently ignored** —
non-empty `operands`, any `spatial`/`placement` block, a partial fusion group, a `for_op` outside
the group, more than one tile dim, a tile dim that isn't every group op's shared row dim, or a
tile size that doesn't divide the bound evenly. This is D27's own lesson applied deliberately: an
adapter that *accepts* an input field it doesn't honor is worse than one that rejects it, because
the caller's intent silently evaporates (exactly what D27 found for `size_kb` against
evaluators/rtl).

**What was verified.** 14 unit contract cases (pure translation, no Stream import) + 7 live tests
against real Stream — including the 4 pre-existing ones, confirming the `mapping=None` path is
untouched: 21/21 green. Real numbers measured by hand before any assertion was written. Full
regression suite green. Docs swept in the same pass: `evaluators/stream/README.md` (the
not-modelled claim removed, the new scope + both pinned facts documented), roadmap's two stale
"not attempted" rows, and docs/ir.md's "fusion … unused by any current adapter" line.

**Implications.**
- `search/*` strategies can now search a fusion axis for multi-op workloads by varying one
  integer in a mapping document — no new search machinery needed, though no strategy does yet.
- The dotted-name finding generalizes beyond Stream: any external tool that parses structured
  names out of ours is a place where Flux's own dotted-id convention can silently mismatch. Worth
  checking first, not last, in the next such adapter.
- Deliberately not built: partial fusion groups (Stream supports cut points; nothing here needs
  them yet), multi-dim tiling, and fusion-aware *search*. Each is a real extension of this
  translation, not a gap in it.

---

## D104. A fusion-tile search axis — and the DSE engine's axis-agnostic claim finally made true

**Decision.** Add `search_kind="fusion_tile"` (function, CHIA node, MCP tool): the first
*mapping*-space search axis here. `generate_fusion_tile_candidates` holds the architecture fixed
and varies a fusion-only Mapping IR document's tile size, which D103's translator turns into real
Stream `intra_core_tiling`. Enabling it required generalizing `run_architecture_dse` to honor an
optional `candidate.mapping`.

**Why, and why it was checked before it was built.** D103 closed noting no strategy searched the
fusion axis. Building one is only justified if the space is worth searching — a monotone space
needs a rule of thumb ("pick the smallest tile"), not a search. So the space was measured first,
on a two-op B=16 chain across the real dual-core architecture, bit-identical across repeated
runs:

    unfused / tile=16  3768.0     tile=4  3648.0  (1.033x)
    tile=8             3568.0     tile=2  3824.0  (0.985x — WORSE than not fusing)
    (best, 1.056x)     tile=1     3736.0  (1.009x)

**Non-monotone, with an interior optimum, and a badly-chosen tile is genuinely worse than not
fusing at all.** That justifies a search — and refutes the obvious heuristic: on the smaller B=4
chain (D103) tile=1 won, so the intuition from one workload does not transfer. Tile size has to
be measured per workload, which is exactly what a search axis is for. The shape itself (not just
the winner) is pinned as a live test: if it ever becomes monotone, this axis stops earning its
keep and that assertion fails loudly rather than the justification quietly rotting.

**The engine generalization, and an honest correction.** `dse.py`'s `_ArchCandidateProtocol`
docstring has long claimed the engine is "candidate-axis-agnostic … and anything else a future
candidate-generator module produces" — but both `Candidate(...)` construction sites hardcoded
`mapping=None`, so the claim was only ever true for *architecture* axes. A mapping-space
candidate was structurally unrepresentable. The fix is two `getattr(c, "mapping", None)` calls:
candidates that carry a mapping get it, candidates that don't are bit-for-bit unaffected (pinned
by its own test). The claim is now true rather than aspirational — the same class of finding as
D103's unused `fusion` block and D96's overclaiming docstrings, and worth naming as a pattern:
**a docstring describing a generalization the code doesn't implement is a bug report written in
advance.**

**A real bug, caught by this arc's own test.** `generate_fusion_tile_candidates` collected op
bounds into a `set` to check agreement — but a dynamic bound is a `{"dyn": [lo, hi]}` dict,
unhashable, so a dynamic-bound workload raised a bare `TypeError` instead of the module's own
typed `NotAFusionSweepCandidate`. Exactly the bare-exception class D96 swept out of the tree,
reintroduced by me and caught within minutes because the test for it was written alongside the
code rather than after. Fixed with a list plus separate type/agreement checks (two distinct
errors: "not static" vs "ops disagree", which are genuinely different caller mistakes).

**What was verified.** 14 unit tests (candidate generation, the engine's new optional-mapping
behavior, and that architecture axes still get `mapping=None`) + 9 live Stream tests including
the end-to-end one: real `flux_search` over `tile_sizes=[16, 8, 2]` against real Stream picks
tile 8 — the real interior optimum — through the real CHIA node. Full regression green. Docs
swept in the same pass (agent-surface's `flux_search` row, `search/architecture/README.md`, the
MCP tool's own parameter docs).

**Implications.**
- The axis count is now five for `flux_search`, but the more useful framing is that the engine
  spans two *spaces* (architecture and mapping) rather than one. A future placement or
  multi-level-tiling axis needs no engine change at all.
- `flux_agentic_dse_loop`'s own `axis` set is deliberately NOT extended here: an LLM-driven
  fusion search would be a different decision with its own verification (the analytic sweep is
  cheap and complete — every divisor — so an agentic search over it would have to justify itself
  against exhaustive enumeration, which for a handful of divisors it probably can't).
- Deliberately not built: multi-dim tiling, partial fusion groups, and fusion combined with an
  architecture axis (a joint mapping×architecture space) — each real, none needed yet.

---

## D105. Contender escalation — and the finding that its precondition isn't met: calibration conflates bias with uncertainty

**Decision.** Build the Pareto-front-relevance escalation trigger docs/calibration.md has named
since D8 and D99 deferred as "needs a search-level view no single `Result` carries" — the DSE
engine *is* that view. `contenders()` returns every candidate whose screening CI overlaps the
leader's (the ones screening data cannot rule out); `run_architecture_dse(escalate_contenders=
True)` escalates exactly that set and re-picks the winner from the higher-fidelity results.
Report gains `escalated_winner()` and `escalation_changed_the_winner()`. Default off; the
default path is unchanged.

**The reasoning.** Escalation previously bought the *point-estimate* winner only, ignoring CIs
entirely. If two candidates' calibrated intervals overlap, screening has not actually ranked
them — yet the engine escalated one and reported it as the winner. "Spend high-fidelity budget
where it changes the answer" means precisely: buy the candidates that could still win (their CI
overlaps the leader's), and don't buy the ones that can't (disjoint CI — no slower measurement
could promote them).

**Then the measurement, which is the more valuable half of this record.** On a real ZigZag width
sweep (4/8/16/32) against real RTL ground truth:

    uncalibrated (empty store): contender set 1 of 4 — point estimates, nothing unresolved
    after 1 real bought residual: contender set 4 of 4, width-32 CI span 23.8x
    after 4 real bought residuals: contender set 4 of 4, width-32 CI span 28.7x  (WIDER)

**The contender set never narrows, and more calibration data makes the CI wider.** The cause is
in the residual statistics: `mean_relative_residual = +1.94` with `std = 0.00` — ZigZag's error
here is a *perfectly-characterized systematic bias*, not uncertainty. But `calibrate_estimate`
computes `factor = 1 + z*(|mean| + std)` and widens symmetrically around the *uncorrected* point
estimate; it never **shifts** by the known mean. A model known with certainty to run 2.94x high
is therefore reported as "somewhere between 4.8x low and 4.8x high" instead of "2.94x high, and
we know it to within ~0%."

Consequences, all real: calibrated CIs span ~24-29x, so on this workload family *every*
candidate is always a contender; contender escalation degenerates to "escalate everything" and
saves no budget; and D102's KPI-row scoping ("≥90% coverage is honest for the per-candidate
bought mode") is true but for an unflattering reason — a CI that wide is nearly unfalsifiable.

**What was verified.** 9 unit tests: the set degenerates to the leader for point estimates,
overlapping/touching/disjoint behavior, both optimization directions, that the default path
still buys only the winner and still encodes `candidate=None`, that contender escalation
genuinely flips the winner when the rung disagrees (and confirms it when it doesn't), that a
ruled-out candidate's budget is *not* spent, and JSON round-tripping of the new
`EscalationStep.candidate`. Full regression green. The saturation measurement above is real,
from live ZigZag + Verilator runs.

**Deliberately NOT done here: fixing the calibration math.** Debiasing (shift by the mean
residual, then widen by the residual *spread*) is very likely the right model, but it changes
the semantics of every calibrated CI in the repo — D8's contract, D98's flywheel, D99's
escalation, D101's adversarial numbers and its pinned test values, and D102's KPI row all read
differently afterward. That is a cross-cutting design decision with real trade-offs (a debiased
estimate is no longer the raw model's own claim; bias may not generalize across a family the way
D101 showed variance doesn't), and it deserves an explicit choice rather than being folded into
a feature record. Raised, scoped, and left for that decision.

**Implications.**
- The feature is correct and tested; its *usefulness* is currently gated by CI width, which is
  gated by the calibration math above. Honest status: built, dormant in this regime.
- A generalizable lesson, third instance this session: the mechanism (escalation) had been
  described for many decisions as spending budget "where it changes the answer" while the code
  bought a fixed candidate — and once implemented properly, it immediately exposed that the
  *inputs* it depends on are miscomputed. Building the thing that consumes a signal is a good
  way to discover the signal is wrong.
- A D96 judgment is now corrected by events: review finding #18 (frozen dataclasses with dict
  fields raise `TypeError` on `hash()`) was deliberately not fixed because "no caller hashes
  them today." A caller appeared within the same session — my own measurement script, keying a
  dict by candidate — and hit exactly that `TypeError`. The library is still unchanged (altering
  `eq`/`hash` semantics for candidate types is its own risk), but the premise "no caller will"
  has expired and should not be reused as a reason.

---

## D106. Calibration corrects known bias instead of fencing it — and a compounding feedback bug found by re-measuring

**Decision.** `calibrate_estimate` now *shifts* by the measured mean residual rather than only
widening around the uncorrected value, in the regime where the data supports it. The residual is
`r = (predicted - reference) / reference`, so `reference = predicted / (1 + r)`: with
`n >= _MIN_TRUSTED_N` residuals the calibrated value becomes `value / (1 + mean)` and the
interval spans only the real spread, `[value / (1 + mean + Z*std), value / (1 + mean - Z*std)]`.
Below that threshold the previous conservative form is kept deliberately. Taken up as its own
arc at the user's direction after D105 measured the need, precisely because it changes semantics
D8/D98/D99/D101/D102 all depend on.

**Why the threshold split.** One or two residuals do not establish that a correction
generalises — D101 measured exactly that failure (a single width-32 residual did not transfer to
width 8; the family residual ranges ~1.93x–2.93x). Correcting on that evidence would trade a
wide-but-honest interval for a narrow-but-wrong one, the worse error for a calibration layer.
The store already encoded this judgment as `_MIN_TRUSTED_N = 3`; the split reuses it rather than
inventing a second threshold. A useful consequence: **D101's own live test and its published
numbers are untouched**, since they run at n=1 — verified by re-running it, not assumed.

**A real compounding bug, found by re-measuring rather than reasoning.** D98's flywheel recorded
`report.declared_value` as the prediction, explicitly justified by the then-true invariant
"`calibrate_estimate` widens only the CI and never shifts `value`". Debiasing falsifies that
invariant, so residuals began measuring the *already-corrected* model and correcting by them
again. It surfaced as an absurd number: the first post-debias sweep produced a *43.2x* interval,
worse than the 28.7x it was meant to fix. `record_conformance_residuals` now takes
`raw_declared_result` as a **required** keyword — not optional-with-fallback, so no call site can
silently keep the old behavior — and all three production call sites pass the uncalibrated
result. `flux_conformance_check` re-evaluates the declared backend raw for this purpose (one
extra fast-model call, on the opt-in path only), because its own `declared_result` comes back
already calibrated.

**Measured effect** — real ZigZag width sweep (4/8/16/32) against real Verilator ground truth,
four bought residuals, before → after:

    interval span (width 32)      28.7x  →   2.1x
    point error vs ground truth    ~194%  →   ~9% (widths 4/8/16), -27% at width 32
    coverage                        4/4   →   4/4   (still honest, no longer vacuous)
    contender set (D105)            4/4   →   1/4   (the ranking is now resolved)

The last row is the arc closing on itself: **D105 built the consumer and discovered the signal
was wrong; D106 fixed the signal and the consumer became functional.** Contender escalation was
recorded in D105 as "built, dormant in this regime" — that status is superseded here, by
measurement rather than by argument.

**What was verified.** Full regression green (907 passed). Two pre-existing D8-era unit tests
encoded the old contract and were deliberately re-contracted, each with the reasoning in its own
docstring: one expected a symmetric `[v/1.2, v*1.2]` interval (the honest reciprocal propagation
of `r in [-0.2, +0.2]` is `[v/1.2, v/0.8]` — a residual band is symmetric in `r`, and `1/(1+r)`
is not symmetric in `r`), and one asserted the interval still contains the *raw* point value
(which is exactly the property debiasing removes — a calibrated interval should contain the
truth, not the model's own claim). Three new tests cover the correction itself, the
below-threshold conservative regime, and the degenerate-denominator fallback. D101's live
adversarial test re-run and passing unchanged.

**Implications.**
- Every calibrated number in this repo is now a *corrected* estimate, not the raw model's claim
  fenced by error bars. That is a real semantic change for consumers: `Estimate.value` after
  calibration no longer equals what the evaluator returned.
- The pattern that keeps repeating this session, now with its sharpest instance: an invariant
  documented in one place ("calibration never shifts value") became false in another, and only
  a *measurement* caught it — the code still ran, returned plausible numbers, and was wrong. The
  fix was to make the dependency explicit and required rather than inferred.
- Still open and unchanged: whether a corrected bias generalises across *workload families* (not
  just widths) — the same question D101 asked about variance, now worth asking about bias, and
  answerable only with a broader corpus (G13).

---

## D107. Validating D106 across workloads — bias generalises by workload, not by architecture width

**Decision.** Immediately validate the semantic change D106 shipped, rather than waiting for it
to be questioned later: the calibration store keys residuals on `(evaluator, metric)` and never
on the workload, so D106's bias correction is applied across every workload from data gathered
on one. Measure whether that is sound. Result: it is sound across workloads, and *not* sound
across architecture widths — recorded here, and documented in docs/calibration.md as a known,
named scope limit rather than silently left in the code.

**Why this couldn't wait.** D106 changed what every calibrated `Estimate.value` in the repo
means, on evidence from a single workload family (`mlp-gemm0`, swept by architecture width).
D101 had already shown that residual *variance* doesn't generalise across widths; assuming
*bias* generalises across workloads without checking would repeat exactly the error this log
keeps catching — a documented claim that the code doesn't actually support.

**Measurement 1 — across workload shapes, fixed 8-lane architecture** (real ZigZag vs real
Verilator):

    B=4  C=32 K=32   1548.0 vs  529.0   +1.926
    B=8  C=32 K=32   3100.0 vs 1057.0   +1.933
    B=4  C=64 K=32   3100.0 vs 1041.0   +1.978
    B=4  C=32 K=64   3084.0 vs 1057.0   +1.918
    B=16 C=16 K=32   3100.0 vs 1089.0   +1.847

Range +1.847..+1.978 — correcting all five by their mean misprices the extremes by ~5%, against
the ~194% error left uncorrected. **Bias generalises across workload shape.** D106's
workload-agnostic residual keying is validated, not merely assumed.

**Measurement 2 — a refuted hypothesis, then the real pattern.** The known width-32 outlier
(+0.93 against +1.92 elsewhere) suggested a mechanism: `K/lanes == 1` is a degenerate
single-K-group case in `mac_array.sv`'s own loop schedule. Predicted before measuring, then
tested — and **refuted**:

    lanes=32 K=64  (K/lanes=2)  +0.936   <- ratio 2, still the low regime
    lanes=16 K=16  (K/lanes=1)  +1.917   <- ratio 1, still the high regime

The residual tracks **architecture width alone** (~+1.92 at widths 4/8/16, ~+0.93 at width 32),
independent of both the ratio and the workload shape. The tidy mechanistic story was wrong; the
empirical rule is simpler and better supported.

**What this explains, retroactively.** D106 measured `std` jumping 0.00 → 0.48 the moment a
width-32 residual joined widths 4/8/16, widening every interval. That is now understood rather
than merely observed: the pool mixes two genuinely different regimes. It also explains why
D101's single-residual non-generalisation finding held — that residual came from width 32, the
minority regime.

**Deliberately not built: architecture-regime-aware residual grouping.** It is the real fix, and
it is out of reach with the current corpus: each regime would need `_MIN_TRUSTED_N` residuals of
its own before any correction applies, and this repo has ground truth for one workload family.
The current pooling errs in the safe direction — a mixed pool inflates the spread, giving a wider
interval that still covers, rather than a tight interval centred wrong — which is why this is a
documented limit, not a defect to hot-fix. Chasing it now would also mean a second calibration
semantics change in one sitting, on thinner evidence than the first.

**Implications.**
- The honest scope statement for D106, now measured rather than hoped: *apply a residual learned
  on one workload to another — sound. Apply one learned at one architecture width to a very
  different width — not sound.*
- A methodological note worth keeping: predicting the mechanism (`K/lanes`) before measuring made
  the refutation cheap and unambiguous. A prediction that survives is evidence; one that dies
  costs two minutes and prevents a plausible-but-false explanation entering the record.
- This sharpens G13 (corpus breadth) from "more benchmarks would be nice" into a specific
  blocker: regime-aware calibration needs multiple real ground-truth points *per architecture
  regime*, which is now the concrete thing a broader corpus would buy.

---

## D108. Correcting D107 within the hour: width 32 is an isolated anomaly, not a regime boundary

**Decision.** D107 concluded, from four sampled widths, that the ZigZag-vs-RTL residual splits
into "two architecture regimes" (~+1.92 at widths 4/8/16, ~+0.93 at width 32) and that the fix
was regime-aware residual grouping. Sampling four more widths refutes that. The residual is
broadly *constant*, and width 32 is a lone outlier:

    w1 +1.938   w2 +1.936   w4 +1.933   w8 +1.926   w16 +1.913
    w32 +0.932  <- anomaly
    w64 +2.098 (K=64)   w64 +2.125 (K=128)

Values on both sides of 32 are normal. Across a 64x span of widths the residual moves only
+1.91..+2.12, which — together with D107's workload-shape result (+1.85..+1.98 across five
B/C/K shapes) — makes ZigZag's bias against RTL **stable in both dimensions**, with one
artifact.

**Why D107 got it wrong, stated plainly.** Its sample was widths 4/8/16/32: three points in the
normal band and the anomaly at the boundary of the sampled range. An outlier at the edge of a
small sample looks exactly like a regime change. Nothing about D107's method was sloppy — the
measurements were real and correctly reported — but the *inference* outran the evidence, and the
cheapest possible check (sample past the edge) had not been run. This record exists because that
check was run afterwards rather than the conclusion being left to stand.

**The leading explanation, labelled as such.** `evaluators/zigzag`'s default target is the
bundled `tpu_like` accelerator, a 32x32 array that spatially unrolls loop dims named K and C
(documented in `ir/workload/examples/mlp-gemm0.yaml`'s own comment). A translated width of
exactly 32 coincides with that template dimension, plausibly letting ZigZag's default spatial
mapping fit in a way it can't at other widths. **Not confirmed inside ZigZag's mapper** — asserted
as the leading hypothesis, not a mechanism, having already been burned once this session by a
tidy-but-refuted mechanistic story (D107's `K/lanes` hypothesis).

**What changes as a result.**
- *The recommended fix inverts.* D107 proposed regime-aware grouping, blocked on needing
  `_MIN_TRUSTED_N` residuals per regime. There are no regimes; there is one contaminant. The
  right treatment is outlier handling, and the store **already has the column for it** —
  `add_record(caveat=...)`, with `residual_stats(exclude_caveated=True)` as the default — built
  long ago for "a real record, known not to be representative". It has never been used for this.
- *D106's pooling is better justified than D107 concluded*, not worse: the residual genuinely is
  stable across both workload shape and architecture width, so a pooled correction is sound.
- *The blocker dissolves.* D107 escalated G13 (corpus breadth) into a hard prerequisite for
  regime-aware calibration. That prerequisite was an artifact of the wrong model. Corpus breadth
  remains valuable for other reasons, but it no longer gates this.

**Deliberately not built here: auto-caveating the anomaly.** Marking width-32 residuals
`caveat="zigzag-template-width-artifact"` is a two-line change, and it is the obvious next step —
but it would encode a hypothesis this record explicitly declines to confirm, and it would silently
drop real measurements from calibration on the strength of it. Naming the mechanism inside ZigZag
first is the honest ordering; the machinery is already there when the evidence is.

**Implications.**
- The generalisable lesson, and the reason this is a full record rather than an edit: **an
  outlier at the edge of a small sample is indistinguishable from a regime change.** D107 had
  four points and drew a boundary; eight points show a spike. Sampling past the edge of an
  apparent boundary is cheap and should be reflexive before any "there are two regimes here"
  claim enters a design.
- Two consecutive records have now had a plausible mechanistic story refuted by a two-minute
  measurement (D107's `K/lanes`, D108's regimes). Predicting first and measuring immediately
  keeps the cost of being wrong at minutes; the alternative is discovering it after building on
  it, which this arc came within one decision of doing.

---

## D109. The anomaly is `lanes == C`: a workload x architecture interaction, predicted then confirmed

**Decision.** Do what D108 said had to happen before its own suggested fix could be encoded —
find the mechanism rather than assume it. D108 hypothesised that the width-32 residual anomaly
was an artifact of `evaluators/zigzag`'s bundled 32-wide `tpu_like` template. That is wrong. The
anomaly occurs whenever the architecture's spatial width equals the workload's **reduction
dimension** `C`, at any width:

    predicted LOW,  lanes=16 C=16 K=32   ->  +0.876   (confirmed)
    predicted HIGH, lanes=32 C=64 K=32   ->  +1.958   (confirmed)
    control,        lanes=32 C=32 K=32   ->  +0.932
    control,        lanes=8  C=8  K=32   ->  +0.772

Both predictions were written down before the run, in opposite directions, so neither could be
satisfied by chance or by post-hoc reading.

**The mechanism, and how far it is established.** ZigZag's own logged spatial-mapping choices
show that at `lanes == C` the option `{D1: {C: n}}` becomes available — it can unroll the
*reduction* dimension completely and drop the temporal reduction loop. `evaluators/rtl`'s
`mac_array.sv` has one fixed hand-written schedule that unrolls K, so it gains nothing from that
coincidence. The fast model therefore looks disproportionately good on exactly that diagonal.
The *behavioural* rule is strongly supported (predictive, both directions, four confirming and
several disconfirming points); the *causal* story is inference from ZigZag's logs, not from
reading its mapper source, and is labelled as such rather than promoted to fact.

**What this corrects, across three records.** The observation has been right since D101 and the
explanation wrong twice:
- D107: "two architecture regimes" — wrong; there are no width regimes.
- D108: "an isolated width-32 anomaly, likely a 32-wide template artifact" — right that it was a
  point anomaly rather than a regime, wrong about the cause and wrong that it was about width.
- Both earlier sweeps looked internally consistent because **neither could see the effect**:
  D107's shape sweep held width at 8 while every sampled `C` was 16/32/64 (never 8), and the
  width sweep held `C` at 32 while only one sampled width was 32. A one-dimensional sweep through
  a two-dimensional interaction reads as "stable" along whichever axis is held fixed. That is the
  generalisable lesson here, and it is a sharper version of D108's: *an interaction is invisible
  to any sweep that varies one factor at a time.*
- D107's headline ("bias is independent of workload shape") must therefore be read with its
  scope: true off the diagonal, false on it.

**What it unblocks, and the question that remains.** D108 set the bar for caveating these records
at "name the mechanism first". The predicate is now named and predictive, so caveating is
justified in principle — `add_record(caveat=...)` and `residual_stats(exclude_caveated=True)`
already exist and already default to excluding. **Deliberately not wired here**, for a layering
reason that needs deciding rather than assuming: the predicate `lanes == C` requires reading a
compute node's `dims` and an einsum op's reduction extent, and `calibration/` (L3) must not learn
to parse architecture internals — that is exactly the coupling the Evaluator ABI exists to
prevent. The honest options are (a) the *caller* computes the caveat and passes it, since callers
already hold both documents, or (b) `evaluators/zigzag` exposes a small predicate helper and
callers use it. (a) is the smaller change and keeps the knowledge where the knowledge lives; (b)
puts it next to the adapter whose behaviour causes it. Left as a real choice.

**Implications.**
- The corrected scope statement for D106's bias correction: pooling is sound within either
  region and unsound across them. Nothing about D106's implementation changes; what changes is
  the precision of the claim about when it is safe.
- Three consecutive records (D107, D108, D109) have now had a mechanistic story refuted or
  corrected by a short measurement, each time before anything was built on it. The pattern that
  keeps paying: write the prediction down, in both directions where possible, then measure —
  which turns "I was wrong" from a rework cost into a two-minute result.

---

## D110. Wiring the `lanes == C` caveat: the finding becomes behaviour, without L3 learning architecture

**Decision.** Turn D109's confirmed predicate into working calibration behaviour.
`flux_evaluator_zigzag.mapping_regime` gains `fully_unrolls_reduction_dim(workload, arch)` and
`caveat_for(...)`; `flux_conformance_check`, `flux_calibrate`'s escalation path, and the
generation loop each ask and pass the answer to `record_conformance_residuals(caveat=...)`. The
store has excluded caveated records from `residual_stats` by default since it was built — that
mechanism finally has its first real user.

**The layering choice, made explicitly.** D109 left two options open. Taken: the predicate lives
in the **ZigZag adapter**, and callers pass the resulting string; `calibration/` (L3) never
learns to read a compute node's `dims` or an einsum's reduction extent. That coupling is exactly
what the Evaluator ABI exists to prevent, and callers already hold both documents, so asking is
free for them. The rejected option — teaching calibration the predicate — would have been fewer
lines at the cost of the boundary that makes evaluators swappable.

Three supporting choices, each deliberate:
- The predicate is phrased as a statement about **ZigZag alone** ("can it fully unroll this
  reduction dimension spatially?"), with no reference-backend knowledge in it. That RTL happens
  not to benefit is the caller's comparison, not the adapter's business.
- It is **conservative and never raises**: no architecture, multi-dim compute node, unparseable
  expr, dynamic bound → `False`. A residual is only ever excluded on a positive,
  well-understood match, and an advisory predicate that could crash a real conformance run would
  be strictly worse than one that says "no".
- Callers import it **lazily and guard `ImportError`**, and only when the declared backend is
  ZigZag — so a deployment without the ZigZag adapter installed still records residuals normally
  rather than failing on an optional refinement.

**What was verified.** 17 unit tests, whose positive and negative cases are the *actual measured
points* from D109 rather than invented examples — including `lanes=32, C=64` (normal), the case
that refuted the "width 32 is special" story. Plus a real end-to-end run recording four residuals
(widths 4/8/16 at C=32, then the `lanes == C = 32` diagonal):

    all records, diagonal included   n=4  mean +1.676  std 0.496
    caveated excluded (the default)  n=3  mean +1.924  std 0.010

**`std` falls 50x and the mean corrects to the true off-diagonal value.** Downstream that is the
difference between a ~2.2x calibrated interval and a ~1.01x one, on the same data. Full
regression green.

**Implications.**
- The D101→D110 thread is now closed end to end: an anomaly observed (D101), mischaracterised
  twice (D107 regimes, D108 template artifact), correctly identified (D109), and handled (D110) —
  with each wrong turn corrected by measurement before anything was built on it. The cost of the
  two wrong explanations was minutes; the benefit of catching them was a calibration pool that is
  now 50x tighter.
- The `caveat` column existed from the beginning with `exclude_caveated=True` as the default and
  went unused until now. Worth noting as a pattern in the opposite direction from the usual one
  here: a mechanism built ahead of its evidence, which turned out to be exactly right when the
  evidence arrived — the same file's `reference_source` tagging has the same character.
- Still open, unchanged: the causal story (reduction-loop unrolling) remains inference from
  ZigZag's logged mapping choices, not from reading its mapper. Nothing downstream depends on
  it — the behavioural predicate carries the weight — but promoting it to fact would need that
  source read.

---

## D111. A real budget leak, found by verifying an interaction rather than reasoning about it

**Decision.** D106 and D110 both changed the *inputs* to D99's escalation policy (bias correction,
then caveat-based outlier exclusion), so verify that the policy still behaves — rather than
arguing that it should. It did not. `flux_calibrate`'s "already spent" gate never latched against
real backends: the reference simulator was re-run on **every** call for the same candidate.
Measured before the fix: 3 calls → 3 real Verilator runs, intended 1. Fixed, re-measured: 3 calls
→ 1.

**The bug.** The gate asked `all(has_exact_match(evaluator, m, ...) for m in result.metrics)`.
Real ZigZag returns `energy_pj` alongside `latency_cycles` regardless of the requested metric set,
and `evaluators/rtl` can only ever produce a *latency* residual — so the energy metric never got a
record, `all(...)` was never true, and the gate never closed. The correct question is "has a
reference measurement already been bought for this exact candidate?", which one record answers:
`any(...)`, matching D99's own stated intent ("the budget was already spent once, not spent
again").

**Why the existing test passed.** D99's own `test_budget_already_spent_is_not_spent_again` used a
single-metric stub, where `all` and `any` are indistinguishable. The test was correct, targeted
the right behaviour, and could not have caught this — the defect lives entirely in the gap between
a single-metric stub and a multi-metric real backend. The new regression test uses a deliberately
multi-metric declared evaluator against a single-metric reference, reproducing the real shape.

**How it surfaced, which is the transferable part.** Nothing failed. No test broke, no exception,
no wrong number — the system produced correct results while silently spending N times its
intended budget. It appeared only from an *unexpected observation during verification*: an
already-calibrated candidate reported `in_domain=False`, which looked like a bug, was chased, and
turned out to be correct-by-design (`calibrate_result` takes the conservative worst per-metric
domain, and energy has no calibration data). Following that non-bug to its cause is what exposed
the real one sitting next to it. The instinct worth keeping: when a verification produces a
surprising-but-explainable result, explain it fully rather than accepting the first plausible
story — the explanation is where the actual defect was hiding.

**Also confirmed by the same verification (no change needed).** Tighter post-D106/D110 intervals
do *not* disable escalation for genuinely-new candidates: the width trigger stops firing
(relative CI width ~1.4%), but the out-of-domain trigger still fires for anything unmeasured, so
the flywheel keeps spinning. That was the original question this verification set out to answer,
and the answer is yes — it just wasn't the most valuable thing it found.

**Implications.**
- Cost of the defect, had it shipped unnoticed: every escalated candidate re-running a real
  Verilator simulation on each call, indefinitely — a silent multiplier on exactly the budget
  D99 exists to conserve.
- A stub that is simpler than reality in a dimension the code branches on is a blind spot, not a
  simplification. Single-metric stubs are fine for logic that never enumerates metrics; this gate
  enumerates them.
- This closes the verification D110 left implied. The calibration thread (D98 → D111) is now
  checked end to end against real backends, not only against stubs.

---

## D112. Reviewing the D96–D111 arc: the fix for the anomaly had created a worse one

**Decision.** Run the same adversarial review on the D96–D111 arc that D96 ran on its
predecessor — two parallel read-only agents (code, docs) — and fix what it confirmed. It returned
14 code findings and 15 documentation findings. The most serious was a defect *introduced by
D110's own fix*.

**The headline finding: D110 made the thing it was fixing worse.** Caveating a `lanes == C`
residual excludes it from the pooled statistics — but the caveated candidate was still *corrected
by that pool*, which by construction does not describe it, while `has_exact_match` (no caveat
filter) reported `distance = 0.0, in_domain = True` and escalation therefore declined to
re-measure it. Measured on real backends: the diagonal candidate came back at **87.9 inside a
±0.7% interval when ground truth is 133.0** — 34% wrong, stamped in-domain, and never scheduled
for re-measurement. Before D110 that same record sat in the pool and at least widened the
interval. The exclusion protected the pool and abandoned the point.

Fixed by letting calibration ask its *own store* — no architecture parsing, so D110's layering
holds: `exact_match_caveat()` reports whether this candidate's own record is caveated, and if it
is, `calibrate_estimate(trust_pool=False)` declines the pooled correction and the domain is
forced out-of-domain. Re-measured after: **257.0, CI [52.4, 1261.0], covering 133.0, in_domain
False, escalation recommended, calibration id present.** Honest and wide instead of tight and
wrong.

**Other confirmed defects, each now fixed and regression-tested:**
- *A zero measured spread produced a zero-width interval.* `std = 0.00` is real (D105 measured it
  for ZigZag), and with debiasing it collapsed the CI to a point — which turns
  `check_conformance`'s `ci_low <= ref <= ci_high` into float equality (conformance always fails)
  and drives escalation's width trigger to 0 (the flywheel stops). Floored the spread at 1% of
  the correction magnitude: a finite sample of identical residuals is not evidence of certainty.
- *The degenerate-denominator guard was a knife edge* (`> 0`), admitting ~5e9-wide upper bounds
  just above zero. Now requires the denominator to keep a real fraction of the centre.
- *`escalated_winner()` preferred a truncated rung over a complete shallower one*, so a
  wall-clock cutoff landing mid-rung returned a 9x-worse design and reported
  `escalation_changed_the_winner=True`. Now only rungs that measured every contender count.
- *Rungs were grouped by name*, so `["rtl", "rtl"]` (or two SystemC configs) merged different
  fidelities into one comparison — the exact mixed-fidelity error the method exists to prevent.
  Grouped by position now.
- *The D105 payoff was invisible over MCP*: `to_dict()` omitted the escalated winner, so an agent
  reading `winner` got the pre-escalation answer. Both fields are now in the payload.
- *`flux_calibrate` swallowed an unknown `reference_backend`* as "not expressible" — the same
  defect D96 fixed in the generation loop, reintroduced in a sibling. Resolved up front now.
- *The predicate's documented "never raises" was false*: a present-but-null `attrs` key made
  `.get("attrs", {})` return None, and the CHIA callers guard only `ImportError`, so a malformed
  document killed a real conformance run. Hardened; 11 parametrised cases pin it.
- *`provenance.calibration` was dropped whenever any metric was uncalibrated* — the routine shape
  for real ZigZag (energy) + real RTL (latency only). Post-D106 that meant a result whose value
  had been silently corrected carried no calibration id at all, contradicting this module's own
  "a result without a calibration id is a bug". Taken per-metric now.

**Documentation, swept in the same pass.** The generated index had rotted since **D37** — 74
entries missing, and the header still said "through D37 (latest)". Regenerated programmatically
from the headings, with its hand-curated Topic column deliberately dropped: a column that stopped
being true 74 decisions ago is worse than no column, and every entry names its own topics. Five
existing anchors were also wrong (hand-written, missing the double dash an em-dash produces) and
are now correct. Also fixed: `calibration.md` claiming "nothing yet auto-dispatches" 77 lines
after describing D99's auto-dispatch; roadmap listing the Pareto trigger as unbuilt (D105 built
it) and layer fusion as "still not started" (D103 built it); `flux/README.md`'s Stream row and
`docs/search.md`'s axis list and budget claim.

**Knowingly left unfixed, named rather than silently carried:**
- The budget gate still fails to latch when the reference produces *none* of the declared metrics
  (e.g. `metrics=["energy_pj"]` against an RTL reference): no record is written, so nothing marks
  the attempt. Fixing it properly needs an attempt log the store doesn't have; fabricating a
  placeholder record would be worse than the leak.
- The gate also ignores *which* reference was bought, so a later call with a different
  `reference_backend` is a silent no-op.
- `run_architecture_dse` raises `KeyError` for a screening result missing the metric, against its
  own "recorded as a failure, not a crash" contract.
- A multi-op workload is caveated if *any* op matches the diagonal, which can exclude a mostly
  off-diagonal residual.
- `_ref_hash`-style callers may pass content-hash strings where the predicate expects dicts, in
  which case caveating silently stops applying.

**Implications.**
- The generalisable lesson is the headline one: **a fix that removes bad data from a shared pool
  must also decide what the excluded case itself gets.** D110 answered the first half and left
  the second half defaulting to the pool — turning a known-anomalous point into the most
  confidently-wrong output in the system. Exclusion is not neutrality.
- Two findings (the swallowed backend error, the bare-exception predicate) are defects D96
  already fixed *elsewhere in the same codebase*. Fixing a class of bug in one module does not
  fix it in its siblings, and this is now the second time that pattern has appeared.
- Regression: 939 passed, 22 skipped, after the fixes and 20 new tests.

---

## D113. Closing the D112 leftovers that were actually fixable

**Decision.** Of the five findings D112 named as knowingly-unfixed, three needed no new machinery
and are fixed here; the remaining two genuinely do, and are restated as the design question they
actually are. Leaving named debt from a review one has just run is the wrong place to stop —
but so is patching the two that need a schema decision.

**Fixed.**
- *`run_architecture_dse` raised `KeyError` for a result missing the metric*, against its own
  "recorded as a failure, not a crash" contract. Reachable without a stub: `evaluators/rtl`
  returns an *empty* metrics dict when the requested metric isn't `latency_cycles`. Now recorded
  per-candidate as a real failure with the metrics actually returned, and rungs missing the
  metric are skipped rather than crashing the ranking.
- *The anomaly predicate caveated a multi-op workload if **any** op sat on the `lanes == C`
  diagonal.* A ten-op workload with one matching op had its entire residual excluded, silently
  shrinking the calibration pool — a false positive, which the "conservative by construction"
  docstring covered only in the false-negative direction. Now every einsum op must be on the
  diagonal, since the residual is a property of the run as a whole. D110's own test asserting the
  `any` behaviour was updated to the corrected contract, with the reasoning in its docstring.
- *Hash-ref callers silently bypassed the predicate.* `WorkloadRef`/`ArchRef` may be a content
  hash, and `caveat_for` returned `None` for a non-dict — so for those callers the D110 exclusion
  simply stopped applying, with no error and no warning. Now raises `TypeError` naming the reason:
  escalation-with-recording is opt-in, so a caller who asked for calibration data to be written
  must supply what makes it correct. Failing loudly beats silently pooling an anomalous residual.

**Restated rather than patched.** The budget gate still doesn't latch when the reference produces
*none* of the declared metrics, and ignores *which* reference was bought. Both are the same
missing capability: the store records **measurements**, not **attempts**, so there is nowhere to
note "we bought `rtl` for this candidate and it yielded nothing shareable". Fixing it means either
a new table or a sentinel record — a schema decision with real consequences for
`residual_stats`, replay, and every existing store on disk. That is a decision to take
deliberately, not a patch to land at the end of a review.

**Also settled: the D100 bridge's upward half is blocked for a sharper reason than recorded.**
D100 said it needs "cycle measurement for generated designs". More precisely: `rtl_bridge`
derives a *combinational* dot product, and a combinational module has no meaningful cycle count
at all — it can never be a latency conformance reference regardless of measurement. The real
prerequisite is *sequential* generation: a design with its own schedule and control (K-group
looping, an FSM), which is a generation problem, not an instrumentation one. Worth correcting
because "add cycle measurement" sounds like plumbing and would have been a wasted afternoon.

**Verified.** 941 passed, 22 skipped.

**Implications.**
- Two of the three fixes were false *positives* in safety machinery — the missing-metric crash
  and the over-eager caveat both made the system reject or discard more than it should. Safety
  code fails in both directions, and the over-cautious direction is the one that hides: nothing
  errors, the pool just quietly gets smaller.
- The attempt-vs-measurement distinction is the real gap left in the calibration store, and now
  has a name.

---

## D114. Attempts are not measurements: the schema decision D113 deferred

**Decision.** Add a `calibration_attempts` table alongside `calibration_records`, and have the
escalation budget gate consult it. This is the schema decision D113 declined to make in passing —
taken deliberately here because both remaining gate leaks are the same missing capability, and
neither can be patched without it.

**The distinction, which is the whole point.** A `calibration_record` says *"this candidate was
measured and here is the residual"*. Nothing said *"ground truth was bought for this candidate"* —
and those come apart in two real ways:
