## D161. All four Timeloop packages build — the port's remaining risk is now the equivalence run

**Decision.** Package `accelergy-cacti-plug-in`, completing the set D149 scoped:

| package | status |
|---|---|
| `accelergy` 0.4 | builds |
| `timeloopfe` | builds against it |
| `accelergy-library-plug-in` | builds, estimator installed for scanning |
| `accelergy-cacti-plug-in` | **builds**, with a working CACTI beside its wrapper |

**Two upstream assumptions this package makes, neither documented, both found by building.** Its
default branch is `master` while the library plug-in's is `main` — the `main` guess 404'd. And its
`setup.py` copies `cacti/cacti` as a data file: the plug-in is *meant* to ship a CACTI binary, which
the image's Dockerfile builds into the source tree first, so a fresh checkout fails with
`can't copy 'cacti/cacti'`. Supplying nixchip's binary at that path before the build satisfies it.

**That substitution is safe because it was measured, not assumed.** D150 ran Accelergy's bundled
CACTI and nixchip's stock build against the same config and got identical numbers to six figures;
the packaged plug-in's binary reproduces them again here (`1.47098 ns`, `0.303592 nJ`). And it is
only *possible* because of the `tech_params` fix (D146): a CACTI needing its data alongside it
could not be dropped into someone else's plug-in directory at all.

**The install location is asserted, not hoped for.** `get_cacti_dir()` searches relative to
`__file__`, so a binary installed anywhere else is useless; `postInstall` fails the build if it is
not executable at that exact path. A packaging step whose only failure mode is a silent runtime
error deserves a check that runs at build time.

**What is left is the part that can still refute all of it.** Every package building says nothing
about the numbers being right — that is D133's lesson, where a complete-looking Accelergy would
have reported dummy energy. The acceptance test has been written since D141: energy equivalence
against the recorded Docker baseline (620000 pJ across three architectures), with D138's guard
catching a plug-in set that fabricates.

**Verified.** All four derivations built with real hashes; the plug-in's installed tree listed; its
bundled binary run from the installed location and its numbers compared against two independently
built CACTIs.

**Implications.**
- Building four packages took less effort than the six rounds of scoping that preceded it, which is
  worth remembering next time an estimate stretches across four decision records.
- The remaining step is a run, not a build, and it is the only one that can still say no.

---

## D162. The four packages were never the blocker — nixpkgs' Timeloop binary is too old

**Decision.** Record that the hermetic port is blocked on a *fifth* component nobody had counted:
Timeloop itself. All four Python packages build and compose into one environment; the run then
fails at the binary.

```
driver exit=1
ERROR: key not found: data-spaces, at line: 0
```

**The front-end worked.** `timeloopfe` parsed the v4 specification and wrote
`outputs/parsed-processed-input.yaml`, then invoked `timeloop-mapper`, which rejected it. So the
Python side of the port is sound and the failure is downstream of everything that was scoped.

**It is the same error D132 measured**, when the bare nixpkgs binary was pointed at this repo's
config files. At the time I read that as "the front-end does real translation the binary cannot
do" — true, and it hid the more important half: **nixpkgs ships Timeloop 3.0.3, and `timeloopfe`
v4 emits a specification format a newer Timeloop understands.** The image builds Timeloop from
source (`/usr/local/src/timeloop`) rather than using a release.

**Five estimates, and the count keeps landing short.** D142 said CACTI needed packaging; D143 said
the migration was cheap; D149 said two plug-ins, not six; D151 raised it to four packages after
`accelergy` 0.4 turned out incompatible; now it is four packages *plus* a from-source Timeloop
build. Each correction came from executing the next step, and each revealed something the previous
scoping could not have seen — which is an argument for doing the first build early rather than
scoping further.

**What this does to the recommendation.** Keeping Docker for this adapter looks better again. The
image is not bundling four Python packages; it is bundling a *matched set* including a Timeloop
built from a specific source revision, and reproducing that set is the actual work. The Python
packages built today are still worth keeping — they are correct, they are cheap, and they will be
needed by whoever finishes this — but "three of four" and even "four of four" were never the
measure of done.

**Verified.** All four packages built and combined with `pkgs.timeloop` into one environment; the
reference bundle run through it; the failure captured from `outputs/run.log`; nixpkgs' version read
as 3.0.3 and the image confirmed to build Timeloop from source.

**Implications.**
- The remaining work is a C++ build of Timeloop at the revision the image uses, then the
  equivalence check (D141) — not more Python packaging.
- The acceptance test never moved and is still the only thing that can say yes. Everything measured
  so far has only moved the *cost*.

---

## D163. The repo already knew: barvinok is the dependency, and the README said so first

**Decision.** Stop the hermetic Timeloop port here and keep Docker, on evidence that was written
into this repo before the port began. The image's Timeloop needs **isl and barvinok 0.41.6**, and
`evaluators/timeloop/README.md` has said so all along:

> "PyTimeloop needs Timeloop built as shared libs plus `islpy` with Barvinok support — a
> well-documented, genuinely painful dependency (docs/gap-analysis.md G11). The project's own
> tutorial infrastructure ships a Docker image for exactly this reason."

**So the original decision was right, for the reason originally given.** Twenty-one decision
records (D142–D163) rediscovered it from the outside: CACTI is packaged, then broken, then fixed;
two plug-ins not six; `accelergy` 0.4 replacing an incompatible nixpkgs package; four Python
packages built; and finally a Timeloop binary too old, whose replacement needs the barvinok chain
the README named in one sentence.

**That is worth recording plainly rather than quietly closing the thread.** I treated a documented
"why" as an open question and paid several hours to reconstruct it. The scoping was not worthless —
it produced four working derivations, a corrected CACTI package upstream (D146), an estimator guard
(D138) and an equivalence baseline (D141), all of which stand on their own. But the headline
conclusion was available for free, in the file describing the adapter I was trying to replace.

**Kept, not discarded:** `flux/nix/{accelergy,timeloopfe,accelergy-library-plug-in,
accelergy-cacti-plug-in}.nix` all build and are correct. Anyone resuming needs only Timeloop
itself — from source, at the image's revision, with isl and barvinok 0.41.6 — and then D141's
equivalence run.

**Implications.**
- Before scoping a replacement for an existing component, read what the component's own
  documentation says about why it exists in its current form. That check costs one file read and
  would have front-loaded the answer here.
- The Docker dependency for this one adapter is now a decision supported by measurement *and* by
  the original reasoning, rather than an unexamined default — which is the outcome D132 set out to
  reach, just by a much longer road.

---

## D164. Two untouched modules, three real defects — a bounded window that silently under-returns, and an ONNX input count that rejects valid models

**Decision.** Review the two packages no prior pass had touched (`knowledge/`, `frontends/onnx/`),
and fix what it found: (1) `knowledge_lookup(query, standard_id=...)` now ranks the whole corpus
before filtering instead of over-fetching a fixed `max(k * 8, 50)` window; (2) the ONNX frontend
counts graph inputs *not supplied by a constant initializer*, rather than raw `len(graph.input)`;
(3) a dropped `Gemm` bias is recorded in the emitted document's `provenance["dropped"]`, and a
node with no named output is refused rather than silently inheriting the previous node's name.

**Why.** The two earlier module reviews this session (`search/agentic/_engine.py`,
`stores/caching.py`) came back clean and were reported as clean, so this pass was not run
expecting a yield. It found three, and all three share the shape this session keeps hitting:
correct on today's inputs, silently wrong on the inputs the code is explicitly designed to grow
into.

The retrieval window is the clearest case. `build_default_index` iterates
`corpus/<standard_id>/` subdirectories precisely so that "adding a new standard is add a
subdirectory, not a code change" — and the filtering path over-fetched 50 results and then
filtered by `standard_id`. With one standard in the corpus that is exact. With two, a standard
whose matches all rank below the window returns *fewer than `k` hits, or none, while real matches
exist* — a silent under-return, not an error. Ranking everything is not the expensive option it
looks like: `search()` already scores and sorts every chunk regardless of `k`, so the only cost
removed by the window was constructing surplus `RetrievedChunk`s.

The ONNX input count is a false negative on real files. ONNX IR version < 4 *requires* every
initializer to also be declared in `graph.input`; only IR >= 4 made that optional. Models from
older exporters therefore legitimately carry `graph.input = [activation, W0, W1, ...]`, and the
raw count rejected them with a message naming the wrong reason ("has 3 inputs; this frontend only
handles a single-input MLP"). This frontend supports those graphs completely.

The bias is the one place the module's own promise — "rather than silently skipping nodes and
producing an incomplete workload" — was not kept. A `Gemm`'s third input was read nowhere. Neither
available fix is free: the IR's `einsum` op genuinely cannot express an elementwise add, and
refusing biased Gemms would refuse nearly every real MLP export. So the loss stays, and stops
being silent — the bias's cost is O(B*N) against the GEMM's own O(B*K*N), so a consumer reading
this IR is not handed a materially wrong workload, and a reader who cares can now see exactly what
was left out.

**What was verified.** Each defect was reproduced before being fixed, none asserted from reading:

- `knowledge_lookup("cache", "std-b", k=5)` over a 60-chunk index (59 `std-a`, 1 `std-b`) returned
  **0 hits**; the `std-b` chunk is a genuine match ranked 59th of 60, below the 50-window.
- This repo's *own* exporter output — a two-layer MLP from `workload_ir_to_onnx_model`, re-saved
  at `ir_version = 3` with its initializers appended to `graph.input`, and accepted by
  `onnx.checker.check_model` — was rejected by `onnx_model_to_workload_ir` as "graph 'mlp' has 3
  inputs". Round-tripping the same model at IR 4 gives 2 ops.
- 5 new unit tests, including one asserting the `std-b` chunk really does rank last (so the test
  fails if the fixture stops exercising the window) and one asserting an unbiased Gemm records
  nothing dropped (so `provenance["dropped"]` cannot become unconditional noise).
- Full regression: **1056 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1051 + 22; the delta is exactly the 5 new
  tests, no existing contract changed).

**Implications.** "Untouched" is a weak prior for "clean" but not a worthless one — two of three
reviews found nothing, and this one found three. The yield here came from a specific question
rather than a general read: *which of these bounds are sized for today's corpus?* Both real bugs
answered it. The bias fix records what the earlier two reviews had no equivalent of — a place
where the code's stated contract and its behaviour had quietly diverged, fixed by changing the
behaviour and the docstring together rather than either alone.

---

## D165. The same question, asked of the sweep: a short batch silently truncated it, and both fallbacks were invisible

**Decision.** Carry D164's question — *which of these bounds are sized for today's inputs?* — into
`run_architecture_dse`, and fix what it found. `swept` was built by `zip(candidates, results)`, so
a `screening_evaluator` whose `evaluate_batch` returns the wrong number of results truncated the
sweep to the shorter list. That case now re-screens one candidate at a time, and
`ArchitectureDSEReport` gains `screening_fallback` naming why the batch path was abandoned — for
the pre-existing raise-fallback too, which was equally silent.

**Why.** The `zip` was assuming a length invariant the ABI never states. `Evaluator.evaluate_batch`
is typed `-> list[Result]` and documented as "batched interface, not necessarily batched
execution"; nothing there or in docs/evaluator-abi.md says the list must be as long as the input,
and nothing checks. That is a bound sized for today's evaluators: every adapter in this repo is a
sequential loop that happens to return one result per candidate, and `ChiaParallelEvaluator`'s
`get(refs)` preserves length. But the ABI exists precisely so third-party cost models can plug in
(`evaluators/abi/protocol.py`: "Any cost model that implements this becomes swappable"), and this
function *already* treats `evaluate_batch` as untrusted — it catches a whole-batch raise and falls
back. A short return is the same class of misbehaviour, and it failed far worse: the raise is
recovered from, the short list was silently believed.

Recovering rather than raising matches the fallback directly above it — a misbehaving batch
shouldn't turn a sweep into a dead end when the per-candidate path can still produce a real
answer. But recovering *silently* was its own version of the problem D164 named: at the 10**3-10**5
candidate counts the batch ABI exists for, falling back serialises the whole sweep, and the caller
saw only an inexplicably slow run. Hence `screening_fallback` on the report and in `to_dict()`, so
the MCP surface carries it too.

**What was verified.** Reproduced before fixing, with a batch evaluator that drops its last result:

- 4 candidates in, **3 in `swept`**, **zero errors recorded**, and the report named width 8 the
  winner. The dropped candidate was width 16 — under the test's `latency = 1000 / width` model, the
  true optimum. So the truncation surfaced as a confidently wrong answer, not merely a short list.
- After the fix, the same evaluator yields 4 swept points, winner width 16, and
  `screening_fallback` = "evaluate_batch returned 3 results for 4 candidates; re-screened one
  candidate at a time".
- 3 new unit tests, including one asserting a well-behaved batch records `screening_fallback is
  None` — so the field cannot quietly become always-on and stop meaning anything.
- Full regression: **1059 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1056 + 22; delta is exactly the 3 new tests).

**Implications.** D164's question generalises past the module it came from, and this is the second
place it paid. Both defects have the same shape: a length or a window that is exact for the inputs
the code sees today, silently lossy for the inputs its own extension points invite. The sweep for
more instances of it came back otherwise clean — the `_MAX_*` constants in `generation/rtl_bridge.py`
refuse rather than truncate, `dse.py`'s wall-clock cutoff already reports `stopped_early`, and the
remaining `[:N]` slices in the repo are hash and error-message truncation. Worth noting what the
fix did *not* do: add a length assertion to the ABI protocol. The invariant is still unstated
there, and the next caller to `zip` against a batch result will have the same hole.

---

## D166. Closing the invariant where it belongs: `evaluate_batch` returns one Result per candidate, stated in the ABI and checked against every backend

**Decision.** State the batch-length invariant in `Evaluator.evaluate_batch`'s own docstring and in
docs/evaluator-abi.md — *if it returns, it returns exactly one `Result` per candidate, in the order
given; an implementation that cannot evaluate a candidate raises rather than dropping it* — and
enforce it with `tests/unit/test_batch_length_conformance.py`, run against every backend in the CLI
registry.

**Why.** D165 fixed the caller that assumed this and got burned. It explicitly left the invariant
unstated, and named the consequence: the next caller to `zip` against a batch result has the same
hole. Fixing one caller defensively is the weaker half of the fix — the strong half is making a
short return a bug in the *implementation*, which requires the contract to actually say so. It
didn't: `-> list[Result]` is the only thing that ever expressed it.

Positional pairing is what makes the length load-bearing. A caller has no other way to tell which
result belongs to which candidate, so a drop in the middle silently re-pairs everything after it
with the wrong candidate — worse than the trailing drop D165 measured, which merely deleted
candidates from the caller's view. Neither is detectable downstream.

**What was verified.** All twelve registered adapters conform today, measured rather than assumed —
each is a one-line `[self.evaluate(c, ...) for c in candidates]`. The new checks:

- Every registered backend, constructed for real from `flux_cli.registry` (none needs its external
  tool present to be built), with `evaluate` stubbed and `evaluate_batch` called on 4, 1, and 0
  candidates: right length, right order, each candidate evaluated exactly once. Stubbing is the
  point rather than a compromise — every adapter's `evaluate_batch` is a pure delegation to
  `self.evaluate`, so the wrapper's own pairing behaviour is exactly what's under test, and the
  check runs with no Docker, Verilator, gem5 or Rust build.
- Registry-driven, so a backend added later is covered without anyone remembering this file — the
  same discipline `test_backend_registry_parity.py` uses, and for the same reason (D119, D26).
- Two guards on the guard: an empty registry fails loudly rather than passing vacuously, and a
  deliberately filtering batch implementation is shown to fail the assertion. Then confirmed
  against a *real* adapter, not only the synthetic one: patching `ZigZagEvaluator.evaluate_batch`
  to swallow refusals gives 3 results for 4 candidates and the check fires.
- Full regression: **1097 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1059 + 22; +38 = 1 registry guard + 12 backends
  x 3 cases + 1 filtering guard).

**Implications.** The realistic way this breaks is not malice but reasonable-looking error handling:
an adapter that catches its own `NotExpressibleError` per candidate and continues looks tidier from
inside the adapter than raising for the whole batch, and is invisible from outside. That is now a
test failure naming the backend. The v0.1 "raise for the whole batch" rule is a real limitation, not
an ideal — per-item error isolation is the better contract and remains unbuilt; what matters is that
the *current* rule is now written down, so the eventual move to per-item results is a deliberate ABI
change rather than an adapter quietly doing it early.

---

## D167. D112's rung grouping was inferred, not recorded — a refused candidate made it compare fidelities anyway

**Decision.** Record each escalation step's rung position on `EscalationStep.rung_index` at append
time and group by it, replacing D112's attempt to recover position from append order. Separately,
`escalation_agrees_with_screening` now compares the winner's screening estimate against *the
winner's own* deepest escalation, not against whichever step happened to be last.

**Why.** D112 was right that grouping by rung *name* is wrong (names legitimately repeat — two
SystemC configs, `["rtl", "rtl"]`), and right about the consequence: comparing a deep measurement
of one candidate against a shallow one of another is a silent wrong answer. Its fix inferred
position from append order — "same name as the last bucket, and this candidate isn't in it yet."
That inference is sound only while every rung measures every contender. A rung that *refuses* one
candidate leaves a gap, so the next rung's first step is a name-match with a candidate not yet in
the previous bucket, and slots into it. The comparison D112 forbade then happens inside a bucket
D112 built.

The second defect is D105 collateral. Before contender escalation, every escalation step measured
the winner, so "the last successful step" and "the winner's deepest measurement" were the same
thing and `successful[-1]` was correct. With `escalate_contenders=True` the last step belongs to
whichever contender was evaluated last, and comparing its value against the winner's screening
estimate answers no question at all.

**What was verified.** Both reproduced against real `run_architecture_dse` runs before fixing:

- Two rungs both named `"rtl"`, the coarse one refusing width 2 and reporting 4000.0 for width 4,
  the deep one measuring width 2 = 5.0 and width 4 = **4.0**. `escalated_winner()` returned
  **width 2** — it had compared 4000.0 (coarse) against 5.0 (deep), while the complete deep rung
  was split across two buckets and never considered. After the fix: width 4 at 4.0, the deep
  rung's real best, and `escalation_changed_the_winner()` flips to `True`.
- A winner escalated to **exactly** its own screening estimate (100.0 vs 100.0) reported
  `escalation_agrees_with_screening(tolerance=1.0)` = **False**, because the other contender's
  step (99999.0) came last. After the fix: `True`.
- 3 new unit tests, including one asserting the recorded indices are `[0, 0, 1, 1]` (so the fix is
  pinned to the mechanism, not just its output) and one asserting a winner refused by every rung
  gives `None` — "can't tell" — rather than borrowing another candidate's measurement.
- Also fixed in passing: `escalation_agrees_with_screening` indexed `result.metrics[self.metric]`
  without checking it was there, so a rung returning a Result without the metric raised KeyError
  out of an accessor. Same omission D112 fixed in `escalated_winner` and didn't carry across.
- Full regression: **1100 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1097 + 22; delta is exactly the 3 new tests).

**Implications.** This is the second time this method has been wrong in the same way, and the
pattern is worth naming: D112 fixed the symptom (name-keyed grouping) with a cleverer inference
rather than recording the fact it needed. The information was never lost — the loop that appends
the steps knows the rung index exactly — it was thrown away and reconstructed. When a reconstruction
depends on "no gaps," the gap case is a bug waiting for the first refused candidate, which is a
routine event in this repo (every adapter refuses workloads it can't express; that's the ABI's
whole posture). D165's fix has the same shape: stop inferring the pairing from position, state it.

---

## D168. A fix that never left the module it was written in: D112's missing-metric hole was still open in all three other search strategies

**Decision.** Treat "the evaluator returned a `Result` that doesn't contain the searched metric" as
a per-candidate failure in `search/annealing`, `search/agentic` and `search/exhaustive`, exactly as
D112 already did in `search/architecture/dse.py` — recorded with the same message shape, never
fatal.

**Why.** D112 found this in the architecture sweep and fixed it there. The same three lines —
`outcome.metrics[self._metric].value` — sat unguarded in the annealing strategy's `observe()`, the
agentic engine's `observe()`, and the exhaustive driver's `_metric_value`. It is not a
hypothetical: `evaluators/rtl/adapter.py` builds its metrics dict inside
`if not metrics or "latency_cycles" in metrics`, so asking the RTL evaluator for `energy_pj`
returns a completely valid `Result` whose metrics dict is empty. D112's own note said as much and
the observation never travelled.

Where it lands differs by strategy, and the exhaustive case is the worst: the annealing and agentic
versions raise from inside `observe()` and kill the loop mid-search, while the exhaustive version
raises from `_metric_value` *after* every candidate has already been evaluated — the search runs to
completion and then throws all of it away. Both are one candidate's problem escalated into total
loss.

**What was verified.** Reproduced with the real workload/architecture examples
(`mlp-gemm0` x `simple-npu-1d-v1`) and an evaluator that reproduces `evaluators/rtl`'s exact
metrics-dict logic:

- Before: `run_simulated_annealing(..., metric="energy_pj")` and
  `run_exhaustive_search(..., metric="energy_pj")` both died with `KeyError: 'energy_pj'`.
- After: annealing returns `best=None` with all three candidates carrying
  `"evaluator returned no 'energy_pj' metric (got [])"`; exhaustive returns `best=None` with
  `skipped_not_expressible == 18 == len(evaluated)`.
- 4 new unit tests. One is the half-and-half case — a metric present for some candidates and
  absent for others — asserting the sweep still ranks the ones that reported it, which is the
  difference between a degraded answer and no answer, and which neither the all-fail nor the
  all-pass test would catch.
- The agentic prompt builders (`architecture_strategy.py`, `joint_strategy.py`,
  `memory_strategy.py`, `noc_strategy.py`, `strategy.py`) index the same way but already guard on
  `e.result is not None`; with the engine fix they now render an honest `FAILED: ...` line for
  these candidates instead of raising while building the LLM's next prompt.
- Full regression: **1104 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1100 + 22; delta is exactly the 4 new tests).

**Implications.** The interesting thing is not the bug, it's that D112 already knew it. The fix was
correct, tested, and written down — and stayed local to one file while three siblings implementing
the same `Strategy` protocol over the same ABI kept the hole. Nothing in the repo makes "an
evaluator may legally omit the metric you asked for" a shared, checked expectation the way D166 has
now made batch length one. That is the more durable fix and it isn't built: the ABI could offer a
single "value of this metric, or a stated refusal" accessor that every consumer goes through,
rather than eleven call sites each remembering to use `.get`.

---

## D169. `Result.refusal_for` — making "the evaluator may not answer for this metric" a shared fact instead of a remembered one

**Decision.** Add `Result.refusal_for(metric) -> str | None` and `Result.value_of(metric)` to the
ABI, and route every consumer that handles arbitrary evaluator output through them. The message a
user sees is now written once. Found and fixed one more instance of D168's bug while doing it:
`sweep_moe_routing` had no guard where its sibling `sweep_dynamic_shape` has had one for a while.

**Why.** D168 ended by naming what it hadn't fixed: eleven call sites each independently
remembering `.get`, with nothing making "an evaluator may legally omit the metric you asked for" a
shared, checked expectation. This is that fix. It is deliberately small — the check was never hard,
the problem was that it was *invisible*, so each new consumer rediscovered the need for it by
crashing.

The history in this one repo makes the case better than the argument does. The same defect was
found and fixed independently three times — D112 in the architecture sweep, an earlier review in
`workload_dynamism/sweep.py` (whose comment still says "not with a raw KeyError after all N samples
have already been evaluated"), and D168 across the three strategies — and each fix stayed local.
`moe_routing.py` sits beside `sweep.py`, aggregates results the same way, and still crashed with a
bare `KeyError: 'energy_pj'` after evaluating every routing sample.

**What was verified.** A survey of all 38 direct `.metrics[...]` accesses outside tests, then a
real crash for the one that wasn't guarded:

- `sweep_moe_routing(..., metric="energy_pj")` against an evaluator reproducing
  `evaluators/rtl`'s metrics-dict logic: **`KeyError: 'energy_pj'`** before, a typed
  `MoeRoutingError` naming the evaluator and the metrics it does emit after — the same message its
  sibling already gave.
- The other consumers were checked rather than assumed, and came back clean:
  `validity/roofline.py` raises `NotIndependentlyCheckable`, `calibration/conformance.py` skips
  metrics the reference lacks, `workload_dynamism/sweep.py` raises after one evaluation, and the
  agentic prompt builders guard on `result is not None`. `flows/chia_nodes/dse_loop.py`'s eleven
  accesses read a `best_result` chosen *by* that metric, so presence is structural there.
- 7 new unit tests for the accessor itself, including: a refusal must name what *is* available
  (a refusal that doesn't is a dead end), `value_of`'s exception must carry `refusal_for`'s exact
  message so the two cannot drift, and a metric present with value `0.0` must not read as missing —
  the truthiness trap a `.get(...)` -based check invites.
- Full regression: **1111 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1104 + 22; +7 accessor tests, +1 moe guard test,
  and one net -1 from replacing a hand-written message assertion).

**Implications.** This does not *prevent* the next consumer from indexing `metrics[...]` directly —
no test can, short of a static rule over 38 call sites that couldn't tell a guarded access from an
unguarded one. What it changes is that the correct thing is now the obvious thing to reach for, and
it lives on the type every consumer already holds. The stronger version of this, still unbuilt, is
the ABI returning a sum type — a value or a stated refusal — so that indexing isn't reachable at
all; that is a v0.2 change to every adapter, not a v0.1 accessor.

---

## D170. The baseline pick, not the winner: three defects on the graceful-degradation path, and a correction to D169

**Decision.** In `flows/chia_nodes/dse_loop.py`: validate the agent-supplied baseline index instead
of indexing with it unguarded; treat a baseline `Result` that lacks the searched metric as a
refusal and fall through to the next candidate; and record a replay whose fresh evaluation stops
reporting the metric as a *failed* replay rather than letting it raise. All three sit on the path
that exists to degrade gracefully.

**Correction to D169.** That entry surveyed the 38 direct `.metrics[...]` accesses and said of this
file's eleven: "read a `best_result` chosen *by* that metric, so presence is structural there."
That is true of five of them — the per-axis `winner_value`, where the search picked the winner by
comparing that metric. It is false of the other five. The baseline is picked by
`_pick_baseline_with_fallback`, whose criterion is "the first candidate `evaluate_candidate`
doesn't raise on" — nothing about metrics — and its callers then read
`baseline_result.metrics[metric].value`. Reading the winner path and generalising to the file was
exactly the kind of inference D167 warned about, made one entry after writing it down.

**Why.** `_pick_baseline_with_fallback` exists so an unlucky default index doesn't blow up the
whole loop, and both new failures escape it in the same way — through a line that isn't inside the
`try`. `candidates[start_index]` is evaluated before the guarded call, so an out-of-range index
raises `IndexError` on the first iteration, before a single valid candidate is tried; the fallback
never engages at all. And a metric-less Result *succeeds* the try, so it is accepted as the
baseline and detonates one frame up.

The index is not an internal detail: `baseline_mapping_index`, `baseline_variant_index` and
`baseline_size_index` are all `flux_agentic_dse_loop` parameters, i.e. things an agent chooses. A
bad one is a caller error, so it now says so — naming the value and the valid range — rather than
being silently clamped to something that would answer a different question than the one asked.

The replay case is the sharpest of the three. `ReplayCheck` exists to detect non-determinism, and
an evaluator that stops reporting the metric on re-evaluation is the most extreme non-determinism
there is — yet it raised `KeyError` out of the node instead of being recorded as the replay failure
it obviously is. A check that crashes on the strongest instance of what it checks for is worse than
one that reports it.

**What was verified.** Both new defects reproduced against the real helper before fixing:

- `_pick_baseline_with_fallback(candidates, 99, ...)` → **`IndexError: list index out of range`**;
  now a `ValueError` naming index 99 and the range `[0, 3]`.
- A baseline evaluator returning `evaluators/rtl`'s real metric-less shape → the pick succeeded,
  then **`KeyError: 'latency_cycles'`** one frame up; now it falls through to the next candidate,
  verified by a fixture where only the third candidate tried reports the metric at all.
- 3 new unit tests, including the all-fail case asserting the error names the *metric* — the
  refusals are what tell a user they asked for something this evaluator doesn't produce, and an
  error that only says "every candidate was rejected" sends them hunting the wrong problem.
- `ReplayCheck.fresh_value` is now `float | None` with a `fresh_error` field, so a missing fresh
  metric reports `matched=False` with the reason attached.
- All ten `.metrics[metric]` reads in the file now go through D169's accessor.
- Full regression: **1114 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1111 + 22; delta is exactly the 3 new tests).

**Implications.** Three of the four defect classes found since D164 have been on error-handling
paths — the fallback, the refusal branch, the "can't tell" case — rather than on the happy path.
That is where this repo's real complexity lives, because its whole posture is that evaluators
refuse things routinely; and it is systematically the least-exercised code, because tests are
written from the feature outward. The generalisable lesson from this entry specifically is smaller
and about me: D169's survey checked one representative access per file and generalised. Two files'
worth of that generalisation held; this one's didn't, and the half that failed was the half no
test covered.

---

## D171. Repetition was buying trust: the calibration gate counted rows, not measured points

**Decision.** `ResidualStats` gains `distinct_points` — how many distinct (workload_hash,
arch_hash) points its `n` records cover — and `calibrate.py`'s `_MIN_TRUSTED_N` gate reads that
instead of `n`, at both sites. `flux_calibrate_against_generated_rtl` now guards its `add_record`
with `has_exact_match`, the guard `calibration/conformance.py` has always had.

**Why.** `n` is the right denominator for mean and standard deviation and the wrong one for "is
this pool big enough to trust." Recording one point three times is one measurement repeated, and
the gate that decides whether to *correct* a prediction — rather than merely widen its interval —
was counting rows.

The reachable path is short and entirely ordinary: `flux_calibrate_against_generated_rtl` calls
`add_record` with no duplicate check, and D117 made the derived design deterministic, so re-running
it on the same candidate measures the identical value. An agent retrying a flow three times, or a
loop that re-calibrates a candidate it has seen, gets there without doing anything unusual.

This is D122's failure mode reached by a different road. D122 fixed *unvalidated* corrections
being reported with narrow bounds; this is a correction becoming trusted at all on evidence that
was never there. Both end in the same place — a confident number that reality doesn't support.

**What was verified.** Measured against the real store and the real calibration path, one point
recorded repeatedly:

| recordings of the same point | n | corrected value | interval | width |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1x | 1 | 210.0 | [94.9, 464.9] | 370.1 |
| 2x | 2 | 210.0 | [94.9, 464.9] | 370.1 |
| 3x | 3 | **529.0** | **[518.6, 539.8]** | **21.2** |

The third recording crosses `_MIN_TRUSTED_N = 3` and the interval collapses by 17x, on zero new
information. After the fix, all three rows give `distinct_points == 1`, the value stays 210.0, and
`in_domain` stays `False`.

- 3 new unit tests: the repetition case, a control proving three *distinct* points still cross the
  gate (so the fix tightened calibration rather than breaking it), and one pinning the `None`
  fallback for hand-built stats.
- Two existing tests changed contract, and the reason is worth stating: both built their "enough
  records" pool by recording the same (wh, ah) point three times with three *different* predicted
  values. No deterministic evaluator can produce that — its prediction is a function of (workload,
  arch, evaluator) — so the fixtures encoded the very misconception the gate had. Rewritten to use
  three real points, which is the only way "enough records" honestly occurs.
- Full regression: **1117 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1114 + 22; delta is exactly the 3 new tests).

**Implications.** The store-level fix was tempting and would have been wrong: a `UNIQUE` constraint
on (workload, arch, evaluator, metric, source) breaks `test_residual_stats_mean_and_std`, which
records the same point three times with different values — and a store genuinely cannot tell a
duplicate from a re-measurement. The distinction only exists one layer up, in what the *gate*
means. Worth noting what stays unfixed: `add_record` will still happily store duplicate rows, and
mean/std still average them. For byte-identical rows that is harmless (the mean is unchanged), but
it does deflate the observed spread — currently masked by D112's `_MIN_RELATIVE_SPREAD` floor, which
is load-bearing here in a way it wasn't designed to be.

---

## D172. `arch=None` was a cache wildcard, and a wrong corpus path was an empty corpus — plus a correction I made mid-fix

**Decision.** `CachingEvaluator._lookup` compares `arch_hash` client-side instead of passing it to
`find_results`, the treatment `mapping_hash` already had. `load_corpus` raises `CorpusRootError`
(new) for a path that isn't a corpus, rather than loading silently as an empty one. A duplicate
entry id inside one partition now says "twice in public/" instead of "in both public/ and public/".

**Why — and a correction, mid-entry, of my own reasoning.** `find_results` documents `None` as
"do not filter on this column", not "match rows where it is NULL". `_lookup` already knew this for
`mapping_hash` and compensated with an explicit client-side comparison and a comment explaining
why. `arch_hash` was passed straight through, so an `arch=None` candidate meant *"any
architecture"* and matched a row stored for a different, real one.

I first read `ArchRef = Union[str, dict]` — not Optional — concluded this was unreachable through
the typed ABI, and started to add a defensive assert mirroring the neighbouring `workload` one. The
assert immediately failed six existing tests, because `workload_dynamism`'s `sweep_dynamic_shape`
and `sweep_moe_routing` really do construct `Candidate(..., arch=None)`. The type annotation was
describing an intent the codebase doesn't hold to, and I had trusted the annotation over the
callers. So the real finding is stronger than the one I set out to write down: this is a live
cross-architecture cache hit in shipped flows, not a hardening exercise — and the fix is the
client-side comparison, not an assert that would have broken those flows outright.

The corpus half is the vacuous-pass class again. `Path.glob` on a directory that doesn't exist
yields nothing rather than raising, so a typo'd `corpus_root` produced `public_entries() == []` —
"checked, genuinely found nothing" and "the path is wrong" made indistinguishable. `leaderboard.py`
names this exact anti-pattern in its own docstring ("never a silently empty standings list that
could be mistaken for 'checked, genuinely found nothing'") while its own data source practised it.

**What was verified.**

- Before: storing a result for `arch-ONE`, then evaluating the same workload with `arch=None`,
  returned `arch-ONE`'s value with **no call to the inner evaluator**. After: two distinct
  candidates, two calls, and each subsequently hits its own row (100.0 and 200.0, stable on
  repeat).
- 3 new caching tests covering all three directions — `arch=None` must not reuse a real arch's
  row, must still cache against itself (or the fix would silently disable caching for every
  `workload_dynamism` sweep), and must not shadow a real arch's row.
- `load_corpus` on a typo, on a nonexistent absolute path, and on `docs/` (a real directory with
  neither partition) now each raise a named error; the real corpus still loads its 8 entries, and
  a `public/`-only corpus with no `holdout/` still loads fine — checked explicitly, since
  over-reaching into rejecting that legitimate layout was the obvious way to get this wrong.
- 4 new corpus tests, including that `public/`-only case and the duplicate-id message.
- Full regression: **1124 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1117 + 22; +7 new tests).

**Implications.** The lesson I'd keep is the one about the type annotation. `ArchRef` not being
Optional is a claim about the code that six tests falsify, and I reached for it as evidence
precisely because it was quicker than reading the call sites. Annotations in this repo are
documentation, not enforcement — nothing runs a type checker in CI (docs/decisions.md D155's
workflow is pytest only). Worth noting the unfixed remainder: `ArchRef` and the sweeps still
disagree, and I have not changed either. Making `ArchRef` Optional would be honest about what
callers do; making the sweeps pass a real architecture would be honest about what the ABI means.
Both are bigger than this entry, and picking one requires knowing which of the two the sweeps
actually intend.

---

## D173. Asking the backends instead of the annotation: `arch=None` is a supported input, and `ArchRef` now says so

**Decision.** `ArchRef` becomes `Union[str, dict, None]`, `Candidate` documents what `None` means
for both `arch` and `mapping`, docs/evaluator-abi.md records it, and
`tests/integration/test_arch_none_conformance.py` checks every registered backend either honours
`arch=None` or refuses it with `NotExpressibleError`.

**Why.** D172 left this open and framed it as needing a decision: `ArchRef` was annotated
non-Optional while `workload_dynamism`'s sweeps constructed `Candidate(arch=None)`, and I wrote
that picking a side "requires knowing which of the two the sweeps actually intend." That was the
wrong place to look for the answer. The backends already had one, and it took one loop to read it:

| behaviour on `arch=None` | backends |
|---|---|
| honours it, falling back to its own default architecture | rtl, systemc, timeloop, zigzag |
| refuses with `NotExpressibleError` naming the requirement | booksim, cacti, dramsim3, gem5, native, noxim, stream, thermal |

Nothing crashed, nothing silently substituted. That is exactly the ABI's "honour it or refuse
loudly" posture, arrived at independently by twelve adapters — which makes `arch=None` a supported
input that the type annotation, alone, disagreed with. `mapping=None` had carried the identical
meaning and the correct annotation since the beginning; `arch` just never got it.

**What was verified.** All twelve backends run against a real `Candidate(arch=None)`, producing the
table above — the split is measured, not declared. The conformance test asserts both directions per
backend: a backend in the default-architecture set must not refuse, and one outside it must not
succeed (which would mean it substituted an architecture the caller never asked for). Two guards on
the guard: an empty registry fails rather than passing vacuously, and a renamed backend is caught
by checking `_DEFAULT_ARCH_BACKENDS` against the registry rather than letting it quietly stop
matching anything. Full regression: **1124 passed, 22 skipped**, unchanged — this decision adds no
unit tests, only the integration file.

**Implications.** The test is an *integration* test, and that placement is itself a correction made
during this entry. I first added it to `tests/unit/test_batch_length_conformance.py`, where it
passed in 13 seconds — because the four honouring backends reached Verilator, Docker and zigzag for
real. That contradicted the file's own docstring ("the check stays runnable without Docker,
Verilator, gem5 or a Rust build") and would have broken D155's per-push CI, which has none of them.
A passing test is not evidence a test is in the right place; this one passed precisely *because* it
was doing something a unit test must not do.

The broader point closes D172's: an annotation is a claim about the code, and the cheapest way to
check a claim about twelve adapters is to run all twelve. That loop took one command and replaced
a question I had recorded as needing the user's judgement.

---

## D174. `protocols/`: protocol facts as data, with the licence check built into the schema

**Decision.** New package `protocols/` (`flux_protocols`): structured, typed descriptions of bus
protocols — signals with widths and directions, parameters, numbered rules — that other modules
consume programmatically. Ships OBI 1.6.0, WISHBONE B4, AXI4 and AXI4-Lite, plus a clocking/reset
vocabulary. Three surfaces as usual: typed functions, three CHIA nodes, three MCP tools (39 now).

**Why this is not `knowledge/`.** `knowledge/` retrieves *prose* via BM25 over AsciiDoc chunks: the
right shape for "what does the spec say about X", answered to a human or an agent. The request here
was for something "other modules can reference/access", which is a different question — "what
signals does an OBI manager drive, how wide is `be`, and which requirement says so" — asked by code.
A codegen backend emitting a bus interface cannot use a paragraph.

**Why the schema enforces licensing.** D31 checked five standards' redistribution terms and found
four closed, recording Arm's own words: "No part of the document may be reproduced in any form by
any means without the express prior written permission of Arm." A store of protocol facts is exactly
the artefact that accumulates such text by accident, so `provenance` is required and two guards are
structural rather than advisory:

- A source marked `redistributable: false` may not carry quoted rules or prose descriptions. It may
  still carry *structure* — names, widths, directions — which is what a consumer needs to generate
  or check an interface, and is not the reproduced expression a licence covers.
- A `normative: false` document (one describing an implementation rather than a standard) must name
  what it implements. This is how AXI is representable at all: the user chose to source it from
  `pulp-platform/axi`, real permissively-licensed RTL, and a reader is told plainly they are
  reading an implementation.

Both failures are silent at the point of use — a fabricated signal width and a sourced one look
identical to the code reading them — which is why the schema refuses them rather than a reviewer
catching them.

**Why it's ingested now, when D31 declined to.** D31 verified WISHBONE B4 is public domain and
deliberately did *not* ingest it, because nothing in Flux consumed bus semantics and it would have
been "corpus content in search of a use". It named the condition for revisiting: ingest "with that
functional work". `resolve_ir_reference` is that work. D31 also recorded that `noc: {model:
"axi4@2.0"}` and `protocol: axi4` were free-text labels no code parsed — "grep -rn 'axi4' across
every .py file in flux/ returns nothing". They are parsed now.

**What was verified.** Every licence read from the primary document, not a summary, per D31's own
process note:

- **OBI**: page 2 of OBI-v1.6.0.pdf — "Copyright 2020 Silicon Labs Inc. This document, all
  associated software, and derivatives thereof are licensed under the Solderpad License, Version
  2.0". Worth noting the repository has *no* `LICENSE` file (404) and a one-line README, so a
  repo-level check would have concluded "no grant" and been wrong.
- **WISHBONE B4**: page 3, "not copyrighted, and has been placed into the public domain". `pdftotext`
  extracted it cleanly, where D31's `WebFetch` attempt failed on the same PDF — worth recording as
  an addition to D31's process note.
- **pulp-platform/axi**: SHL-0.51 at tag v0.39.10 (`a8c53cee2520`), signals read from `axi_intf.sv`
  and widths from `axi_pkg.sv` typedefs.
- **The IR references now resolve or explain themselves.** `axi4@2.0` correctly does *not* resolve —
  this build ships facts read from pulp-0.39.10, not Arm's v2.0 — and says so naming what is
  available. Bare `axi4` resolves. That is the honest outcome, not a gap to paper over.
- 24 new unit tests, mostly on the guards: each required provenance field, both licence guards, and
  crucially that a closed source can still carry structure (a guard that made closed protocols
  unrepresentable would have over-reached). Two check the data against its source in ways that would
  catch memory-writing: AXI signals must carry *no* descriptions, and AXI4-Lite must be a strict
  subset of AXI4 computed from the documents rather than asserted.
- Full regression: **1148 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1124 + 22; +24 new tests).

**Implications.** Writing the WISHBONE document surfaced the failure mode this schema is built
against, in my own work: I drafted `STB_O` and `WE_O` descriptions and a rule id from the pattern of
the surrounding entries rather than from the text, then checked and found the descriptions truncated
and `RULE 3.05` a guess that happened to be correct. The guess being right is the point — nothing
downstream could have distinguished it from a sourced fact, and the schema cannot catch it either,
because provenance was present and the licence permitted quotation. What the schema prevents is a
whole *document* with no source; what prevented this was reading the PDF again. Worth stating
plainly: `coverage_note` on each document exists for the same reason, since silence about a gap
reads as completeness — the clocking file lists setup/hold, CDC and metastability as deliberately
absent, because IEEE 1800 is not redistributable and writing them from memory is precisely the move
this entry is about.

---

## D175. AXI4-Stream, from a second implementation — closing a gap I had recorded rather than filled

**Decision.** Add `axi4-stream@verilog-axis-48ff7a7e` to `protocols/`, sourced from
`alexforencich/verilog-axis` (MIT). The user's request named AXI "stream, lite, full"; D174 shipped
lite and full and left stream out with a stated reason. A stated reason is not the same as a
delivered scope.

**Why a different source.** `pulp-platform/axi` — where D174's axi4 and axi4-lite come from — has no
AXI-Stream typedefs, checked rather than assumed. `verilog-axis` is a widely-used MIT-licensed
AXI4-Stream implementation, and the licence was read from the MIT grant in the source file's own
header. That makes two implementations behind the three AXI documents here, which is worth being
explicit about: their naming conventions are their own and need not line up, so a consumer must read
each document's `provenance.document` rather than assuming the AXI entries share a source. A test
asserts they differ, so a later edit that quietly unified them would fail.

**What was verified.**

- Signals, widths and directions read from `axis_register.v`'s port list: tdata, tvalid, tready,
  and the optional tkeep, tlast, tid, tdest, tuser.
- **Which signals are optional comes from the source's own `*_ENABLE` parameters**, not from what a
  reader might expect AXI4-Stream to make optional. Asserted directly: required is exactly
  {tdata, tvalid, tready}, optional exactly the five gated ones, and each gate parameter exists.
- The naming difference is handled rather than smoothed over: the source writes `s_axis_tdata` /
  `m_axis_tdata` because a module carries both a sink and a source interface, so the `s_`/`m_`
  prefix identifies the *port*, not the signal. Signals are recorded unprefixed with direction in
  driver/receiver, and `coverage_note` says so.
- A structural test that a stream has no address or response channel while the axi4 bus does —
  the difference a consumer choosing between them needs, checked from the data rather than
  described in prose.
- Full regression: **1151 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1148 + 22; +3 new tests).

**Implications.** D174's closing note listed AXI4-Stream as "deliberately absent", and that framing
was doing more work than it deserved. Recording a gap honestly is necessary but it is not the same
as closing one, and the distance between them here was one search for a permissively-licensed
implementation. The `coverage_note` convention is still right for genuinely unavailable things — the
clocking document's setup/hold and CDC entries stay absent because IEEE 1800 is not redistributable
and there is no open substitute — but "no verified source was checked" deserves a check before it
becomes a note.

## D176. Deriving the stream from the bus, and checking the derivation against a source that shares none of its own

**Decision.** `flux_protocols.derive_stream_from_bus` constructs the stream form of an AXI-family
bus by keeping the write-data channel and dropping the address and response channels — the user's
suggestion, after the search for a usable AXI4-Stream specification came up empty. It is a function,
not a document in `specs/`, and `derived_matches_reference` checks its output against the
independently-sourced implementation.

**Why not a document.** Arm's AXI4-Stream specification (IHI0051) is closed on D31's finding, and
re-checking Arm's page produced nothing quotable — a JavaScript shell with no extractable terms —
so D31's own rule stands: absence of a grant is not a grant. Hunting further implementations also
stopped cleanly rather than being abandoned: SpinalHDL and LiteX both report `NOASSERTION` on their
licence metadata, which is not a permissive grant, so neither was used.

That leaves construction, and construction has a specific hazard this module is built against. The
mapping (`w_data`→`tdata`, `w_strb`→`tkeep`, and so on) is *my* reasoning, not a quotation from
anything. A file in `specs/` asserts "a source states this"; nothing states this. So it lives in
code, where its provenance can say "derived, not quoted" and be true.

**What was verified — and this is the part that makes it credible.** The derivation reads the
pulp-platform documents (Solderpad); the reference it is checked against is
`alexforencich/verilog-axis` (MIT). The two share no source, no author and no lineage, so agreement
between them is evidence rather than restatement:

| derived from | agreed | underived | **invented** |
|---|---|---|---|
| `axi4` | tdata, tkeep, tlast, tready, tuser, tvalid (6) | tid, tdest | **none** |
| `axi4-lite` | tdata, tkeep, tready, tvalid (4) | tid, tdest, tlast, tuser | **none** |

`invented` empty in both directions is the load-bearing result: the subtraction restructures facts
rather than producing them. It is **sound but incomplete** — it under-produces, which is the safe
direction to be wrong in. `tid` and `tdest` are unreachable for a structural reason worth recording
rather than papering over: a bus carries transaction ids on its address and response channels, not
on write data, and has no analogue at all of a stream destination, since it routes by address.

Also pinned: widths and directions carry through (`tdata` keeps `AXI_DATA_WIDTH`, `tready` runs
back toward the source like `w_ready`), the derived protocol carries **no rules** (no document
states requirements about something Flux constructed), and deriving from OBI or WISHBONE is refused
rather than silently returning an empty stream — the mapping is specific to AXI-family channel
naming, not a general bus-to-stream transform. 6 new tests; full regression **1157 passed, 22
skipped** (was 1151 + 22).

**Implications.** The honest framing of "generate our own" turned out to be "generate, then find
something independent to disagree with it". Deriving alone would have produced a confident-looking
signal list with nothing behind it — the same artefact as writing one from memory, just with more
steps. What makes it usable is that a source with no relationship to the inputs agrees on every
signal it produces. Worth noting the limit that leaves: the derivation says nothing about *timing*
or *ordering* semantics, only structure. Both sources are RTL and neither states requirements in a
form this schema can carry, so a consumer needing stream ordering rules still has nothing here —
and `coverage_note` says so rather than letting the six agreed signals imply completeness.

## D177. Emitting interfaces from the protocol documents — the consumer that can be wrong in ways a lookup cannot

**Decision.** `flux_protocols.emit_sv_ports` / `emit_sv_module` generate a protocol-conformant
SystemVerilog port list for one role of a protocol, and
`tests/integration/test_protocol_emit_verilator.py` runs real Verilator over every shipped protocol
and role.

**Why.** D174 met D31's "ingest with the functional work" bar with `resolve_ir_reference`, which
resolves IR protocol strings. That is a real consumer but a weak test of the data: a lookup returns
whatever the document says and cannot be caught being wrong. Generating an interface exercises the
widths, the directions and the role model together, and a tool outside this repo passes judgement
on the result.

**What was verified.** Nine interfaces across five protocols, plus the derived stream from D176,
all lint-clean under real Verilator: OBI manager/subordinate, AXI4 master/slave, AXI4-Lite
master/slave, AXI4-Stream source/sink, WISHBONE master, and the derived stream source. Spot-checks
pinned separately in unit tests, chosen for what fails invisibly: an OBI subordinate must *receive*
`req` and *drive* `gnt` (a reversed pair lints perfectly), and `be` must come out as
`DATA_WIDTH/8` evaluated — 8 bits at DATA_WIDTH=64.

Two refusals are load-bearing and tested. A width naming a parameter with no value given is an
error, never a default: a silently 1-bit data bus lints clean and means nothing. And a `DATA_WIDTH`
the source's own `be` relationship cannot hold for (12) is refused rather than rounded.

Full regression **1164 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1157 + 22; +7 unit), plus 13 integration tests.

**Implications — two corrections found by using the thing.**

First, my own API lied. The error for a width the specification leaves open said such widths "must
be supplied explicitly by the caller", and there was no parameter to supply them with — WISHBONE's
`ADR_O` was simply unemittable. Writing the message was not the same as building what it promised.
There is now a `widths=` override, and a test that the error names it *and* that it works.

Second, the linting is deliberately not `-Wall`, which this repo otherwise keeps strict for
generated designs (D153/D154). These modules are intentionally empty, so every output is undriven
and every input unused by construction; under `-Wall` all nine fail on exactly those two warnings.
Keeping `-Wall` here would have been a check calibrated to the wrong artefact — the strictness that
is right for a generated *design* is noise for a generated *interface*.

The limit worth stating: Verilator proves the output is well-formed SystemVerilog, not that the
documents are right about their protocols. A reversed direction in a YAML file produces a module
that lints perfectly and is wrong. Only provenance speaks to that, which is why the emitted header
carries the source document, its licence, and — when the source is an implementation rather than a
specification — a note saying the specification governs where the two could differ.

## D178. Checking RTL against the protocol document — and two parser defects that only real third-party RTL could surface

**Decision.** `flux_protocols.check_module_conformance` checks an existing SystemVerilog module's
ports against a protocol document for a given role, reporting per-signal findings. Exposed as
`flux_check_protocol_conformance` (CHIA node and MCP tool — 40 now).

**Why.** D177 emitted interfaces *from* documents and named the gap it left: Verilator proves output
is well-formed SystemVerilog but says nothing about whether a module matches the protocol it claims,
because a reversed `req`/`gnt` pair lints perfectly. This is the other direction, and it lands on
D39/D43's split — "verification owns structure, LLM owns behaviour". `generation/` produces
LLM-written RTL and nothing checked that a generated bus interface was structurally right. Now the
model proposes and a sourced document decides, with nothing resting on the model having remembered
AXI correctly.

**What was verified — including the part that went wrong.** The round trip works (emit an OBI
subordinate, check it, clean) and the invisible-to-Verilator cases are caught: reversed `req`/`gnt`
reports both signals, a 16-bit `wdata` reports the width against `DATA_WIDTH`, a removed `we`
reports a missing required signal.

Then I ran it against real third-party RTL — `alexforencich/verilog-axis`'s `axis_register.v`, the
source behind D175's axi4-stream document — and it reported **every signal missing, on both
interfaces**. Two defects, neither reachable from my own emitter's output:

- The module-header regex matched a parameter block as `#\s*\([^)]*\)`, which stops at the first
  `)`. `parameter KEEP_ENABLE = (DATA_WIDTH>8)` — ordinary Verilog — truncated the match and took
  the port list with it. Replaced with balanced-paren scanning.
- Global signals were per-interface prefixed. Real RTL declares a bare `clk` beside
  `s_axis_tdata`/`m_axis_tdata`, because one clock serves both interfaces, so every global read as
  missing.

After both fixes, `axis_register` conforms as a **sink** on its `s_axis_` side and a **source** on
its `m_axis_` side, ten signals each. That is cross-validation rather than self-consistency: the
module was written by someone else, and D175's document was read from a different file in the same
project, so both sides conforming is evidence the document describes the protocol rather than
itself. 7 new unit tests; full regression **1171 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1164 + 22).

**Implications.** The failure mode is worth naming precisely, because it is the same one this whole
session keeps circling: the broken parser did not error or return nothing recognisable. It returned
a complete, confident, structured report saying every required signal was absent — indistinguishable
in shape from a correct verdict on genuinely broken RTL. Had I only ever tested it against my own
emitter (which produces no parameter block and prefixes nothing), it would have passed every test I
wrote and been wrong about every real module it ever saw. The general lesson is about fixture
provenance: a checker validated only against the generator it was written alongside is validated
against a shared set of assumptions, not against the world.

Also stated on the report itself rather than left implied: `conforms=True` means the interface is
*shaped* right — names, directions, widths — never that the design speaks the protocol. Ordering and
handshake timing are unchecked because the sources mostly do not state them in a form this schema
carries (D176's closing note), and a checker implying otherwise would be worse than none.

## D179. The same parser bug was already shipped: D127's unpacked-array guard silently passed on ordinary Verilog

**Decision.** Extract the balanced-paren module-header scanner D178 wrote into
`flux_codegen_rtl_harness.sv_parse`, and use it from both callers: `synth.py`'s unpacked-array
guard and `flux_protocols.conform`'s port checker.

**Why.** D178's parser bug was a regex matching a parameter block as `#\s*\([^)]*\)`, which stops
at the first `)`. Having fixed it in new code, the obvious question was whether the shape existed
in old code — and it did, in `codegen/rtl_harness/synth.py`, essentially character for character.

That guard is not decorative. D127 added `unpacked_array_ports` because Yosys rejects unpacked-array
ports with `syntax error, unexpected '['` pointing into generated code the caller never wrote, and
the guard exists so the failure names the real limitation instead. With a parenthesised parameter
default the guard returned `[]`, passed, and handed the design to Yosys — reproducing exactly the
confusing failure it was written to prevent, in the one case where a design is complex enough to
have such a parameter.

**What was verified.** A module with an unpacked-array port `a` and `parameter KEEP = (WIDTH>8)`:
`unpacked_array_ports` returned **`[]`** before and `['a']` after. The control — the same module
with `parameter KEEP = 1` — returned `['a']` both times, so the fixture isolates the parentheses
rather than something else. 2 new tests there; full regression **1173 passed, 22 skipped** (was
1171 + 22), and D177's Verilator integration suite still passes against the shared scanner.

One implementation rather than two copies, deliberately: D168 recorded a fix that stayed local to
one file while three siblings kept the same hole, and duplicating a subtle parser across two
packages is how that happens again. `protocols` depends on `codegen/rtl_harness` for it, which is
the right direction — the lower-level package owns SystemVerilog parsing and the higher-level one
borrows it.

**Implications.** This is the third time in this session that a defect found in one place turned out
to already exist elsewhere (D168's missing-metric crash across four modules, D169's `moe_routing`
guard, and now this). The pattern is consistent enough to be worth acting on rather than just
noting: **when a bug is found, grep for its shape before moving on**. It cost one command here, and
the thing it found was a guard that had been silently inoperative for exactly the designs it was
meant to protect. The corollary is less comfortable — D127's guard was tested, and its tests passed,
because every fixture written for it used a parameter list simple enough to survive the regex.

## D180. Raw markup in 10 of 195 corpus chunks: the AsciiDoc cleaner ran per line on constructs that span lines

**Decision.** Split `adoc.py`'s cleanup into per-line substitutions (macros, index entries) and
paragraph-level ones (anchored spans), applying the latter after a paragraph's lines are joined.

**Why.** D179 ended by recommending that a found bug be grepped for by shape before moving on, so I
swept the repo for regexes with the same brittleness. The AsciiDoc connector's
`_ANCHOR_SPAN = \[#[^\]]*\]#([^#]*)#` was applied by `_clean_line` to one line at a time, and an
AsciiDoc anchored span routinely straddles a line break — `m-st-ext.adoc` opens one on line 23 and
closes it on line 25. The substitution could never match those.

The consequence is exactly the kind that hides: not a crash, a slightly wrong answer. An agent whose
`knowledge_lookup` returned that chunk read `[#norm:mul_op]#mul performs an XLEN-bit×XLEN-bit
multiplication of...` instead of the sentence, and BM25 indexed the marker's fragments as if they
were content — `norm`, `mul`, `op` as tokens the specification never wrote.

**What was verified.** Measured against the real corpus, not a fixture: **10 of 195 chunks** carried
raw `[#...]#` markup before, **0** after, and the example chunk now reads "mul performs an
XLEN-bit×XLEN-bit multiplication of `rs1` by `rs2` and places the lower XLEN bits in the destination
register." The same sweep found the other regexes clean — no chunk carried an unstripped macro, an
index entry, or an attribute line. 3 new tests, one of them ingesting the actual corpus and
asserting no residual markup in any chunk, with a size assertion so an empty ingest cannot pass
vacuously. Full regression **1176 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1173 + 22).

**Implications.** This is D178's fixture-provenance lesson in a second setting, and the mechanism is
identical. `test_knowledge_adoc_connector.py` had tests for anchored spans, and they passed — every
one of them written on a single line, because that is how you naturally write a test fixture for an
inline construct. The real document wraps at 80 columns, so the real input has a property no
hand-written fixture had. Both defects this session that survived their own test suites survived the
same way: the fixtures shared an assumption with the code, and only real input broke it.

Worth noting what the sweep did *not* find, since a clean result reported honestly is the point of
running it: the other five bracket-scanning regexes here and in `synth.py` handle their real inputs
correctly, and `_RANGE_RE`'s `[^\]]*` is safe because packed ranges do not nest in any design this
repo generates or ingests.

## D181. Two simulator parsers silently truncated scientific notation — wrong by 10**6 and 10**7, into Result.metrics

**Decision.** `evaluators/booksim` and `evaluators/noxim` capture their statistics with a float
pattern that accepts an exponent, matching what `evaluators/timeloop` and `evaluators/dramsim3`
already did.

**Why.** Continuing D179's "grep for the shape" sweep into the highest-stakes parsers in the repo —
the ones that turn simulator output into the numbers every downstream decision rests on. Four
regexes captured values as `([\d.]+)`, which cannot match an exponent. C++'s default `ostream`
formatting switches a double to scientific notation outside a narrow range, so those captures do not
fail on such a value; they match the mantissa and stop.

The contrast within the repo is what made this findable: Timeloop's patterns are `[\d.eE+-]+` and
DRAMSim3's are `[-\d.eE+]+`. Two adapters had learned this and two had not, which is the same
"a fix that never travelled" shape as D168 and D179.

**What was verified.** Rather than assume how C++ prints these, a real program was compiled with
`g++` and run:

| real value | what C++ actually prints | old capture parsed | error |
|---|---|---|---|
| `1234567.0` cycles | `1.23457e+06` | **1.23457** | 10**6 too small |
| `1e-07` flits/cycle | `1e-07` | **1** | 10**7 too large |
| `0.00123` flits/cycle | `0.00123` | 0.00123 | correct |

Both wrong values are silent and plausible: a latency of 1.23 and a throughput of 1.0 are numbers a
reader would accept. 4 new tests pinning the exponent cases and one asserting the looser class still
does not match `nan`. Full regression **1179 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1176 + 22).

**Implications.** The reachability argument is the uncomfortable part. These magnitudes are not
exotic inputs — they are what these simulators produce precisely when the answer matters. Booksim
reports large packet latencies exactly when a network saturates, which is the regime a NoC sweep
exists to find; Noxim reports tiny throughputs exactly when a network is nearly idle. So the parser
was correct across the ordinary middle of the range and wrong at both ends, where the interesting
designs are.

Worth stating what remains unverified: this was checked against C++'s formatting behaviour, not
against captured output from real Booksim2 and Noxim runs, because neither tool's output is stored
in this repo. The integration suites do run both for real (D25, D64) and their pinned numbers are in
the ordinary range, so they would not have caught this and do not now confirm the fix at the
extremes. Capturing real output at saturation would.

---

## D182. Running the real simulator to check D181's claim — the fix is right, the justification I gave for it was not

**Decision.** Build and run real Booksim2 to test D181's reachability argument, store the captured
output as `tests/golden/booksim_congested_output.txt`, and **correct D181**: the scientific-notation
fix is correct and stays, but the reason I gave for it was overstated for Booksim.

**What D181 claimed.** That these magnitudes "are what these simulators produce precisely when the
answer matters" — Booksim reporting large latencies exactly when a network saturates. It read well.
It was reasoning from C++'s formatting rules plus an assumption about simulator behaviour, and D181
itself flagged that no real captured output existed to check it against.

**What running it actually showed.** A depth-1 clone built with `make -j4`, then run across
injection rates on a 4x4 mesh, and finally on a deliberately pathological configuration — 8x8 mesh,
transpose traffic, `injection_rate = 0.95`, `num_vcs = 1`, `vc_buf_size = 1`, `packet_size = 8`:

| configuration | packet latency average |
|---|---|
| 4x4 mesh, uniform, rate 0.05 -> 0.60 | 19.65 -> 24.31 |
| 8x8 mesh, transpose, rate 0.95, 1-entry buffers | **4928.11**, then "Too many sample periods needed to converge" |

Booksim2 aborts — "Average latency for class 0 exceeded 500 cycles. Aborting simulation." — long
before an average could reach the ~1e6 needed to cross into scientific notation. So for Booksim
specifically, the case D181 said was the important one is one the tool declines to report at all.

**What remains true.** The mechanism is confirmed from both tools' own sources, which is what the
fix rests on: neither sets stream formatting at these print sites (`trafficmanager.cpp` writes
`<< _plat_stats[c]->Average()` bare; Noxim's `GlobalStats.cpp` writes `<< metrics.
network_throughput_flits_per_cycle` bare, its only two `std::fixed` uses being unrelated hub lines).
Default `ostream` formatting therefore applies, and the truncation D181 demonstrated with a compiled
C++ program is real. Noxim's throughput is the more plausible case — a *small* value crossing the
1e-5 threshold rather than a large one crossing 1e6 — and I have not run Noxim, so that stays
unverified rather than claimed.

**What was verified.** The captured congested run is now a fixture, and the parser is tested against
real tool text for the first time: it reads 4928.11 correctly. The fixture's header records that it
contains *no* scientific notation, because that absence is the finding. 1 new test; full regression
**1180 passed, 22 skipped**.

**Implications.** The fix cost nothing and removes a real class of silent error, so it stays on its
merits. What does not stand is the confidence of D181's reachability paragraph, and the failure mode
there is worth naming precisely: I verified the *mechanism* empirically (compiled C++, measured the
truncation) and then reasoned about *reachability* from plausibility, in the same entry, in the same
voice. A reader could not tell which half was measured. Running the simulator took one build and
four commands.

Also worth recording as process: while adding the tests I created
`tests/unit/test_booksim_translator.py` and `tests/unit/test_noxim_translator.py`, not noticing the
real files are `test_*_architecture_translator.py`. Appending with `cat >>` creates a file rather
than failing, so the tests ran and passed in a home of their own. Merged into the real files and the
strays deleted.

## D183. Running Noxim closed D182's other open item — and found a real misdiagnosis instead

**Decision.** Build and run real Noxim to test D181/D182's remaining unverified claim, and split the
adapter's error handling to distinguish "the delay line is absent" from "the delay line is present
and its value is not a number".

**What D182 left open.** That Noxim's *throughput* was the more plausible scientific-notation case —
a small value crossing the 1e-5 threshold rather than a large one crossing 1e6 — and that it was
unverified because Noxim had not been run. It is now run: built from source through the adapter's
own path (SystemC 2.3.1 plus a CMake build), on a 10x10 mesh with poisson traffic.

| `-pir` | received flits | delay (cycles) | throughput (flits/cycle) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.00001 | 216 | 16.8148 | 0.0113684 |
| 0.000001 | 8 | 16 | 0.000421053 |
| 0.000001 (another run, same arguments) | **0** | **`-nan`** | 0 |

**So the scientific-notation claim is not confirmed for Noxim either.** Throughput does not shrink
toward 1e-7; it bottoms out at exactly `0`, because with no flits received the quotient is zero
rather than tiny. Noxim also refuses `-pir` values below about 1e-6 outright (`Assertion "Invalid
pir format" failed`), so the regime cannot be reached from the command line at all. The D181 fix
still stands on the mechanism — neither tool sets stream formatting, so the truncation is real if a
value ever crosses — but after running both simulators, **neither has been shown to produce such a
value in practice**. That is a weaker justification than D181 gave, and it is the accurate one.

**What running it found instead.** With zero flits received, real Noxim prints `-nan` for the
average delay. The adapter's regex correctly does not match that, and then reported "Could not find
a 'Global average delay (cycles):' line in Noxim output" — when the line is right there. A reader
gets sent after a parsing or version problem for a simulation that simply carried no traffic. Now a
separate label-only regex distinguishes the two, and the no-traffic case says so and suggests
raising the injection rate.

**What was verified.** 4 new tests. The real low-injection capture is stored as
`tests/golden/noxim_low_traffic_output.txt` and parsed by one of them. The `-nan` case is a literal
in the test rather than a fixture, and the test says why: the zero-flit outcome is probabilistic, a
run with identical arguments received 8 flits, and labelling a hand-written string as "captured"
would be the fabrication this repo's whole discipline is against. Full regression **1185 passed, 22
skipped** (was 1180 + 22).

**Implications.** Two simulators built and run to check one claim, and the claim came back
unconfirmed both times while the running turned up a different, real defect neither had been looked
for. Worth stating what that costs and buys: D181's fix was cheap and remains correct, but I would
not have written its confident reachability paragraph had I run the tools first — and running them
took one background build each. The general form: when a fix is justified by a claim about what real
tools do, the tool is available and the claim is cheap to test.
