## D184. A security control that any later call could silently switch off: `register_pdk` allowed a downgrade

**Decision.** `flux_redaction.policy.register_pdk` refuses to re-register an already-confidential
PDK as non-confidential unless `allow_downgrade=True` is passed explicitly. Tightening and
idempotent re-registration remain unrestricted.

**Why.** `redaction/` is the module docs/gap-analysis.md G15 exists for — "Proprietary PDKs and IP
cannot be sent to public frontier models" — and `require_not_confidential` is the gate the raw,
unredacted synthesis path calls before returning real absolute numbers. That gate reads a
module-global registry that `register_pdk` wrote with a bare `_REGISTRY[pdk_name] = ...`.

So the guarantee held only as long as nothing else in the process called `register_pdk` again with
looser terms. Measured: register `acme7` as confidential, confirm `require_not_confidential` raises,
call `register_pdk('acme7', confidential=False, ...)`, and the raw path is allowed — no error, no
warning, `is_confidential` now `False`. The rest of the module is carefully fail-closed (an
unregistered PDK raises `UnknownPdkError` in both accessors, "refusing to assume either way"), which
is what makes this the one seam worth closing: everything else refuses to guess, and this quietly
accepted being overruled.

**What was verified.** The bypass reproduced end to end before the fix, and after it: a downgrade
raises `ConfidentialPdkError` naming the existing registration's reason, re-affirming identical
terms works, and tightening a public PDK to confidential works. 3 new tests covering all three
directions. Full regression **1185 passed, 22 skipped**.

The safe directions are deliberately left open rather than locked down, because an existing
integration test (`test_rtl_synth_asap7_live.py`) temporarily re-registers the real, public ASAP7 as
confidential to prove the CHIA node refuses — a *tightening*, which still works untouched. It
restores afterwards by assigning `_REGISTRY` directly, which bypasses this guard entirely; that is a
test reaching into a private and is its own business, but worth noting that the guard protects the
public API, not the module's internals.

**Implications.** The correction is deliberately narrow: a registration made in error must stay
correctable, so the fix blocks *silence*, not the change itself. `allow_downgrade=True` is a single
greppable token that makes a relaxation visible in review, which is the property that was missing.

Worth naming the shape, since it is not the same as this session's other findings: nothing here
computed a wrong number or crashed. The code did exactly what it said, and the defect was that what
it said was too weak for what it guards. A control whose strength depends on no other code ever
calling it again is not a control.

---

## D185. A bookkeeping failure reported as a design limitation: the residual write sat inside conformance's own try

**Decision.** In `generation/architecture.py`, narrow the `except ValueError` around the conformance
check so it covers only the reference evaluation and `check_conformance`, and move the opt-in
residual recording outside it, where a failure is recorded in the transcript instead of being fatal
to the conformance result. Also guard the replay's fresh-metric read, which had D170's exact shape.

**Why.** The `try` wrapped both the reference evaluation *and* the calibration-flywheel write. Those
two failures mean completely different things. A `ValueError` from the reference evaluator is a real
structural fact about the candidate — the backend cannot express it — and reporting it as
`conformance_error` is exactly right. A `ValueError` from `record_conformance_residuals` is a fact
about an opt-in bookkeeping step, and `CalibrationStore.add_record` raises precisely that for a zero
reference value.

Because the write happened after `conformance` was already assigned, the `except` clause then set
`conformance = None` — discarding a successful, completed conformance report and replacing it with a
message that reads as representation lock-in. The two conclusions could hardly be further apart: one
says the design cannot be checked against this reference at all, the other says a database write was
rejected. A reader is told the benign-sounding version of a problem they do not have, and loses the
result they did have.

The code's own comments show the intent was already the opposite: the caveat lookup immediately
above is wrapped in its own `try` labelled "advisory only — never break a real generation run over a
caveat". The recording itself just never got the same treatment.

**What was verified.** Reproduced with the module's own stub evaluators and
`record_conformance_residuals` patched to raise the real message `add_record` produces: before,
`conformance=None` and `conformance_error="reference_value must be non-zero..."` despite the check
having succeeded. After, `conformance` is a real report, `conformance_error` is `None`, and the
advisory failure appears in the transcript. A control test confirms a genuine
`not_expressible_in: [rtl]` refusal is still caught and reported as `conformance_error` — narrowing
the scope must not stop the case the clause exists for. 2 new tests; full regression **1187 passed,
22 skipped** (was 1185 + 22).

**Implications.** This is the fourth defect this session whose damage is a *misattribution* rather
than a crash or a wrong number — after D170's "can't tell" reported as disagreement, D178's parser
reporting every signal missing, and D183's Noxim no-traffic run reported as a missing output line.
The pattern is specific enough to name: an over-wide `except` turns "something else went wrong" into
a confident statement about the subject under test. The tell is a `try` block that spans two
operations which fail for unrelated reasons, and this repo has a strong local convention against it
that simply was not applied here — every other advisory step in the same function is individually
wrapped.

---

## D186. Comments say what the code does and why it resists an obvious simplification; the log holds the story

**Decision.** Cut the long narrative comments in `flake.nix` and the worst-offending Python modules,
on one rule: **a comment keeps the operative fact and the decision pointer; the decision record keeps
the narrative.** `flake.nix` 503 -> 411 lines (161 -> ~105 comment lines); ~170 net lines removed
across 15 files. No behaviour changed; full regression unchanged.

**Why.** These comments were mine, and they had drifted into retelling. A 30-line block in
`flake.nix` re-narrated D23 and D85's investigation of a CHIA submodule packaging bug — including a
dangling-gitlink finding confirmed via GitHub's API — when what a flake reader needs is three lines:
CHIA isn't on PyPI, it's pinned, `doCheck = false` because the submodules are empty and its tests
need docker. The investigation is in the log, permanently, and the log is where someone goes when
they want it.

The cost of the drift is not just length. A comment that spends fifteen lines on history buries the
one sentence that stops the next reader breaking something.

**What was kept, and why that distinction is the whole rule.** Comments were cut where they
narrate and kept where they are *operative* — where deleting them invites a plausible-looking
change that reintroduces a bug:

- `evaluators/booksim`: "Take the LAST match, never the first." Without it, `findall()[-1]` looks
  like a candidate for simplification to `.search()`, which is exactly the bug D25 found.
- `stores/caching.py`: compare hashes client-side, never via `find_results`, because `None` there
  means "don't filter" rather than "match NULL" (D172).
- `calibration/calibrate.py` was largely left alone at 25% comment density. Every constant in it
  needs a reason — why the interval is multiplicative, why the spread has a floor, why `Z=2` is
  flagged rather than asserted — and those are dense, not redundant. Only one passage of mine from
  today, which recited a measurement already in D171, was trimmed.

**Implications.** The rule generalises to what I write next, which is the actual point: state the
fact and the pointer, and let the log carry the reasoning. Two comment shapes are worth keeping at
any length — the operative "don't simplify this, here's what breaks" note, and a constant's
justification. Everything else is the log's job, and duplicating it there ages badly: the log is
append-only and dated, while a comment silently becomes wrong when the code around it moves.

---

## D187. Schema validation reported one error at a time, against a three-attempt repair budget

**Decision.** `flux_ir.validate` now reports every schema violation it finds (capped at 10), each
with its path in the document, instead of raising on the first.

**Why.** The main consumer of that message is a repair loop. `generation/architecture.py` catches
`SchemaValidationError`, feeds `str(exc)` straight back to the LLM, and retries — with
`max_repair_attempts=3` by default, meaning three attempts *total*. `jsonschema.validate` raises on
the first error only, so a candidate with three independent mistakes required three repair rounds
even from a model that fixed exactly one per round and introduced none. The budget could not cover
it, and the run would report `success=False` as if the model had failed.

Measured on a document with three real problems (`schema_version`, `id`, `hierarchy`): the old path
reported `'0.1.0' was expected` and nothing else; `iter_errors` finds all three. The failure was
invisible from the outside — a generation run that exhausted its attempts looks exactly like a
model that could not produce a valid document, which is the more natural explanation and the wrong
one.

**What was verified.** Errors are sorted by path for a deterministic message, each prefixed with its
location (`hierarchy/0/level: 123 is not of type 'string'`) — a bare "is not of type 'string'" does
not say *where* in a nested document. 3 new tests: all three errors present in one message, nested
paths named, and a single error still reading naturally as "1 error" rather than list-formatted.
Full regression **1190 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1187 + 22).

**Implications.** Worth recording a mistake I made writing the tests for this, because it is the
same one this session keeps finding in code. My first path-reporting test asserted that
`attrs: {dims: "not-a-dict"}` produces an error — it does not; the schema places no constraint
there, and the document is valid. The test failed, and the honest reading was that my *fixture*
encoded an assumption about the schema I had not checked, not that the code was wrong. Replaced
with a constraint the schema genuinely has (`level` must be a string). A test written from an
assumed constraint would have passed vacuously had I picked a case the schema did happen to
reject for some other reason.

---

## D188. A constraint that constrains nothing was reported as checked and passing

**Decision.** `check_declared_constraints` no longer counts a constraint with neither `max` nor
`min` toward its `checked` total. It stays in the denominator, so the gap between declared and
checked remains visible.

**Why.** The Architecture IR schema requires only `kind` on a constraint; both bounds are optional.
So `{"kind": "area_mm2"}` is a schema-valid constraint that compares nothing — and the checker
incremented `checked` before looking at the bounds, then reported
`checker_version="constraints-v0.1:checked=1/1"` with `ok=True`. Measured against a result carrying
`area_mm2 = 999999.0`.

That defeats the precise distinction this function's own docstring promises: "`checked=<n>/<total>`
so a caller can tell the difference between 'checked and fine' and 'nothing to check'." And it is
inside `validity/`, which docs/gap-analysis.md G14 and docs/evaluator-abi.md both name as the
primary anti-reward-hacking mechanism — the component whose reports are supposed to be the thing
you can trust when the cost model has no opinion. A clean `1/1` on a vacuous constraint is the
weakest possible form of that guarantee.

**What was verified.** The vacuous constraint reproduced end to end (schema-validated first, so the
document really is legal), and after the fix reports `checked=0/1` with `ok=True` — nothing was
violated, because nothing was checkable, and the counter now says so. A control test with a
bound-less constraint beside a real one reports `checked=1/2` and correctly fails the real one.
2 new tests; full regression **1192 passed, 22 skipped**.

**Implications.** This is a weakness in the mechanism rather than a bug in the arithmetic — nothing
computed a wrong number, and the same shape as D184's registry downgrade: a control reporting
success for work it did not do. Both were found by asking what the component *promises* and then
checking whether a legal input could make the promise false, which is a different question from
"does this code do what it says".

Worth also recording a repeat of D182's process slip: adding these tests I ran `cat >>` against
`test_validity_constraints.py` on the assumption it held the constraint tests. It does exist, but
the tests live in `test_validity.py`; `cat >>` created a second file rather than failing, exactly as
D182 described. Caught by the missing `_result` helper, stray removed, tests moved. Twice now — the
lesson is to read the target file before appending, not to check whether the name is plausible.

---

## D189. `flux replay` dropped the mapping — the command docs/stores.md holds up as the determinism check

**Decision.** `cmd_replay` restores the stored mapping document and passes it to the evaluator,
refuses outright when a `mapping_hash` is present but its document is missing, and wraps the
re-evaluation in the same "print `error:`, exit 1" shape every other path in that file uses.

**Why.** The candidate was rebuilt as `Candidate(workload=..., arch=..., mapping=None)` while the
record carried a `mapping_hash` the store round-trips perfectly. So replaying any mapping-carrying
result re-evaluated a *different design*.

What makes this worse than an ordinary bug is where it sits. docs/stores.md presents "deterministic
replay is one command" as the guarantee, and `flux replay` is that command. A difference caused by
silently dropping an input therefore presents as **non-determinism in the evaluator** — the reader
is handed a MISMATCH and pointed at the wrong culprit. The same shape as D170, D178, D183 and D185:
the damage is a confident misattribution, not a crash.

Reachable through the CHIA nodes rather than the CLI: `flux eval` has no `--mapping` flag, so it
cannot store one, but `flux_agentic_dse_loop` with `axis="mapping"` stores a mapping alongside its
winner, and every mapping-space search (exhaustive, annealing, agentic) produces exactly that.

**What was verified.** The store round-trips a mapping document intact, confirming the input was
available and simply unused. 3 new tests with a mapping-sensitive stub evaluator — chosen because
the question is which candidate `cmd_replay` builds, not what a backend computes: replay now hands
over the stored mapping, a dangling `mapping_hash` is refused rather than degrading into a
mapping-free replay (the original bug wearing an error case), and a genuinely mapping-free result
still replays. Full regression **1195 passed, 22 skipped** (was 1192 + 22).

**Implications.** Worth separating from the fix: `flux eval` still has no `--mapping` flag, so the
CLI cannot evaluate a mapping-carrying candidate at all. That is a feature gap, not a defect, and it
is why the bug survived — the CLI's own tests could never have produced a result that exposed it.
The evaluator error path was tightened in passing for the same reason it existed everywhere else in
the file: a refusal now prints an error and exits 1 instead of surfacing a traceback.

---

## D190. `flows/mcp` reviewed and clean — plus a guard for the one silent failure a wrapper layer has

**Decision.** Review `flows/mcp/tool.py` (1586 lines, the largest surface never given a pass) for
the defect class a thin wrapper layer actually has: arguments forwarded to the wrong parameters.
**No defect found.** A mechanical check is added to `test_mcp_surface_parity.py` so it stays that
way.

**Why that class specifically.** These 42 methods mostly exist to forward to a CHIA node with an
agent-facing docstring attached. A wrong *keyword* raises `TypeError` immediately and loudly. A
wrong *order* in a positional call does not: the values land in the wrong parameters and, for
same-typed neighbours like `(protocol_id, role)` or `(workload, arch)`, produce a plausible answer
to a question nobody asked. That is the same silent-misattribution shape as D170, D178, D183, D185
and D189, and it is invisible to the existing parity tests, which check that every node is
*reachable*, not that it is called correctly.

**What was verified.** 42 tool methods; 8 forward positionally; **0 order mismatches**. A second
pass over every keyword argument passed to any node from this file: **0 names the node does not
accept**. Full regression **1196 passed, 22 skipped**.

**Implications.** The process note is the part worth keeping. My first version of this check
reported "0 mismatches" and I nearly wrote that down — but it had introspected `ChiaTool`, the base
class, and examined **2 methods**, not 42. The real class is `FluxTool`. A clean result from a check
that looked at nothing is indistinguishable from a clean result from a check that looked at
everything, which is precisely what this session has spent twenty entries finding in other people's
code and has now produced in its own analysis twice (D183's Noxim capture that did not contain the
case it was named for, and this).

So the committed test asserts a **floor on what it inspected** — `forwarded >= 5` — with a message
explaining that a refactor to keyword arguments should lower the bound deliberately rather than let
the check quietly stop seeing anything. A guard that cannot go vacuous is worth more than the one
finding it did not produce.

---

## D191. The agentic strategies fell back to random search whenever the model wrote "Here is my proposal:"

**Decision.** Make `search/agentic/llm.py`'s `strip_markdown_fence` accept any language tag and
tolerate text around the fence, matching `generation/architecture.py`'s own stripper — which
already accepted any tag — and give both the prose tolerance neither had.

**Why.** Five agentic strategies share one fence stripper, so its limits are the package's limits.
It matched `^```(?:json)?...```$`: lowercase `json` only, and only when the fence was the *entire*
response. Measured against ordinary model habits:

| response shape | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| ` ```json ` | ok | ok |
| ` ```JSON ` | **fail** | ok |
| ` ```yaml ` | **fail** | ok |
| `Here is my proposal:` then a fence | **fail** | ok |
| a fence then `Hope that helps!` | **fail** | ok |

Each failure raises `InvalidLLMProposal`, which the engine handles *gracefully* by falling back to
a random unvisited candidate. That is why this was invisible: nothing errors and no test fails —
the run simply spends its bounded iteration budget on random proposals. An agentic search that
silently degrades to random search when the model is cooperating is failing at the one thing it
exists to do, and the report says `used_fallback=True` for a reason a reader would attribute to the
model.

**What was verified.** All five shapes above, through the real strategy rather than the helper
alone, asserting `used_fallback is False` — the observable that distinguishes "the model's proposal
was used" from "something else was". 5 new parametrised tests. Full regression **1201 passed, 22
skipped** (was 1196 + 22).

**Implications.** The divergence is the tell: two strippers for the same job, one already accepting
any tag, and no reason recorded for the difference — the D168/D179 shape again, an improvement made
in one place and not its sibling. They are still two implementations, deliberately: sharing one
would make `generation` depend on `search/agentic` or need a new home for four lines. Each now
carries a comment naming the other, which is the weakest form of the fix and worth saying so — if a
third consumer appears, that is the point to give it a real home rather than a third copy.

---

## D192. `codegen/systemc_harness` reviewed clean, and what "reviewed" was taken to mean

**Decision.** Review `codegen/systemc_harness` (916 lines, never given a pass). **No defect found.**
Recorded because a settled state is defined as much by what has been checked as by what has been
fixed, and an unrecorded clean review is indistinguishable from no review.

**What was checked, and why those three things.** The module shares `DesignSpec` with
`codegen/rtl_harness` — `rtl_harness` imports it from here — so the risks are the ones a shared
type creates between two generators that consume it differently:

- **Feature parity with the spec.** Array ports (`Port.dims`) exist in the shared spec and are an
  RTL-harness capability. The SystemC side refuses them outright in both `driver_gen` and
  `compose`, with typed errors citing D120 and D128, rather than dropping the depth and generating
  `sc_signal<int>` for something that is not an int. A *guarded* divergence, which is the correct
  shape — the silent version of this is what D168 and D191 were.
- **Reserved-word collisions.** Twelve realistic C++/SystemC probes (`class`, `template`, `signal`,
  `wait`, `operator`, `sc_module`, ...) and ten SystemVerilog ones are all refused by their
  respective `keywords.py`.
- **Generated-name collisions.** The driver declares one `sig_<port>` per port, so a spec
  containing both `x` and `sig_x` was worth testing: `x -> sig_x`, `sig_x -> sig_sig_x`. The
  prefix map is injective, so no collision is constructible.

**Implications.** This is the second module this session to come back clean (with `flows/mcp`,
D190), against seven that did not. Worth stating what that does and does not license: it says these
specific failure modes were looked for and are absent, not that the module is correct. The three
axes were chosen from what this session has actually found elsewhere — silent feature divergence
between siblings, and generated identifiers colliding with user-supplied ones — so a clean result
is evidence against *those* patterns and no others.

---

## D193. The golden reference could hold values the generated ports could not, so a correct design would fail

**Decision.** `derive_design_spec` refuses a derivation whose accumulator cannot represent every
value its own declared input precision allows, rather than emitting golden vectors the generated
module cannot hold.

**Why.** The derived ports are `dtype: "int"`, which the RTL harness emits as
`logic signed [31:0]`. The golden `acc` for each test vector is `sum(x * y for ...)` computed in
Python, at unbounded precision. Nothing connected the two.

At the 8-bit precision every workload example in this repo declares, that gap never opens: 64 lanes
of 8x8 products peak near 1.05e6, comfortably inside 2.147e9. At 16-bit it opens almost immediately.
Measured on real derivations:

| lanes | precision | golden vectors exceeding a 32-bit signed port |
|---|---|---|
| 16 | I=W=16 | 0 of 4 (max 1.61e9 — inside, but only just) |
| 32 | I=W=16 | **1 of 4** |
| 64 | I=W=16 | **3 of 4** |

The consequence is the session's recurring shape. The RTL wraps where the reference does not, so a
*correct* multiply-accumulate fails its own verification — and `generate_architecture_candidate`
hands that failure to the model as a repair prompt, spending its budget instructing it to fix a
design that was never wrong. The harness's limitation, attributed to the design.

**What was verified.** The guard refuses on the *worst case* the declared precision permits, not on
the vectors actually drawn, because the golden data is randomly seeded from the candidate hashes: a
data-dependent check would accept a spec for one (workload, architecture) pair and reject the same
shape for the next. Refusals now cover 16-bit at 4, 32 and 64 lanes; 8-bit derives unchanged at 4, 8
and 64 lanes, with a test asserting every drawn vector lands inside the port range. 2 new tests;
full regression **1203 passed, 22 skipped**.

**Implications.** This one had never fired, and could not have, because every workload example here
declares `I: 8, W: 8` — so the entire test corpus sits inside the safe region. That is the same
reason D178's parser bug survived (fixtures that shared an assumption with the code) and D189's
replay bug survived (the CLI could not produce the input that exposed it). The bridge reads
`precision` from the workload and the schema permits any value, so the failure was one 16-bit
workload away, and nothing in the suite would have distinguished it from a bad generation.

Worth naming what is *not* fixed: the ports are still fixed-width, so a 16-bit workload cannot be
bridged at all rather than being bridged with a wider accumulator. Refusing is honest; widening is
the real fix and is a spec-level change (`dtype` carries no width today).

---

## D194. Clipped quantiles collapse onto the bound, and the sweep paid for every duplicate

**Decision.** `sweep_dynamic_shape` memoises its evaluations per sample value. Duplicates stay in
`samples`, so the aggregate is unchanged; only the redundant evaluator calls go.

**Why.** `quantile_sample_points` clips every point into a workload's declared `{dyn: [lo, hi]}`
bound, which is deliberate and documented — real conversations genuinely exceed a small `hi`, and
clipping keeps the point inside a physically valid range. The consequence is that every quantile
above `hi` collapses onto the same value. Measured with this repo's own `kv-cache-len-v1`
distribution at n=8:

| declared `hi` | distinct sample points |
|---|---|
| none / 4096 | 8 of 8 |
| 512 | **4 of 8** |
| 128 | **2 of 8** |

The sweep then evaluated all eight. This module exists to drive real evaluators — its docstring is
about aggregating real evaluations into an honest interval — so at `hi=128` that is six redundant
Timeloop or RTL runs for one extra data point.

**What was verified.** The duplicates are *not* noise and had to survive: seven points at the same
value is real probability mass, and dropping them would turn the probability-weighted mean into an
unweighted one over distinct values, changing the answer. Measured after the fix on 8 points with 2
distinct values: **2 evaluator calls**, and an aggregate byte-identical to before —
`value = (170 + 7x1280)/8 = 1141.25`, `ci = [170.0, 1280.0]`. 1 new test asserting both halves:
one call per distinct point, and the weighted mean preserved. Full regression **1204 passed, 22
skipped**.

**Implications.** This is the one finding in the unreviewed-module sweep that is not a correctness
defect — the module's output was always right, it just bought the same answer repeatedly. Worth
distinguishing in the record rather than filing it alongside the others: D187 through D193 were
things that produced wrong or misattributed results, this is a cost. It is also the reason the
clipping design is worth keeping as-is: the temptation on finding duplicate sample points is to
de-duplicate them at the source, which would silently drop the probability weight and quietly change
every aggregate this module has ever produced.

---

## D195. The flake described a package layout it did not have, and I preserved the claim while cleaning it up

**Decision.** Correct `flake.nix`'s description of `localSrcDirs`, drop the package counts from it
and from the CI comment, and add `tests/unit/test_flake_local_packages.py` to check the list against
the filesystem in both directions.

**Why.** The description stated that seven adapters —
`evaluators/{booksim,noxim,cacti,gem5,thermal,dramsim3,native}` — "are outside `localSrcDirs` on
purpose", and that their callers "add each `src/` to PYTHONPATH explicitly, per each adapter's
README". **All seven are in the list.** Checked one by one, not inferred: `grep` finds every one of
them, and a filesystem comparison shows 32 packages listed and 32 on disk with no difference in
either direction.

Two counts were stale alongside it: the description had said 24 packages and the CI comment 31, at a
moment when there are 32.

**The part worth recording is how it survived.** D186 rewrote this exact description four hours
earlier, compressing 82 lines to 44 on the rule "keep the operative fact, drop the narrative". I
preserved this claim verbatim — it *reads* like an operative fact, which is precisely why it needed
checking rather than copying. A cleanup pass is the moment prose is most likely to be re-attested
without being re-verified, because the work feels editorial. The stale counts were visible in the
same block and I did not check those either.

**What was verified.** Both directions, and both matter: a package absent from `localSrcDirs` is
importable in a developer's own environment and missing in CI, which is the worst version of the
failure; a listed directory with no package is a dead entry that is harmless to run and misleading
to read. Neither exists today. 3 new tests, filesystem-driven for the same reason
`test_backend_registry_parity.py` is — the check has to notice a package nobody remembered to
mention. Full regression **1207 passed, 22 skipped**.

**Implications.** The counts are now removed rather than corrected. A number in prose that must be
maintained by hand is a defect waiting for its next edit, and this one had already drifted twice;
the test carries the invariant instead. What the description keeps is the *reason* the heavy
adapters are listed — being on PYTHONPATH costs nothing until something imports them — which is the
part a reader actually needs and the part that cannot go stale.

---

## D196. Every hand-maintained count in the living docs was stale, including one I broke this morning

**Decision.** Remove the node/tool counts from `docs/agent-surface.md`, `docs/roadmap.md`,
`docs/gap-analysis.md` and `flux/README.md` rather than correcting them, applying D195's own
conclusion to the rest of the documentation.

**Why.** D195 found `flake.nix` describing a package layout it did not have. The obvious follow-up
was whether other *checkable* claims in prose had gone false, and the answer was all of them:

| location | claimed | actual |
|---|---|---|
| `docs/agent-surface.md` heading | thirty-six nodes/tools | **40** |
| `flux/README.md` | "all thirty-six nodes" | **40** |
| `docs/roadmap.md` | "thirty-six CHIA nodes/MCP tools total" | **40** |
| `docs/gap-analysis.md` G12 | "36 CHIA nodes / MCP tools" | **40** |

The drift is mine and it is hours old: this session added four tools (three protocol lookups plus
`check_protocol_conformance`), and I updated the count inside `flows/mcp/tool.py`'s own docstring
each time while never touching the four places outside it. Every one of those edits felt complete.

The roadmap also carried a positional claim — "the 25th, `flux_leaderboard`" — which is a worse
form of the same thing: it is wrong whenever anything is inserted before it, and nothing about
adding a node prompts you to renumber a sentence in a different file.

**What was verified.** The real numbers were read from the code, not counted by hand: 40 exported
`flux_*` nodes from `flux_chia_nodes`, 40 `add_tool` calls in `FluxTool.setup`. Full regression
**1207 passed, 22 skipped**, unchanged — these are documentation edits only.

**Implications.** Counts are removed, not corrected, for the reason D195 gave and this entry
demonstrates: a number maintained by hand in prose is a defect waiting for its next edit, and four
separate files proved it within a day. What survives is the pointer — `agent-surface.md`'s table is
the list, and it is generated from nothing, but it lives next to the thing it describes and the
parity tests (D119, D190) already fail if a node is missing from it.

Worth stating the limit honestly: no test now asserts these documents are accurate, because there
is no number left in them to assert. That is the trade — a claim that cannot go stale because it is
no longer made, rather than a maintained claim plus the machinery to maintain it.

## D197. The table D196 called authoritative was missing the module built the same day

**Decision.** Add the four protocol tools to `docs/agent-surface.md`'s table and `flux-protocols` to
`flux/README.md`'s package table, and check the table against the tool registry in
`test_mcp_surface_parity.py`.

`agent-surface.md`'s table is the list and needs no number beside it. That argument only holds if

of `protocols/` in **every** living document — README, architecture, roadmap, agent-surface — for a

So D196 replaced a stale number with a claim about a table, without checking the table. The
decision log had the module; nothing a reader would actually consult did.

**What was verified.** 40 registered tools against the table, both directions, now asserted in
`test_mcp_surface_parity.py` — the guard the counts should have been all along. Also swept the
living docs for broken relative links while looking: **673 checked, 0 broken** (one apparent hit was
an angle-bracketed URL containing parentheses that the check mis-split, not a real break). Full
regression **1208 passed, 22 skipped**.

**Implications — a correction inside this entry.** My first version of the table check reported
`flux_find_results` as undocumented, and I began adding a row for it. It is documented: the table
gives it a shared row, `flux_get_result / flux_find_results`, and my regex captured only the first
backticked name per line. The insert failed loudly (no matching anchor row), which is the only
reason I looked rather than committing a duplicate entry.

That is the third time in this session a check of mine has produced a confident wrong answer about
its own subject — after the `ChiaTool`-instead-of-`FluxTool` introspection (D190) and the Noxim
capture that did not contain the case it was named for (D183). The pattern in all three is the
same: the check ran, produced a plausible result, and nothing about the result announced that the
extraction underneath it was wrong. Two were caught by an assertion failing; this one by an insert
having nowhere to go. None were caught by reading the output.

## D198. Auditing the suite for the failure my own checks kept making

**Decision.** Audit every test whose cases come from *discovery* — a glob, the backend registry,
`inspect.getmembers`, a regex over source — for a floor assertion on what it actually found. One of
eight lacked one; fixed.

**Why.** D197 closed by naming a pattern in my own work: three times this session a check produced a
confident, plausible, wrong answer because its extraction step silently matched nothing or the wrong
thing (D183's Noxim capture, D190's `ChiaTool`-instead-of-`FluxTool` introspection, D197's
first-name-only table regex). None was caught by reading the output. The repo already has the
antidote — the "guards the guard" assertion this codebase writes by convention — so the question was
whether it is applied where it matters rather than where it was remembered.

**What was verified.** Eight test files build their cases from discovery. Seven assert a floor.
The eighth, `test_backend_health.py`, asserted
`[b.name for b in report.backends] == available_backends()` — an equality between two values drawn
from the *same* source, which an empty registry satisfies while checking nothing. Now floored at 12
backends. Full regression **1208 passed, 22 skipped**, unchanged, as expected for a test-only
addition that was already true.

**Implications.** Seven of eight is a better result than this session's average, and worth reading
correctly: the convention is real and mostly held, and the exception was the case where the
vacuousness hides behind a comparison rather than an iteration. A parametrised test over an empty
list obviously runs zero cases; `[] == []` looks like a passing assertion.

Deliberately not built: a meta-test asserting that discovery-based tests carry a floor. Detecting
"has a floor assertion" needs a regex over test source, which is exactly the kind of extraction that
produced three wrong answers today — a guard whose own failure mode is silently matching nothing is
not an improvement. The audit is recorded here instead, to be re-run by hand when tests are added.

---

## D199. The full integration suite, actually run — two real failures, one primer, and a lesson about diagnosing from one sample

**Decision.** Run all 81 integration files. Two failed. Both were the D153/D154 width-literal class
that the `_WIDTH_PRIMER` exists to prevent, in shapes the primer did not name; extended it, and both
now pass.

**What the suite says.** 81 of 81 files, **0 failures**. The generation demos were re-run after the
primer change and pass repeatedly (`toy_cpu` twice consecutively, having previously failed all three
repair attempts).

**The two failures were real and specific.** `test_rtl_toy_cpu_demo_live`: the model wrote
`opcode == 2'sd2` against a 32-bit port; Verilator rejects it under this repo's strict `-Wall`
(D153), the error was fed back, and **the model returned identical code three times**.
`test_rtl_register_file_demo_live`: `sel[1'b0]` — a 1-bit index into a 32-bit value — and when told
the index was too narrow, it changed the *port* to `[1:0]`, which then failed where the harness
binds to it.

All three are the same mistake wearing different syntax, and D154's primer named only `4'h0` and
`4'b11` — constants in comparisons. It now also covers sized literals as bit-select indices
(`sel[0]`, never `sel[1'b0]`) and states that port widths are fixed, since narrowing the port is the
"fix" the model reaches for when told a comparison is too narrow. Same approach D40 and D154 took:
correct a specific, repeated mistake up front rather than through repair rounds the model does not
converge on.

`test_rtl_register_file_demo_live` also **passed** in one run and failed in another before the
change, which is worth recording plainly: these tests depend on a 7B local model's sampling, so they
are inherently flaky, and the primer reduces that rather than removing it.

**Implications — three process failures of mine, all in how the run was managed.**

*Diagnosing from one sample.* I checked `ps` once, saw no pytest process, concluded the background
run had died, and started a second one. It had not died — it was between files, and it later
reported completion normally. Two runs then raced, appending to one summary and overwriting each
other's logs, producing ten duplicate entries. A long-running process is not dead because it is idle
at the instant you look.

*Reporting a green result from a partial file.* I said "zero failures" several times while the
summary was still being written; both failures appended later. The number was true when read and
false as a claim about the suite.

*A harness bug that made my own records meaningless.* My foreground batches recorded `rc=$?` after a
pipeline, which captures `tail`'s status, not pytest's — so every one of those lines says `rc=0`
regardless. The failures were caught from the *text* ("1 failed"), not the code I recorded. Both
failing files were re-run individually to confirm.

## D200. `flux-llm`: four copies of the same two things, and D191 had only found two of them

**Decision.** New package `llm/` (`flux_llm`) holding the `LLMProposer` Protocol,
`InvalidLLMProposal`, and `strip_markdown_fence`. All four consumers now import it;
`search/agentic/llm.py` is deleted and the local copies in `generation/architecture.py`,
`flows/chia_nodes/generate_rtl.py` and `generate_systemc.py` are gone.

**Why — and the count is the argument.** D191 found two markdown-fence strippers, fixed a
prose-intolerance bug in both, and concluded that a *third* consumer would be the moment to give
them a real home. There were already four. The two I did not find are in `flows/chia_nodes`, and
both still carried the anchored `^```...```$` pattern D191 had just replaced — so a model prefacing
its answer with "Here is the module:" would have had its fence left in place there, which is exactly
the bug D191 fixed elsewhere the same day.

The proposer Protocol was duplicated too, in `generation/architecture.py` and
`search/agentic/llm.py`, with the same one-method shape and the same reasoning in both docstrings.

`generate_systemc.py`'s copy even documented *why* it was separate: the shared helper "only
special-cases a ` ```json ` fence", true when that copy was written. The shared one grew to handle
any tag; the note explaining the fork stayed, and nothing connected the two.

**What was verified.** 12 new tests over the real fence shapes this repo's own backends produce —
`json`, `JSON`, `yaml`, `cpp`, prose before, prose after, no fence at all — plus first-block-wins
for a model that emits two, and a structural check that any object with `propose` satisfies the
Protocol (`@runtime_checkable`, matching `flux_evaluator_abi.Evaluator`). The two node test files
that imported the deleted `_strip_code_fence` now import the shared name. **1187 unit + 33
conformance passing.**

**Implications.** The general lesson is about how I looked, not about the code: D191 compared the
two implementations it already knew about and generalised from a sample of two, exactly the mistake
D190 and D197 record in a different form. `grep` for the *shape* — `_FENCE_RE`, `def _strip` — takes
one command and finds four. "If a third appears" was the wrong trigger; the right one was to count
before concluding.

## D201. `Result.metric` — the ABI's missing value-or-refusal type, and a failure message that explains itself

**Decision.** Add `MetricOutcome` (a value or the reason there isn't one), `Result.metric(name)`
returning it, and `MetricMap` — a `dict` subclass used for `Result.metrics` whose missing key raises
`MissingMetricError`, a `KeyError` subclass carrying the standard explanation.

**Why.** An evaluator may legally return a `Result` without a metric that was requested;
`evaluators/rtl` does it routinely. Until now `metrics[name]` was the only way in, so every consumer
had to *remember* to guard — and six did not: the four search strategies (D168), `moe_routing`
(D169), and the DSE loop's baseline path (D170). D169 added `refusal_for`, which made the check
available but left the unguarded path exactly as inviting, and said so: "no test can prevent the
next consumer indexing `metrics[...]` directly".

Both halves are now covered. `metric()` makes the handled case the natural one — branch on
`outcome.ok`, or read `.value` where absence would be a bug. And the unhandled case explains itself:
a bare `KeyError('energy_pj')` becomes a message naming what the evaluator *did* return and which
accessor to use instead.

**What was verified.** 8 new tests: presence, absence with the returned set named, `.value` raising
on a refusal, `value_or` for callers with a real fallback, a `0.0` metric being present rather than
falsy, direct indexing still working while explaining itself, `MissingMetricError` still catchable
as `KeyError`, and a `Result` round-tripping through `to_dict`/`from_dict` unchanged. **1195 unit +
33 conformance passing**, with no adapter modified — `__post_init__` converts a plain dict literal,
so all twelve construct exactly as before.

**Implications.** This is deliberately not the sum type that makes indexing *unreachable*: `metrics`
is still a dict, because it is serialised, iterated and membership-tested throughout, and hiding it
would touch every adapter and every consumer for a guarantee the message now largely delivers. What
changed is that the wrong path is no longer silent, and the right path is shorter than the wrong one.

## D202. Ports carry a width, so a 16-bit workload is bridged instead of refused

**Decision.** `Port` gains `bits` (2..64, `int` only, defaulting to the historical 32). The RTL
harness emits declarations *and literals* at that width; `derive_design_spec` sizes the accumulator
from the declared precision instead of refusing; the SystemC harness refuses an explicit width
outright rather than silently emitting 32 bits.

**Why.** D193 found the golden reference could hold values the generated ports could not — a 64-lane
16-bit dot product overflows 32 bits, the RTL wraps, the Python reference does not, and a *correct*
MAC fails its own verification while the repair loop tells the model to fix it. D193 refused those
derivations, which was honest but was a limitation dressed as a guard: `dtype` carried no width, so
refusing was the only option available.

**What was verified.** Sizing is `in_bits + w_bits + ceil(log2(lanes))`, from the worst case the
declared precision permits rather than the vectors actually drawn — the golden data is seeded from
the candidate hashes, so a data-dependent width would differ between two derivations of the same
shape. Measured:

| lanes | precision | accumulator | every golden vector fits |
|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 8-bit | 32 (unchanged) | yes |
| 4 | 16-bit | 34 | yes |
| 32 | 16-bit | 37 | yes |
| 64 | 16-bit | 38 | yes |
| 64 | 32-bit | 70 -> **refused** | past the 64-bit port ceiling |

All four supported cases were then linted by **real Verilator under `-Wall`**, generating the
testbench and a matching DUT — and that is what caught the half of this change I had missed. At 38
bits the *golden literals* failed `WIDTHEXPAND`: an unsized decimal is 32 bits in SystemVerilog, so
a wide expected value does not fit the port it is assigned to. `_verilog_literal` is now width-aware
too, emitting a sized literal past 32 bits and the unchanged plain decimal below it. 9 new tests
across the spec and the bridge; **1204 unit + 33 conformance passing**, plus `test_rtl_harness_live`
and `test_generate_rtl_module_live` re-run green.

**Implications.** The SystemC refusal is deliberate and matches D120/D192's shape: a narrower port
needs `sc_int<N>` and a reference model that truncates identically, and generating a 32-bit signal
for a 16-bit port would compile and verify the wrong design. Divergence between the two harnesses is
fine when it is *stated*; what D168 and D191 record is the version that is silent.

Worth noting how the literal bug surfaced, because it is the session's own lesson applied to my own
change: unit tests over the derivation all passed — they check the spec, and the spec was right. It
took running the actual toolchain over the actual generated file, which is the same reason D177
linted every emitted interface instead of trusting the emitter.

---

## D203. Widths in the SystemC harness too, closing the divergence D202 had just opened

**Decision.** A sized port generates `sc_int<N>` in the SystemC harness — driver, composite module,
and internal nets — replacing the refusal D202 added one entry earlier. Composite top-level ports
carry their declared width, and a net joining ports of different widths is refused.

**Why.** D202 gave `Port` a `bits` field and taught the RTL side to honour it, then had the SystemC
harness refuse it outright, on the reasoning that a narrower port needs `sc_int<N>` and a reference
model that truncates identically. That reasoning was right about the requirement and wrong about the
cost: `sc_int<N>` *is* SystemC's fixed-width integer, it truncates at N bits by construction, and
the harness already generates every signal declaration it needs. The refusal was a day's-end
boundary, not a real limitation.

`sc_int<N>` rather than a wider native type matters for the same reason the width exists at all: the
point of declaring 16 bits is that the DUT and the reference agree on overflow, which a plain
`long long` would not give.

**What was verified — by compiling and running, not by inspecting the emitted text.**

- A 16-bit/40-bit design through real g++ and SystemC: **3 of 3 vectors**, including
  `-32768 + -32768 = -65536`, which does not fit in the operand width and so fails against any
  harness that quietly reused it.
- A 16-bit *composite* — leaf, top ports, and the net between them — compiled and verified,
  **1 of 1**.
- An unsized spec still emits plain `int`, so every pre-width spec generates byte-identical code.
- 3 integration tests and 3 unit tests; `test_systemc_harness_live` (10) and
  `test_systemc_compose_live` (3) re-run green. **1207 unit passing.**

**Two defects in my own D202 change, both found by running the composite path rather than the
leaf.** `compose.py` declared top-level ports with `Port(name=..., dir=..., dtype=...)` and no
`bits`, silently dropping a declared width — so a composite would have emitted a 32-bit port and
bound it to a 16-bit leaf. And internal nets were typed from the dtype alone, so a net joining a
16-bit output to a 32-bit input would have been declared plain `int`; that is now a refusal, since
one net cannot be both and picking either truncates or sign-extends everything crossing it.

**Implications.** The RTL and SystemC harnesses now agree on widths, which removes the divergence
rather than documenting it — D192 recorded that a *stated* divergence is fine and a silent one is
not, and this is the better outcome still: no divergence to state. The remaining one is array ports,
which the SystemC side still refuses (D120), and that refusal is real — arrays need `sc_vector`
binding, not just a type name.

---

## D204. Timeloop v4 builds hermetically — the binary half of the Docker dependency is solved, the estimator half is not

**Decision.** Package `barvinok` (`nix/barvinok.nix`) and Timeloop v4 (`nix/timeloop.nix`). Both
build. Docker is **not** removable yet: Accelergy does not register its estimation plug-ins in this
environment, so energy estimation still fails. Recorded now rather than when finished, because the
half that is done overturns two things D132/D163 concluded.

**What D163 said was blocking, and what actually was.** D163 closed this as "keep Docker", naming
"Timeloop itself from source with isl and barvinok 0.41.6" as the remaining chain. barvinok is
genuinely not in nixpkgs and is genuinely required — Timeloop's `src/SConscript` links it
unconditionally, `--with-isl` notwithstanding. But it packages in ~40 lines: the release tarball
bundles its own isl and polylib, and the only real friction is that polylib is pre-C99 code that
GCC 14 rejects on implicit declarations, the same class of workaround D64 records for 3D-ICE.

**D132's diagnosis was subtly wrong, and it cost the most time here.** It attributed
`ERROR: key not found: data-spaces` to nixpkgs shipping Timeloop 3.0.3 rather than v4. Two findings
correct that:

- The error is **not** version-related. It reproduces with a freshly built v4 binary run directly
  on this repo's reference YAML, because those files are inputs to `timeloopfe`, not to the binary
  — the front-end assembles them first. D132's own conclusion ("the Docker dependency is the
  front-end, not the binary") was right; the evidence it gave for it was not.
- The upstream is **`NVlabs/timeloop`, not `Accelergy-Project/timeloop`**. The working image's
  `accelergy-timeloop-infrastructure` pins the former as a submodule. The latter's master is 18
  months older and still spells 8 config keys `data-spaces` where the front-end emits
  `data_spaces` — so building it produced exactly the error D132 blamed on v3. Pinned now to
  `32370826`, the same commit the image uses.

**What was verified.** All six binaries build and run. `timeloopfe` + `accelergy` + both plug-ins
compose into one environment with them. The adapter's own driver script — `tl.Specification.
from_yaml_files(...)` then `tl.call_mapper(...)` — runs this repo's reference config through the
front-end, produces `parsed-processed-input.yaml`, and invokes the mapper, which exits **0** and
calls Accelergy. Two real defects were found and fixed on the way: `nix/accelergy-cacti-plug-in.nix`
copied CACTI's binary without its `tech_params/` and `contention.dat`, which is D145's finding
recurring (that entry traced five wrong CACTI predictions to those exact files); and
`nix/timeloopfe.nix` pins `rev = "main"`, a moving reference of the kind D38 pinned gem5 to avoid.

**What remains, precisely.** Accelergy loads the plug-ins but registers no components —
`accelergy -l` prints an empty "Supported Components", and estimation fails with "Can not find an
energy estimator for DRAM(type=LPDDR4, ...)". The plug-in directory matches the image's file for
file after the `tech_params` fix, and `cacti_wrapper.py` imports cleanly and defines `CactiDRAM`.
So the gap is in how Accelergy discovers estimators from a Nix-installed plug-in, not in Timeloop.
That is a different subsystem from the one this entry set out to solve.

**Implications.** Also worth recording as an operational hazard: Accelergy writes
`~/.config/accelergy/accelergy_config.yaml` containing **absolute store paths**, and reuses it. A
rebuilt environment leaves that file pointing at the previous one, so plug-ins silently vanish —
which cost a debugging cycle here, and would silently degrade any real run. Any hermetic path needs
a controlled `HOME` or a regenerated config, exactly as the Docker path gets a fresh container each
time.

---

## D205. Accelergy's estimators do run under Nix — two root causes, both about how Nix installs things

**Decision.** Establish the working hermetic recipe: Timeloop v4 + Accelergy + both plug-ins produce
a complete Timeloop run with no Docker. Two root causes found, neither in Timeloop.

**Root cause 1: `os.walk` does not follow symlinks.** Accelergy discovers estimators by walking its
configured plug-in directories looking for `*.estimator.yaml` — `plug_in_path_to_obj.py`'s
`iter_files_recursive` uses `os.walk(p)` with the default `followlinks=False`. Every directory in a
Nix `buildEnv` or `python.withPackages` environment is a **symlink** into the individual package's
store path, so the walk descends into none of them. Measured directly on our environment:

    os.walk(plug_in_dir)                   -> []
    os.walk(plug_in_dir, followlinks=True) -> ['library.estimator.yaml', 'cacti.estimator.yaml',
                                               'dummy.estimator.yaml']

That is the whole reason `accelergy -l` reported an empty "Supported Components" and D204 stopped.
It is not a version problem, not a missing plug-in, and not `tech_params` — the same three files
were sitting there the entire time, unreadable by a walk that would not follow a link.

**Root cause 2: the CACTI wrapper writes inside its own installation directory.** With discovery
fixed, `CactiSRAM` registered at 80% accuracy and genuinely invoked CACTI — then failed with
`PermissionError: [Errno 13] ... /nix/store/...-accelergy-cacti-plug-in/cacti_inputs_outputs`. It
creates a scratch directory next to itself, which is read-only in the store by construction.

**Both are fixed by one mechanism**, which is the useful part: copy the plug-in directories into a
writable working directory at runtime and point Accelergy's config there. Copying makes them real
directories (so the walk finds them) *and* writable (so CACTI can scratch). Verified end to end —
the run produced the full output set, `timeloop-mapper.stats.txt`, `ERT.yaml`, `ART.yaml`,
`map.txt` and the rest, with no container involved.

**What is NOT yet verified, and it matters.** The run above used the reference `problem_base.yaml`
as-is, not the problem instance the adapter substitutes per workload, so its `Cycles: 1` /
`Energy: 0.00 uJ` are not comparable to the pinned Docker numbers in
`tests/golden/timeloop_energy_baseline.json` (512/1024/256 cycles, 620000 pJ). **No claim is made
here that the hermetic path reproduces those.** That check requires wiring the path into
`TimeloopEvaluator` and running D141's acceptance test, which is the next step and is not done.

**Implications.** Accelergy's config also stores absolute store paths and is cached in `$HOME`
(D204), so the runtime materialisation has to regenerate it rather than reuse whatever is there.
Between that, the symlink walk and the read-only scratch directory, every obstacle to running this
under Nix turned out to be an assumption the tool makes about being installed into a mutable prefix
— none of them about the tool's actual function. Worth remembering the shape when the next
Python-packaged EDA tool refuses to work here.

---

## D206. The hermetic Timeloop path is wired in, opt-in, and reproduces the Docker numbers exactly

**Decision.** `TimeloopEvaluator` gained `use_local`, selecting the Nix-built Timeloop from D204/D205
instead of the Docker image. It is **opt-in**: `use_local=True`, or `FLUX_TIMELOOP_LOCAL=1` for callers
that construct through `make_evaluator`. The default is Docker *even inside* `nix develop .#timeloop`.
`provenance.evaluator` reports `timeloop-nix@local` on that path and the unchanged
`timeloop-docker@<image>` otherwise. The four Python derivations plus the two new C++ ones are now
reachable from `flake.nix` as a third shell, `.#timeloop`; `nix/timeloopfe.nix`'s floating
`rev = "main"` is pinned to `5603893c0ff75183b5ffd6839aba33774fc3b6fe`.

**Why.** D205 built the pieces and stopped one step short: it proved a hermetic Timeloop *runs*, and
said in as many words that no claim was being made about whether it produces the same numbers. That
was the whole question — D133 measured the failure mode where a Nix-assembled Timeloop runs happily,
reports correct cycles, and fabricates energy from a dummy plug-in. Correct-looking output is the worst
available shape, so "it runs" is not a result.

Opt-in rather than auto-detect, and this is the load-bearing part: `shutil.which("timeloop-mapper")`
returning a path is not a request. Auto-detection would mean the same call produces numbers from a
different tool depending on which shell it ran in, with `provenance.evaluator` the only trace anyone
could use to notice. D147 took exactly this shape for `CACTI_BIN`. Asking for local without one
installed raises rather than falling back to Docker — a silent fallback is how a run that was supposed
to be hermetic gets recorded as hermetic while an image produced the numbers.

Its own shell rather than the default one because Timeloop and barvinok are from-source C++ builds
costing minutes on a cold cache, and nobody doing Phase 1 Python work should pay that to get a shell.

**What was verified.** All three architectures in `tests/golden/timeloop_energy_baseline.json` run
through the hermetic path and match the pinned Docker values **exactly**, not approximately:
simple-npu-1d-v1 512 cycles, v2 1024, v3 256, all 620000 pJ. That is D141's acceptance test, which had
never been run against anything.

Equality of totals proves nothing by itself, so the estimators were read rather than assumed: Accelergy
used `CactiSRAM`, `CactiDRAM` and `Library` — the same real plug-ins the Docker image reports, no
`dummy`/`placeholder` anywhere. The committed check reads them *inside* `reject_placeholder_estimators`
rather than from a path saved for later; the first version of that test failed because the adapter's
`TemporaryDirectory` is already deleted when `evaluate` returns, and an absent file makes
`estimators_used` return an empty set — which passes the rejection guard vacuously. It now asserts the
set is non-empty before asserting what is in it.

The `timeloopfe` pin was verified to be a no-op today before being applied: `nix-prefetch-url` on the
explicit commit produced `sha256-/HO6QOoB9sUv2WztH+54Y9EahpKRmvx1+dRFTT27kXQ=`, byte-identical to what
the floating `main` had. A moving ref with a fixed hash is a build that breaks whenever upstream
pushes, which is intolerable for the package whose entire job is reproducing pinned numbers.

Both runners execute the same driver script, differing only in path prefix (`/work` under a container
mount vs. the working directory locally) — asserted by string equality under substitution, with a
floor assertion that the two strings differ at all so the equality cannot hold trivially.

Regression: 1250 unit + conformance passing (up from 1240), 22 skipped. The 4 new integration tests
pass under `.#timeloop` and skip elsewhere. `test_timeloop_energy_baseline_live.py` gained a skip on
`FLUX_TIMELOOP_LOCAL`, since it goes through `make_evaluator` and would otherwise measure the hermetic
path while asserting the Docker provenance string.

**Implications.** D132's "dropping Docker is an adapter rewrite, not a package swap" and D163's
"keep Docker" are both superseded on the packaging question — the obstacle was barvinok, and the
adapter needed no rewrite at all. Docker remains the default and the CI path; nothing changes for
any existing caller. What is now available is a Timeloop that runs where no daemon exists, with
measured equivalence rather than assumed equivalence.

Two things stay true and unfixed: `area_mm2` is 0.0 on both paths (Timeloop reports no area for
these architectures), and the equivalence is established on three 1-D architectures and one workload
— it is a calibration check, not a proof over the input space.
