## D207. The equivalence is wider than three numbers, and CI now runs the hermetic path

**Decision.** The nightly workflow gained a `timeloop-hermetic` job that builds `.#timeloop` and runs
the equivalence file plus the four Timeloop live-integration files on the hermetic runner. Two
integration tests that asserted `provenance.evaluator.startswith("timeloop-docker@")` now accept
either runner by prefix. `tests/integration/` docstrings that said "requires a working `docker`
daemon" say what is actually required.

**Why.** The nightly sweep runs every file in `tests/integration/` under the default shell, where
`test_timeloop_local_equivalence_live.py` skips itself — and a file whose tests all skip exits 0. So
the from-source Timeloop build could rot completely and CI would stay green. That is the failure mode
D129 recorded in different clothing: an unknown reading as a pass. Its own job because it needs its
own shell, and the skip is asserted against explicitly rather than trusted to an exit code.

**What was verified.** Running the four Timeloop live files on the hermetic runner found **three
failures**, and the run was worth doing for what they turned out to be:

- Two were tests pinning the Docker provenance string. Not adapter defects — the *numbers* passed,
  including `test_timeloop_adapter_live`'s pinned 512 cycles / 100000 pJ against the vendored
  `reference/` bundle, which is a fourth architecture agreeing exactly and one the golden baseline
  does not cover. Fixed by asserting the contract (one of the two known prefixes, so a bare
  `"timeloop"` still fails) instead of the runner, since those tests' subject is the numbers.
- One was `test_arch_none_conformance[systemc]` failing because `.#timeloop` ships no SystemC. An
  environment artifact of running a cross-backend conformance test in a single-backend shell, not a
  defect, and not something to "fix" by adding SystemC to that shell.

With those corrected: **20 Timeloop integration tests pass identically on both runners** — sparsity
(D78's real `sparse_optimizations`/`densities` path), architecture translation, mapping translation
and the adapter's own pinned numbers. The Docker path was then re-run to confirm the loosened
assertions did not stop testing anything: 39 tests, all passing.

That re-run mattered independently. D206 refactored `_run_timeloop` and `_driver_script`, which both
runners share, and had only ever executed the *local* branch afterwards. Unit tests covered the
script text; nothing had actually invoked Docker through the changed code until now.

Regression: 1250 unit + conformance passing, 22 skipped. Both CI steps were run locally verbatim,
including the skip guard, rather than being reasoned about from the YAML.

**Implications.** The equivalence evidence is now four architectures and several mechanisms rather
than three pinned scalars, and it is checked nightly instead of by hand. It is still calibration, not
proof: everything measured is 1-D, single-workload, and `area_mm2` is 0.0 on both paths, so area
remains untested by construction.

---

## D208. Three follow-ups on the hermetic path: dead config, a health tool that lied, one definition of "opted in"

**Decision.** `_materialise_accelergy_env` no longer writes a `primitive_components` path;
`flux_backend_health` reports on the Timeloop runner that would actually run rather than on Docker
unconditionally; and the `FLUX_TIMELOOP_LOCAL` parsing has one definition, `local_runner_requested()`,
used by both the adapter and the test that gates on it.

**Why.** All three are the same shape — something written *during* D206 that reads as correct and
isn't checked by anything.

The config entry pointed at `share/accelergy/primitive_component_libs`, which **does not exist**:
this Accelergy installs only `estimation_plug_ins` there and the package ships no YAML at all. Runs
succeeded anyway, which is the problem — a config naming a fictional directory that never fails is
config nobody will ever discover is wrong. Now an explicit `[]`, and the key is kept rather than
dropped because Accelergy rewrites a config with missing keys, and a rewrite is exactly how absolute
store paths from a previous environment come back (D205).

`flux_backend_health` treated `timeloop` as a Docker-only backend, so in a `.#timeloop` shell with no
daemon it reported the backend unusable — while the backend worked. That is worse than a stale
comment: agents route around "unusable", so the health tool would have steered work away from a
working evaluator. It now branches on the evaluator's selected runner. An installed-but-unselected
hermetic Timeloop still reads as unusable, which is honest — the adapter will not switch runners on
its own — but the detail says the fix is an environment variable rather than a daemon.

The env parsing had two copies, one in the adapter and one in the skip guard of
`test_timeloop_energy_baseline_live.py`. Both were correct on the day. The recurring defect in this
repo is not a wrong copy, it is the *second* copy: a fix that never travels to its sibling (D186,
D197).

**What was verified.** The missing directory was confirmed by listing `share/accelergy/` in the real
shell before changing anything, not inferred from the code. After the change, the equivalence suite
still passes and still reports `CactiSRAM`/`CactiDRAM`/`Library` — so the removed entry was carrying
no load.

The health probe was tested three ways (local selected, installed-but-unselected, no hermetic build
at all) and then run for real in the hermetic shell both with and without the environment variable,
because mocked agreement with reality is a claim, not a measurement. The local-selected case asserts
Docker is not mentioned in the detail at all — a floor, since a passing `usable` flag could otherwise
coexist with an answer still gated on the daemon.

The equivalence test gained a stronger assertion while this was being checked: `dummy_tables` **is**
installed in the environment under test, so the real plug-ins winning is a live outcome rather than a
consequence of nothing else being available. Without that floor, "no dummy estimator was used" would
be satisfiable by an environment that has no dummy estimator to use.

Regression: 1253 unit + conformance passing (up from 1250), 22 skipped; 13 hermetic and 5 Docker
integration tests re-run after the changes.

**Implications.** None of this changes a number. It removes one lie from a config file, one from a
tool agents consult to decide what to run, and one opportunity for two copies of a rule to disagree.

---

## D209. A push to main was cancelling the nightly sweep, and the workflow file now has tests

**Decision.** The `concurrency` group includes `github.event_name`, and `cancel-in-progress` is
`${{ github.event_name != 'schedule' }}`. `tests/unit/test_ci_workflow.py` asserts five structural
invariants of the workflow. Generated output moved out of the checkout into `$RUNNER_TEMP`.

**Why.** The group was `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}` with `cancel-in-progress: true`. A
scheduled run and a push to the same branch share both keys, so **any push to `main` cancelled a
nightly already running on `main`** — and the integration sweep is a 350-minute job. On an active day
it would never once finish.

What makes this worth a decision rather than a one-line fix is the reporting: a cancelled run shows as
*cancelled*, not failed. No red mark, no notification, no failing check on any PR. The job that exists
because "nothing runs the integration suite" (D155) could have gone months without completing, and the
only visible evidence would have been an absence — the same "an unknown reads as a pass" shape D129
records, one level up in the stack. Both halves of the fix are needed: the event in the group so the
runs stop competing, and the exemption so a scheduled run is never a cancellation target.

CI is the one part of this repo whose failures are invisible by construction — a job that is
cancelled, skipped, or covering nothing still leaves a page that does not look wrong. That is
precisely the case for testing it like code.

**What was verified.** `actionlint` (which shellchecks the `run:` blocks) reports no findings on the
file. The five new tests were **mutation-checked, not just run**: the concurrency keys were reverted,
a named test file renamed, and `set -o pipefail` deleted in a scratch copy of the real workflow. Three
tests failed — exactly the three whose invariants were broken — and the two untouched ones stayed
green. The file was then restored and confirmed byte-identical by `diff`.

The extraction in `test_every_test_file_the_workflow_names_exists` carries a floor (at least four
paths found) because a token scan that silently matched nothing would pass its own "all exist" loop
with an empty set — the failure this repo keeps rediscovering (D190, D197).

Regression: 1258 unit + conformance passing (up from 1253), 22 skipped.

**Implications.** The nightly sweep and the hermetic Timeloop job can now actually complete on a
branch that receives pushes. Nothing here was found by a test failing; it was found by reading the
workflow file. The tests exist so the next regression is found the other way.

Not addressed: the hermetic job's 90-minute budget is a guess against a cold cache for two
from-source C++ builds, unverified because it can only be measured on a GitHub runner. If it is
wrong the job fails visibly, which is the acceptable direction to be wrong in.

---

## D210. timeloop.nix: the homepage named the wrong fork, and an empty install is now impossible

**Decision.** `nix/timeloop.nix`'s `meta.homepage` points at `NVlabs/timeloop` (the repo `src`
actually fetches), and a `postInstall` assertion fails the build unless `timeloop-mapper` and
`timeloop-model` — the two binaries `timeloopfe` drives — landed in `$out/bin`.

**Why.** The homepage said `Accelergy-Project/timeloop` while the derivation's own header comment
explains at length why that fork is precisely the wrong repo (its master still spells the config
keys that produce D132's `key not found: data-spaces`). A reader following the metadata would land
on the repo the file exists to avoid — the misattribution defect class, in metadata.

The assertion exists because both install loops tolerate an empty glob: if upstream's build layout
moved, the globs would match nothing, install nothing, and the derivation would stay green — an
empty-but-green package, the same shape `accelergy-cacti-plug-in.nix` already asserts against
(D204). Asserted on the two binaries this repo calls, not all six, which upstream may grow or
shrink without it mattering here.

**What was verified.** The `version` date was checked against the pinned commit before assuming it:
`32370826` was committed 2025-06-09, matching the string — no change needed, and now it is a checked
fact rather than a plausible one.

The rebuild with the assertion in place succeeded and installs all six binaries plus both shared
libraries. The assertion itself was then mutation-checked, and the first attempt is worth recording
for what went wrong with it: with a nonexistent binary added to the list, the rebuild failed — **but
for the wrong reason**. GCC died with `internal compiler error: Aborted` during the IPA modref pass,
minutes before `installPhase` ran. An rc=1 that proves nothing about the thing under test, and
counting it would have been exactly the vacuous-verification defect this log keeps finding in code.
Rather than pay another ten-minute rebuild, the mechanism was isolated: two probe derivations with
the identical shape (overridden `installPhase` calling `runHook postInstall`, assertion in
`postInstall`). The negative probe fails with the assertion's own message (`missing present-not` is
the last line of its build log); the positive probe passes. What the probes cannot re-prove — that
timeloop's real globs find the real binaries — the green full build already had.

The mutation was then reverted; the shell resolves back to the already-built store path, the
equivalence suite passes against it, and the full regression is unchanged (1258 + 22 skipped).

**Implications.** One less lie in metadata; upstream layout drift now fails the build instead of
producing an empty package. Separately observed and worth keeping: the Timeloop scons build can die
nondeterministically under memory pressure (`-flto -O3 -j$NIX_BUILD_CORES` × GCC ICE) — it happened
twice this session on a many-core machine and succeeded on retry both times. The CI hermetic job
builds this from source on a cold cache, so its first-ever run may flake for this reason; a retry is
the fix, not a code change.

---

## D211. Direct `Result.metrics[...]` indexing is now unreachable in production code

**Decision.** All 27 production subscript sites were converted to D201's accessors —
`Result.value_of()` where only the number is read, a new symmetric `Result.estimate_of()` where the
CI bounds, unit or method are needed — and `tests/unit/test_no_direct_metric_indexing.py` makes the
subscript form a test failure in every production `src/` tree. Tests keep indexing directly, on
purpose. This closes the last of the three "remembered but not enforced" items (D200/D202 closed
the other two).

**Why.** D201 built the handled path and made the unhandled one explain itself, but left the
subscript *reachable*, and reachable means new code will reach it: the D112 crash (a search dying
on a legally-omitted metric) was fixed in `search/architecture` and then independently re-written
in `search/agentic`, because nothing stopped it. The fix for a recurring defect class is a fence,
not a fourth careful caller.

The scope split is deliberate. In production, a missing metric is either handled (`metric()`) or a
reasoning error that should explain itself (`value_of`/`estimate_of`). In tests, direct indexing
*is* the assertion — `MissingMetricError`'s message is exactly what a failing test should print —
so banning it there would trade nothing for churn across ~40 files.

Every converted site was classified first rather than converted blind: at all 27, presence is
established upstream (an explicit membership guard in `roofline`/`conformance`/`moe_routing`, the
`metrics_present` intersection in the two aggregators, `refusal_for` filtering in both search
engines, or a `min`/`max` whose key already read the metric). So the crash-preserving accessors are
the correct spelling everywhere, and no behavior changed — only what the failure says.

**What was verified.** The lint is AST-based, not a grep: the ban is on the code shape
`<expr>.metrics[...]`, while prose stays free — `dse_loop.py` quotes the historical crash verbatim
in a comment, and history should not be reworded to satisfy a linter. The detector is itself tested
on synthetic code (flags the banned shape; passes prose mentions, `value_of`, `.get()`, and plain
dicts merely named `*_metrics`) — a matcher wired to the wrong node type would otherwise report an
empty offender list forever.

The scan carries two floors, and one of them caught a real bug in this very test before it was ever
committed: the package-coverage assertion looked for `flux_search_architecture` in the roots'
*parent* paths, where it never appears (it is inside `src/`), and failed — on the first run, for the
right reason. Fixed to check the package directory itself. A floor that fires on its own author is
the mechanism working.

Regression: 1260 unit + conformance passing (up from 1258), 22 skipped. The integration files
exercising the changed aggregation and calibration paths (`test_moe_routing_sweep_live`,
`test_calibration_live`, 19 tests) pass against real evaluators.

**Implications.** The residue list loses an item: `Result.metrics` remains a public dict (hiding it
was the rejected cost), but the subscript is no longer a thing new production code can quietly do.
`estimate_of` is now the sanctioned spelling for "give me the whole Estimate or explain why not."

---

## D212. OBI handshake semantics are machine-checkable: a `handshakes` block and a Verilator-proven SVA emitter

**Decision.** Protocol documents may carry a `handshakes:` block — clock, active-low reset, and
request/accept phases with reset obligations and no-retraction rules — under one hard constraint:
**every field that states a behavior must cite a rule id the same document quotes**, enforced at
parse time. `emit_sv_assertions(protocol)` derives a SystemVerilog checker module from the block,
each `assert property` carrying the source rule's own number and text. `obi-1.6.0.yaml` carries the
first block (address req/gnt per R-3/R-3.1.2/R-2.1, response rvalid/rready per R-4/R-4.1.2/R-2.2).

**Why.** The `protocols/` residue said "no ordering or handshake-timing semantics are represented
anywhere", and the wall behind it — Arm's AXI specification is not redistributable, IEEE 1800 has no
open substitute — is real but was hiding a door: OBI's own specification is Solderpad-licensed and
already vendored *with its rules quoted verbatim*. For that document the semantics were sitting in
prose one representation away from being checkable.

The citation constraint is the design's load-bearing part. A semantics block that could say anything
would let machine-checkable claims drift free of the normative text; requiring every claim to name a
quoted rule means the block can never say more than the document does — and it composes with the
existing licence guard for free: non-redistributable documents cannot carry rules, therefore cannot
carry handshake semantics, with no new licence code written. Cross-validation also rejects citations
of undefined signals, requester roles that contradict the document's own driver column (a phase
claiming the manager requests via subordinate-driven `gnt` refuses to parse), and multi-bit control
wires.

**What was verified.** The emitter's output was judged by a real simulator on real waveforms, in
both directions. Verilator (`--binary --assert --timing`) accepted the generated checker, a
compliant OBI trace ran clean, and three violation scenarios — retracting `req` before `gnt`,
driving `req` during reset, retracting `rvalid` before `rready` — each tripped **exactly its own
assertion by name** (`a_address_no_retract`, `a_address_req_low_in_reset`,
`a_response_no_retract`). Both directions matter: a checker that never fires is decoration, and one
that fires somewhere on a violation is not the same as one that fires at the rule being broken. All
four scenarios are now `tests/integration/test_protocol_emit_verilator.py` parametrized cases; the
schema validations (unquoted rule id refused, undefined signal refused, contradicted driver refused,
assertion-less documents refuse to emit) are unit tests.

Regression: 1264 unit + conformance passing (up from 1260), 22 skipped; 17 integration tests in the
Verilator file (13 pre-existing + 4 new).

**Implications.** `check_module_conformance` still answers only "is this interface shaped right",
but the answer to "does this design speak the protocol" is no longer uniformly "unrepresentable" —
for OBI, a slice of it is an artifact a simulator can enforce. The residue narrows rather than
closes: ordering and payload-stability rules are still prose-only (R-3.1.x stability is not among
the vendored rules), AXI stays structural for licence reasons that no code can fix, and the emitted
checker asserts exactly three rule shapes — reset-low, no-retract, and nothing else, stated in its
header rather than implied.

---

## D213. Address-phase stability is asserted, response-phase stability is deliberately not — and two vendored rules were paraphrases

**Decision.** `handshakes` phases may carry `stable_until_accept` obligations; OBI's address phase
asserts R-3.1.1 stability over `addr`/`we`/`be` with parametric widths (`parameter int ADDR_WIDTH`,
`DATA_WIDTH`), so one emitted checker binds beside any legal configuration. R-3.1.1 and R-4.1.1 are
newly vendored, verbatim, from the primary document. R-4.1.1 (response stability) is vendored but
**not** machine-checked, and a unit test pins both halves — the coverage and the restraint.

**Why.** The residue named payload stability as prose-only. The primary PDF was fetched and read
before writing anything, which is the methodology, and it paid twice:

First, the two retract rules vendored in D174 turn out to be **paraphrases, not quotes**: the YAML
said req may not retract "until after the address phase transfer has been accepted" where the
document says "until after **the last cycle of the address phase**" (same for rvalid). Semantically
equivalent, but the module's whole claim is that rules are citable verbatim — a reader comparing the
YAML against the PDF would find text the document never contains. Every other vendored rule matched;
both paraphrases fixed to the document's words.

Second, the document's own elaboration under R-3.1.2 — "Request retraction is allowed during reset
activation" — is exactly what the emitted `disable iff (!reset_n)` already models. The exception in
the SVA is the document's own exception, not a tool convenience.

The restraint on R-4.1.1 is the decision's substantive half. Every response payload signal is either
optional (`err`, `rid`, `ruser`) or conditional on transaction direction (`rdata` is undefined for
writes, per the document's own qualifier), and the block cannot yet express a `we`-conditional
obligation — so asserting response stability would alarm on compliant traffic. A rule the block
cannot state truthfully stays prose, with the reason in a YAML comment beside the omission. The same
qualifier excludes `wdata`/`wuser` from the address-phase set. Validation grew the matching guard: a
stability claim on a signal the requester does not drive (e.g. the manager "holding" the
subordinate's `rdata`) refuses to parse.

**What was verified.** Rule texts came from `pdftotext` on the fetched OBI-v1.6.0.pdf and were
diffed against every vendored rule, not just the new ones. In simulation: changing `addr` mid-phase
trips exactly `a_address_addr_stable` and nothing else; a multi-cycle pending request with held
payload runs clean; changing everything the cycle *after* acceptance runs clean — the assertion
window ends where the document says the phase ends. Both new scenarios are parametrized cases in
`tests/integration/test_protocol_emit_verilator.py` (19 tests there now).

Regression: 1267 unit + conformance passing (up from 1264), 22 skipped.

**Implications.** The OBI checker now covers reset, retraction and unconditional address-phase
stability — every rule shape the vendored subset states unconditionally. What remains prose is
remaining for stated reasons: conditional stability needs a schema extension (`we`-gated
obligations), and ordering (R-10's aid/rid mirroring) needs sequence-carrying assertions; neither is
misrepresented as covered. The D174-era lesson generalizes: vendored "quotes" that predate this
check should be treated as unverified until diffed against their primary document — OBI's are now
clean; the WISHBONE and Solderpad-licensed AXI implementation documents have not had the same diff.

---

## D214. Six of fourteen OBI "quotes" were unfaithful, D213's diff was incomplete, and verbatim is now a test

**Decision.** Four more rule texts in `obi-1.6.0.yaml` were restored to the document's exact words
(R-3.2.1 paraphrased a parenthetical; R-14 dropped "(when not in reset)"; R-21 truncated its
sentence; R-21.1 dropped "(nor on gntpar or rvalidpar)"), plus the same R-3.1.2 paraphrase and R-21
truncation where they were re-quoted in `definitions-clocking-v1.yaml`. The extracted text of both
redistributable primary documents is vendored under `protocols/specs/reference_text/`, and two new
unit tests make the discipline permanent: every vendored rule text must appear verbatim (normalized
whitespace and typographic quotes) in its primary document, and a rule quoted in two spec documents
must be byte-equal in both.

**Why, and what this corrects.** D213 claimed "every other vendored rule matched". That claim was
wrong, and wrong for an instructive reason: the enumeration behind it came from a grep window that
ended at R-10, so R-14 and the R-21 family were never compared at all — an incomplete iteration
read as a complete one, the same defect class as D197's first-backtick-only regex. The systematic
re-diff (every rule, programmatically, against the normalized PDF text) found six unfaithful texts
out of fourteen where D213's manual pass had found two.

One of the six changes meaning, not just wording: R-14 without "(when not in reset)" states an
unconditional obligation the document does not impose — a parity assertion derived from the
truncated text would false-alarm during reset, precisely the class of wrongness the citation
discipline exists to prevent. The R-3.1.2 paraphrase surviving in `definitions-clocking` after D213
fixed it in the OBI document is the fix-that-never-travels defect in its purest form, caught within
the hour by the new cross-document test — which then immediately caught a third copy of the R-21
truncation in the OBI document itself.

Vendoring the extracted text (66KB + 229KB, licence-clean: Solderpad-2.0 and public domain, each
file headed with its extraction provenance) is what turns the diff from a one-time investigation
into an offline test: no network, no pdftotext at test time, and a future "quote" that is really a
paraphrase fails CI the day it is written.

**What was verified.** After the fixes, all 14 OBI rules, all 3 WISHBONE rules and all 13
definitions-clocking quotes check verbatim — the test floors at 25 rules checked so an id-format
drift cannot pass it vacuously. WISHBONE's three rules were verbatim on first check; the AXI
documents carry no rules (implementation-derived, licence-constrained) so there is nothing to diff
there by construction. Regression: 1269 unit + conformance passing (up from 1267); the 19
Verilator integration tests still pass — the emitted assertions cite rule ids, not rule prose, so
correcting texts changed comments only.

**Implications.** D213's residue note ("other documents have not had the same diff") is resolved —
every quoted rule in the repository is now machine-diffed against its primary source on every test
run. The R-14 fix matters beyond hygiene: any future `reqpar` parity assertion must carry the reset
qualifier, and now the vendored text it would be derived from does.

---

## D215. Timeloop consumes 2-D compute arrays, and the equivalence set gains its first 2-D point

**Decision.** `architecture_ir_to_timeloop_architecture_yaml` accepts a compute node with two dims:
`spatial: {meshX: <first>, meshY: <second>}`, C parallelised along meshX and M along meshY via an
explicit 8-entry permutation (`[G, N, P, Q, R, S, C, M]`) and `split: 7`, with **no**
`maximize_dims`. Three or more dims are refused (Timeloop containers have no third mesh axis), as
is `spatial_dim` on a 2-D array (both spatial dims are fixed by construction — accepting and
ignoring a mapping constraint would report it honoured). The 1-D path is byte-identical to before.

**Why this shape, and why the experiment came first.** The naive extension — add `meshY`, move the
`split` — produced zero valid mappings, and the transpiled v3 config the binary actually consumed
explains why, in two parts that were both invisible from the v4 input. First, the `maximize_dims`
constraint macro expands to *fixed* factors maximising the product to the total fanout (measured:
`M=32, C=2` against an 8x8 mesh) with no awareness of the per-axis split, so every mapping it
forces overflows one axis. Second, the front-end prepends `G` to the permutation, shifting every
index the split points at — which is why the emitted permutation lists `G` explicitly. Neither
fact is in any documentation found; both came from reading `parsed-processed-input.yaml` out of a
kept work directory after the failure. Writing the translator first and debugging it through the
adapter's deleted tempdirs would have been strictly worse.

**What was verified.**
- The recipe against the real tool before any translator code: mlp-gemm0 on the 8x8 array maps
  `C in [0:8) Spatial-X, M in [0:8) Spatial-Y` (read from `timeloop-mapper.map.txt`), 64 cycles at
  100% utilisation — the 4096-MAC / 64-lane compute roofline exactly.
- **Both runners agree on the new point**: `timeloop-nix@local` and `timeloop-docker@…` each report
  64.0 cycles / 340000.0 pJ — the first non-1-D entry in the D206/D207 equivalence evidence.
- ZigZag on the same architecture and workload: 210 cycles, 154167 pJ. Not expected to match —
  different model, and its cycles include memory-stall serialisation — but both respect the same
  64-cycle roofline, and a true same-architecture 2-D cross-backend comparison is now possible at
  all, which is the thing `simple-npu-1d-v1.yaml` was invented to work around.
- The conformance matrix was **re-probed, not edited**: both new cells measured 64.0 (mlp-ffn0's
  two layers aggregate 32+32 through the one-invocation-per-layer path), `my-npu-v3` still refuses
  (3-D), `generic-riscv-soc-v1` still refuses (no dims). The suite then ran under Docker, so the
  pinned cells are Docker-measured as well as hermetic-measured.
- The stale integration test asserting the 2-D *refusal* was retargeted to 3-D, keeping its actual
  subject (inexpressible architectures fail before paying for a runner) rather than deleting it.

Regression: 1272 unit + conformance passing (up from 1269), 22 skipped; 5/5 in the architecture
translation live file on both runners.

**Implications.** The "1-D only" caveat on the Timeloop adapter is gone; the honest residues are
now 3-D-and-up (refused loudly) and the C-on-meshX/M-on-meshY assignment being a fixed convention
rather than a searched choice. `simple-npu-1d-v1.yaml` stays load-bearing for its pinned golden
baselines. The D207 equivalence caveat "everything measured is 1-D" no longer holds; "one
workload family" still does.

---

## D216. Objective IR: the fourth document kind, and what a campaign means

**Decision.** `objective.schema.json` joins workload/architecture/mapping in `flux_ir` and the
store's `_VALID_KINDS`. An objective declares: `objectives` (metric + direction, optional weights),
`mode` (`pareto`|`weighted`), hard `constraints` (metric bounds + the independent validity checker),
`workload`/`base_arch` docrefs (hash or inline), `backends` (screening + escalation rungs, by
registry name, never instances), the `search` space (reusing `flux_search_architecture`'s
vocabulary), a `strategy` (`grid`|`agentic`), a hard `budget` (≥1 of evaluations/wall_clock_s/usd)
and `stop` criteria. Semantic validation beyond the schema lives in `parse_objective`: weighted mode
requires weights everywhere, a grid strategy may not carry `llm_model` (a field that would be
silently ignored misleads the reader about what ran), `memory_size` needs its `level`.

**Why.** The campaign work (this arc's goal: standalone agentic work over a time frame) needs a
declarative answer to "what does *improve* mean" that outlives any one process. Making it an IR
document buys the existing machinery for free: content hashing gives campaigns identity and lineage
(D220), the store's `documents` table gives durability, and the schema gives agents a checkable
contract instead of a prose convention. `budget.evaluations` meters *real* screening calls only —
cache hits are free (they spent nothing) and escalation draws wall-clock, mirroring how
`run_architecture_dse` budgets its own escalation.

**What was verified.** Round-trip through the real schema validator and the real store: the parsed
objective's `flux_ir.content_hash` equals the store's document hash for the same YAML. Semantic
rejections measured (weighted-without-weights, grid-with-llm_model, missing budget). Naming note
recorded: `flux_store` already exports a corpus-level `Objective` (D58) — the campaign one lives in
`flux_search_campaign`, no import collision, but the two concepts share a word.

**Implications.** An agent can now hand Flux a document saying "minimize latency and energy on this
workload over these widths, screen with zigzag, escalate the survivors through RTL, spend at most 64
evaluations" — and everything after that is bookkeeping the rest of this arc builds.

---

## D217. Campaign state lives in the ResultStore's SQLite file, and the database is the checkpoint

**Decision.** `flux_store.CampaignStore` composes `ResultStore` on the *same* file and connection
(WAL journaling): `campaigns`, `trials` (with a `result_id` foreign key into the existing `results`
table), and an append-only `campaign_events` log. One trial = one transaction: the intent row
(`status='running'`) commits *before* evaluation starts; result insertion and trial completion
commit together after. The budget ledger and the Pareto frontier are **derived** — `SUM` over trial
rows plus top-up events; a pure function of ok trials — never stored.

**Why.** A long-horizon loop's failure mode is dying between "measured" and "recorded". Sharing the
connection makes the result row and its trial row atomic — the alternative (separate campaign DB
with cross-DB refs) loses exactly that and was rejected. Deriving ledger and frontier means an
interrupted process *cannot* leave them disagreeing with the trials: there is nothing to disagree.
The intent row is what turns a crash into a classifiable fact: a `running` row found at load time
belongs to a dead process, is relabeled `interrupted` (itself an event), and its candidate returns
to the un-visited set.

**What was verified.** Beyond unit tests (atomicity, double-completion refused, derived arithmetic,
top-ups): a real **SIGKILL** mid-trial-2 of a live zigzag campaign, DB reopened cold — the intent
row survived as `running`, resume classified it, re-proposed the candidate, completed all four
widths, and the event log reads `started / interrupted_trials_found / resumed / stopped`. The plan's
own caution (exception injection is not a process death) was honored: both were tested. The
exception-injection variant is the committed integration test; resumed-vs-uninterrupted stores are
trial-equivalent (same candidates, same metric values, same frontier) with the interrupted row
present and honest.

**Implications.** `run_campaign_steps` is also the resume path — resuming IS running. Anything that
can open the SQLite file can audit a campaign completely; there is no state anywhere else.

---

## D218. Multi-objective dominance with calibrated CIs — and one deliberate divergence from `contenders()`

**Decision.** Two distinct sets. The **frontier** uses point-value dominance: crisp, deterministic,
what stop criteria and reports need. The **contender set** (what escalation buys) generalizes
`dse.contenders()`'s closed-interval overlap rule: a candidate is eliminated only when another is
interval-BETTER on ≥1 objective, interval-WORSE on none, **and point-worse on none**. The last
clause is the multi-objective addition: an interval can cleanly beat on metric A while its point
value quietly loses on metric B inside overlapping intervals, and eliminating the point-B winner on
that evidence would buy the wrong candidate. Refusals never enter dominance in either direction.

**Why the divergence is deliberate.** Single-objective equivalence with the real `contenders()` is
unit-tested by calling it, not restating it — and the test construction surfaced a genuine semantic
difference: `contenders()` is *leader-relative* (only the point-minimum's band eliminates), so with
mixed point/CI estimates it keeps a candidate whose interval lies strictly above a non-leader point
estimate — a candidate that provably cannot win. The campaign rule eliminates it. The containment is
one-directional and safe (campaign ⊆ dse, proven: dse-elimination implies leader interval-dominance
implies campaign elimination), so the tightening never buys less than dse would keep needed. Both
properties are pinned: exact membership equality on uniformly-CI'd inputs, strict-subset-with-the-
divergent-candidate-named on the mixed input.

**What was verified.** Unit matrix over point/CI/maximize/refusal/mixed cases; the equivalence and
containment tests against the imported `dse.contenders()`; and on real data: the zigzag width
campaign's multi-objective frontier contains the single-metric winner for *each* objective computed
independently (they coincide at width 32 — measured monotone physics, not an assumption; a gbuf
size probe was run looking for a real trade-off and found none in this corner, so non-trivial
frontiers are exercised synthetically).

**Implications.** With uncalibrated point estimates everything degenerates to classical dominance
and the contender set to the leader — an uncalibrated campaign escalates exactly what
`run_architecture_dse` would. Calibrated CIs (D98's flywheel) are what make the contender set grow,
and the escalation budget with it; that consequence should be re-measured on calibrated data rather
than assumed (still open).

---

## D219. Resume determinism is a per-trial recorded fact, not a promise

**Decision.** Every trial row carries `deterministic`, and for agentic trials: the model name and
sha256 hashes of the exact prompt and response, plus `used_fallback`/`fallback_reason` when a bad
proposal fell back to a seeded-random unvisited candidate. Grid resumes are deterministic by
construction (proposal order is a pure function of objective + visited set). Agentic resumes rebuild
the LLM's prompt history from the store — non-deterministic but not amnesiac — and the `resumed`
event marks the boundary. An agentic campaign without an LLM factory refuses loudly
(`make_llm` is the runner's injection point; the campaign package stays LLM-client-agnostic, the
CHIA/Ollama adapter lives in the `flux_campaign_*` nodes).

**What was verified.** Grid: resumed-vs-uninterrupted trial equivalence against real zigzag
(integration) and the SIGKILL variant (manual, D217). Agentic: a live campaign against real
qwen2.5-coder:7b via Ollama + real zigzag, stepped 2 trials then resumed — all four widths covered,
every row `deterministic=0` with model and both hashes present, zero fallbacks needed that run; the
step boundary preserved the prompt history.

**Implications.** "Is this campaign replayable?" is now a query, not a guess:
`nondeterministic_trials` in the status payload. CI covers the grid path; the agentic path is
Ollama-gated like every other generation test (the known CI hole).

---

## D220. campaign_id = objective_hash: same objective, same campaign

**Decision.** A campaign's identity is its objective document's content hash. `start_campaign` is
INSERT-OR-IGNORE: starting an objective that already ran resumes it (one `started` event, ever).
Terminal campaigns (stopped/done) refuse resume; any change to the document — a weight, a width, a
budget — is a different hash and thus a different campaign. No fork mechanism until a real need
shows up; if one does, an explicit fork field belongs in the objective (changing the hash), not in
the store.

**Why.** Idempotency is the agent-friendly property: an agent that lost its notes can recover its
campaign from the objective it still has, and a retried `start` call cannot fork a silent sibling
that splits the budget. The cost — two independent campaigns over one objective in one DB are
impossible — is the point, not a limitation.

**What was verified.** Unit: restart resumes (same id, `created=False`, single `started` event).
Wire: the MCP lifecycle test drives start→step→status→frontier→stop→double-stop over the real
protocol against real zigzag; the double stop is refused carrying the original reason, and `usd`
spend reports null (unknown), never 0.0, when no backend priced anything. The six tools passed
`test_mcp_surface_parity` only after `docs/agent-surface.md` gained their rows — the parity test
caught the missing docs before any human did, which is that mechanism working.

**Implications.** 47 MCP tools. The campaign surface is the first place the "standalone agentic
work over a time frame" goal is operational: an agent can start a bounded campaign, come back
later — across processes — and the store answers for everything that happened in between.

---

## D221. Weighted mode was accepted but not acted on; now it acts, and two more axes are reachable

**Decision.** `pareto_frontier` and `frontier_contenders` branch on the objective's mode: `weighted`
keeps the trial(s) achieving the minimal weighted scalar point value (ties all kept, so the stop
criterion's membership test stays exact), and its contender set is `dse.contenders()`'s own rule on
the scalarized axis (closed-interval overlap with the leader's scalar band). Symmetrically,
`mode: pareto` now *rejects* weights instead of ignoring them. And the campaign search space gained
`joint` (width x memory size) and `noc_topology`, mapping to the existing
`flux_search_architecture` generators.

**Why.** Reviewing the just-shipped foundation for a status answer found that `mode: weighted`
parsed, validated, had a tested scalarizer — and changed nothing: the runner computed a Pareto
frontier regardless. A field that validates but does not act is the exact defect the parser already
rejects elsewhere (grid + `llm_model`), sitting in the same file. The pareto-with-weights rejection
closes the mirror image of the same hole. The axes widening is the smaller half: the NoC and joint
generators existed and were reachable from one-shot tools but not from an objective document.

**What was verified.** Unit: a genuine trade-off keeps both trials on the pareto frontier while
weighted mode picks the one the weights favour — and flipping the weights flips the winner, which
is what proves they are load-bearing; weighted contenders with a single unit weight reproduce the
real `dse.contenders()` membership (called, not restated); ties all stay. Integration, real
backends: a weighted zigzag campaign whose winning scalar recomputes exactly from the stored
estimates (263 + 0.001 x 193768); a joint campaign covering the full 2x2 Cartesian product with the
frontier at (width 32, gbuf 64) — the direction a gbuf-size probe measured, not assumed; a
`noc_topology` campaign through real Booksim2 where the torus beats the mesh at equal dimensions —
asserted as physics (wrap-around links), not as a pinned magic number. The objective-IR checks that
had lived only in a scratch script during the build are now `tests/unit/test_objective_ir.py` — a
check that ran once proves nothing about next week.

**Implications.** All four architecture-side axes the one-shot DSE tools cover are now campaign
axes. Agentic proposals still cover width only, stated in the strategy's own error message.

---

## D222. Calibration is wired into the campaign, and the contender-set question is measured: it grows exactly at the extrapolation

**Decision.** `run_campaign_steps(calibration_db_path=...)` applies D98's flywheel to every
screening result *before* classification and recording — the stored trial carries the corrected
estimate with its residual CI, so the frontier, contender set, and every status payload see
calibrated numbers with no further plumbing. A cache-hit re-calibrates against today's pool (the
pool may have grown since the raw result was stored) and records its own trial row. It is a runtime
argument, not an objective field, deliberately: the objective's content hash must not change
because two machines keep their residual pool at different paths; which calibration actually
applied lives per-result in `provenance.calibration`, the honest place.

**Why.** The D218 record left one consequence explicitly unmeasured, and the "Still open" list
carried it: with point estimates the contender set degenerates to the leader (verified), but what
calibrated CIs do to it had only been reasoned about. Measuring it required the hook — which turned
out not to exist: nothing connected `calibrate_result` to the campaign loop at all.

**What was measured.** Real ZigZag screening, real RTL (Verilator) references populating the pool
for widths 4/8/16, campaign over widths 4/8/16/32:

- ZigZag's latency bias re-measured at 2.94x (the documented near-constant ratio), and calibration
  corrected it to near-exact RTL agreement for every in-pool width — 1057.4 / 529.1 / 264.9
  calibrated vs 1057 / 529 / 265 RTL-measured — with tight CIs (<10% of value).
- The held-out width 32 got an honestly wide interval, [53.3, 1297.5] around a corrected 89.5 —
  extrapolation priced as uncertainty rather than stated as confidence — wide enough to overlap the
  runner-up's [259.7, 270.3].
- **The consequence:** the contender set grew from {32} (uncalibrated) to {32, 16} — the campaign
  would now buy one extra RTL measurement, at exactly the point where the residual pool has no
  evidence. That is D105's "screening data cannot rule out" made operational by the flywheel, and
  the escalation-budget cost of calibration is quantified: +1 rung evaluation per unsupported
  extrapolation in the frontier's neighbourhood, not an unbounded blowup.

All of it is pinned in `tests/integration/test_campaign_calibrated_live.py`, which re-measures the
bias ratio rather than assuming it and asserts CI shapes and set memberships, not just totals.
Regression: 1304 unit + conformance passing (up from 1290), 22 skipped.

**Implications.** The "Still open" item is resolved by measurement. A calibrated campaign is
strictly more honest than a raw one and modestly more expensive in escalation — the trade the
architecture intended. The residual risk is unchanged from D98: calibration quality is bounded by
the pool's coverage, and the wide held-out interval is the system saying so out loud.

---

## D223. Generated RTL is graded on vectors the LLM never saw

**Decision.** `derive_design_spec` accepts a `vector_seed_salt` (empty salt reproduces the
historical seed byte-identically — every pre-existing derived spec unchanged, unit-pinned), and
`flux_generate_rtl_for_architecture` re-verifies a successful generation against a **holdout** set:
fresh golden vectors from the same candidate-pair seeding under the salt `"holdout"`, at least
twice as many as were shown, same ports, same module, same golden model. The report carries all
three verdicts separately — derivation, generation-against-shown, holdout — plus an explicit
`overfitted_repair` flag; `success` requires the holdout.

**Why.** The repair loop's strength is its weakness: `failing_vector_lines` are fed back to the
LLM, so the vectors a design is graded on are *disclosed*, and a repair can converge onto them
without implementing the behavior. Nothing re-checked on undisclosed data. This is the repo's own
holdout discipline (docs/roadmap.md's calibration principle) applied to generation — and it was
the genuinely missing piece of the "verification ladder" gap: the seeded-random golden-model
vectors this analysis assumed were missing already existed (`n_vectors`, content-addressed
seeding); what was missing was that every one of them leaked.

**What was verified, both directions, with real tools.**
- **The guard catches the attack:** a deliberately memorizing module (exact-match lookup over the
  shown vectors, `'0` otherwise — what a fully overfitted repair amounts to) passes **4/4** shown
  and **0/8** holdout vectors through real Verilator.
- **The guard does not punish correctness:** an honest hand-written dot product passes both sets;
  and the full node with real Ollama (qwen2.5-coder:7b) generated a correct implementation on
  attempt 1 that passed **8/8** holdout — a genuine implementation, distinguished from a memorized
  one by measurement rather than by trust.
- Salt properties unit-pinned: empty salt byte-identical, salts vary vectors only (ports, module
  name and behavior text unchanged), zero overlap with the shown set, distinct salts give
  distinct sets.

Regression: 1305 unit + conformance passing, 22 skipped; the three-test holdout integration file
runs in ~90 s.

**Implications.** `success=True` from the architecture→RTL bridge now means "implements the
behavior on data it never saw", not "fits the examples it was shown". The same leak exists on the
sequential and GEMM derivation paths (their seeds already carry `seq:`/`gemm:` prefixes, so the
salt mechanism extends directly); those nodes have not been wired yet — a known, named residue,
not a silent one. The calibration flywheel composes cleanly: `calibrate_against_generated` records
measured cycles from designs that now clear a holdout, strengthening what a "reference" means.

---

## D224. The sequential and GEMM paths needed no holdout wiring — composition already is one, measured

**Decision.** D223's residue ("the sequential and GEMM derivation paths have the same
disclosed-vector leak") is resolved by measurement, not by code: no wiring was added, and two
parametrized integration tests pin why.

**Why the residue was wrong.** The leak model assumed those paths grade on what they disclose.
They do not: the LLM implements only the combinational *leaf tile*, whose shown vectors are three
fixed hand-picked values (a positive, a negative, a zero — chosen in `leaf_port_spec` for
reproducibility), while the composed top verifies against the wrapper driving *seeded-random*
candidate-pair data the LLM never sees. The disclosed set and the graded set were disjoint by
construction all along — composition is a de facto holdout.

**What was measured.** A deliberately memorizing leaf (exact-match lookup over its three disclosed
vectors, `'0` otherwise, one lookup chain per output port) passes its standalone verification 3/3
on BOTH paths and fails the composed verification 0/1 on both, through real Verilator. The first
GEMM attempt also caught a real assumption in the experiment itself — the broadcast-MAC leaf has
multiple output ports where the script assumed one, and Verilator rejected the malformed cheat
before it could prove anything; fixed and re-run rather than counted.

The committed tests assert the full chain: memorizer fits disclosed perfectly, composed run
catches it. If either derivation ever starts showing the wrapper's own data to the LLM, the tests
start failing — the alarm working, not breaking.

**Implications.** All three architecture→RTL generation paths now grade on undisclosed data: the
combinational bridge by D223's explicit holdout, the wrapped paths by their own structure —
verified rather than assumed. The still-open item is removed.

---

## D225. The synthesis rung is real: OpenROAD places ASAP7 cells, and area_mm2 stops being 0.0

**Decision.** `evaluators/openroad` (backend #12, `nix develop .#physical`): Yosys maps the
candidate's derived MAC datapath onto the D92 ASAP7 liberty, OpenROAD 26Q2 floorplans and places it
on newly-vendored ASAP7 platform files (tech LEF + RVT cell LEF + flow fragments, same pinned ORFS
commit as D92, licences verified per file class), and the ABI reports measured `area_mm2`,
`power_w` and `worst_slack_ps` with `validity.ok` as the timing verdict at a stated clock.
**OpenROAD over Hammer**, answering the question that started this arc: Hammer is a flow-abstraction
layer whose primary value is commercial-EDA portability and whose open-source plugin drives OpenROAD
anyway — for a hermetic, licence-free repo it would wrap the tool installed regardless.
`evaluators/hammer/README.md` stays as the documented commercial-flow alternative.

**The packaging.** nixpkgs ships openroad 26Q2 but broken-marked via or-tools, whose *vendored*
pybind11 (let-bound inside its package, unreachable by scope overlays — measured: the overlay
applied to `python3Packages.pybind11` while or-tools' drv hash did not move) fails one test under
python 3.14 on a changed TypeError wording. Fix: or-tools on python 3.13 plus `doCheck = false` for
its own ctest (a python-contrib dependency check openroad, which links only the C++ libraries,
never touches). Four build attempts, each failing one layer deeper; the flake's `.#physical` shell
reproduces the final recipe to the identical store path.

**What running the real tools corrected — five findings, none guessable from documentation:**
1. **`mac_array.sv` is simulation-only.** Its operand memories are testbench-loaded via
   `$readmemh`, so under synthesis they are never written and Yosys constant-folds the entire
   datapath away — LANES 8 vs 32 differed by *ten cells*. The adapter therefore places the derived
   combinational datapath (D223's spec family) as its canonical LLM-free implementation instead;
   `evaluators/rtl` keeps `latency_cycles` for the simulated design, and this rung deliberately
   reports neither latency nor energy (another rung's runtime would be borrowed provenance).
2. Yosys `-q` suppresses the very `stat` report being parsed; `-l <file>` is the answer.
3. `stat -liberty`'s total row switches its area column to scientific notation past ~1e3 um^2
   (`19321 1.93E+03 cells`) — **D181's exponent-truncation defect class, reproduced live** after
   that record spent a paragraph noting no real instance had ever been observed.
4. OpenROAD's structural netlist reader rejects `input signed [31:0] x;` (STA-0171); on a mapped
   netlist signedness carries nothing, so it is stripped, with a declaration-only regex.
5. `report_design_area` spells `um^2`, `report_worst_slack` interposes `max`, and the first run's
   1 ns default clock failed timing on the reference design itself — the default is now 2 ns,
   because a validity gate that flags every default run is miscalibrated, not strict. Also caught
   before any tool ran: `acc`.startswith("a") counted the output port as a ninth lane and the
   generated module referenced a nonexistent `a8*w8`.

**The first real numbers, and their physics.** 8 lanes: 1928 um^2 / 27.9 mW / +293 ps at 2 ns.
The two clock runs cross-check exactly (2000 - 293 = 1707 = the 1 ns run's critical path). The
width family scales 2.004x and 2.002x per lane doubling — one multiplier per lane, as it must —
and slack degrades 293 -> 68 -> -225 ps as the adder tree deepens, so the 32-lane array honestly
fails 2 ns and `validity.ok` says so. Unit tests pin every parser against captured real output;
the live integration file (skips without `openroad`) pins the reference point, the scaling slope,
and the validity flip. Regression: 1316 unit + conformance passing (up from 1305; parametrized
suites grew with the registry automatically).

**Implications.** `area_mm2` finally has a backend whose number comes from placed silicon rather
than 0.0 or a gate count, and campaigns can escalate `zigzag -> rtl -> openroad` for
latency+energy+area+power across three fidelities of the same candidate. Honest limits, stated
where they bite: flow depth is placement (CTS/routing named as the next rung), ports are the
spec's 32-bit carriers so multipliers are 32x32 even for int8 workloads, and the first
`.#physical` entry pays a from-source or-tools+openroad build.

---

## D226. Mixed-fidelity objectives: a metric may be measured at escalation only, and the frontier composes per-metric at equal fidelity

**Decision.** An objective entry may declare `measured_at: escalation` (default `screen`).
Screening then requires, requests and ranks on the *screened* metrics only; an escalation rung's
trial is ok when it carries at least one objective metric (rungs are partial by design); and the
escalated frontier becomes a **per-metric equal-fidelity composite**: for each objective metric,
every contender's number comes from the deepest source — screening or a rung — whose ok trials
cover the full contender set on that metric, with the fidelity recorded per metric in the payload.
The composite is empty until every declared metric has a covering source: a frontier missing a
declared objective would be the screening frontier wearing a deeper label.

**Why.** Registering `openroad` as a campaign rung exposed the gap before any test ran: a campaign
minimizing latency *and* silicon area was structurally impossible. `_classify` refused any trial
missing an objective metric; ZigZag cannot produce `area_mm2`, OpenROAD cannot produce
`latency_cycles`, so every trial of such a campaign — screening or escalation — would be refused.
The refusal machinery (D112/D201) was doing its job on each result while making the composition of
partial backends unreachable. Declaration over detection, per D216's own principle: an
auto-detected "this metric never appears at screening, defer it" would turn a screening backend
regression into a silent semantic change of the campaign; `measured_at` makes the split part of
the objective's content hash.

The per-metric rule generalizes D112's equal-fidelity lesson rather than replacing it: comparing
a's deep number against b's shallow one on the SAME metric is still forbidden (a rung covering a
subset of contenders supplies nothing), while mixing fidelities BETWEEN metrics is legitimate
precisely because every candidate gets the same source per metric.

**What was verified, real backends end to end.** A live campaign with objectives
`latency_cycles` (screen) + `area_mm2` (escalation), zigzag screening widths 8/16/32, OpenROAD
rung: screening ranked on latency with every trial legally area-free; the contender set
degenerated to width 32 (point estimates, D218); exactly one real OpenROAD run bought its area;
and the composite frontier reports width 32 with latency 263.0 at `fidelity: screen` and its real
placed area (7733 um^2, within 5% of D225's family measurement) at `fidelity: openroad`. Parse
rejections: a deferred metric with no escalation backends, and all-deferred objectives (screening
would have nothing to rank on). The prior escalation test's payload assertion was updated to the
per-metric fidelity shape — a deliberate format change, not an accident — and the full campaign
suite re-run. Regression: 1316 unit + conformance, 22 skipped, unchanged.

**Implications.** Campaigns can now optimize across metrics no single backend serves:
latency+energy from analytic screening, silicon area and power from the physical rung, each
number carrying the fidelity that produced it. The screening request set shrank to what screening
measures (part of cache identity — an honest request reads honestly in provenance). Residue: the
stop criterion `target` on a deferred metric can never fire during screening and is only
evaluated against screened metrics today — a campaign whose stop condition is "area under X"
runs to space or budget exhaustion instead; wiring stop-targets into the composite is a small,
named follow-up.

---

## D227. Three small closures: composite stop-targets, a de-rotted docstring, and axis-generic agentic proposals

**Decision.** Three named residues closed in one pass:

1. **Stop-targets on deferred metrics fire** (D226's residue). `_stop_target_met` runs against the
   per-metric equal-fidelity composite: checked *before each rung* (a target the previous rung
   satisfied saves every deeper rung's spend) and again after escalation, where the final event now
   says which way it ended — "stop.target met by the composite frontier" versus "stop.target NOT
   met". Ending by exhaustion and ending by achievement are different facts, and the event log
   states which. The `_CompositeMeasurement` gained `value_of`/`refusal_for`, so the existing stop
   logic runs on composites unchanged.
2. **`flux_evaluate`'s docstring stopped hand-listing backends.** Three sites named five of the
   registry's thirteen; each now points at `flux_backend_health` as the live source of truth with
   three illustrative examples. A hand-list here would rot, and had — D119's lesson applied to
   prose instead of tests.
3. **Agentic proposals are axis-generic.** `AgenticStrategy` no longer hardcodes the width axis
   with a width-specific parser: it proposes from the SAME finite candidate list `GridStrategy`
   walks, asking the LLM to pick one unvisited parameter object verbatim, so validation is pure
   membership and every `search.kind` — width, memory size, joint, NoC topology — gets agentic
   proposals through one mechanism. A per-axis prompt/parser pair is the fix-never-travels shape,
   avoided by construction. Listings cap at 64 candidates (a thousand-line prompt is noise, not
   choice; the cap names itself in the fallback reason when it bites).

**What was verified, real backends throughout.** The stop-target: both outcomes live against real
ZigZag + real OpenROAD — a 1.0 mm^2 target met (event says met), a 1e-9 target unmet (event says
NOT met), parametrized in the mixed-fidelity suite. The agentic generalization: the existing width
campaign still covers its space through the generic mechanism (same provenance rows), and a NEW
memory-size agentic campaign — real qwen2.5-coder picking gbuf sizes, real ZigZag measuring —
covered [2, 8, 64, 512] KiB and put 2 KiB on the frontier, matching the D221 probe's measured
energy-rises-with-size physics. Regression: 1316 unit + conformance, 22 skipped, unchanged.

**Implications.** Campaign feature-completeness against its own declared scope: every search kind
has both strategies, every objective mode acts, stop criteria fire at every fidelity, and the one
tool agents use most no longer misstates what exists. The remaining campaign-adjacent residues are
infra (Ollama CI runner) and fidelity depth (CTS/routing, true-precision ports), not semantics.

---

## D228. True-precision datapath ports: the int8 area was overstated 4.8x, and correcting it exposed a synthesis pathology

**Decision.** `derive_design_spec` sizes ports to the workload's own declared precision: an int8
workload gets 8-bit operand ports and an exactly-sized accumulator (8+8 product bits + lane bits —
the 32-bit floor `_ACC_BITS` is gone, replaced by the harness's own 2-bit minimum). The generation
prompt renders each port's true width instead of a hardcoded `[31:0]`, and the width primer is
width-generic ("match each port's declared width; plain decimals are always safe") instead of
asserting everything is 32 bits. The OpenROAD canonical datapath emits explicit exact-width
per-lane products. Golden vectors are unchanged by construction — they always drew from the true
precision range; only the containers were oversized.

**Why.** D225 stated the caveat and D228 removes it: with 32-bit carriers, the physical rung
placed 32x32 multipliers for an int8 workload. Measured, not estimated: the 8-lane datapath is
**401 um^2 at true precision versus 1928 um^2 in carriers — a 4.8x overstatement** that would have
poisoned any calibration or Pareto decision resting on the old numbers. Power similarly: 11.1 mW
vs 27.9 mW. This ranked above CTS/routing because it is a *meaning* error, not a fidelity limit —
flow depth is stated per report; "whose datapath is this" was not.

**What running the real tools surfaced — two findings beyond the plan:**
1. **Verilog expression sizing builds the wrong multipliers silently.** `assign acc = a0*w0 + ...`
   extends every operand to the 19-bit assignment context — 19x19 multipliers for int8 inputs, the
   overstatement reappearing one layer down. The canonical source now declares per-lane product
   wires at exactly `a_bits + w_bits` and sums those.
2. **A synthesis pathology the 32-bit era masked:** on true-width structures, `synth`'s internal
   generic ABC pass plus a full liberty ABC took 420 s for 8 lanes and did not finish 16 lanes in
   ten minutes — while producing a 6x SMALLER netlist. The 32-bit truncating multipliers had
   synthesized to a structure ABC happens to map quickly; exact-width products do not. Recipe,
   measured stepwise rather than guessed: `synth -noabc` + `abc -fast -liberty` -> 0.7/1.2/2.5 s
   for 8/16/32 lanes, at a uniform ~15% cell-count cost versus full mapping (3792 vs 3271 cells at
   8 lanes) that applies to every candidate identically, leaving rankings unaffected. Also
   process-honesty: two intermediate edits were killed mid-apply by tool timeouts and the runs
   after them measured the OLD code — caught both times by grepping the file before believing the
   number.

**The corrected physics.** 401 / 807 / 1618 um^2 and 11.1 / 24.9 / 52.6 mW for 8/16/32 lanes —
scaling 2.01x and 2.00x per doubling, unchanged in shape, ~4.8x smaller in level. Slack: 768 /
574 / 525 ps at 2 ns — **all three widths now meet timing**; D225's 32-lane miss (-225 ps) was the
32-bit carriers' deeper adder tree, and the validity-flip test now pins monotone degradation with
everything positive instead. D225's absolute numbers are superseded by these; its scaling and
cross-check claims stand.

**What was verified.** The whole downstream chain re-run against real tools: the D223 holdout
suite (memorizer still caught 4/4->0/8, honest module passes, live qwen generation at mixed
8/19-bit ports succeeds with the new primer), the generation live suite, the OpenROAD family with
re-measured pins, the mixed-fidelity campaign (composite area pin 7733 -> 1618 um^2), both
stop-target outcomes, and the full regression: 1316 unit + conformance, 22 skipped. The
`_derive(64, 8) == 32` unit pin — the old floor, pinned as "never narrowed" — now pins 22, the
exact worst case.

**Implications.** `area_mm2` and `power_w` now mean the workload's datapath. The sequential/GEMM
leaf specs still use 32-bit ports (their hand-written wrappers assume it) — those paths feed
`evaluators/rtl` simulation, not the physical rung, so no number they produce changes meaning;
noted, not hidden. Anything calibrated against pre-D228 OpenROAD numbers must be re-measured —
nothing was, which is why this ranked first.

## D229. The routed flow depth is real — and building it exposed that the D92 liberty could not time a single flip-flop

**Decision.** `run_ppa_flow(flow_depth="routed")`: global + detailed routing (TritonRoute) and
OpenRCX extraction against the platform's own `rcx_patterns.rules` (newly vendored, same pinned
ORFS commit), with clock-tree synthesis running exactly when the design has a real clock port — a
combinational datapath has no clock net to build a tree on, and the conditional says so rather
than erroring. `OpenRoadEvaluator(flow_depth=...)` exposes it; placement stays the default
(~10 s vs ~90 s per candidate) and provenance reads `openroad@asap7-<depth>`. Also from this
block: `full_mapping=True` restores exact liberty mapping at its measured 600x cost, and the
sequential/GEMM leaf-precision tightening was assessed and deliberately NOT done — the 32-bit
assumption is woven through ~12 sites of two hand-written simulation-only wrapper templates whose
numbers D228 already established change no meaning; recorded, not hidden.

**The find.** The first clocked design through the flow reported **worst slack INF** with 547
cells and 51 DFFs placed. Not a flow bug: the D92 merged liberty reused the SIMPLE file's header,
silently dropping three table templates that only the SEQ file's header defines
(`delay_template_7x7`, `power_template_7x7`, `passive_power_template_7x1`). ABC never noticed in
ten months of use — area mapping reads no timing tables — but OpenSTA warned `template not found`
per DFF timing group and priced every sequential arc as unconstrained. **The vendored liberty
could not time any flip-flop, and nothing that consumed it before this flow could have told.**
The repair extracted the three blocks from the same SEQ source (same commit, same licence, same
brace-depth parsing), verified every referenced template is now defined programmatically, and
re-verified the D92 area pins byte-for-byte (9/9 in `test_rtl_synth_asap7_live.py` — templates
change no mapping). PROVENANCE.md carries the correction.

Also corrected en route: my own "the design got gutted" hypothesis — 66 um^2 for 547 ASAP7 cells
is consistent (~0.11 um^2/cell, matching the datapath family's density); only STA was blind. And
`worst slack max INF` is a legitimate report the parser now maps to float("inf") instead of
rejecting.

**Measured.** Combinational 8-lane int8, routed: area unchanged at 401 um^2 (routing moves no
cells at this utilization), slack +891.5 ps extracted vs +768 ps placement-estimated — the
estimator was ~14% pessimistic here, a real calibration fact about the estimator — power 10.8 vs
11.1 mW. Clocked PipeMac: finite reg-to-reg slack at last (1292.8 ps placed / 1321.9 ps routed),
CTS visible in the numbers (one buffer of area, real clock-tree power). Runtime ~90 s routed vs
~10 s placed. All pinned in `test_openroad_ppa_live.py` (5 tests); regression 1316 unit +
conformance and the RTL-reference calibration suite unchanged.

**Implications.** The OpenROAD rung now spans two honest fidelities under one provenance scheme,
and clocked designs are timeable for the first time — which un-blocks any future
sequential-design PPA. The liberty lesson generalizes D214's: a vendored artifact is only as
verified as the deepest consumer that ever read it, and each new consumer class (STA, after ten
months of ABC-only use) deserves its own verification pass before its answers are believed.

## D230. The physical rung joined CI, and the roadmap stopped pointing at solved problems

**Decision.** A `physical` nightly job builds `.#physical` and runs the OpenROAD-gated integration
files with the same explicit skip-guard the `timeloop-hermetic` job carries. `docs/roadmap.md` was
re-checked against D216-D229: the rank-1 synthesis-rung item is retired as built (on OpenROAD, not
Hammer — its two named blockers dissolved rather than being solved), the D100 "blocked on cycle
measurement" clause is struck (D115/D118/D121 built it; `flux_calibrate_against_generated_rtl`
records the references, D223/D224 holdout-strengthened), and a new rank-0 item names the actual top
gap: **workload breadth** — every calibration, equivalence and campaign claim rests on the
`mlp-gemm0` degenerate-GEMM family, a caveat stated per-decision but fixable as one capability
(ONNX frontend -> workload IR -> derivation -> campaigns, plus golden baselines on genuinely
different shapes).

**Why.** The CI gap is the D129/D207 defect class, third instance: the nightly sweep runs every
file under the default shell, where the openroad tests skip, and a skipped file exits 0 — the
from-source build, the D229 liberty repair, and the routed flow would all rot green. The roadmap
rot is the misattribution class at its most expensive: a planning document ranking a completed
capability as the top blocked item would send a future session to re-solve a solved problem with
the wrong tool (Hammer).

**What was verified.** The CI step was run verbatim locally, skip-guard included: 9/9 (the PPA
family, routed depth, clocked CTS, mixed-fidelity campaign, both stop-target outcomes),
skip-guard clean. actionlint clean. The workflow unit tests pass with the new job — the
file-existence check now also guards the physical job's named files, and the pipefail check
covers its tee. Roadmap edits were made against the decision log, not memory (the D100 clause was
verified resolved by reading what D115/D118/D121 and the calibrate node actually do). Regression:
1316 unit + conformance, 22 skipped, unchanged.

**Implications.** Every backend with its own shell now has its own nightly job; nothing
skip-rots. The roadmap's ranked list is current through D229, and the top-ranked open item is the
one this session's evidence actually points at. The 180-minute budget for the physical job's
cold-cache or-tools+openroad build is a guess of the same kind D209 made for the hermetic job —
wrong in the visible direction if wrong.

## D231. Workload breadth: ONNX-born workloads flow through the whole stack, and the path needed verification, not construction

**Decision.** `tests/integration/test_onnx_to_campaign_live.py` pins this repo's first golden
baselines beyond the hand-written `mlp-gemm0` family, on two structurally different ONNX-born
workloads: a chained 3-layer classifier head (32x784x256x128x10 — non-square, non-power-of-2
output) and a single wide projection (8x512x64). Pinned: ZigZag latency/energy for both
(2,822,445 cycles / 2.02 mJ and 98,958 cycles / 70.9 uJ on the reference 1-D NPU), real Verilator
cycles for the single-op shape (32,833 at 8 lanes), true-precision derivation (8-bit operands,
19-bit accumulator from the ONNX defaults), and a full mixed-fidelity campaign whose composite
frontier reads latency 8,209 at `rtl` fidelity and energy at `screen` fidelity for width 32.

**Why, and the honest finding.** The roadmap's rank-0 item assumed a path needed *building*. It
did not: `onnx_model_to_workload_ir` -> zigzag -> `derive_design_spec` -> rtl -> campaigns worked
end to end with **zero code changes** — the frontend's einsum chains, the derivation's precision
defaults, and the campaign machinery composed on first contact. What was genuinely missing was
verification and pins: nothing had ever run the chain, so nothing could honestly claim it worked,
and no baseline would catch drift on non-`mlp-gemm0` shapes. The distinction matters for the
standing caveats: D207/D222/D228's "one workload family" qualifiers now have a second family with
its own pinned numbers, though calibration-store residuals for the new shapes remain future work
(the pins are baselines, not calibration references yet).
