honestly contribute below its floor is its own measured periphery: at DETAILED print level
it reports `Area efficiency (Memory cell area/Total area)` — a real per-configuration number
chia's CONCISE runs omit (measured).

Built on (3): the D255 bitcell floor is refined to `bits x published-7nm-bitcell / CACTI's
own array efficiency at the native node` — both inputs sourced (TSMC N7 HD 0.027 um2;
the tool's own report), the single assumption (periphery fraction carries across nodes)
stated in every provenance note, and far weaker than logic-scaling the whole macro. The
interval is anchored: ci_low = the bitcell floor (physical bound), ci_high = the larger of
the two estimates (logic-scaled vs bitcell/efficiency — neither established as an upper
bound alone). `measure_area_efficiency` runs the one extra DETAILED-level CACTI invocation;
the rung's probe is injectable (callable = scripted for tests, False = off, None = real),
after a unit test was caught invoking the real binary through the default.

**What was verified.** Live: the refinement produces the size-dependence the flat floor
missed, from the tool's own numbers — 4KB at 73.6% efficiency -> 0.0367 um2/bit (1202 um2),
32KB at 81.8% -> 0.0330 um2/bit (8656 um2), each with interval [bitcell floor, estimate]
and the full derivation in provenance. Unit (2 more + 1 reworked): the efficiency parser
pinned against the tool's real output line; refined math + assumption in the note + rejected
out-of-range efficiency; the rung test now uses a scripted probe and asserts the anchored
interval. The D254 macro-flow live test re-pinned to the refined 4KB macro (1202 um2;
combined placement 1609 um2) and re-run green. Regression: 1395 passed, 22 skipped.

**Implications.** The 7nm SRAM area chain is now: real CACTI at a native node -> published
bitcell anchor -> the tool's own periphery fraction — every number sourced, the residual
assumption named. Beyond this sits only a real FinFET memory model: FinCACTI if it
resurfaces, an SRAM compiler if ASAP7 ever ships one, or SPICE characterization against
ASAP7's own device models (BSIM-CMG; a genuine arc, recorded as the end of this road).
Energy/access-time at 7nm remain unscaled (the macro liberty carries CACTI@32nm timing,
labeled pessimistic) — the same refinement pattern would need published energy anchors first.

---

## D257. Timing and power join the scaled chain: measured inverter ratios first, polynomials for voltage studies

**Decision.** The D253-D256 area chain gains its delay/energy/power siblings, from the same
primary source, as TWO methods whose disagreement was measured before choosing a default.
The paper's remaining tables were extracted: Table 2 (simulated FO4-inverter delay/energy/
power per node at its ITRS nominal voltage — 32nm@0.97V: 9.8 ps / 0.51 fJ / 2.47 uW;
7nm@0.8V: 2.47 ps / 0.111 fJ / 0.789 uW; only clearly-legible rows vendored) and Table 5
(the Eq. 5-7 polynomial coefficients per node and device type). The polynomial
implementation validates EXACTLY against the authors' own corrected worked example (their
errata page: EF(32HP,0.9V)=0.4571, EF(65bulk,1.3V)=2.604, 1 pJ -> 0.1755 pJ — reproduced to
0.1756). Cross-checking both methods at nominal voltages: DELAY agrees within ~7% (poly 3.69x
vs measured 3.97x for 32->7), but the ENERGY and POWER polynomials deviate ~1.8x from the
measured points (energy 8.2x vs 4.6x; power 5.6x vs 3.1x) — quadratic fits over a wide
voltage sweep are loose at the range's edge. Therefore: `scale_delay_ns` /
`scale_energy_pj` / `scale_power_w` default to method="measured" (Table 2 ratios — direct
simulated points at exactly the nominal-voltage use case), and method="polynomial" exists
for custom-voltage studies with the measured deviation carried as a caveat IN ITS OWN NOTE.
Non-vendored nodes are refused, never interpolated, both methods.

**What was verified.** Unit (1 more, all golden-vectored): the three measured ratios
straight from the vendored rows; the errata polynomial vector to 4 digits; the caveat
present on polynomial energy notes; typed refusals for non-vendored nodes and missing
voltages. Live: the 4KB gbuf's real CACTI@32nm access time (0.2651 ns) scales to 0.0668 ns
at 7nm and its leakage (2.45 mW) to 0.78 mW; the D254 macro-flow test now carries the real
scaled access time instead of an arbitrary constant, provenance naming both chains, re-run
green. Regression: 1396 passed, 22 skipped.

**Implications.** Every macro number now has a sourced chain: area (bitcell + CACTI's own
efficiency, D256), access time and leakage (measured inverter ratios, this record). The
known limits, stated where they act: inverter scaling is a LOGIC proxy for SRAM timing
(SRAM-specific 7nm timing data would be better and does not publicly exist — same road-end
as D256); the macro liberty consumes access time but not yet leakage (a cell_leakage_power
attribute is a small follow-on); per-access energy at 7nm is available via
`scale_energy_pj` but deliberately still not composed into workload energy anywhere.

---

## D258. Validated against real ASAP7 macros: area survives, delay scaling is refused, leakage is caveated

**Decision.** The user judged the D257 timing/power numbers unconvincing; they were right,
and the check that settles it existed all along: OpenROAD-flow-scripts SHIPS ASAP7 SRAM
macros (`flow/platforms/asap7/lef|lib/fakeram7_*`) — an independent, published 7nm reference
this repo had not consulted. Fetching `fakeram7_256x32` (8192 bits at 0.7V: 351.1 um2 LEF
footprint, 218 ps `cell_rise`, 128.9 uW leakage) and comparing our chain:

| quantity | ours | reference | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| area | 0.0367 um2/bit | 0.0429 um2/bit | 0.86x (close, optimistic as stated) |
| access time | 66.8 ps | 218 ps | **0.31x — 3.2x too fast** |
| leakage | 23.9 nW/bit | 15.7 nW/bit | 1.5x (same order, conservative) |

The delay gap is a MODEL error, not a tolerance: an FO4 inverter chain scales with transistor
speed, while SRAM access time is dominated by bitline/wordline RC that does not. So
`scale_delay_ns` now REFUSES by default with the measured discrepancy in its message;
`allow_inverter_proxy=True` still returns the factor but stamps "3.2x optimistic" into the
note; and `reference_access_ns` returns the published 218 ps with its citation and an
explicit statement that size dependence is NOT modeled (the fakeram7 family varies little in
access time, and inventing a size law would be exactly the fabrication this repo forbids).
`scale_power_w` survives the check and now carries "validated within 1.5x (conservative)".
D256's area method is INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATED at 0.86x — the bitcell+efficiency route was
the right call.

**What was verified.** The comparison above, each reference number read from the fetched
files. Unit (1 more + 2 reworked): the delay refusal with its reason, the opt-in carrying the
warning, the published reference and its no-size-law disclosure, the leakage validation note;
the golden-vector test now opts in explicitly (the factor arithmetic is still correct — it is
the APPLICATION to SRAM that was wrong). Live: the macro-flow test now builds its macro with
the reference access time (3.2x slower and honest — the design still closes at 2 ns) and
gained a standing cross-check that our area-per-bit stays within 15% of the shipped
reference macro, so a drifting area chain fails a test rather than a report. Regression:
1397 passed, 22 skipped.

**Implications.** The lesson generalizes past this arc: when a published artifact of the
target technology exists, comparing against it beats any amount of internal consistency —
and this one was two HTTP fetches away while three decisions reasoned about scaling factors.
The fakeram7 macros are now the standing 7nm sanity reference. Deliberately NOT done:
vendoring them wholesale (they are a specific set of sizes; our generator serves arbitrary
ones), and back-fitting our chain to match them (that would make the reference unusable as an
independent check).

---

## D259. Sizes, shapes and ports: what the reference actually models, and where the dependence really comes from

**Decision.** Asked whether the scaling holds across sizes and ports, and whether access and
leakage should track bitcell count and efficiency the way area does, the whole fakeram7
family (9 macros, 1344 to 79872 bits) was fetched and tabulated. The result CORRECTS D258's
characterization of that reference and changes the access-time model.

**What the reference actually models.** Its LEF footprint and liberty area vary properly
(61.7 to 3387 um2; 0.0424-0.0950 um2/bit). Its access time is **218 ps in all nine files**
and its leakage **128.9 uW in all nine** — constants, not size-modeled values. So D258's
"3.2x too fast vs the reference" was a comparison against a placeholder: the PHYSICS
conclusion stands (an FO4 chain scales with transistor speed, SRAM access with bitline RC —
and 67 ps for a 4KB macro at 7nm is not credible), and 218 ps remains the number OpenROAD's
own ASAP7 flow closes timing against, but the reference is evidence for AREA only. D258's
leakage claim is likewise corrected: "validated within 1.5x" compared our size-varying
number against a constant, which validates nothing — our CACTI-derived leakage is the more
informative of the two.

**Where the dependence really comes from — measured.** CACTI models what the reference does
not (all at 32nm): access 148.8 ps at the reference geometry, 265.1 ps at 4KBx64, 315.0 ps
at 32KBx64; leakage 0.649 / 2.451 / 19.701 mW, i.e. ~75-79 nW per bit — nearly constant per
bit, so leakage really does track bitcell count as the question supposed; array efficiency
0.707 / 0.736 / 0.818, growing with size. And SHAPE matters as much as size: at identical
16384 bits, a wide 64x256 array runs 0.358 efficiency (0.4171 um2/bit) against 0.715
(0.2091) for a deep 256x64 — a 2.0x spread, which the published family independently shows
(0.0950 vs 0.0426 um2/bit for its own wide/square pair). Our area chain already captures all
of this, because the efficiency probe runs CACTI on the ACTUAL configuration rather than
assuming a constant.

**The change.** `anchored_access_ns` replaces the flat constant: access = the published
218 ps x CACTI's own access ratio between this configuration and the reference geometry AT
THE SAME NODE. Taking the ratio at one node cancels the technology term entirely, so no
delay-scaling factor is needed — precisely the factor D258 measured to be invalid for SRAM.
Absolute from the published macro, relative from the tool's own array model: 388 ps for a
4KBx64 buffer, 461 ps at 32KBx64, 222 ps at 2KBx256. **Ports**: the architecture translator
and CACTI both handle multi-port SRAM (attrs.ports r/w/rw), but the macro GENERATOR emits a
fixed 1RW pin interface — it now refuses anything else with a typed error rather than
emitting a LEF/liberty that misrepresents the requested ports.

**What was verified.** The nine-macro table and the five CACTI configurations above, every
number from a real fetch or run. Unit (2 more + 1 reworked): anchoring returns the reference
value at the reference geometry and a strictly larger value for a bigger array; the
size/shape dependence including the 2.0x wide-vs-deep area spread surviving the scaling
chain; the multi-port refusal. Live: the macro-flow test now builds with the anchored 388 ps
(not the flat 218, not the proxy's 67) and still closes at 2 ns. Regression: 1399 passed,
22 skipped.

**Implications.** Access, leakage and area now all vary with size and shape, each from the
source that actually models it. Remaining honest gaps: multi-port macros are refused rather
than generated (CACTI would cost them correctly — the pin-generation work is the blocker);
the anchor is one published macro at one shape, so the ratio carries CACTI's array model
into 7nm on the assumption that RELATIVE geometry effects scale, which is weaker than an
absolute claim but stronger than the flat constant it replaces; per-access energy remains
uncomposed.

---

## D260. OpenRAM cross-check: a real compiler bounds the analytical path, and the gap is periphery

**Decision.** The memory-area chain gained the strongest check available to it: OpenRAM (in
nixchip, now in the `.#physical` shell) is a real memory COMPILER — it generates an actual
layout and characterizes it, where CACTI solves analytical equations — and both support 45nm
(OpenRAM's freepdk45 vs CACTI's native node). So the same geometry can be built twice with
NO scaling in between, isolating the base of the chain from every 7nm question.

Measured, 256 words x 32 bits (8192 bits) at 45nm, both tools real:

| | OpenRAM (compiled layout) | CACTI (analytical) | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| area | 16004 um2 (1.95 um2/bit) | 3426 um2 (0.42 um2/bit) | **4.7x** |
| access | 293 ps | 209 ps | 1.4x |

At 64x32 the area ratio widens to 8.7x — small arrays are periphery-dominated, and the
compiler pays that in real layout while the analytical model assumes it away. The gap is
NOT the bitcell: CACTI's own reported efficiency here (70.7%) implies a ~0.30 um2 45nm 6T
cell, which is plausible; its optimism lives in the periphery/routing it assumes. An
academic compiler is also not a commercial one — OpenRAM's layouts are deliberately
conservative — so a real 45nm macro sits BETWEEN the two, which is why the new test asserts
a BAND (3.5-6.0x area, 1.2-1.8x access) rather than an equality.

**What was verified.** The table above, from real runs of both tools; the whole comparison
is now a reproducible integration test (`test_openram_crosscheck_live.py`, ~3 min, gated on
`openram-ram`, added to the physical CI job) that pins both absolutes, the two ratios, and
the implied-bitcell decomposition — so a drift in either tool, or in this repo's plumbing to
them, fails a test rather than sitting unnoticed in a report.

**Implications, stated carefully.** This does NOT invalidate the 7nm numbers: against the
published ASAP7 fakeram7 macro our 7nm area lands at 0.86x (D258), and that reference is
itself built from a bitcell-plus-efficiency model of the same family as ours. What it DOES
establish is the direction and rough magnitude of the analytical path's optimism at small
sizes — a 4.7x compiled-vs-analytical spread at 8 Kb, widening as arrays shrink. A campaign
comparing memory sizes is comparing consistently-derived numbers and remains sound; a
campaign whose ABSOLUTE area budget matters should read the band, not the point. The obvious
follow-on, now cheap because the tool is wired in: OpenRAM as a real macro source for
sky130/freepdk45 flows (it emits LEF and liberty directly, no generated black box needed) —
at 7nm it cannot help, since it has no FinFET technology.

---

## D261. The interconnect demo: a fabric DSE that answers a real question, and the two gaps it found

**Decision.** A runnable, LLM-free demonstration of the whole DSE stack on a posed problem:
28 clients x 128 bits reaching 32 banks CONCURRENTLY, minimize fabric area subject to
>= 600 MHz. New package `evaluators/interconnect` (deterministic RTL generators plus two
evaluators), a new search kind `interconnect_topology`, and `demos/interconnect_dse.py`.

Topology families, each reporting blocks, pipeline stages, peak concurrency and expected
served-per-cycle (analytic occupancy model for bank conflicts, stated as a model):
`xbar_multistage` with 1-3 stages and an explicit intermediate rank per stage (`ports: []` is
the direct crossbar; `[16]`, `[12, 6]` etc. concentrate), and `butterfly` radix-R networks.
Screening is an instant structural evaluator; escalation runs REAL Yosys + OpenROAD on ASAP7
per distinct arbitrated selector.

**The measured answer** (the demo's own output): the direct crossbar closes at **483 MHz** —
it FAILS the 600 MHz floor — and costs 0.0425 mm2; the radix-4 three-stage network makes
829 MHz at **0.0133 mm2**, a 3.2x area saving at identical concurrency (18.8 words/cycle
under uniform traffic) for 3 cycles of latency. The fabric is 17% of the 0.0765 mm2 of memory
it serves. The obvious answer is both too slow and too big, which is exactly the kind of
result a DSE exists to produce.

**Four real-tool findings, each fixed rather than worked around.** (1) A standalone 28:1 x
128b block has 3718 ports; place_pins refuses it (PPL-0024) and, forced onto a huge die, its
wire delay swamps the logic (-29.7 ns slack for ~0.5 ns of logic). Blocks are therefore
measured at widths that place at normal utilization and FITTED (`area = a + b*W`,
`delay = c + d*log2 W`); which widths fit is computed from pin count, not chosen. (2) Clocked
designs had no I/O delays, so input->flop paths were unconstrained and slack read INF — every
crossbar path is input->mux->flop, so the flow now sets them (`all_inputs -no_clocks`;
`remove_from_collection` does not exist in this OpenSTA). (3) No buffering step: a 5-bit
select driving ~3500 mux cells measured -127 ns until `repair_design` was added, opt-in so
every previously pinned number (D225/D237/D254) stays valid. (4) A round-robin arbiter
written with modulo arithmetic synthesized to a 28-deep chain (417 MHz); the mask-based
rewrite reaches 613 MHz at the same arity, and a shift-based mask update failed Yosys
outright — the arbiter, not the datapath mux, sets this block's frequency.

**Two campaign-machinery gaps the demo exposed, both closed.** (a) A CONSTRAINT on a metric
only a deeper rung produces (fmax) was demanded of screening trials, refusing every one:
`measured_at` now exists on constraints as it already did on objectives, and the deferred set
unions both. (b) A contender the rung RESOLVED negatively (measured, constraint violated)
still counted as missing coverage, so the composite frontier could never form — such
candidates are decided, not missing, and are now excluded from the coverage set.

**What was verified.** The demo runs end to end in the physical shell and prints the table
above; regression 1407 passed, 22 skipped. The repo's own registry-parity and conformance
tests then caught the packaging: one directory provides one backend, so the code is a shared
library (`interconnect/`, the topologies and RTL) plus two thin adapter packages
(`evaluators/interconnect_struct`, `evaluators/interconnect_phys`), and both evaluators gained
the ABI's `evaluate_batch`. Exactly the D26-class unreachability those guards exist for. Honest limits, stated
in the code: the 128-bit numbers are a fit over measured widths (identical in method across
topologies, so the comparison is sound); the throughput model assumes uniform independent
targets; the butterfly's reported throughput is an upper bound (internal blocking is not
modeled); inter-block routing between fabric stages is not placed, so the fabric's own
top-level wiring is not in the area.

**Implications.** The stack now demonstrates its capability on a question a designer would
actually ask, with no model in the loop. Named next steps: place the composed fabric as one
design (rather than composing measured blocks) to capture top-level routing; model
concentrator arbitration fairness; and a real NoC family via the existing booksim rung for
latency-under-load, which structural concurrency cannot express.

---

## D262. The search discovers its own space, and the demo is driven through the agent surface

**Decision.** Two corrections to D261's demo, both from the same objection: a DSE that
evaluates a list its caller wrote is not searching, and a demo that imports the campaign
runner is not exercising the product. (1) `search.kind: interconnect_topology` now accepts a
PROBLEM STATEMENT — `{clients, banks, width_bits, max_stages}` — and `enumerate_space`
derives the candidates: every divisor of the client count and of the bank count (ranks that
partition evenly), plus the powers of two in range, taken as 2-stage intermediate ranks and
as ordered PAIRS for 3-stage fabrics, plus every radix the port count admits; structurally
identical candidates collapse by block signature. From 28 clients and 32 banks that is **69
distinct topologies**, including the asymmetric shapes a power-of-two sweep never reaches
(7-then-8, 4-then-7) — 7 is a divisor of 28 and of nothing else in sight. An explicit
`variants` list still works for the case where a caller genuinely wants to pin the space.
(2) The demo drives `flux_campaign_start` / `_step` / `_status` / `_frontier` — the functions
the MCP tools wrap — instead of `run_campaign_steps`.

**What the search then found, with no list from anyone.** All 69 screened instantly; the
CI-aware contender set kept 11; the physical rung measured 7 as ok and REJECTED 4 on the
600 MHz floor (the 1-stage direct crossbar among them, at 483 MHz). Frontier: the radix-4
3-stage network at 0.0133 mm2 with full concurrency. Radix-16 at 622 MHz and radix-32 at
1012 MHz appear in the measured set — points a hand-written variant list would very likely
have omitted, since nothing about the problem statement suggests them.

**What was verified.** The demo runs end to end through the tool surface and prints the table
in `demos/README.md`; regression 1407 passed, 22 skipped. The budget latch is visible in the
demo's own history: at 32 evaluations the campaign stopped mid-screen with
`budget_exhausted` — correct behavior, and the grant is now sized to the discovered space.

**Implications.** The remaining hand-authored input is the topology FAMILY set (multistage
crossbar, butterfly): a family the library cannot express is invisible to the search, which is
the honest boundary of "discovery" here. Two named extensions: the `generative` strategy
(D233) could propose fabric structures outside the enumerated families, and the `agentic`
strategy could choose which contenders to escalate when the physical rung is expensive —
neither is needed at this space size, where screening the whole space costs nothing.

---

## D263. Parallel-switch fabrics: the structure the rank model could not express

**Decision.** A fourth topology family, `xbar_staged`, taking stages as explicit parallel
switches — `[{switches: 7, in: 4, out: 4}, {switches: 4, in: 7, out: 8}]` for "first stage
4x4, second stage 7x8". This is not a re-parameterization of `xbar_multistage`: there a stage
is one monolithic crossbar between consecutive ranks, so a 28->28 stage costs 28 selectors of
arity 28; here the same transition costs 7 switches x 4 outputs = 28 selectors of arity FOUR,
which is why real fabrics are built this way. Chaining, admission and drive are validated
(stage i's emitted links must equal stage i+1's taken links; the first stage must admit every
client, the last must drive every bank), and internal blocking is explicitly NOT modeled, so
the reported throughput is an upper bound like the butterfly's. `search.extra_variants` lets a
caller name such a structure alongside the discovered space, since enumeration covers families,
not every structure a designer might have in mind.

**Measured, in the same run as everything else** (real Yosys + OpenROAD, ASAP7):
7x(4x4) -> 4x(7x8) is **0.0198 mm2 at 829 MHz**, 2 stages, full concurrency; the mirrored
4x(7x7) -> 7x(4x5) is 0.0192 mm2 at the same frequency. Both sit between the radix networks
(0.0133-0.0250) and the rejected direct crossbar (0.0425 at 483 MHz), and both beat every
monolithic 2-stage crossbar the search enumerated (0.0500 at best) — the parallel-switch
decomposition buys a 2.5x area saving at identical rank structure, which is exactly the effect
the rank model could not see.

**What was verified.** The demo prints all nine measured contenders and the four
constraint-rejected ones; regression 1407 passed, 22 skipped. The family's structural
validation is exercised by the demo's own two specs (a mismatched chain raises rather than
silently mis-costing).

**Implications.** The search now covers three families by enumeration (multistage crossbar,
butterfly, and — via extra_variants — staged) and one by naming. The honest gap is unchanged
and now sharper: enumeration cannot invent a family, so a structure like a Benes network or a
ring is invisible until someone adds it or a generative strategy proposes it. Blocking-aware
throughput (booksim, which this repo already has as a rung) is the natural next fidelity step
for the families whose numbers are currently upper bounds.

---

## D264. Widening rounds, a bigger space, and a measurement the store was throwing away

**Decision.** Three changes, from the question "69 candidates seems pessimistic, and can it
widen gradually?". (1) `enumerate_staged` enumerates the parallel-switch family from the
problem — for each first-stage switch count, each fan-out, and each way of chaining into
following stages — which is where Clos-shaped fabrics live (a middle stage wide enough to be
non-blocking is just one of the enumerated chains). With `breadth="wide"` the space for 28
clients / 32 banks grows from 69 to **1242 candidates**; screening stays instant because it
is structural. (2) The demo runs WIDENING ROUNDS: 2-stage narrow, 3-stage narrow, 2-stage
wide, 3-stage wide (16, 71, 279, 1242 candidates). Each round is its own campaign identity
but shares one result store, so a later round re-measures nothing — the durable store turns
"widen the scope" into a cheap operation rather than a restart. `--rounds`, `--budget` and
`--db` are flags; the final table aggregates every fabric measured across all rounds.
(3) `CampaignStore.trials` now returns the stored `Result` for EVERY status, not only `ok`.

**Why (3) matters more than it looks.** A constraint_violated trial is a MEASUREMENT that was
paid for: the direct crossbar really was synthesized and placed and really did come out at
483 MHz. The loader silently withheld that Result from every reader — the demo could not
print why a fabric was rejected, and D243's knowledge mining could never learn "this shape
misses timing at this frequency". `ok_trials` still filters by status, so nothing that ranks
or escalates changes; only the readback does.

**What was verified.** The 2-round run completes end to end through the agent surface and
prints nine measured fabrics with the winner at 0.0133 mm2; regression 1407 passed, 22
skipped after the store change. `demos/README.md` now carries the exact commands plus the
two verification recipes — re-querying the frontier through the same MCP-wrapped tool, and
dumping each measured number's provenance (evaluator string, per-block areas and delays, the
fit widths used).

**Implications.** Space size is no longer the limiting factor; the physical rung is, and it is
bounded by DISTINCT selector arities rather than candidate count (the fit cache), which is why
1242 candidates cost barely more than 71. The named residue from D263 stands: enumeration
widens within families, so a family nobody wrote — ring, mesh, buffered crossbar,
multipumped fabric — is still invisible, and the last of those is the one our own measured
frequency headroom (829 MHz against a 600 MHz floor) argues hardest for.

---

## D265: Three ways a fabric flattered itself, and the fits that were not comparable

**Context.** The interconnect DSE reported `xbar_staged-28x1x1-28x1x2` as the smallest fabric
meeting every constraint. The reaction to that — "I doubt it has full throughput or is as small
as it claims, same with many other xbars" — was correct on three separate counts, and each one
had a different cause.

**Decision.**

*Reachability is a constraint, not an accident of arithmetic.* `staged_crossbar` checked only
that consecutive stages' link counts chained and that the last stage drove enough ports. A
chain of 28 switches of 1x1 into 28 switches of 1x2 satisfies both and is not a crossbar: a
client entering a 1x1 switch reaches two banks, not thirty-two. The product of per-stage
fan-outs must be at least the bank count, or every client cannot address every bank and the
structure does not solve the stated problem. The wide enumeration fell from 1242 to 1108 valid
candidates, and the shapes that vanished were exactly the ones topping the ranking.

*Multistage fabrics were being credited with a crossbar's throughput.* The model charged bank
conflicts only, so a radix-4 network and a direct crossbar both reported 18.85 words per cycle
while differing several-fold in area. Replaced with stage-by-stage load propagation (Patel,
IEEE Trans. Computers C-30, 1981): a switch output's load is `1 - (1 - p/out)**in`, applied
per stage. For a one-stage crossbar this reduces to the occupancy result, so the two agree
exactly where they should; the radix-4 network fell to 13.13.

*Composed cell area prices gates and not wires.* Summing measured block areas systematically
flatters a fabric of many tiny switches, because what connects them is invisible to the sum.
`interstage_link_bits` is now a first-class metric and objective, so the omitted burden is
visible and rankable rather than silently absent.

*And the physical fits were not comparable across arities.* A 32:1 selector reported a FASTER
128-bit path than a 28:1 one, which no arrangement of transistors can do. Two causes, both
methodological. The fit widths were chosen per arity by what would place within a single pin
layer pair, so different arities were extrapolated from different data; extra pin layers now
buy the capacity for one width set (8, 16, 32) shared by every arity. And the width term was
fitted per arity over three points, which fits noise: delay is nearly FLAT in width — a 8:1
selector measures 902, 898, 872 ps at 8, 16, 32 bits, because a mux's critical path is its
select tree and widening replicates the datapath in parallel. Per-arity slopes ranged from -15
to +436 ps per octave; extrapolated two octaves to 128 bits, that noise swamped the real arity
ordering. The width slope is now pooled across all arities and only the intercept is per-arity.

*And the escalation stopped after one wave.* Contenders are the screened frontier, so once the
direct crossbar dominated every screened objective it was escalated alone, failed the 600 MHz
constraint, and the round ended with a single measured fabric — the constraint had eliminated
the only candidate that had earned measurement, and nothing took its place. `_run_escalation`
now loops: after each wave it recomputes the contender set over the trials NOT yet eliminated
by a constraint violation, and escalates whatever newly surfaces, up to twelve waves or the
budget. A round that measured one fabric now measures fourteen.

**Consequence.** The 128-bit fits became monotone in arity — 2:1 at 1241 MHz down to 32:1 at
406 MHz — and with it the whole answer changed: no single-stage 28-to-32 crossbar reaches 600
MHz, because its selectors are arity 28 and 32. The frequency target can only be met by
fabrics built from switches of arity 8 or less, which is a real engineering conclusion the
earlier arithmetic had hidden. A butterfly was also found pricing only its request path while
every other family priced its response muxes too; a radix-32 butterfly over 32 ports IS a
direct crossbar, so the two must cost about the same, and now do.

**Implications.** Every one of these was invisible until the search put incomparable things on
one table, which is an argument for breadth in a DSE independent of finding a better design.
The first unit tests for this subsystem landed with the fixes.

---

## D266: The throughput number, measured

**Context.** Of the three numbers the interconnect DSE reported, area and frequency came from
Yosys and OpenROAD on real ASAP7 and throughput came from a model. That asymmetry is exactly
where D265's flattery had lived, and no amount of fixing a model settles what a model asserts.

**Decision.** Generate the WHOLE fabric as synthesisable SystemVerilog — every switch of every
stage, wired by shuffle — drive it with uniform-random traffic under Verilator, and count the
transfers the banks accept. One offered request per client per cycle, dropped and retried on a
lost arbitration, which is precisely the analytic model's own assumption, so the two are
comparable. Throughput on the escalation rung is now this measurement, at ~5-8 s per fabric
against minutes for place-and-route.

Building it for real forced two things the model never had to face. Routing became
CONSTRUCTIVE: the generator computes which output port reaches which bank over the actual
wiring and refuses a topology where some client cannot reach some bank, which is the sufficient
condition D265's fan-out product only approximates. And route selection became explicit, which
turned out to matter more than any topology parameter (see D267).

**Consequence.** Measured against RTL, the analytic model is exact for a direct crossbar
(18.85 both ways) and for single-path parallel-switch fabrics (14.89 against 14.88), 9% high
for a concentrating multistage, and 21% LOW for a Clos at m = n — it assumes each switch picks
among its outputs at random, so it understates any fabric whose router load-balances across
several valid paths. An earlier reading of this repo's own numbers, that the model was up to
47% optimistic for butterflies, was an artifact of the generator's first routing policy and is
withdrawn; under rotating path selection radix-4 measures 13.54 against a modelled 13.13.

A second latch fired in the same place and is worth separating from the first. A screening
trial spends one evaluation from a campaign's grant exactly as a place-and-route does, so the
demo's flat per-round grant of 400 starved its own widest round: 1137 candidates consumed the
entire budget on screening, the round ended `budget_exhausted` having escalated NOTHING, and the
printed frontier was built entirely from the narrower rounds while the output still announced
four. Grants are now sized to the round's own space plus escalation headroom. The round that had
measured nothing measures thirty-two, and one of them — a parallel-switch fabric reaching 17.10
words/cycle at 0.0276 mm2 and 746 MHz — is arguably the best design in the study and appears in
no other round. A campaign that stops early is visible in its status; a REPORT that silently
aggregates such a campaign is not, which is why the demo now prints candidates against screened
per round.

**Implications.** The screen model stays where it belongs, ranking a thousand candidates
cheaply, with its error now characterised rather than assumed: use it to rank, not to quote.

One operational note, recorded because it cost a full run: a Verilator build directory is tens
of megabytes, a widening round measures hundreds of fabrics, and the first version kept every
one of them. The temp filesystem filled mid-campaign and took the run down with it. Measurement
harnesses that run per-candidate have to clean up per-candidate.

---

## D267: An IP catalog that has to build what it lists

**Context.** The ask was for referenceable IP alongside the specs and mined facts — standard
crossbars, Clos networks, simple NoCs — on a lightweight interface such as OBI or AXI-Stream.

**Decision.** A catalog with one rule: an entry is listed only if Flux can BUILD it. Every
entry names a generator that produces a `Topology`, which produces SystemVerilog, which the
simulator and the ASAP7 flow then measure — so "the catalog offers a Clos" means the tool can
construct, route, simulate and place one. Entries carry parameters, cost shape, when to use,
known limits, published references, and, kept deliberately separate from those references,
what this repo has measured. Status is `constructible`, `evaluable_only` (a mesh NoC, reachable
through the BookSim and Noxim evaluators, whose numbers are not comparable to placed silicon),
or `not_implemented` (a ring, listed so its absence is explicit). Reachable as
`flux_ip_catalog`, which also instantiates an entry into the Architecture IR a campaign takes.

Interfaces are described to the same standard. OBI is a NATIVE fit and the reason is
structural: a lost arbitration is exactly `req` asserted without `gnt`, which is the
drop-and-retry the switches already implement. AXI4-Stream is NOT, and the catalog says so —
AXI-Stream forbids withdrawing an unaccepted `tvalid`, so it needs a per-input skid buffer that
is not generated here and that would change the measured throughput. Picking an interface on a
false compatibility claim is the mistake a catalog exists to prevent.

Clos was the family genuinely missing, and adding it was worth it twice over. Its parameters
carry published conditions — strictly non-blocking for m >= 2n-1 (Clos, 1953), rearrangeably
non-blocking for m >= n (Benes, 1965) — that are about CIRCUIT switching, and the catalog
refuses to translate them into packet-mode promises. Measured instead: C(n=4,m=2) 9.00
words/cycle, C(n=4,m=4) 15.46, C(n=4,m=7) 15.47. The knee is at m = n; satisfying the
strict-sense condition added ~75% more inter-stage wiring for 0.01 words per cycle.

**Consequence.** The first attempt measured 4.86 for m = 2, 4, 7 AND 8 — identical — because
the router took the first path that reached the destination, so every request used middle
switch 0 and the rest of the middle stage was built and unreachable. A Clos is non-blocking
BECAUSE something chooses among the middle switches. Routing tables became lists of every
valid port and each input rotates among them. That fixed half of it; the other half was that
all inputs of a switch advanced their rotation counters in lockstep from zero, so they picked
the same port in the same cycle, collapsing an m-way stage to one usable port. Seeding each
counter to its input index fixed it, and only then did m matter.

A smaller bug rode along and is worth naming because it is the kind that survives review: every
Clos was labelled `clos`. Labels are what tables, frontiers and reports identify a fabric BY, so
thirty measured configurations collapsed into one row and twenty-nine measurements were invisible
behind whichever was written last. The label builder is now one importable function that must
name every distinguishing parameter, and the proposer REFUSES to generate two different variants
sharing a label rather than trusting that function to stay complete.

**Implications.** Routing policy is a first-class design variable and is not currently in the
search space: the same radix-4 butterfly measures 8.92 or 13.54 depending on it alone, a wider
spread than most topology choices in this study produce. A quoted throughput without its
routing policy is not a number.

---

## D268: A throughput number is not a correctness claim, and a store outlives its evaluator

**Context.** Two questions about the interconnect demo's own output — is every fabric really
implemented in RTL, and is any of it tested for correctness — landed on a table that contained
a `butterfly-radix32` row reading 0.0250 mm2 at 1012 MHz. That row is impossible under the
current method: a radix-32 butterfly over 32 ports IS a direct crossbar, its selectors are
32:1, and 32:1 measures 406 MHz.

**Decision, part one: the evaluator's identity carries its method version.** The row was real,
and it was measured — by code that no longer exists. A campaign store is durable by design, so
it outlives the evaluator that filled it, and the demo's final table aggregates every campaign
in the store. Its provenance said `interconnect_phys@asap7`, which is the same string the
current code writes, so nothing distinguished a result produced by the superseded per-arity fit
(D265) from one produced after it. The evaluator id is now
`interconnect_phys@asap7/<method>`, bumped whenever a change moves measured values — fit
widths or slope, what blocks a topology is charged for, where throughput comes from — and the
demo excludes results from any other method version, counting and NAMING them rather than
silently dropping or silently mixing them.

**Decision, part two: the simulation checks the fabric, not just its rate.** The testbench
counted transfers accepted at the banks and nothing else. A fabric that delivered every word to
the wrong bank would have reported exactly the same words-per-cycle as a correct one; so would
one that corrupted payloads, or starved a client outright. Throughput measures how much a
structure moves. Three checks now ride along on stimulus that already carried what they need:

* **Routing** — the destination is derived from the payload itself, so a word arriving at bank
  b must satisfy `data mod BANKS == b`. One assertion covers the routing tables, the shuffle
  wiring and every switch's port selection, end to end.
* **Integrity** — the next 32 payload bits carry the complement of the first 32, so any bit
  dropped, held or crossed between payloads is caught.
* **Starvation** — the next 8 carry the client id, giving a per-client delivery census. A
  client that some bank cannot serve shows up here and in no aggregate number.

A routing or integrity failure RAISES rather than returning, and the evaluator deliberately
does not catch it into its analytic-model fallback: a fabric that delivers to the wrong bank is
not a slow candidate, it is a broken one, and a modelled number would keep it in the running
with a clean-looking score.

**Consequence.** All five families pass with zero misroutes and zero corrupted payloads, and
per-client delivery ratios of 0.86 to 0.96. The negative control is the part worth keeping: one
swapped entry in a crossbar's last-stage routing table produces 3,269 misdelivered words over
3,000 cycles and fails the measurement. A check that has only ever passed is not evidence.

**Implications.** What is verified is behavioural, under uniform-random traffic, on the
generated netlist — not a proof, and not a check of the placed silicon, which remains a
per-arity block composition rather than one placed fabric. Deadlock and fairness under
adversarial patterns are untested, and the bufferless drop-and-retry design is what makes that
tolerable for now: there is nothing to deadlock on.

---

## D269: The local model on the proposing side, and only there

**Context.** The interconnect demo used no model at all — by request, it had to run without
Claude — and the observation that followed was fair: nothing in the flow decides, generates or
interprets, and the local Ollama sits idle. The ask was to use the local model to improve
generation and orchestration.

**Decision.** A fourth proposer strategy, `generative_interconnect`, in which a local
qwen2.5-coder:7b proposes fabric STRUCTURES directly rather than picking from an enumerated
grid. What makes that safe rather than reckless is the division of labour: the model proposes,
and the deterministic machinery disposes. Every proposal is built by the real constructor
(which refuses stages that do not chain and fabrics that cannot reach every bank), routed
constructively, screened, placed on ASAP7 and simulated with D268's correctness checks —
exactly what an enumerated candidate faces. A bad proposal costs one evaluation. It cannot
produce a wrong answer, and it cannot reach the results table without being measured.

The honesty contract of the existing LLM strategies carries over unchanged: `deterministic=
False`, the model name, sha256 of the exact prompt and response, and a seeded deterministic
fallback whose reason is recorded rather than silently swapped in.

**Consequence.** Three findings, all measured against the real model on this machine.

*A 7B model cannot do the arithmetic, so it should not be asked to.* Proposing stages as
`{switches, in, out}` failed three times in four, always the same way: consecutive stages
disagreeing on their link count ("stage 1 emits 112 links but stage 2 takes 32"). That is
consistency across three coupled numbers, not a design decision. The model now chooses only
what IS a decision — switch count and fan-out per stage — and the input counts are derived, so
the rule cannot be broken because it is no longer expressible. This is the same shape as D235's
primers: do not ask a small model for what it will get wrong.

*A refusal the model never sees is a lesson it cannot learn.* Feeding the previous rejection
reason into the next prompt took the valid-proposal rate from one in four to, in the full
demo round, ten out of ten with no fallback used at all.

*An open-ended proposer must be capped, or it never stops proposing.* The runner advances to
escalation when a proposer returns `None`; it never consults `done()`. The first LLM round
therefore proposed until the budget latched and measured nothing it had proposed — the same
failure as the flat per-round grant, arriving by a different route. `strategy.max_proposals`
now ends the screening phase, and the cap is expressed as `None` from `propose()` because that
is what the runner actually reads.

**Implications, stated plainly.** On this problem the model found nothing the enumeration had
not: its best proposal, `7x(4x4) -> 4x(7x8)` at 0.0198 mm2 and 746 MHz, is already on the
enumerated frontier — though it is notable that a 7B model reached it unaided, having been
given only the problem and this repo's measured arity-to-frequency table. That is the expected
result where exhaustive enumeration is affordable, and it locates where this is actually worth
spending: spaces too large to enumerate, and families nobody has written a generator for. The
model still cannot invent a ring, a mesh or a buffered switch here, because it can only propose
within families `build()` knows. Orchestration proper — deciding the next round's scope from
what has been measured, rather than following a fixed round table — remains deterministic.

---

## D271: The rank-named crossbar was the parallel-switch fabric all along

**Context.** A direct question — what is the difference between `xbar_staged` and
`xbar_multistage`, and can they be merged — with a better answer than expected: not only are
they the same family, the duplication was producing two concrete faults.

**Decision.** `multistage_crossbar` now builds the `xbar_staged` fabric it has always
described, keeping only its naming. A rank transition is a row of parallel switches like any
other: rank `n` means `n` switches, each concentrating ceil(prev/n) inputs into one link. The
conversion was already written and already used — `canonical_stages` had to do it before any
RTL could be generated — so the family had two implementations of one idea, and they had
drifted.

**Consequence.** Both faults were invisible from inside either implementation.

*Its throughput model charged hardware it never built.* For `ports=[8]`, the stage-load model
saw one 28-input, 8-output stage while the block accounting bought eight arity-4 selectors. The
screen and the silicon were describing different fabrics, measured as the 9% screen-versus-RTL
gap this family alone showed (D266). The merged form reports the switches it actually buys.

*Three-rank forms did not chain.* `ports=[7, 8]` produced a stage emitting 7 links into a stage
taking 8 — a fabric no generator can wire. Those candidates were enumerated, screened,
escalated and placed, and their throughput silently fell back to the analytic model because
their RTL could not be built. Every 3-rank crossbar in the study was therefore unverified. With
stages derived rather than stated, every form chains and routes, and `[7, 8]` correctly dedups
into `[7, 7]` — seven links cannot feed eight ranks, so that fabric IS `[7, 7]`.

**Implications.** The enumerated space shrank without losing anything real: the duplicates it
lost were duplicates. The general lesson is narrower than "merge similar things" — it is that a
conversion function written to serve one consumer (here, RTL generation) is often the proof
that two abstractions are one, and leaving both in place lets them disagree about the same
design.

---

## D272: One RTL for both questions, and what composition was hiding

**Context.** "When running the demo, are area and fmax based on OpenROAD place-and-route from
synthesis? If not we should base ourselves on actual evaluation and not analytical models."
They were real tool output, and they were not what the question meant.

**Decision.** Generate one RTL that is both simulated and synthesised, and measure the WHOLE
fabric, not a composition of per-arity blocks.

The fabric had two descriptions and neither was checked against the other. Throughput came
from a switch module with routing ROMs, destination decode and modulo arithmetic — simulatable
under Verilator, rejected outright by Yosys (`localparam int RT [32]`). Area and frequency came
from `arbitrated_selector_rtl`, a mask-arbitrated mux containing NO routing logic at all, placed
once per arity in isolation and multiplied by count. So the composed numbers priced a design
that was missing the destination decode, the routing tables, and every wire between switches.

The switch RTL is now synthesisable: routing tables packed into flat constant vectors, the
rotation modulo unrolled into conditional subtraction, and the same mask-and-priority arbiter
the standalone selector uses. Behaviour is unchanged — the same throughput to four digits and
the same zero misroutes — which is the point of having the D268 checks.

**Consequence.** Placing the complete design says something the composition could not, and it
is not a margin. Measured on ASAP7 at 128 bits, composed against whole-fabric:

| fabric | composed | whole | composed | whole | whole |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | mm2 | mm2 | MHz | MHz | mW |
| staged 7x(4x4)->4x(7x8) | 0.0198 | 0.0122 | 746 | 120 | 16.0 |
| staged 4x(7x8)->8x(4x4) | 0.0209 | 0.0130 | 746 | 71 | 34.1 |
| staged 2x(14x4)->4x(2x8) | 0.0112 | 0.0067 | 608 | 187 | 23.7 |
| butterfly radix-8 | 0.0286 | 0.0169 | 754 | 43 | 68.0 |

Composition is pessimistic on area by ~40% (it multiplies a standalone block's periphery by
count, where synthesis optimises across the design) and optimistic on frequency by 5x to 17x.
Worse, it does not preserve the ORDER: it calls the radix-8 butterfly the fastest fabric in the
study, and placed whole it is the slowest; it calls `2x(14x4)->4x(2x8)` the slowest qualifier,
and placed whole it is the fastest. A screen that mis-ranks is still useful for pruning and
must not be reported as the answer.

The gap is wiring. A 128-bit fabric moves 3,584-bit buses between stages, and the placement
shows it: 5,617 repair buffers, 708 slew violations, 1.4 million um of half-perimeter
wirelength on a 170 um die. It is not missing registers — every switch registers its outputs,
so stages are already flop-to-flop, and boundary-registering the I/O moves 100 MHz only to 138.
Power, which the composed rung never reported at all, arrives with this measurement.

**Implications.** The whole-fabric number carries its own pessimism and should not be quoted as
final either: the design is placed standalone with ~7,880 top-level pins and no floorplan, so a
placer that knows nothing about which switches belong together spreads buses across a die sized
for the pins. A real block would be floorplanned by stage. The defensible claim is the
direction and the re-ranking, not the absolute 43 MHz. What follows is that this study's
frequency conclusions need re-stating against whole-fabric numbers, and that routing (rather
than placement) is now the next fidelity step worth paying for.

---

## D273: The generated switch, made worth synthesising

**Context.** The first synthesisable fabric placed at 120 MHz for a topology a person had built
close to 600 MHz. The topology was not the problem.

**Decision.** Three RTL faults, each on the critical path, each fixed without changing what the
fabric does (throughput identical to four digits, zero misroutes throughout):

* **A runtime modulo.** Reducing a free-running rotation counter modulo the number of valid
  ports, by unrolled conditional subtraction, is a serial chain of subtractors per input. It is
  folded into the ROM at generation time: the table is indexed by (destination, raw counter)
  and stores the port, so rotation costs one lookup and no arithmetic.
* **Per-input work done per output.** Which port an input wants depends only on the input, and
  it was computed inside the per-output loop, so a 32-output switch built 32 copies of the
  decode. Hoisted.
* **No register inside the switch.** Decode, ROM lookup, eligibility, a fan_in-deep priority
  arbiter and a 128-bit mux were one combinational path between the stage registers. The switch
  is now two pipeline stages, decode then arbitrate-and-mux, and the arbiter resolves to a
  one-hot grant (`x & -x`) that drives the mux enables directly instead of an `integer` index
  feeding one 32-bit comparator per input.

**Consequence.** A standalone 7x8 switch went from 427 to 524 MHz. Latency is two cycles per
stage now, and the evaluator reports it — a pipeline register that quietly halved the reported
latency accuracy would have been worse than the frequency it bought.

**Implications.** These were RTL faults, not design faults, and none of them was visible in
simulation: Verilator resolves a variable part-select and a barrel shifter identically. Only
synthesis distinguishes them, which is the argument for generating RTL that goes through both.

---

## D274: Four ways to measure a frequency that is not the design's

**Context.** "How do we get actual values of the interconnect with correct fmax?" Every number
this study had reported was wrong, and each was wrong for a different reason.

**Decision.** Measure the fabric IN CONTEXT, with the whole datapath live, with the reset
excepted, and read the timing path rather than inferring it. Each of those four exists because
its absence produced a confident, wrong number.

*Standalone placement is pin-limited.* The fabric's client and bank buses are top-level ports —
about 7,880 at 28x128 into 32x128 — and a placer sizes the die to fit that perimeter, landing
at 41% utilisation on a die far larger than the logic needs. `synthesis_harness_rtl` wraps the
fabric in a synthesisable generator and signature checker, so those buses become internal nets
and the die is sized by cells.

*Synthesis prunes what is not driven and not observed, and the pruning is silent.* Three
separate versions of that harness measured a fabric nobody asked for: one drove 32 live bits
into a 128-bit datapath (three quarters constant-folded away); one drove lanes that differed
only by a constant, so synthesis built one lane's mux and XORed the rest; one observed only the
low 32 bits of each bank, so the upper three quarters had no reader. Each looked like a
frequency improvement — 287 MHz, 298 MHz — and each was a smaller design. Cell count against
the standalone build is what caught it: 64,748 where the real fabric is 256,009.

*A reset port is not a datapath, and it dominated everything.* Driven from a pad, `rst_n` fans
out to every flop: measured at 18,568 sinks, 10.4 pF, 17.9 ns through one weak NAND. That path
set every frequency this study reported — 120, 67, 55 MHz — until the timing report was read.
Real flows build a reset tree during CTS, which a placement-only flow does not run, so
`run_ppa_flow` gained a `reset_port` that excepts it. Stated rather than hidden: reset
recovery/removal is now unchecked and a real implementation still owes the tree.

*Guessing at a critical path is not analysis.* Three wrong guesses were made in a row — a barrel
shifter from a variable part-select, a missing pipeline register, the harness's own XOR fold —
each plausible, each producing a real improvement to the RTL, none of them the actual limiter.
The flow now emits `report_checks` alongside the slack number, and the reset path was obvious
the moment it was printed.

**Consequence.** With all four in place, at 128 bits on ASAP7, placement-only:

| fabric | composed mm2 | mm2 | composed MHz | MHz | mW | cells |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| staged 7x(4x4)->4x(7x8) | 0.0198 | 0.0229 | 746 | 392 | 71.2 | 256,009 |
| staged 4x(7x8)->8x(4x4) | 0.0209 | 0.0237 | 746 | 345 | 79.9 | 266,295 |
| staged 2x(14x4)->4x(2x8) | 0.0112 | 0.0164 | 608 | 327 | 61.7 | 170,865 |
| butterfly radix-8 | 0.0286 | 0.0270 | 754 | 374 | 80.9 | 318,116 |
| direct crossbar | 0.0425 | 0.0333 | 406 | 215 | 135.0 | 452,908 |

The composed screen now reads as what it is: optimistic on frequency by roughly 2x and
understating area, but broadly order-preserving — the crossbar is worst on both, the staged
fabrics best. That is a usable screen. It was not usable when it claimed 746 MHz against a
measured 55.

**Implications.** 392 MHz against the ~600 MHz a person reached by hand is a gap worth naming
rather than closing on paper: this is placement-only with no routing and no floorplan, and the
switch microarchitecture is this repo's own. Routing, and stage-level placement constraints,
are the next fidelity steps. What should not survive is any published number from before the
reset was excepted.

---

## D275: RTL changes that helped, and one that did not

**Context.** A person who had built the same topology by hand reported 600+ MHz where this
repo's generated switch measured far less, and asked for the RTL to be fixed rather than
explained.

**Decision.** Three changes to the generated switch, each measured, plus one reverted.

*Fold the rotation into the ROM.* Reducing a free-running counter modulo the valid-port count
by unrolled conditional subtraction is a serial chain of subtractors per input. The table is
now indexed by (destination, raw counter) and stores the port directly.

*Drop the rotation entirely where there is one path.* Most fabrics are single-path at every
switch; the counter, its register and half the ROM index are then pure overhead. Measured
effect on frequency: none — Yosys was already constant-folding it — but the RTL is smaller and
says what it means.

*Make the counter wrap at the PORT COUNT.* It spanned a power of two, so seven middle switches
were served by eight counter values and port 0 was chosen twice as often as its peers. A Clos
C(n=4, m=7) measured 14.35 words/cycle against the 15.47 a uniform rotation gives. The
correctness harness did not catch this — it is not incorrect, only unfair — which is worth
noting about what harnesses do and do not cover.

*And one revert.* Replacing `grant = active & (~active + 1)` with a prefix-OR, on the reasoning
that an increment is a ripple-carry chain and a prefix could be a log-depth tree, measured
314 MHz against the increment's 524. A sequential prefix loop synthesises to a literal ripple,
while the increment maps onto the library's own carry logic. The comment stays in the code so
the next reader does not retry it.

**Implications.** None of these was visible in simulation — Verilator resolves a variable
part-select and a barrel shifter identically — and two of the four intuitions were wrong in a
way only measurement settled. Generate RTL that goes through both a simulator and a synthesiser,
and measure before believing.

---

## D276: Vendoring proven IP, and the front end that made it possible

**Context.** Asked to vendor `xbar_varlat` — the PULP logarithmic interconnect, whose
`rr_arb_tree` muxes data as it arbitrates — and to use the same ideas for the other fabrics.

**Decision.** `interconnect/vendor/` carries the IP byte-identical to upstream (PULP
`cluster_interconnect` @ 2967d8d1 and `common_cells`, Apache-2.0 WITH SHL-2.1, plus the OBI
wrapper and types from github.com/choelzl/rtl-lab), with provenance recorded per file.
`vendored.py` assembles it into the same topologies `topology.py` describes: one `crossbar`
instance per switch, wired stage to stage by the same shuffle, routed by address bit-slices
derived from the stage fan-outs. `supports()` states what it cannot express — address-slice
routing needs power-of-two fan-outs multiplying to the bank count, so a Clos with seven middle
switches is out — rather than failing at elaboration.

**Consequence.** Yosys's built-in reader cannot synthesise this IP: type parameters, `$bits` of
a type, `unsigned'()` casts, module-header package imports, `return` in functions, and
packed-array width inference all sit outside its subset. Five yielded to documented,
behaviour-preserving rewrites applied at load; the sixth did not. `yosys-slang` — already in
nixchip, which this repo already cherry-picks from — reads all of it unmodified, and is now in
the `.#physical` shell with `run_ppa_flow(sv_frontend="slang")` to use it. That is a general
capability: this repo can now synthesise real SystemVerilog IP, not only the subset it
generates for itself. The rewrite layer survives as a labelled fallback, and every result says
which front end produced it.

**Implications.** The comparison the vendoring was for now runs: at 7x(4x4) -> 4x(7x8) on ASAP7,
the vendored fabric measures 240 MHz / 0.0159 mm2 / 6.7 mW against the generated one's
454 MHz / 0.0230 mm2 / 70.4 mW. The generated switch is pipelined two deep per stage and the
vendored one is combinational across both levels, so the trade is legible rather than a verdict:
the generated fabric buys frequency with latency and area, the vendored one is a quarter of the
power and two thirds of the area. An earlier claim here that the generated switch was "several
times slower" than the vendored one is withdrawn — it was not, and the difference was the flow.

---

## D277: Four measurement artifacts, each of which looked like a design

**Context.** Chasing a frequency that would not rise, on a design a person had built faster by
hand. Each artifact below was found by reading the timing path, and each had been silently
setting the number before it was.

**Decision and consequence.**

*The reset net.* Driven from a pad, `rst_n` reaches every flop — 18,568 sinks, 10.4 pF, 17.9 ns
through one weak NAND. It set every frequency this study reported until it was excepted;
55 MHz became 392. CTS builds this tree in a real flow, and a placement-only flow does not run
CTS, so `run_ppa_flow` gained `reset_port`. Stated, not hidden: reset recovery and removal go
unchecked and a real implementation still owes the tree.

*The harness's own readout.* `signature <= acc[rd]` is a 128-to-1 mux of 32-bit words, and every
one of the four worst paths started at its read pointer. Replaced by a chain in which each
accumulator feeds the next, so all banks stay observed at two XOR levels of depth. This was the
THIRD time the measuring rig was the thing being measured — the others being a 128-deep XOR fold
and a datapath that synthesis had pruned for want of observation.

*Design rules imposed without measuring them.* `set_max_fanout 16` was added because a fanout-33
net looked wrong, and it makes `repair_design` split every wide net into groups of sixteen with
weak `HB3xp67` buffers — six in series at ~200 ps each, becoming the critical path itself.
Removing it took the vendored fabric from 145 to 240 MHz and the generated one from 216 to 454.
Design-rule targets are now opt-in, and the path afterwards contains zero repair buffers.

*A log tail too short to hold the evidence.* The verbose timing report is longer than the 2,000
characters kept from the OpenROAD log, so the startpoint — the one field that identifies a path
— was always the field that overflowed. Widened, and a compact summary now prints alongside.

**Implications.** Every one of these was mine, none was in the design under test, and each was
found the same way: by reading `report_checks` rather than reasoning about what ought to be
slow. Three wrong guesses preceded the first path report. The rule this leaves is narrow and
worth keeping — when a measurement disagrees with someone who has built the thing, suspect the
measurement, and read the path before touching the design.

---

## D278: The synthesis flow had never been asked to optimise for timing

**Context.** A vendored, proven crossbar measured 240 MHz where the person who wrote it gets
600+. After D277 removed four measurement artifacts the number was still less than half what it
should be, and the remaining insistence that it should be better was correct.

**Decision.** Three defects in this repo's own synthesis and placement flow, each of which had
been setting every frequency number this repo has ever published.

*`abc -fast`.* Technology mapping ran at minimum effort unless a caller asked for
`full_mapping`, which nothing did. Full mapping is worth about 40% of the frequency AND 29% of
the area on this design — 240 MHz to 333, 15,879 um2 to 12,295 — so it was not even the
area/speed trade it looks like. Full mapping is now the default for fabric measurement.

*`repair_timing` was never run.* `repair_design` fixes DESIGN RULE violations; setup violations
are a different command, and the flow simply did not contain it. Every frequency this repo has
reported came from a netlist on which no timing optimisation had been performed at all.

*`set_wire_rc -layer` set nothing.* ASAP7's tech LEF carries no RESISTANCE or CAPACITANCE
values, so naming a layer had no effect — which is exactly why sweeping the signal layer M3 /
M5 / M7 produced byte-identical results, a null result that should have been suspicious and was
instead read as "the wire model is not the lever". It also meant `repair_timing` refused to run
at all: "could not find a resistance value for any corner". The platform ships `setRC.tcl` for
precisely this and the flow now sources it.

**Consequence.** At 7x(4x4) -> 4x(7x8), 128 bits, ASAP7, placement:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| vendored `xbar_varlat` | 240 MHz | **530 MHz** |
| generated fabric | 216 MHz | **622 MHz** |

Both are now in the region the hand-built design reaches, and the vendored IP is a quarter of
the generated one's power at two thirds its area while being combinational across both levels
rather than pipelined — the trade is real and legible, which it was not while the flow was
losing a factor of two.

**A routing attempt, and what it cost.** `flow_depth="routed"` — CTS, global and detailed
routing, RCX extraction — was run on this fabric to replace the placement estimate with
extracted parasitics. It timed out after five hours without finishing. Detailed routing a
250,000-cell design is not something this repo can do per candidate, so placement with the
platform's wire RC is the practical ceiling for fabrics at this scale, and every interconnect
number here is placement-grade by necessity rather than by choice. Routing stays feasible for
the small datapath blocks, where it is already exercised.

**Implications.** Every absolute frequency in D261 through D277 predates this and should be
re-measured before being quoted; the relative comparisons within a single run survive, since
every candidate went through the same broken flow. The wider lesson is about null results: three
layers gave identical numbers and that was reported as "the wire model is not the lever" when it
was evidence the knob was disconnected. A parameter that changes nothing is a finding, not a
measurement.

---

## D279: The vendored core under every topology, and two failures that looked like success

**Context.** With `xbar_varlat` vendored, the obvious next question is whether the other
families can use it too. The OBI wrapper routes on an address bit-slice, which restricted it to
power-of-two fan-outs multiplying to the bank count — no Clos with seven middle switches, no
radix-8 butterfly over 32 banks.

**Decision.** That restriction is the WRAPPER's, not the IP's. `xbar_varlat` takes `add_i` —
the target port for each input — as an ordinary input, so driving it from the routing tables
this repo already computes puts the proven arbiter tree under every topology it can express. A
second switch backend does exactly that, with a port list identical to the generated switch, so
the fabric assembly, the traffic harness and the correctness checks of D268 are unchanged and
`switch="generated" | "vendored"` swaps one for the other. Eleven cores for the staged fabric,
twenty-three for a Clos, eight for a radix-8 butterfly.

**Consequence.** The two backends now cross-validate: identical throughput to within 0.02
words/cycle across staged, Clos, butterfly and direct crossbar, with zero misroutes — two
independent switch implementations of the same network agreeing is a far stronger statement
than either measuring correctly alone.

Getting there produced two failures that a naive check would have called perfect.

*Zero throughput, zero misroutes.* `xbar_varlat` permits no outstanding transactions, so with
`vld_i` tied low every input stalled after its first request. The fabric measured 0.00
words/cycle and the routing check was spotless, because a fabric that delivers nothing
misroutes nothing. Correctness checks that only inspect what ARRIVES cannot see a fabric that
never delivers; the throughput number is what caught it.

*Routing correctly is not routing well.* Taking the first valid port rather than rotating gave
4.86 words/cycle on a Clos where rotation gives 15.46, and 8.93 on a radix-4 butterfly against
13.54 — precisely the numbers this repo recorded before path diversity existed (D267). Every
word went to the right bank; the fabric was simply using one path where it had several.

**Measured, both backends, same flow, same topologies (ASAP7, 128 bits, placement):**

| fabric | switch | MHz | mm2 | mW | cells |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| staged 7x(4x4)->4x(7x8) | generated | 622 | 0.0209 | 72.9 | 188,634 |
| staged 7x(4x4)->4x(7x8) | vendored | **737** | **0.0154** | 67.8 | 136,654 |
| Clos C(n=4,m=4) | generated | 470 | 0.0275 | 76.3 | 248,267 |
| Clos C(n=4,m=4) | vendored | **707** | **0.0193** | 63.7 | 173,600 |
| butterfly radix-8 | generated | 448 | 0.0251 | 82.6 | 238,405 |
| butterfly radix-8 | vendored | **739** | **0.0174** | 72.5 | 159,138 |

The vendored core is 18% to 65% faster and about 30% smaller on every family, and the margin is
widest exactly where the generated switch struggles most. An arbiter tree that muxes its payload
as it arbitrates is simply a better structure than eligibility, priority resolution and a
separate wide mux, and the gap is large enough that the generated switch should be regarded as
the fallback for topologies the vendored core cannot express rather than the primary.

**Implications.** The vendored backend needs the slang front end, and `measure_whole_fabric`
did not select it — the failure was a Yosys synthesis error rather than a wrong number, which
is the good kind. What this does NOT yet do is feed the search: the demo screens on composed
per-arity fits of the GENERATED selector, so the vendored core is available for verification
and comparison but is not what the DSE ranks by.

---

## D280: The decision rung, and what a screen is allowed to decide

**Context.** With both switch backends measured, the generated one is 18% to 65% slower and
about 30% larger than the vendored `xbar_varlat` on every family (D279). Asked to make the final
ranking and the decision on the vendored IP, on the grounds that the fully generated quality is
lacking. It is, and the request is right for a reason worth writing down.

**Decision.** The demo gains a DECISION RUNG, separate from everything above it. The rounds
screen; the escalation rung measures composed per-arity blocks; and the decision rung places
each finalist WHOLE, on the vendored core, and ranks by what that measures.

Nothing above the decision rung is allowed to settle the choice, and each has a specific reason:

* the structural screen ranks a thousand candidates on an analytic model whose error is
  characterised (D266) but which is not silicon;
* the composed rung prices each selector arity in ISOLATION and multiplies by count, so it sees
  no wire between switches at all — and it does not preserve the ORDER (D272), which is the
  disqualifying property for a decision;
* the generated switch is a working reference implementation that a proven one beats
  substantially (D279), so ranking on it ranks on an implementation nobody would ship.

The rung is opt-in per candidate count (`--decide-on-finalists N`), because placing a fabric
whole costs minutes where screening costs nothing, and it states its criterion rather than
implying one: meet the frequency floor on placed silicon, then take the most throughput per mm2
of fabric. Throughput itself is memoised across the rung — the two backends agree to within
0.02 words/cycle (D279), so it does not change when the switch implementation does.

**Implications.** This makes the flow's fidelity ladder explicit all the way to the end:
analytic screen -> composed measurement -> whole-fabric measurement on production-grade IP, with
the decision at the bottom. What it does NOT do is change what the search optimises: the rounds
still rank by the composed rung, so the decision rung re-ranks a shortlist rather than steering
the exploration that produced it. A shortlist chosen by a mis-ranking screen can exclude the
fabric the decision rung would have preferred, and the honest fix — screening on the vendored
core — costs a whole-fabric placement per candidate and is not affordable at a thousand.

---

## D281: Pointing the proposer at the gap

**Context.** The local model's round proposed into a vacuum. It was given the problem, this
repo's measured arity-to-frequency table, the IP catalog, retrieved design guidance, mined
facts, the history of what had been tried and the reason its last proposal was refused — and
nothing at all about which part of the trade-off was already well covered.

The consequence was visible in the results rather than inferred. It clustered at the throughput
end and produced a Clos-into-radix-8-into-crossbar hybrid that topped the screened table at 17.5
words/cycle, cost 2.7x the area of its nearest rival, and then placed at 430 MHz on the decision
rung (D280) — the slowest of eight finalists. A good proposal against the objective it was
shown, and not one anybody would build.

**Decision.** The prompt now carries the measured Pareto frontier and names the single widest
gap in it: "the widest gap is between 9.9 words/cycle at 0.0104 mm2 and 13.0 at 0.0128 — a
fabric inside that gap improves the frontier; one outside it has to beat an existing point
outright." Dominated points are not shown, because a list of everything tried is history and a
list of what currently wins is direction.

The frontier is recomputed per proposal, and the runner evaluates a non-grid strategy one
candidate at a time, so the target moves as the model fills gaps — the round is an iterative
directed search rather than ten independent guesses. Below two measured points there is no gap
to name and the paragraph is omitted rather than padded.

**Implications.** This steers the proposer with the SCREEN's frontier, which is the frontier
the search itself ranks by, and D280 established that the screen mis-ranks against placed
silicon. So the model is now aimed accurately at a target that is itself somewhat wrong: it
will fill gaps in screened area-versus-throughput, and whether those survive placement is a
separate question the decision rung still has to answer. Feeding decision-rung measurements back
into the proposer's history is the obvious next step and is not done — it would close the loop
from the most accurate measurement in the flow to the thing generating candidates, which is
where a knowledge flywheel of this kind actually pays.

---

## D282: Capacity is a count, and it does not move with the traffic

**Context.** The results table gave each fabric's measured throughput and nothing to read it
against. 16.2 words per cycle is not interpretable alone: it could be a fabric leaving half its
capability unused, or one within a whisker of what its structure permits.

**Decision, after getting it wrong once.** The column reports `max/cyc`: how many transfers the
fabric can carry AT ONCE, an integer fixed by its narrowest point — the client count, the bank
count, and every stage's total link count.

The first attempt reported the bank-conflict bound instead, `banks * (1 - (1 - 1/banks)**
clients)`, which is 18.85 for 28 clients into 32 banks. Two things are wrong with that under the
heading "max". A cycle either carries a word on a path or it does not, so a capacity is a count
and cannot be fractional. And 18.85 is an EXPECTATION under one specific traffic pattern, so
labelling it a maximum made a fabric's ceiling move when the traffic model changed, which a
capacity must not do. The same fabric has the same capacity under uniform, strided or
single-bank traffic.

The conflict bound is still worth knowing and is now stated once in the header, as what it is:
under uniform-random targets even a perfect crossbar averages 18.8 of its 28, because clients
collide on banks.

**Consequence.** The two readings separate cleanly. Wide fabrics all carry 28 and differ only in
how much of it this traffic uses, 62% down to 52%. Narrow ones are capacity-bound and say so:
`7x(4x2) -> 2x(7x16)` carries 14 and uses 79% of it, `8x(4x2) -> 2x(8x16)` carries 16 and uses
69%, and both measure exactly 11.0 words per cycle. Identical rates, different engineering
statements: one is near structurally saturated, the other is leaving capacity idle. The raw
throughput column cannot tell them apart and the capacity column can.

**Implications.** The share column is still traffic-dependent even though the capacity is not,
and it is labelled that way: it reads as "of what this traffic uses", and a hot-bank or strided
pattern moves every percentage in it while leaving every capacity untouched. That split is the
point of separating the two.

---

## D283: Full concurrency as a constraint, enforced where it is free

**Context.** The problem states that 28 clients access 32 banks AT THE SAME TIME. A fabric whose
narrowest point carries fewer than 28 transfers cannot serve that, however little silicon it
uses, and the search had been ranking such fabrics rather than refusing them: the cheapest
entries on every results table were exactly the capacity-limited ones.

**Decision.** A second declared constraint alongside the frequency floor: the structural capacity
(D282) must be at least the client count. It is checked at SCREEN, where the capacity is a
property of the dimensions and costs nothing to compute, so a fabric disqualified by its own
shape never earns a place-and-route.

The proposer is told the same rule rather than merely being refused by it. A model that does not
know a constraint spends its whole round on candidates discarded before any tool runs, so the
rule is stated where proposals are made, with the arithmetic that decides it: every stage needs
`switches * out >= clients`, seven switches with out=2 carry 14 and are refused, the same seven
with out=4 carry 28 and are not.

**Consequence.** Round 4 refused 340 of 1,101 candidates at the screen, and the measured set fell
from nineteen fabrics to eight, saving twenty-two place-and-route jobs. Every survivor carries
the full 28. The eight differ only in how much of that capacity this traffic uses, 62% down to
53%, which is the comparison the constraint was meant to leave behind.

**Implications.** The cheap end of the curve is gone, and that is the constraint working rather
than a side effect: the old table bottomed out at 0.0065 mm2 serving 3.9 words per cycle with a
capacity of 2. The area span across qualifying fabrics narrows from 4.3x to 1.8x, and the
smallest admissible fabric is `7x(4x4) -> 4x(7x8)` at 0.0153 mm2, which also happens to run at
871 MHz. A consequence worth watching: the local model's hybrids all concentrate somewhere in
the middle and are now inadmissible as a class, so a proposer that had been contributing to the
frontier may contribute nothing until it learns to keep every stage wide.

---

## D284: Mixed topologies, enumerated rather than only proposed

**Context.** A direct question about the demo: where are the mixed fabrics, a crossbar with a
butterfly or the like. The `hybrid` family had existed since D270, builds correctly and is
