verified in RTL, and the answer was still that a deterministic run contains NONE of them. They
were reachable only through the LLM proposer, so whether the study considered a mixed structure
depended on whether a model happened to think of one that round.

**Decision.** The wide rounds enumerate hybrids directly: radix-R networks into a crossbar at
one and two routing stages, and Clos ingress stages into a crossbar, over the fan-outs that
divide the bank count. Thirty-seven survive dedup in the three-stage wide space, twenty-nine of
which carry every client and are therefore admissible under D283. The combinations are chosen to
keep every stage wide, because a narrower one is refused anyway and enumerating it spends a
screening slot on a fabric that cannot win.

**Implications.** This is deliberately a bounded selection rather than a general product of
every layer against every other: the layer vocabulary is four families deep and a full crossing
would swamp the space that already exists. The proposer remains the route to combinations nobody
enumerated, which is the division that makes both worth having — rules cover what can be
covered, the model reaches past the edge of it.

---

## D285: One family, two spellings, one name

**Context.** `xbar_multistage` and `xbar_staged` were merged into a single implementation in
D271, and kept separate `kind` labels afterwards. A results table therefore listed one family
under two names, and the reasonable question followed: why keep the convention when a single
crossbar name makes more sense.

**Decision.** It does. The rank form is a SPELLING of a staged fabric, not a sibling of it:
`ports` names the intermediate rank sizes where `stages` names the switch dimensions, and both
produce the same `xbar_staged` topology through the same constructor. The kind is now
`xbar_staged` in every case, distinguished in the label by which spelling was used —
`xbar_staged-direct`, `xbar_staged-8`, `xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8`. The catalog collapses to one
crossbar-family entry documenting both spellings. `xbar_multistage` is still accepted as an
input kind, and never emitted, so a store or document written before this keeps parsing.

**Implications.** The distinction the two names carried was real but belongs at the level of
the label, not the family: a monolithic rank costs selectors of that rank's full arity, which is
exactly why `ports=[]` misses 600 MHz where the switch forms clear it. That contrast is more
legible on one table of one family than as two families that happened to be the same code.

---

## D286: Repair before refusal, and a demo that does not switch the AI off

**Context.** Two objections to how the interconnect demo behaved, both correct.

**Refusing a proposal discards the part that was chosen.** A model's fabric is usually refused
over arithmetic, not over intent: a stage one link too narrow to carry every client (D283), a
fan-out product short of the bank count. The whole fabric was then thrown away and replaced with
an entry from the deterministic pool, which has nothing to do with what the model was reaching
for. Seven switches fanning out to two carry 14 of 28 and are refused; seven switches in two
stages was a perfectly good structural decision and only the fan-out was wrong.

Proposals are now REPAIRED where the violated rule says how. The repair only widens, never
renarrows, and it leaves switch counts alone because those are the model's decision — only
fan-outs move, upward, to the smallest value that satisfies the broken rule. A repair that still
does not validate is abandoned rather than iterated, so it cannot loop, and input that is not a
fabric at all still takes the recorded fallback. Every repair is recorded on the candidate
("stage 1 fan-out 2->4 to carry all 28 clients"), because a silently corrected proposal would
misreport what the model did unaided.

**A tool about AI for chip design should not demonstrate itself with the AI off.** The proposing
round was opt-in and defaulted to zero, so the headline run was fully deterministic and the
model was a footnote. It is now on by default at twelve proposals, `--llm-round 0` turns it off
for a bit-reproducible run — which is what the determinism was actually protecting — and a
machine with no local model reachable degrades to the enumerated rounds with that stated, rather
than failing.

**Implications.** Repair moves work from the fallback path to the model's own structures, and
the honest accounting of that has to survive: a repaired proposal is not evidence the model
proposed a valid fabric, and the trial record now distinguishes proposed, repaired and
fell-back. What this does NOT yet do is repair candidates refused by MEASUREMENT rather than by
construction — a fabric that misses the frequency floor could often be fixed by splitting the
stage whose selector arity is too high, and nothing attempts that. That is the more valuable
repair of the two, because it acts on a real measurement rather than on arithmetic.

---

## D287: Two model roles, and coverage that cannot go quiet

**Context.** The local model proposed fabrics in a single round bolted onto the end of a fixed
plan. Two objections, both fair: it should act across the whole search rather than once at the
end, and it should be able to decide what the search does next. Flux's own architecture already
names these as separate module types, an Orchestrator and a Generator, so running one model in
each role is the design rather than an embellishment.

**Decision.** Two local models with different jobs. The GENERATOR designs fabrics, as before.
The ORCHESTRATOR chooses the next step from a fixed menu — enumerate at one of four scopes, ask
for proposals, or stop — given the measured frontier and which scopes have already run.

I argued against the orchestrator role before building it, on the grounds that the four scopes
are cheap, cached and already well ordered, so choosing among them has little leverage, while
varying the plan per run costs the reproducibility that makes "1,101 candidates screened" a
checkable claim. That objection was about a RISK, not about the design, and the risk is
addressable: every scope the orchestrator does not run is reported at the end. A study that
looked at less now says so, in the output, next to the results it is drawing conclusions from.
The model directs the search; it cannot quietly shrink it.

Both roles fail soft. An unusable plan falls back to the next un-run scope with the reason
recorded, a failed proposing step drops back to the fixed plan, and a machine with no local
model runs the enumerated rounds and states that it did.

**Consequence.** Written when the local model store had emptied mid-session, this record
originally said the orchestrator had never made a decision and claimed nothing about its
quality. It has since made them, on a 27.3B qwen3 build, and the observed behaviour is worth
pinning: probed with different search states it chose `narrow/2`, then `narrow/3` where the fixed
plan's next scope was `wide/2`, then the single remaining scope. In a full run it opened on
`wide/3` — the LARGEST scope, 1,134 candidates, the exact inverse of the fixed plan's order — and
then filled in the rest. So it is choosing rather than echoing an order, and it prefers depth and
breadth early.

Whether those are GOOD choices is a separate question this does not answer. Biggest-scope-first
spends the budget where the space is widest, which is defensible, but no run has yet compared a
directed search against the fixed plan on the same store with the same grant, and until one does,
"it decides" is the claim and "it decides well" is not. The degradation contract is separately
confirmed, twice: with no model reachable every call fell back and coverage reported all four
scopes, and when the Ollama server was restarted mid-run the driver took the connection error,
backed off, retried, and continued.

**Implications.** The reproducibility concern is reduced rather than removed. Coverage is now
visible, but a directed run and a fixed-plan run still explore different spaces, so two runs
remain comparable only through the coverage line. Anyone comparing results across runs has to
read it, which is why it prints unconditionally rather than only when something was skipped.

---

## D288: A frontier that measured nothing, twice over

**Context.** The interconnect demo reported a plausible result table while measuring nothing at
all, and it did so for two unrelated reasons discovered within an hour of each other. Both are
worth recording together because the SYMPTOM was identical and benign-looking: a populated
frontier, printed confidently, containing not one number the run had produced.

**Cause one: a degenerate screening front.** `area_mm2` is declared `measured_at: escalation`, so
it does not exist when the screen ranks candidates. That left the screen front decided by
`throughput_words_per_cycle` (maximise) and `interstage_link_bits` (minimise) — and the plain
crossbar maximises the first at ZERO of the second, so it strictly dominates every other fabric,
including `butterfly-radix32` at 18.82 words/cycle against its 18.85. Exactly one contender
escalated per round, in all four rounds; it then failed the 600 MHz constraint; the round measured
nothing and the demo printed rows the campaign store already held from earlier days.

The fix is `mux_bits` as a fourth objective, minimised, visible at screen where it is free. It
earns the role by MEASUREMENT rather than plausibility: across the 23 fabrics in this repo's own
store carrying both a screened `mux_bits` and a placed `area_mm2`, Pearson r = 0.95, near-monotone
from 86,016 bits / 0.0153 mm2 to 391,680 / 0.0500. Contenders escalated per round went from 1, 1,
1, 1 to 4, 15, 4.

**Cause two: the measured rung could not run.** The demo was started from the default nix shell
rather than `.#physical`, so `openroad` was absent. Every escalation failed with
`OpenRoadError: openroad binary 'openroad' not on PATH`, one per candidate, and the run CONTINUED
— tallying the failures per round as an `error` count and printing a table at the end. With a warm
store that table is fully populated, from rows measured on an earlier day, and nothing in the
output says the current run contributed none of them.

`check_toolchain()` now refuses to start when `openroad`, `yosys` or `verilator` is missing, names
which is missing and what it was needed for, and prints the shell that carries them. A hard exit,
not a warning: a run that cannot measure should not produce a table to be misread.

**What this says about the demo's claims.** Every "measured, not modelled" statement in the demo's
README was true of the STORE and not necessarily of the RUN. The two are only the same thing when
the run actually escalates, which the first cause quietly prevented and the second cause quietly
survived. Provenance per number was already recorded; what was missing was any signal that THIS
run added nothing to it.

**Not established.** Whether `mux_bits` remains a good area proxy outside this node, width and
family set. r = 0.95 is over 23 fabrics at one node (ASAP7) and one width (128 bits), and the
proxy prices gates rather than the wire between them, which is exactly the error that D280 already
measured for composed frequency. It is a screening aid and is not quotable as area.

---

## D289: Reasoning models, and a model tag that outlived its pin

**Context.** The local model was swapped from `qwen2.5-coder:7b` to a 27.3B qwen3 build. Three
distinct failures followed, none of them about model quality.

**One: the tag was pinned in 30 places.** Fourteen modules in `flows/chia_nodes`, `flows/mcp`,
ten live integration tests, the knowledge-efficacy harness and the demo each hard-coded
`qwen2.5-coder:7b` independently. When the store changed underneath them, every one silently
skipped, fell back, or errored. `flux_llm.default_local_model()` is now the single source, with
`FLUX_LLM_MODEL` to override. The harness additionally LOGS the model before its first arm,
because its own report named its model only in prose — which is why refreshing that report meant
re-running the experiment rather than editing a label.

**Two: reasoning traces are not the answer.** qwen3 emits `<think>...</think>` before answering.
`strip_markdown_fence` now removes the trace BEFORE searching for a fence, and the ordering is the
substance: a model reasoning about JSON drafts JSON, often fenced, INSIDE the trace and then
rejects it — search for a fence first and the caller receives a discarded draft that parses
cleanly. An unterminated trace, the shape a truncated response takes, is left empty rather than
passed off as an answer.

**Three: a trace that does not fit is fatal, not wasteful.** The reasoning is charged to the same
budget as the answer. Under Ollama's default 4,096-token serving window, a 1,818-token guidance
prompt left so little room that every proposal in a generation round died with
`finish_reason="length"` — the model was still thinking when it was cut off. `suppress_reasoning`
appends qwen3's `/no_think` for models whose tag says qwen3. Measured: 108.7 s to 36.1 s on the
same prompt, clean JSON both ways.

**What is NOT claimed.** That suppressing reasoning is free, or an improvement. It is a workaround
for a trace that does not FIT, and the two roles are not alike: choosing among four enumerated
scopes leaves reasoning little to add, while inventing a fabric under coupled constraints is
exactly where losing it could cost real quality. `FLUX_LLM_THINK=1` restores it, both as the A/B
arm that would settle this and as the right default once the window has room. The comparison
cannot be run at 4,096 tokens, because the thinking arm produces nothing to compare.

**A note on the environment, recorded because it cost an hour.** The serving window was 4,096
despite the unit file setting `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768` — the assignments were joined by
SEMICOLONS in a single systemd `Environment=` line, which is space-separated, so the value became
one long string, not an integer, and both it and `OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=30m` were silently discarded.
Two independent observations agreed before the file was read: `ollama ps` reporting `CONTEXT 4096`
and a keep-alive counting down in five minutes rather than thirty.

---

## D290: Measuring contenders together, because the tools are single-threaded

**Context.** Screening was already batched (D238) and escalation was not, which is backwards with
respect to where the time goes. Screening a topology is instant; escalating one runs OpenROAD,
Yosys and Verilator, each a single-threaded process. Observed during an interconnect run on a
64-core host: placements happening one at a time, load average near 12, roughly fifty cores idle.

**Decision.** `escalation_parallelism` measures a rung's contender set concurrently, defaulting to
1 so the existing path is untouched. Threads, not Ray: the work is a subprocess wait, and the GIL
is released for its whole duration, so the machinery is a `ThreadPoolExecutor` and not another
dispatch layer.

Unlike screening, this applies to EVERY strategy rather than to grid alone. The reason D238 had to
exclude agentic and generative screening is that proposal t+1 legally depends on outcome t, so
batching would change what the strategy is. A contender set has no such property: it is chosen in
full before any of it is measured, so measuring its members together changes nothing about the
choice.

**What had to hold, and how.** Concurrency is confined to the measurement. Intent rows are written
before dispatch and outcomes recorded after, all on the calling thread, so a SQLite connection is
never touched by two threads and an interrupted batch leaves exactly the `running` rows
`classify_interrupted` already handles. Outcomes are recorded in SUBMISSION order rather than
completion order, so the durable trial log of a parallel run reads the same as a serial one's.
Per-candidate error isolation is kept — one candidate raising is one `error` trial, not a lost
batch — which is the posture D238 deliberately preserved for screening by falling back to
sequential calls when a batch raised.

**A prerequisite that had to be fixed first.** The physical evaluator's caches were checked outside
the lock, with the expensive measurement in the gap. Serially that is harmless. Concurrently,
several fabrics sharing a selector arity would each start the same fit — three OpenROAD placements
apiece — so per-key single-flight locks now make later arrivals wait for the first result rather
than duplicate it. Correctness never depended on this, because every flow already runs in its own
temporary directory; the cost did.

**Not established.** The speedup. The mechanism is unit-tested for concurrency, equivalence,
ordering, isolation and no-trial-left-running, but a real end-to-end number on real tools is not
recorded here. Concurrent OpenROAD instances contend for memory and filesystem bandwidth, so the
scaling is a property of the host and the default is deliberately conservative — cores/4, capped
at 8, overridable by `FLUX_ESCALATION_WORKERS`.

---

## D291: The orchestrator decides when the search is finished

**Context.** The directed run was capped at the number of enumeration scopes plus two, which made
the model a chooser of ORDER and never of DEPTH: after four steps the search ended whether or not
the frontier was still moving. That cap was an artefact of the fixed plan the orchestrator
replaced, not a judgement about when a study is done.

**Decision.** A directed run continues until the orchestrator stops it. Every scope is enumerable
once; after that `propose` is the only step that can still find anything, and it is worth
repeating, since each round asks a design model for different fabrics. The prompt now states the
trade-off it is being asked to make — stopping early leaves silicon on the table, spending steps
after the frontier stops moving wastes them — and `--max-rounds` (default 16) is a runaway guard
rather than a plan. An undirected run still follows the fixed schedule exactly.

**One override, on evidence.** A model free to keep proposing can keep proposing the same fabrics.
Two consecutive proposal rounds that attempt no fabric not already tried end the run regardless of
what the orchestrator wants. This is the single place its judgement is overruled, and it is
overruled by a fact from the store rather than by a policy about how many rounds are reasonable.

**And a number for how much was tried.** `FABRICS ATTEMPTED` reports distinct fabrics, printed
beside `COVERAGE`: coverage says which scopes were looked at, this says how much was tried inside
them, and a study is only as strong as both. Distinct fabrics rather than trials, because the same
fabric screened in three overlapping scopes is one fabric that was tried and counting trials would
inflate the figure exactly where scopes overlap. Refused candidates are counted as attempted — a
fabric ruled out by its own dimensions was still considered, and omitting it would make the search
look narrower than it was. Measured on a live run mid-flight: 1,156 distinct fabrics attempted,
18 measured with real tools, 351 refused by constraint, 2 failed to build.

**Established since, and it is not flattering.** Three model-directed runs now exist and they show
BOTH failure modes. One ran nine steps, repaired its own coverage gap mid-search and chose to stop
after the yield went quiet — which this record originally cited as evidence the model stops
sensibly. Two later runs corrected that: one locked onto a single action and repeated it four
times until it was killed, and one stopped after TWO steps with five of six scopes unexplored.

So the honest claim is narrower than the one made here first: the model decides WHAT to do
competently, choosing among enumerate, propose and measure with reasons that hold up, and decides
WHEN TO FINISH badly, in both directions. The safeguards are what make that tolerable — the barren
backstop catches the looping mode, and the coverage line makes the quitting mode visible instead
of letting a one-scope study present itself as a finished one. Neither safeguard is decoration.

---

## D292: The knowledge block that outgrew its window

**Context.** The generation round failed at `finish_reason="length"` even after reasoning was
suppressed. The cause was not the answer but the QUESTION: 7,272 characters of curated guidance
plus 11,052 of mined facts is roughly 4,581 tokens, and the serving window was 4,096. The prompt
alone did not fit, so no amount of retrying or trace-suppression could help.

**The part that matters beyond this machine.** The block GROWS WITH THE STUDY. Mined facts come
from the campaign's own store — 33 in an early run, 76 by the fourth round of a later one — so the
generator works while the campaign is ignorant and fails once it has learned something. That is
exactly backwards, and it is a property of the design rather than of any window size: a bigger
context postpones the failure, it does not remove it.

**Decision.** The knowledge block is fitted to a character budget
(`FLUX_PROMPT_BUDGET_CHARS`, default 9,000) before it is sent, and says what it dropped.

Guidance gets 60% and no more. A first cut gave guidance first claim on the whole budget, and it
took all of it, leaving ZERO facts — a model that knows every family exists and nothing about the
run it is advising, which is the precise failure D270 built two knowledge surfaces to avoid. Both
halves are load-bearing in different ways: the catalog supplies the vocabulary to name a fabric,
the facts say what this silicon actually did.

Cost is measured on the RENDERED block, not on the fact objects — rendering adds framing and each
fact carries the limits that must travel with it, so `str(fact)` is not what lands in the prompt.
Measured after the change: 5,316 characters of guidance and 4 facts, about 2,101 tokens, leaving
room for an answer where there had been none.

**Reported, not hidden.** A trimmed block tells the model it is seeing 4 of 76 facts and that the
omitted ones are not evidence against anything — the same posture COVERAGE takes for scopes
(D287). A model reasoning from a narrowed view should know the view is narrowed.

**Not established.** What this costs in proposal quality. Dropping 72 of 76 measured facts is a
large narrowing, and whether the four that survive are the four worth keeping is untested — they
are simply the first that fit. Selecting facts by relevance to the current frontier, rather than
by order, is the obvious next step and has not been done.

---

## D296: A tree shaped like the architecture

**Context.** The repo had grown to 25 top-level directories and 41 packages, and none of it said
what the system is. The architecture has four module types (Orchestrator, Generator, Evaluator,
Mentor) and the layout reflected none of them: generation lived in `generation/` AND `codegen/`,
orchestration in `search/` AND `flows/`, knowledge across `knowledge/`, `corpus/` and
`protocols/`. Worse for the future, the interconnect study was smeared over four top-level
locations, so a SECOND design problem would have added three or four more.

**Decision.** Twelve top-level directories, four of them named for the module types, plus
`applications/` for problem domains, `core/` for the shared substrate, and `interfaces/` for the
ways the system is driven. Every move was `git mv`, so all 423 changes are recorded as renames and
the history of each file survives.

`applications/<name>/{lib,demo.py,experiments/}` is the part sized for growth. An interconnect
study is not infrastructure and should not sit beside `core/ir/`; it is one problem, and the next
one takes the same shape rather than more top-level directories. Adding a design problem should
not change the top level at all.

**Where a domain's evaluators go, and why not with their application.** They go under
`evaluator/`, with everything else that implements the Evaluator ABI, including the two that only
make sense for interconnect. Cohesion argues the other way and lost to a concrete symptom: with
them filed under their application, the backend-parity test had to scan two trees, which means a
future adapter moved into an application would silently escape the check. A module type split
across two locations is the thing this record set out to remove. The domain LIBRARY does live with
its application, because a topology builder is not an evaluator.

**`build/`, and one constraint that is not a preference.** `nix/` and `containers/` both hold
inputs that build things rather than run them, so they are now `build/nix/` and
`build/containers/`. `build/nix/` cannot move OUT of `flux/`: the flake is `flux/flake.nix` and
Nix can only reference paths inside the flake directory, so relocating it would mean moving the
flake as well, for no gain.

**A real collision, found by moving.** Two different directories were called `corpus`:
`knowledge/corpus/` holds DOCUMENTS to retrieve from, and the top-level `corpus/` holds design
POINTS in public and holdout partitions. The word was doing two jobs, and during the move a path
was repointed at the wrong one and a test caught it. The design-point store is now
`mentor/benchmarks/`, which says what it holds.

**What was NOT changed, deliberately.** Importable package names. `orchestrator/campaign/` still
provides `flux_search_campaign`, which is incoherent and known. Renaming distributions touches
every import in every package, every test and the docs, and mixing that into a 423-file move would
have made a failure impossible to bisect. Layout first, names as a separate pass that can be
verified on its own.

**The bug class this exposed.** Three separate places derived a root by counting parents
(`Path(__file__).parents[N]`), which silently breaks the moment nesting depth changes, and one
test derived the repo root by walking up from the package under test rather than from itself.
A depth-counted root is a hidden dependency on the tree's shape. They now derive from their own
file, and the backend-parity test keys adapters by PACKAGE name rather than directory name, since
a directory is a fact about the filesystem and a package name is the identity being checked.

**Verification.** 1,428 unit tests pass, and the interconnect demo runs end to end from its new
home and reproduces the same answer (0.0153 mm2 at 871 MHz).

---

## D293: Reasoning models answer through a different door

**Context.** A generation round produced nothing for hours on qwen3.8 (27.3B, CPU). The symptoms
moved every time they were chased: truncation at `finish_reason="length"`, then calls hanging to
the client timeout, then whole rounds recording no trial at all.

**The cause, measured rather than reasoned about.** A qwen3-family model does not put its scratch
work in `<think>` tags in the response. It puts it in a separate `thinking` field and leaves
`response` EMPTY until the reasoning finishes. With the same 1,435-token prompt:

    /no_think via the OpenAI-compatible /v1   600 tokens, done_reason=length, response=''   160s+
    think:false via the native /api/generate  214 tokens, done_reason=stop,   response=JSON    53s

Generation runs about 5.5 tok/s here, so the client's 16,000-token output budget is roughly 48
minutes of reasoning before anything is returned. Every symptom above is that one fact.

**Decision.** `NativeOllamaProposer` talks to Ollama's native endpoint, which accepts
`think: false`; the OpenAI-compatible `/v1` endpoint has no equivalent field and the prompt-level
`/no_think` switch is not honoured by this build. `FLUX_LLM_CHIA_CLIENT=1` restores the previous
client for anyone who needs its tool surface and is not using a reasoning model.

**What this cost, recorded because the pattern is the lesson.** Three earlier diagnoses were each
plausible, each partly true, and none was the blocker: stripping `<think>` tags (this model emits
none), shrinking the knowledge block (real, but not why calls hung), and raising the client
timeout from 600s to 3600s (which made a stuck call take an hour instead of ten minutes). The
question that ended it was not "what else could be slow" but "what does the response actually
contain" — `done_reason` and an empty `response` named the bug in one call.

**Not established.** That other reasoning models behave this way, or that this one will keep to
it. `done_reason` is now recorded per call, so the next occurrence is visible rather than
inferred.

---

## D295: Where the wall-clock actually went

**Context.** A run spends its time in four unrelated places — external tools, local model
inference, the search's own bookkeeping, and waiting — and none of them were separable. A
generation round that produced nothing looked exactly like one that was merely slow, and an hour
went into diagnosing "the demo is stuck" when the answer was a single 48-minute model call.

**Decision.** `flux_profile`: a dict, a lock, a context manager. Instrumented at four choke
points rather than at call sites — the one function that launches Yosys and OpenROAD, the
Verilator build and run, and each model call — so the accounting cannot drift out of step with
the code.

**Two clocks, and reporting one of them would lie.** Phases sum time spent INSIDE each category
across every thread, so with concurrent escalation the sum legitimately exceeds elapsed
wall-clock: eight placements running together contribute eight seconds of tool time per second of
real time. Both print, and their ratio is the concurrency ACTUALLY achieved rather than the
concurrency requested. Measured on one round: 124s of tool time over 58s elapsed, 2.2x.

**What it immediately showed, none of which was suspected.** Verilator BUILD dominates at 82s
across 7 fabrics, more than OpenROAD (26s) and Yosys (15s) together, while the simulation itself
is 0.5s: compiling the simulator, not running it. The search's own bookkeeping is unmeasurable
next to one tool invocation. And on a model-directed run, 77% of the wall clock was the local
model thinking against 11% for synthesis and placement — the AI is the bottleneck, not the EDA
tools.

**Not established.** That these proportions hold on other hardware. Every figure is a fact about
one 64-core CPU host with no GPU, which is why the report prints them rather than hard-coding any
expectation.

---

## D297: Conclusions, and an orchestrator that remembers

**Context.** Mining turns a campaign store into typed facts — 100 of them here: 42
`measured_point`, 51 `refusal_pattern`, 7 `frontier_outcome` — so "what happened" is automatic and
durable, failures included. What was missing was "what it MEANT". The statement "arity, not switch
count, sets the critical path" earned its place in the design-guidance corpus because a person
read the measurements and wrote it down; nothing carried it back for a later run to use. And the
orchestrator received none of it: its prompt carried the problem, the scopes run, and the
frontier, so it rediscovered the shape of the space every run.

**Decision, in two parts.** A `conclusion` fact kind, drawn by a model FROM mined facts, and a
lessons digest that reaches the orchestrator's prompt (conclusions plus grouped refusals, capped,
because that prompt is sent on every decision and prefill is the whole cost of a call).

**A conclusion is a different kind of claim, and is held to a stricter contract.** A mined fact is
computed from stored rows and is wrong only if the arithmetic or the store is wrong. A conclusion
is an inference and can be plausible, confident and false. So: its statement carries
`(INFERRED by <model>, not measured)` inseparably; it must cite the fact ids it was drawn from; it
must state what it does NOT establish, and is refused outright without one; and `supersedes` lets
better evidence retire an earlier belief without erasing that it was held.

**Measured, and the reason the guard rails matter.** Of the first two conclusions drawn from the
real store, one was sound — ten trials sharing an identical fmax to fourteen significant figures
indicates a deterministic ceiling, with the right advice attached. The other was confidently
false: it claimed a peak of "21 words/cycle" and values that were "discrete integers" against a
store whose measurements are 12.06, 13.51 ... 18.85 and never 21, and it confused the structural
capacity of 28 with achieved throughput. It cited real facts and described them wrongly, which is
the one failure mode that looks exactly like a good conclusion.

**Not established.** That a model of this size can do this reliably. One in two was wrong on the
only sample taken. What the design bought was not correctness but CHECKABILITY: the false one was
caught in a single query because it cited its evidence and carried its label. D303 adds the
numeric check that would have refused it mechanically.

---

## D298: A demo that is mostly not about its subject

**Context.** `demos/interconnect_dse.py` had grown to 1,069 lines with `main()` alone at 362, and
most of it was not about interconnects: getting a local model, fitting a knowledge block to a
context, counting what a study attempted, digesting a frontier, isolating results from a
superseded evaluator, refusing to start without tools, and the whole directed-search loop. Any
second application would have needed all of it, and would have copied it.

**Decision.** Move the generic parts into the packages that own that concern —
`flux_llm.local_proposer` / `fit_to_budget`, `flux_search_campaign.campaign_tally` /
`frontier_digest` / `next_proposal_series` / `measured_results` / `tally_lines`,
`flux_knowledge_mining.lessons_digest`, `flux_evaluator_abi.preflight.require_tools`,
`flux_profile.outside` — and make the search loop itself a package, `flux_directed_search`.

**The loop's menu is data, which is the part worth keeping.** It used to hard-code its two
capabilities in three places at once: the menu inside the prompt, an `if/elif` dispatch, and a
fallback list. Three copies of one list. An `Action` now carries its name, the line the model
reads, its example, its validator and its callable, and the prompt menu is GENERATED from the
registry, so menu and dispatch cannot disagree. Adding a third capability (`measure`, D304) was a
registration and touched neither the loop nor the prompt.

**Result.** 1,069 lines to 731, and the demo now declares only what is about interconnects.

**What was NOT extracted, and why it is a judgement call.** The results table, the decision rung
and the objective document stay in the application. They read as generic and are not: the columns,
the finalist ranking and the constraint set encode what this study is asking, and a framework that
owned them would have to be told all of it anyway.

---

## D299: Router networks, and where their waist actually is

**Context.** The space held crossbars, staged fabrics, Clos networks, butterflies and hybrids —
every one of them feed-forward. Asked to evaluate NoC-style options, the honest answer was that
none were in it.

**Decision.** `ring`, `mesh` and `torus` as topology families, priced the same way as everything
else: each router is `arity` arbitrated selectors of `arity` inputs, doubled for the response
path as D265 requires.

**A modelling choice that was WRONG, and how it was caught.** Capacity was first set to the
BISECTION — the links crossing the narrowest cut of the graph — reasoning that this is a router
network's waist as a rank width is a staged fabric's. From that followed a confident headline: a
ring carries 2 transfers however long it is, a 6x6 mesh carries 6, 8 of the 13 enumerated router
networks are refused outright, and for 28 concurrent clients a NoC either cannot carry the load or
costs an order of magnitude more silicon.

Simulation disproved it (D306). The 6x6 mesh whose capacity was asserted to be 6 measures 12.58
words/cycle with zero misroutes. A structural capacity that the fabric BEATS is not a capacity.

The error is precise and worth keeping: bisection bounds traffic CROSSING the middle cut, not
total delivery, because most transfers in a grid are short and never cross it. What bounds
delivery is ejection — each router accepts at most one word per cycle into its local bank — which
is `min(clients, banks)`, the same bound every other family here has. Bisection remains reported
as the bandwidth property it is.

**So the finding this record originally claimed is withdrawn.** Router networks are not refused on
capacity, they compete on their merits, and the refusals that followed from the bisection model
were an artifact of it. What made the difference was generating the RTL and running it, which is
the argument for measuring rather than modelling, made against my own model.

**Superseded on comparability.** This record originally stated that router throughput was
MODELLED while area and frequency were measured, because the RTL generator built feed-forward
fabrics only. D306 builds the cyclic generator, so mesh and torus throughput is now measured on
generated RTL through the same harness and the same three correctness checks as everything else.

---

## D300: A proposer that can see what has already been tried

**Context.** The generator kept re-proposing fabrics the store already held — 23 distinct
proposals across many rounds, most of them repeats — and the obvious reading was that the model
was weak. It was not the reading the code supported.

**Cause.** Three things, all structural. `_signatures` started EMPTY every campaign, so structural
dedup only caught repeats within a single round. The prompt showed only the last 12 candidates of
the current round. And `visited` came from `store.visited_keys(campaign_id)`, which is
per-campaign — 16 keys where the store held 1,170 — and the interconnect strategy assigned it and
then never consulted it at all. The model could not propose "something not yet covered" because it
was never told what WAS covered.

**Decision.** `store.visited_keys_all()` for generative strategies, signatures seeded from every
candidate the store holds, and a coverage line in the prompt: `1170 fabrics already tried:
xbar_staged x1084, hybrid x38, clos x30, torus x5, mesh x5, butterfly x5, ring x3`, with the note
that a structural repeat is refused. Per-campaign visitedness stays right for a grid strategy,
where re-screening a cached candidate is nearly free; it is wrong for a strategy spending a model
call per proposal.

**Not established.** Whether it changes what the model proposes. The mechanism is in and the
information is now present; no run has yet compared proposal novelty before and after.

---

## D301: A parameter that was accepted and ignored

**Context.** `enumerate_space(max_stages=4)` returned exactly the candidates `max_stages=3`
returned. The parameter was accepted, documented, and silently did nothing, so "search deeper" was
a no-op that looked like it worked.

**Cause.** The staged enumerator was hand-unrolled to three nested loops.

**Decision, and the mistake in between.** Rewritten to build stage chains level by level, so depth
is whatever the caller asks for: 178 candidates at 2 stages, 1,499 at 3, 3,380 at 4. The first
rewrite was recursive and depth-first, which fixed the depth and introduced something worse — under
`max_candidates` a depth-first walk spends the entire cap going deep on the FIRST first-stage it
tries, so a truncated space is not a sample of the space but one branch of it. Building by depth
means a cap truncates the deepest level and every shallower level is complete. The symptom that
exposed it was non-monotonicity: depth 4 returned FEWER candidates than depth 3, which is
impossible for a superset.

Separately, `enumerate_space` never forwarded the caller's `max_candidates` to the staged family,
so a caller's cap was silently replaced by a default — the same class of bug in the same function.

**Not established.** Whether 4-stage fabrics are worth their latency. Each rank costs a cycle, and
the space now contains them so the question can be measured rather than assumed.

---

## D302: Routing policy is a dimension, not an implementation detail

**Context.** This repo had already measured route selection as the largest single lever in the
whole interconnect study: the SAME radix-4 butterfly served 8.92 words/cycle when each request
took the first valid path and 13.54 when requests rotated among equivalent paths. A 52% swing on
identical silicon, wider than most topology choices produce — and it was hard-coded, so every
fabric was evaluated at one policy and the space was missing its strongest dimension.

**Decision.** `routing` is part of a topology's identity, carried in its params, honoured by the
RTL generator, and enumerated for the families that HAVE a choice of path (butterfly, Clos,
hybrid); on a single-path fabric the policy is a no-op and enumerating it would double the space
to measure the same thing twice. Three policies: `rotate` (per-input counter, the previous
behaviour and every prior measurement), `static` (fixed by input index, no counter), and `first`.

`first` is kept precisely because it is bad. A space containing only good policies cannot show
what policy is worth, and the 8.90 measurement is what makes the 13.55 mean anything.

**Reproduced, and one new result.** Re-measured through the new parameter: `first` 8.90, `rotate`
13.55, against the 8.92 and 13.54 on record. And `static` also serves 13.55 — the same throughput
as rotation with no advancing counter and one less register per input, a candidate the space could
not previously express.

**Two bugs this exposed, both about duplicated identity.** `enumerate_space` deduped by
`(blocks, stages, peak_concurrency)`, which routing does not change while changing the answer from
8.90 to 13.55, so every policy variant was deleted as a duplicate. Worse, the generative
strategy's `_validate` kept its own INLINE copy of that signature: when the stored one gained
routing the two stopped matching and structural dedup stopped catching anything at all, including
exact repeats. A duplicated definition is the defect; the drift is only how it surfaces.

**Not established.** How policy interacts with the physical rung. Removing the counter makes
`first` and `static` slightly smaller, and whether that shows up in placed area at this width is
measured per candidate rather than assumed.

---

## D303: A conclusion may not quote a number it was not shown

**Context.** D297 built model-written conclusions with a structural contract: cite your evidence,
state your limits. The first pair drawn from a real store showed that was not enough. One
conclusion claimed a peak of "21 words/cycle" and that values were "discrete integers" against a
store whose measurements are 12.06, 13.51, 14.89 ... 18.85 and never 21, and it confused the
structural capacity of 28 with achieved throughput. It cited real facts and described them
wrongly.

**Decision.** Every number in a conclusion must appear in the evidence it cites, or the conclusion
is refused and the refusal printed. The prompt says so too, because a rule that is only enforced
teaches nothing.

Three deliberate looseness choices, each of which would otherwise reject good work: numbers match
as PREFIXES, so evidence of 534.6707230352188 supports "534.67" and "534"; bare integers of 100 or
less are exempt, because they are almost always counts a model is entitled to compute ("10 trials
across two campaigns" is 4 + 6) rather than measurements it is quoting; and a refusal names what it
rejected rather than silently returning fewer conclusions.

**What this does and does not catch.** It catches invented magnitudes, which was the observed
failure. It does NOT catch a conclusion whose numbers are all real and whose reasoning about them
is wrong — "throughput is set by discrete structural choices" quotes nothing and is still a claim
about mechanism that these measurements do not establish. Numeric grounding is a floor, not a
proof, and the `(INFERRED, not measured)` label is still doing the important work.

---

## D304: Asking for real silicon mid-search

**Context.** The composed screen prices each selector arity in isolation and sees no wire between
switches, so it runs optimistic on frequency by 100 to 200 MHz (D280). Until now only the decision
rung could settle that, once, at the very end. A search that became unsure about a candidate had
no way to spend a real placement on it and find out.

**Decision.** `measure` as an action the orchestrator may choose: name a fabric already in the
store and it is placed WHOLE on the vendored core with real Yosys and OpenROAD, mid-search. It
cost a registration and no change to the loop, which is the first real test of D298's claim that
the action menu is data.

**A guard this required, and would have broken without.** The barren backstop counted new
candidates, and a measurement finds none — so a measure step read as a wasted step and three of
them would have stopped a search that was working. `Outcome.progressed` lets an action say it
accomplished something without finding anything, defaulting to `gained > 0` so an action that
finds things need say nothing. The yields digest now carries a step's own words, so the NEXT
decision sees `xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8 PLACED WHOLE: 0.0154 mm2 at 737 MHz (measured, not
composed)` rather than "0 candidates".

**Not established.** Whether a model uses it well, or at all. It has been exercised with a
scripted model to prove the registry and the loop, and no local model has yet chosen it in a real
run. A capability that is never selected is worth exactly nothing, and that is measurable the next
time one runs.

---

## D305: A screen that learns from the silicon it was checked against

**Context.** Every screened `fmax_mhz` in the interconnect study is a COMPOSED estimate: per-arity
blocks priced in isolation, no wire between switches. D280 measured what that costs — 100 to 200
MHz optimistic against placed silicon — and the screen is what applies the 600 MHz constraint, so
that optimism decides which fabrics survive to be measured and which are discarded unmeasured.

Meanwhile `flux_calibration` already existed: a residual store, `calibrate_estimate`, and a runner
that accepts `calibration_db_path` and corrects every screening result BEFORE it is classified
(D98/D222). The interconnect study never passed it, and `flux_campaign_step` did not even expose
the parameter, so the machinery was built, tested and unreachable from the agent surface.

**Decision.** Expose it, and record a residual from every whole-fabric placement — from the
`measure` action mid-search and from the decision rung at the end. Each placement already produces
the pair that matters: what composition predicted and what silicon did.

**Measured, on this study's own numbers.** From three placements the flywheel learns the composed
screen runs +20.7% optimistic (sd 3.2%), and corrects a composed 871 MHz to 721 MHz with an
interval of [686, 761] against a placed truth of 737. The bare point estimate was 134 MHz wrong;
the calibrated one is 16 MHz low and its interval contains the answer. A placement stops being
worth one row and starts improving every screen that follows it.

**A one-word bug that would have voided the whole thing.** The residual was first recorded with a
`caveat` set, and `records_for` excludes caveated records from residual statistics by default. The
records would have accumulated and never been used — a flywheel spinning without turning anything,
with no error and no missing output to notice. The caveat field is for comparisons that are not
clean; a composed estimate against placed silicon is precisely the comparison being calibrated,
and the nuance belongs in `reference_source`.

**Also fed to the orchestrator.** Each residual is written as an `estimator_bias` fact, so the
lessons brief carries lines like "composed fmax read +18% against placed silicon for
xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8 (871 vs 737 MHz)". That is what tells a model which estimates to distrust,
and therefore which fabric is worth the next real placement — a choice that was previously a guess.

**Not established.** Whether one residual per shape generalises. The correction is currently a
single pooled mean across every fabric shape, and a 4-rank fabric's composition error is not
obviously the same as a 2-rank one's. The store keeps `arch_hash` per record, so a per-shape
correction is available later; nothing yet measures whether it is warranted.

---

## D306: A mesh you can actually run

**Context.** Ring, mesh and torus entered the space with measured area and frequency and a
MODELLED throughput (D299), because `fabric.py` builds feed-forward fabrics: a transfer crosses
each rank once, there are no cycles, and routing is a table lookup per stage. A mesh is a graph and
breaks every one of those assumptions, so its throughput column could not honestly be compared
with the rest of the table.

**Decision.** A second generator, `router_fabric.py`, emitting a rows x cols network of five-port
routers with dimension-order routing. It presents the SAME module interface as the staged
generator, so the traffic harness and all three correctness checks — every word verified at the
bank it claims, its payload checked against its own complement, per-client delivery counted —
apply unchanged.

**Why there are no virtual channels, which is the hard part of a real NoC.** A buffered network
can deadlock: packets hold buffers while waiting for buffers, and a cycle of such waits never
resolves. This network is BUFFERLESS and inherits the contract every fabric here already has — a
transfer that loses arbitration is not granted and the client retries. Nothing is held, so no cycle
of holding can form, and deadlock is impossible by construction rather than by protocol. That is a
real simplification, stated on every number it produces: what is measured is a bufferless mesh
under drop-and-retry, which loses throughput a buffered design would recover. It is not a claim
about NoCs in general.

**Measured, and immediately useful.** A 6x6 mesh serves 12.58 words/cycle and a 6x6 torus 14.53,
both with zero misroutes and zero corrupted payloads, every client delivering. The torus beating
the mesh by 15% on identical router count is the wrap links doing what they are for — and it is a
measurement rather than an assertion, which is the whole point.

**What it disproved on its first run.** D299 had asserted that a router network's capacity is its
bisection, and drew a confident conclusion from it about NoCs being unable to carry this problem.
The 6x6 mesh beat that stated capacity by a factor of two. The model was wrong, the RTL said so
within a minute of existing, and D299 is corrected rather than left standing.

**Not established.** Anything about buffered NoCs, adaptive routing, or virtual channels. Adaptive
routing is exactly what would reintroduce the deadlock this design avoids, so the path diversity
of these networks is 1.0 per hop by construction and reported as such. Large meshes are also not
practically simulatable — a 28x28 grid is 784 routers, and Verilator build time already dominates
the measured cost of a small one — so the sizes the space enumerates are not all sizes it can run.

---

## D307: Three ways to enumerate a candidate nobody needed

**Context.** Three separate enumeration bugs, found by running the search rather than reading it,
and grouped because they share one shape: a candidate was offered that could not, or need not,
exist.

**A policy variant where there is no choice of path.** D302 offered routing variants for the
families that have multiple paths — butterfly, Clos, hybrid — filtering by FAMILY. A radix-8
butterfly over 32 ports has exactly one path per destination, so its policy is a no-op, and the
decision rung duly placed `butterfly-radix8`, `butterfly-static-radix8` and `butterfly-first-radix8`
at identical area, frequency and throughput: three real place-and-route runs to measure one fabric
three times. The family is not the property that matters; path multiplicity is, and it is now
tested by building the candidate and asking its router. 35 variants became 33, all of them on
fabrics that genuinely have a choice.

**A grid too small to hold its endpoints.** Client `i` injects at router `i` and bank `i` ejects
from router `i`, so a router network needs at least `max(clients, banks)` routers. A 5x5 mesh has
25 and this problem has 32 banks, so the generated RTL referenced routers that do not exist and
failed in the Verilator compile — at measurement time, after the candidate had been screened,
escalated and queued. It now raises at construction, which means it is simply not in the space.

**A grid too large to simulate.** Build cost grows faster than router count: 49 routers build and
run in 15s, 100 in 78s, 196 in 95s, and the space enumerates up to 32x32 = 1,024. Past a threshold
(`FLUX_MAX_SIM_ROUTERS`, default 256) measurement is refused explicitly and the caller falls back
to the analytic model, which it already reports as modelled. The alternative was a round that
stops for many minutes on one candidate with no indication why.

**What these have in common.** Each was invisible to 1,433 unit tests and obvious within one real
run. Two of them cost real place-and-route time before they surfaced, and the third would have.

**A result worth keeping from the same measurements.** Mesh throughput FALLS as the grid grows:
12.23 words/cycle at 7x7, 10.72 at 10x10, 8.81 at 14x14. Longer paths mean more hops, more
contention and more drops in a bufferless network, so for this problem the smallest valid grid is
the best one. That is the opposite of the intuition that a bigger network carries more.

---

## D308: Scopes that nested instead of partitioning

**Context.** A round enumerated a "scope" chosen by the orchestrator from six: `narrow` or `wide`
breadth, at up to 2, 3 or 4 stages. An operator noticed the rounds looked like they were doing the
same thing repeatedly and asked whether one round would do.

**Measured, and the answer was worse than the question implied.** Every scope is a strict SUBSET of
`wide/4`, with ZERO candidates unique to it: narrow/2 has 29, wide/2 180, narrow/3 138, wide/3
1,561, narrow/4 138, wide/4 7,410. So the six scopes were a nested chain and one round covers all
of them.

Two consequences, both bad. The orchestrator's scope choice was not a search decision at all — it
was a budget dial wearing a search dimension's clothes, and every "the model chose wide breadth at
up to 3 stages" in this repo's logs was a choice between a set and its own superset. And the
coverage line was wrong in both directions: a run enumerating `wide/4` alone reported 1 of 6 while
covering 100% of the space, and a run doing narrow/2 plus wide/2 reported 2 of 6 while covering
2.4% of it.

**Decision.** A round enumerates one FAMILY — staged, butterfly, Clos, hybrid, router — at full
depth and breadth. Families are disjoint, each reaches structures no other does, and "which
families were covered" is a claim that means something. Enumerating the Clos family versus the
router family is a real bet with different yields; narrow versus wide never was.

**Not established.** Whether family is the best partition. It is A partition, which is the property
that was missing, and the sizes are wildly uneven — staged holds 7,272 of 7,419 candidates while
router holds 9 — so a round's cost depends heavily on which family it picks. Splitting staged
further, by depth into disjoint bands rather than nested ceilings, is available and unmeasured.

---

## D309: Searching around a good answer, not just across the space

**Context.** The demo could enumerate what the rules express, propose what they cannot, and
measure a candidate for real. None of those answers "is there something slightly better next
door", which is the question a person asks after a good result and the one a Monte-Carlo or
annealing search is built around. The `narrow`/`wide` dials LOOKED like they meant this and did
not (D308): they were nested subsets of a static enumeration, with no incumbent anywhere in them.

**Decision.** `perturb {"from": <label>, "radius": small|large}` — a fourth action, defined against
an INCUMBENT, so the space it explores depends on where the search already is. That is the
difference from enumeration and the reason both are worth having: enumeration covers the codified
space once, perturbation exploits whatever turned out to be good in it.

`small` changes one decision by one step and the result is recognisably the same design;
`large` changes the shape — counts double or halve, a rank is added or removed, a mesh becomes a
torus. Measured on the current winner, `small` yields five buildable neighbours: two switch-count
changes, one fan-out change, and the two alternative routing policies.

**Two correctness properties, both learned from earlier failures here.** A stage's INPUT count is
re-derived from the chain rather than carried over, because copying it is exactly how a mutated
staged fabric stops chaining (D269's lesson, in a new place). And every mutant is BUILT before it
is returned, so a perturbation that cannot chain is simply not a neighbour rather than an error
discovered at measurement time.

**A bug this surfaced.** A perturbation round enumerates nothing — its space is the neighbour list
— which meant passing an empty family list. That list was tested for truthiness, so "enumerate
nothing" read as "enumerate everything": the round would have screened the entire 7,419-candidate
space beside the twelve neighbours it existed to measure.

**Not established.** Whether a model uses it, or uses it well. The orchestrator now chooses between
exploring a family, exploiting a good result, inventing something new, and verifying with real
silicon — a genuinely strategic menu — but no run has yet shown it choosing `perturb`, and D304
records what happened the last time a capability was added without that evidence.

---

## D310: A model applied to a structure it was not written for

**Context.** Router networks were never escalated: the screen put a 7x7 mesh at 4.7 words/cycle
where the RTL measures 12.23, a 2.6x underestimate, so they lost at screening and nothing measured
them. That made the conclusion "NoCs lose here" unusable — it could not be distinguished from
"a model that does not apply to them said they lose".

**Cause.** The stage-load model (Patel, 1981) charges a packet for arbitration at every element of
`switch_stages`, which is right for a feed-forward fabric where every transfer crosses every rank.
A router network's `switch_stages` was set to its DIAMETER, so a 7x7 mesh was charged twelve
applications of load-thinning. A packet in a grid does not traverse the diameter; it traverses its
own path and ejects on arrival, and the mean Manhattan distance between uniform endpoints is
`2(k^2 - 1)/3k` — 4.6 hops, not 12.

**Decision.** Charge the mean path, not the worst one. `stages` still reports the diameter, because
that is the depth and the worst-case latency; `switch_stages` now carries the mean hop count,
because that is what a packet actually pays. Measured after the change: 7x7 mesh 8.17 against 12.23
(was 4.7), 6x6 mesh 10.42 against 12.57, 6x6 torus 12.13 against 14.48.

**Still pessimistic, and stated as such.** The corrected model runs 17-35% low, comparable to the
21%-low behaviour already recorded for a Clos at m = n, and for a related reason: it assumes a
packet contends for all five ports at every hop, when traffic under dimension-order routing is not
uniform across ports and ejecting packets free capacity. Getting to the ~10% this model achieves on
single-path staged fabrics would need a bufferless-mesh throughput analysis, which is not built.

**The outcome did not change, which is the point.** With a fair estimate the mesh is still
dominated on ALL THREE screen objectives — 8.17 words/cycle against 14.88, 313,600 mux bits against
86,016, 9,856 link bits against 3,584 — so it is correctly not escalated. Router networks lose on
hardware cost, decisively, and that can now be said without the caveat that the model was unfair to
them. A correction that changes no decision is still worth making when it changes what the decision
is EVIDENCE for.

---

## D311: One definition of "the same fabric"

**Context.** Five places answered the question "are these two fabrics the same": the enumerator's
deduplicator, the proposer's repeat check, the proposer's validator, the decision rung's shortlist
and the demo's throughput cache. They were written at different times, for locally sensible
reasons, and they drifted.

**What the drift cost, all of it observed rather than imagined.**

* The proposer's validator kept an INLINE copy of the signature. When the stored one gained
  routing (D302) the two stopped matching and structural deduplication stopped catching anything
  at all — including exact repeats, which is what it was built for.
* The decision rung keyed by routing unconditionally, so a single-path fabric and its `-static`
  and `-first` aliases were three entries in a five-slot shortlist: three real place-and-route
  runs to measure one design, and two candidates crowded out.
* The throughput cache keyed by `(kind, blocks, stages)` with NO routing, so a fabric and its
  `-first` variant shared an entry. That one is the sharpest: a cache hit would have returned
  13.55 words/cycle for a fabric that measures 8.90, a 52% error delivered silently.
* Perturbation offered routing neighbours unconditionally, wasting two of five on a single-path
  fabric — the same waste D307 had already removed from enumeration, reintroduced by writing the
  rule again somewhere else.

**Decision.** `structural_key_of(topo)` in one place, used by all of them: blocks, depth, and
routing ONLY where the fabric has a choice of path. `has_path_choice` is public for the same
reason — three callers needed that predicate and three copies would drift the same way.

**And consolidating found an over-merge nobody was looking for.** The enumerator's old key included
`peak_concurrency` and raw routing but could not see path multiplicity, so a Clos at n=4,m=4 and a
staged fabric with the same blocks, depth and concurrency were treated as duplicates and one was
DISCARDED. They are not duplicates: the Clos rotates among middle switches and the staged fabric
cannot, which D302 measured as worth up to 52% of throughput. Three designs were being deleted from
the space on every enumeration.

**The pattern, since this is the fourth instance in one session.** Each drift began as a correct
fix applied in one place — routing added here, a filter added there — and the failure was never in
the logic but in the assumption that a rule lives where it was last written. A duplicated
invariant does not announce itself when it drifts; dedup that has stopped working looks exactly
like dedup that has nothing to do.

---

## D312: Code that is never run is code that is already broken

The `experiments/` harnesses are the only code here that CI never executes. Each buys a number
that costs too much to buy often — an hour of real place-and-route for the escalation speedup, a
few hundred local-model rounds for the thinking comparison — so they are scheduled by hand and can
sit untouched across many refactors of the code they drive.

`escalation_speedup.py` had accumulated three independent breaks and had never been run once. It
called `run_round` with the arity it had before nested depth/breadth scopes became flat families
(D308); it called a `check_toolchain` that had moved into the evaluator ABI as `require_tools`
(D298); and it imported the demo from a `demos/` directory the reorganisation around the four
module types had deleted (D296). Any one of them kills it on its first line of real work.
`thinking_efficacy.py` carried the same dead import path and a `fabrics_attempted` that had become
`campaign_tally`.

None of this was subtle. It was invisible, which is different: every check in the suite was green,
because nothing in the suite touched these files. The harnesses read as working code. A harness
that has never run is not "untested" — it is a file that has never once been proven to do anything,
and the honest prior is that it does not work.

**What now checks it.** `tests/unit/test_experiment_harnesses.py` checks statically what running
one would check dynamically: every harness imports; every import resolves, including the
function-local ones written to keep module import cheap and which therefore hide a stale module
name from everything short of execution; every `demo.<f>(...)` call binds against the signature the
demo has today; and the family a harness names is one the demo actually offers, since a stale
family string fails as an empty enumeration rather than a crash — an experiment that measures
nothing and reports a speedup.

Each of the four checks was confirmed by re-introducing the break it exists for. That step earned
its keep: three of the four caught their break, and the fourth did not. The test file puts the
harnesses' own `sys.path` directories on the path so function-local imports resolve, which made
`import demo` succeed whether or not the harness's insert pointed anywhere real — the check was
masking the exact break it was written for. Hence a separate check that the directories a harness
adds to `sys.path` exist. A rot detector that has not been shown to fail is itself untested code,
which is the subject of this record.

**What this does not do.** It confirms the harnesses still fit their sockets. It says nothing about
whether they produce a meaningful number, which only running them establishes, and neither has been
run. Both remain open work rather than results: D290's escalation speedup is still an unmeasured
claim, and D289's `/no_think` adoption is still a workaround backed by no quality comparison.

---

## D313: Monte-Carlo that actually walks, and the objective it nearly optimized away

`perturb` (D309) was named for a Monte-Carlo search and was not one. It called `mutate` once, got
the parent's entire neighbourhood back deterministically — seven designs for a typical staged
fabric, so its `limit=12` never bound — screened all seven and stopped. Its `variant_key` then
recorded the (parent, radius) pair as done, so asking again spent a step and did nothing. That is
exhaustive local enumeration: no sampling, no acceptance test, and no way for the search to move.
Two attempts found no improvement, which is the expected yield of looking at seven neighbours of
one design once.

The fix was not a bigger neighbourhood. A seven-neighbour ball is ample if the chain walks, since
each accepted move lands on a new incumbent with a ball of its own. `anneal.py` walks: Metropolis
acceptance, geometric cooling, and a widening of the radius only once a chain stalls, on the
grounds that a run of rejections means the incumbent sits in a basin one decision cannot leave.

It is simulated annealing, not MCMC. The proposal is uniform over neighbourhoods of varying size
and no Hastings correction is applied, so the chain does not target a Boltzmann distribution. The
distinction is worth keeping because it governs what may be concluded at the end.

**The mistake, which is the part worth remembering.** The first version minimized `mux_bits`
subject to the structural-capacity constraint. It beat the exhaustive enumeration by 30% in
seconds — 57,344 mux_bits against 81,920 — and the design was junk: 4.5 words/cycle of delivered
throughput against the enumerated optimum's 13.9. The constraint it satisfied was
`max_served_per_cycle`, the traffic-agnostic waist, which asks only whether 28 clients *could* be
carried. What a fabric actually delivers is `expected_served_per_cycle`, a screen objective in its
own right, and nothing was defending it. The walk bought its area saving by discarding three
quarters of the throughput.

This is the ordinary way a Monte-Carlo optimizer fails against a surrogate: it finds the hole in
the objective, quickly, and reports a number that looks like progress. Collapsing a `mode: pareto`
study to one scalar was the error, and it was caught only by looking at the winning design instead
of at its score. The walk now carries the objective vector the demo screens on — `mux_bits`,
delivered throughput, inter-stage wiring — with weighted scalarization for acceptance and Pareto
dominance for the archive.

**What it is worth, measured against exhaustively enumerating 1,217 feasible designs (front 18).**

| chains | steps | crossover | seconds | archive | outside the enumeration | strictly dominating |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 600 | 80 | 15 | 21 | 14 | 1 |
| 16 | 1200 | 200 | 34 | 28 | 21 | 1 |
| 32 | 2000 | 400 | 77 | 35 | 35 | 1 |
| 64 | 3000 | 800 | 175 | 37 | 37 | 1 |

Searching harder pays until roughly 32 chains and then saturates: 2.3x the time buys two designs.
At that point every archive member lies outside what enumerating 1,217 designs can express.

The last column is the honest headline and it is not the flattering one. The walk almost never
strictly dominates an enumerated front member. It **widens the trade-off surface** rather than
winning on any axis — the best single-objective values still come from enumeration, which is what
exhaustive search of a codified space is good at. Reporting this as "Monte-Carlo found smaller
fabrics" would repeat the error above in prose.

**Why crossover is there.** Every move `mutate` offers changes one design and none of them changes
`kind`, so a chain's family is fixed at its start: an ensemble seeded on staged fabrics had never
once looked at a butterfly. Crossover splices one staged fabric's leading ranks onto another's
trailing ones, which is a jump no sequence of single edits was going to make. It is defined only
for the staged form, where a cut point is a real structural boundary; for a butterfly's radix or a
mesh's grid, splicing is just picking one parent's number, which mutation already does.

**The economics this rests on.** The analytic screen runs at ~30,000 designs/second while one real
placement costs minutes. Spend the cheap thing without counting and the expensive thing only on
what survives — 4,800 proposals cost 15 seconds, and the two designs an ensemble surfaced were
screened and placed for real in 38.

**Still a screen.** Every metric the walk reads is a screen metric. `mux_bits` is an area proxy
(r = 0.95 against placed area over this repo's 23-fabric store) and frequency does not exist at
screen time at all, so a walk cannot know whether what it found closes at 600 MHz. The archive is a
list of candidates for measurement, never a result.

**Open.** The cross-family jump remains beyond the walk: one butterfly entered a 35-design archive.
Monte-Carlo cannot make that move and crossover cannot either. The local model can, which is what
pairing the two is for, and it is not yet demonstrated.

---

## D314: The flywheel was learning from failures only

A run stored this, as a lesson for later runs to read:

> "A maximum throughput of 28 words per cycle is currently unreachable within the tested design
> space, as all observed throughput failures were below this minimum requirement."

The same run's results table, printed one screen earlier, listed thirty-one fabrics achieving
exactly 28. A second conclusion quoted a place-and-route frequency to thirteen significant figures.
Both passed validation and were written to the fact store, which is fed into the next run's prompt.

**Why the guards missed it.** `unsupported_numbers` checks that every number in a claim appears in
its cited evidence. "28" is a bare integer under 100 and therefore exempt as a count; the
thirteen-digit frequency was *literally present* in the evidence, so it passed on the merits. The
check asks whether a number is supported, never whether the claim is true or the precision sane.

**The actual cause was upstream of the model.** The caller ranked refusals first and truncated to
eighteen facts. The store held 506 — 261 refusals, 210 measured points, 35 frontier outcomes — so
the model was handed eighteen failures and not one success. It was not reasoning badly. It was
reasoning correctly about a sample containing no counterexample, because none had been shown to it.
A conclusion drawn from failures alone can only be pessimistic.

Evidence is now selected round-robin across kinds, so every kind present contributes before any
kind contributes twice: 6/6/6 in place of 18/0/0.

**Three further guards, and the one that mattered least.** Numbers are trimmed to six significant
figures before the model reads them, since it copies what it is given and the prefix-matching
check still accepts a trimmed quote against its untrimmed source. Absolutes — "unreachable",
"never", "all observed", "no fabric" — are refused outright: a model shown two dozen facts out of
hundreds can support claims about what was seen and never about what does not exist. This last one
is blunt and will occasionally refuse a true universal, which costs a lesson; the alternative cost
a false one that fed forward.

Worth recording that the balanced evidence did nearly all the work. Re-run against the same store,
the model wrote conclusions of a different character entirely — comparing radix-2 against radix-8
butterflies across throughput, area, link bits, mux bits and frequency, with the trade-off stated
in both directions. No guard would have produced that. It came from showing the model what had
worked.

**And then they were thrown away.** Those good conclusions were never stored. The model replied
`{"conclusions": [...]}`; the parser accepted a bare array or a lone dict, wrapped the envelope as
a single item, found no `statement`, and `continue`d — silently, because the malformed-item path
recorded no refusal. Zero conclusions with zero explanation, which reads exactly like a model that
had nothing to say and sent the search looking somewhere else entirely. A lone list-valued key is
now unwrapped, and every dropped item reports what it was missing.

The same silence hid a second failure: the conclusion call timed out at 300s on every run and said
so nowhere, because `draft_conclusions` swallowed the exception. Balanced evidence is a richer
prompt and a reasoning model takes longer over it — measured at over five minutes for this store —
so the budget is 900s and a failed call now says which exception ended it. An optional step may
fail quietly; it may not fail invisibly.

**A related fix in the orchestrator, from the same run.** `NOT YET DONE` is assembled from unrun
*declared variants*, and only an action with a finite variant set can appear there. In this demo
exactly one action had one — `enumerate`, over the five families — so the line read "not yet done:
<families>" every round while the Monte-Carlo step, the proposer and the perturber went unmentioned.
The model chose `enumerate` twice against a space it had exhausted and never once chose `anneal`.
The line was arguing for one action by omission.

Naming the repeatable actions in that line was not enough: the next run stopped after two steps,
still without annealing. What worked was giving `anneal` declared variants of its own, so it is
outstanding work rather than a standing offer. The run after that chose `enumerate clos`, then
`anneal 32x2000`, then `anneal 16x1200`, then `enumerate butterfly`, then `perturb` — 64,000
screened proposals seeded from 2,560 designs the store already held, which is the memory the
Monte-Carlo work was for. Five new fabrics against two.

**Not fixed.** The best fabric is unchanged at 0.0153 mm2, 871 MHz. Nothing here found a better
design; it fixed a search that was recording false lessons, ignoring half its capabilities, and
reporting neither.

---

## D315: A flake's `nixConfig` does not apply when the flake is an input

The dev shell stopped evaluating with `attribute 'zigzag-dse' missing`. The cause was a refactor,
not a pin: `zigzag-dse` and `stream-dse` had been built here from PyPI in roughly two hundred lines
of derivation, and were replaced by `chipPkgs.zigzag-dse` — but nixchip only began exporting them
after the rev this repo pinned. Simplification is the right direction; it just needed the input
moved with it.

Moving it exposed the thing worth recording. nixchip declares a binary cache in its own flake:

    nixConfig.extra-substituters = [ "https://nixchip0.cachix.org" ];

**A flake's `nixConfig` applies only when that flake is the top-level one being evaluated. It is
ignored when the flake is an input.** Consuming nixchip therefore consulted its cache never, and
the shell compiled OpenROAD from source — for hours, silently, with no indication that a cache
existed and was being skipped. Repeating the substituter and its public key in this repo's own
`flake.nix` is what makes it apply. It further needs `accept-flake-config = true` in nix.conf, or
`--accept-flake-config`, since nix ignores a flake's substituters otherwise and does so quietly.

With the cache actually consulted, the dry run reduced from a full rebuild to two derivations:
OpenROAD and the shell. 200 of OpenROAD's 201 closure paths were already in nixchip0 — that cache
was well populated all along and had simply never been read.

**Which is why the obvious fix was wrong.** Reverting to nixchip's own nixpkgs pin was tried first
on the reasoning that following it preserves binary-cache hits. It does, but the argument had been
inverted: overriding the pin was not what forfeited the hits, omitting the substituter was. Two
further attempts were needed to find the pair that evaluates at all — at nixos-unstable 1559d3da
the default interpreter is Python 3.14 and nixchip's stream-dse has no ortools wheel for it. The
only combination where both evaluators resolve is nixchip's own pin, which is where its packages
are built.

OpenROAD took eight minutes on 64 cores rather than the hours feared, and has been pushed to
nixchip0, so the next machine downloads it. The interpreter moved 3.12.13 -> 3.13.13 in the
process; the full suite passes unchanged on it.

**The general lesson.** A cache that is configured but never consulted is indistinguishable from no
cache at all, except that it looks fine in the config. The `nixConfig` block was present, correct,
and inert, and the only symptom was a build everyone assumed was necessary.

---

## D316: The frontier ranks on an estimate that is 20% optimistic

**This record replaces an earlier version of D316 that got the cause wrong.** It claimed an
OpenROAD bump had moved measured frequencies ~20% and pushed cached results across the 600 MHz
constraint. The measurements behind it were real; the attribution was not.

`interconnect_phys@asap7/m2` — the evaluator every row of the results table comes from — is the
COMPOSED estimate: real Yosys and OpenROAD per distinct selector arity, fitted over widths 8/16/32
and evaluated at 128b. `measure_whole_fabric` is a different rung: one placement of the entire
fabric. Re-measuring 45 stored rows with the latter and comparing against the former compares two
rungs, not two toolchains. Composed-against-composed across the same toolchain change is stable to
about a percent (`xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8`: 0.0153 mm2 at 871 vs 879 MHz). The toolchain bump was
close to neutral. The gap was the fidelity ladder, in plain sight.

The run's own log had already said so, on the line above the one that was read:

    xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8 PLACED WHOLE: 0.0155 mm2 at 738 MHz (measured, not composed)
    learned: composed fmax read +19% against placed silicon (879 vs 738 MHz)

**What survives, and it is the more useful finding.** D280 recorded that the composed screen runs
