optimistic on frequency by 100-200 MHz. What nobody had done is ask what that costs the frontier.
Placing 45 of the store's fabrics whole says: **25 of them do not meet the 600 MHz constraint they
are reported as meeting.** The median placed frequency is 0.80x the composed one and the spread
runs 0.59x to 0.96x, so no single correction factor recovers the ranking. Area moves the other way,
median 0.89x, because the composed model prices no shared placement.

Both of the demo's headline answers move. The reported highest-throughput fabric,
`xbar_staged-15x2x4-4x15x8`, places at 597 MHz and fails. The smallest reorders:
`xbar_staged-8x4x4-4x8x8` at 0.0154 mm2 / 799 MHz displaces `xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8` at 0.0155.

**Why the run cannot see this itself.** `measure` — the action that places one fabric whole — was
chosen ONCE in fourteen steps. The calibration flywheel then learned a +19% correction from that
single point and applied it as one pooled factor, which a 0.59-0.96 spread does not support. The
ladder exists and is correct; the search simply never climbs it before reporting.

**The wrong lesson to draw** is that composed estimates are broken. They cost about a second
against several minutes and they rank the space well enough to find candidates worth placing.
The error is reporting a screening number under a heading that says "MEASURED", against a hard
constraint, without placing the handful of designs the answer actually rests on.

**Kept from the superseded version**, because it is independently worth having: the toolchain
fingerprint recorded once per store, in a sidecar rather than on every result row. It did not
catch this and was never going to — but a store does outlive the flake that filled it, and the
check costs nothing. Its warning text has been corrected to stop claiming a precedent that did not
happen.

**How this was caught, and it is not flattering.** The wrong attribution came from comparing a
number I had just measured against a number in the store without checking they were the same kind
of number. The run's own log named the distinction explicitly, one line away. The lesson is the
one D314 already recorded from the other side: a confident claim assembled from two real
measurements that were never comparable.

---

## D317: The loop had stages but no way back

Reading the CHIA loop figure alongside a real Flux run made the difference obvious. Both are
staged: cheap checks first, expensive ones last, a gate between each. CHIA's diagram is mostly
RED — every gate has a fail edge, and each one runs back to a model whose job is to fix what
failed. Flux had every stage and not one fail edge. A design that missed its gate was recorded as
`constraint_violated` and abandoned.

The store says what that cost: **17 fabrics reached real tools, carry all 28 clients, and miss
600 MHz — one of them by five megahertz.** Another 24 failed to build and were never looked at
again. These are the most informative failures the search produces, and they were the only results
nothing consumed.

They are also diagnosable without guessing. The evaluator already records per-arity delays, so
`selector_28x128b: 32 x 417.0 um2, 1773 ps` sits on the row of a fabric measured at 564 MHz — and
1/1773 ps is 564 MHz. The record names the rank that set the clock.

**So there are now two model roles, deliberately separate.** The ORCHESTRATOR chooses what the
search does next and never sees a netlist. The REPAIR model sees one failed design, its measured
frequency, its shortfall and its per-arity delays, and returns a fixed spec — which is then built,
screened and placed exactly like any other candidate. It cannot choose strategy, and a repair that
quietly widens the waist to buy frequency is rejected: `kind`, `clients`, `banks` and `width_bits`
are pinned over whatever it returns, and an unbuildable or unchanged answer is a failed step, not
a stored result.

**Two other things this changed.**

`_done` started EMPTY on every run, so a warm store was re-enumerated from scratch each time. 78%
of this repo's screen trials are cache hits and 94% over recent runs — the evaluations were free,
but the enumeration is Python, and one round spent 2,448 seconds, 38% of a whole run, re-deriving
3,307 topologies to find nothing. It is now seeded from the store by parsing campaign ids, scoped
to the problem, and counting only numeric rounds: `rounda4-staged` is an anneal that inherited a
family tag, and reading it as an enumeration would retire a family nobody enumerated. A run
against the existing store now skips all five families and goes straight to work.

`perturb` was removed. It looked at one deterministic neighbourhood and stopped, could not be
repeated, and drew 5 of 14 steps in a real run with 2 of those wasted on repeats it could not see
(D313). `anneal` does the same thing by walking, and now takes an optional `from` naming a design
to start every chain at — the one capability perturb had that annealing lacked. Five actions, none
redundant.

**A test gap worth recording.** Removing `perturb` also removed `_anneal` and `_population`, and
all 1,538 tests passed while the demo died with a `NameError` on its first line of real work. The
actions are nested functions inside `main()`, so nothing imports them and nothing calls them.
There is now a static check that every name the action registry references actually exists, which
is the check the interpreter would do at a point the suite never reaches. It was confirmed by
deleting `_anneal` again and watching it fail.

**Not fixed.** The repair edge exists and its near-miss detection is tested against real store
rows, but no repaired fabric has yet been measured end to end — whether the model can actually fix
a critical path it has been handed is untested. `propose` remains the weakest action on evidence:
28 proposals over this store's history produced 4 placed fabrics, all valid, none competitive
(best 0.0184 mm2 against 0.0138 enumerated). It is kept because it is the only action that can
cross families, which D313 left open, and not because it has earned its place.

---

## D318: One correction for a family whose bias has more than one shape

The screen's frequency estimate is corrected by a single pooled residual per (evaluator, metric).
D316 measured what that pool actually contains: over 45 fabrics placed whole, the composed rung
reads a mean +0.29 optimistic with a standard deviation of 0.156 — a correction whose spread is
more than half its own size. That is not one bias measured imprecisely. It is several biases
averaged.

Split by depth, the same 45 records:

| pool | n | mean residual | sd |
|---|---|---|---|
| pooled | 45 | +0.287 | 0.156 |
| depth 1 | 23 | +0.349 | 0.167 |
| depth 2 | 17 | **+0.186** | **0.082** |
| depth 3 | 4 | +0.395 | 0.067 |

The pooled figure is wrong for depth-1 and depth-2 in opposite directions, by about 0.1 each way,
and depth-2's spread is half the pool's. Leave-one-out over the same data: trusting the screen
costs 167 MHz of mean error, the pooled correction 62, and a per-depth correction 51.

`CalibrationStore` now carries an optional `bucket` per record and `records_for` can narrow to
one. Omitting it pools everything, which is what every existing caller does and continues to do;
the column is added on open, so a store written before this still opens with its rows unbucketed.

**Depth, and nothing finer.** Arity, family and link count were all available and all correlate
to some degree. With 45 points a finer split starves every pool, and a correction fitted on three
residuals is exactly the failure D101 recorded. Depth is also the mechanism rather than a
correlate: each rank is another selector delay in series. Thin buckets are not special-cased —
depth 3 holds four records and depth 4 holds one, so `calibrate_estimate`'s existing
`_MIN_TRUSTED_N` gate declines to correct on them and widens instead, which is what that gate is
for.

**Where this does NOT help, which is half the records.** Depth 1 comes out at sd 0.167, slightly
worse than the pool it was split from. It lumps single-stage crossbars in with butterflies and
routers, and depth does not separate those because they are all one rank. The gain here is
concentrated in depth 2 and 3; depth 1 needs a different cut, and this record does not have the
evidence to say which.

**Left on the table.** A LINEAR correction beats a ratio: leave-one-out gives 44.5 MHz against
51.0 for per-depth ratios, because the overestimate grows with the claim (`placed = 161 + 0.56 x
composed`, and the correlation between ratio and composed frequency is -0.46). The calibration
layer is built end to end on relative residuals — D105, D106 and D122 all reason in those terms —
and swapping the model is a deeper change than adding a dimension to the pool. The 18% available
from bucketing is taken here; the further 13% is not.

**Not yet demonstrated in a run.** The buckets are recorded and readable, and the numbers above
come from real placements replayed through the real store. What has not happened is a search that
selects its contenders using a bucketed correction and lands somewhere a pooled one would not.
Until that is measured, this is a better-conditioned estimator and not yet a better search.

---

## D319: The demo's headline answer was a fabric that cannot route

Turning the decision rung on by default (D316) had an effect nobody was looking for. Five
finalists were placed whole, and three of them did not place at all:

    xbar_staged-7x4x4-7x4x4-28x1x2   vendored placement failed: client 4 cannot reach banks [8,...
    xbar_staged-8x4x4-8x4x4-32x1x2   vendored placement failed: client 4 cannot reach banks [0,...
    xbar_staged-7x4x4-7x4x8          vendored placement failed: client 4 cannot reach banks [8,...

The first of those was the run's own reported answer: **SMALLEST that meets timing:
xbar_staged-7x4x4-7x4x4-28x1x2 — 0.0138 mm2**. It cannot carry a single word.

`build` succeeding means a shape is CONSTRUCTIBLE. It does not mean every client can reach every
bank, and a chain whose ranks do not cover the banks builds fine. The routability check existed —
`routing_tables` raises `UnroutableFabricError` — but it ran only at the decision rung, minutes of
Yosys and OpenROAD later, and until D316 that rung was off.

**Why the search preferred them, which is the part that matters.** A missing connection is a
missing mux, and `mux_bits` is the area proxy. The broken fabric costs 64,512 against the real
answer's 86,016, so it is cheaper *because* it is broken. Unroutable designs are 0.5% of the
enumerated space and were 60% of the finalists: a search minimizing area does not stumble into
them, it hunts them. Rarity in the space says nothing about frequency in the results when the
objective rewards the defect.

The check now runs in the screening evaluator. It costs 178 us against the screen's 36 — five
times the screen and four orders of magnitude under one placement. An unroutable fabric is
reported as zero capacity rather than raising, because the study already refuses a fabric whose
waist is too narrow and this is the narrowest waist there is; every existing caller then refuses
it without knowing the check exists. The provenance note carries the reason, so nobody has to
place it to find out.

**A correction to D313.** That record described the design minimizing `mux_bits` alone as buying
area by giving up three quarters of its throughput, and answered it by making the search
multi-objective. The design was unroutable. Its "4.5 words/cycle" was the Patel model computed on
a fabric that delivers nothing, and the regression test written to pin that story used the broken
fabric as its fixture. The test now asserts what was actually wrong. The multi-objective change
stands on its own merits — a cheaper, slower fabric and a dearer, faster one are genuinely two
points on a trade-off — but it was not what fixed that case, and with routability enforced the
cheapest routable design (81,920 mux_bits, 13.9 words/cycle) is a perfectly good one.

**What this says about the ladder.** Every rung above the screen was working: the composed rung
ranked, the decision rung placed, and the placement failure was reported clearly and immediately.
The defect was that the cheapest rung answered a question it had not been asked — "is this
shape buildable" instead of "does this fabric solve the problem" — and everything above inherited
the answer. Three of five placements were spent discovering something a 178-microsecond check
knew.

**Still open.** The repair action added in D317 has still never run end to end. And the store
holds these unroutable designs as screened, valid rows; they are refused going forward but the
existing frontier was computed with them in it.

---

## D320: Paths written inside data files fail nowhere

The nightly integration sweep failed. The cause was the reorganisation around the four module
types (D296), which moved `ir/` to `core/ir/`. Every source import was updated, because Python
fails loudly on a bad import and the fast suite would not run otherwise.

Paths written *inside data* have no such property. Eight corpus entries under
`mentor/benchmarks/` and twelve locators in `tests/golden/calibration_baseline.json` still
pointed at a directory that no longer exists, and nothing anywhere noticed for an entire session
of work on top of them.

**How it surfaced, which is worse than a missing file.** `test_calibration_live.py` selects its
corpus by workload path:

    _PUBLIC_ENTRIES = [e for e in _CORPUS.public_entries()
                       if e.workload_path == "core/ir/workload/examples/mlp-gemm0.yaml"]
    GEMM_WORKLOAD = FLUX_ROOT / _PUBLIC_ENTRIES[0].workload_path

The test string had been updated; the data had not. The filter matched nothing, and the module
died at COLLECTION with `IndexError: list index out of range`. Not one assertion failed — an
entire file's worth of tests never ran, and pytest's exit code was the only evidence.
`test_drift_detection.py` would have failed differently, opening a golden-listed file that is
not there.

**Why the fast suite stayed green.** Both live only in `tests/integration/`, which runs in the
nightly sweep. Every check that could have caught this was in the job that runs least often, so
the failure was authored in the morning and discovered by CI overnight.

So the checks now live in the fast suite, where they cost microseconds: every `*_path` in every
corpus entry resolves, every locator in the drift golden resolves, and — the case that actually
happened — the corpus still contains an entry with the workload path its tests filter for. A
corpus where every path resolves and which describes nothing anyone asks for fails just as hard,
one layer later. Confirmed by re-breaking one entry and watching it go red.

**The general shape.** A reorganisation is checked by the compiler for code and by nothing at all
for data. Anywhere a path, a module name, or an identifier is written as a *string in a data
file*, a rename is silent, and the only question is how long until something reads it. Here it
was three days and one nightly run. This is D312's lesson — code that is never run is already
broken — applied to data that is read rarely.

**Not addressed.** Stale paths remain in YAML *comments* ("# Paired with ir/workload/…"), which
mislead a reader but break nothing, and are left rather than swept so that the functional check
above is not diluted into a prose linter.

---

## D321: The repair edge works once the model stops writing JSON

The fail edge added in D317 had never run. Run against three real near-misses, it failed all
three, and the failures were identical in kind:

    final stage drives 16 outputs < 32 banks
    stage 1 emits 96 links but stage 2 takes 48

Asked to author a repaired spec, the model changed the rank that was slow and did not carry the
consequences through the chain. Chaining a staged fabric is an invariant — each rank's outputs are
the next rank's inputs, and the last must cover every bank — and a language model does not hold it
while writing JSON. The validator caught every one, so nothing bad reached the store; the
capability simply produced nothing.

`mutate` enforces that invariant by construction. So the model now CHOOSES rather than authors: up
to twelve neighbours are built, screened, checked for routability, and listed with the one number
that decides the clock — the widest selector each one leaves — and the model picks an index and
says which arity it is attacking. It does the part it is good at, judging which structural change
attacks a critical path, and never the part it is bad at.

Re-run against the same three fabrics, all three were repaired:

| fabric | was | after | widest selector |
|---|---|---|---|
| `xbar_staged-14x2x3-2x21x16` | 595 MHz | **651 MHz** | 21:1 -> 14:1 |
| `xbar_staged-16x2x6-4x24x8` | 571 MHz | **697 MHz** | 24:1 -> 16:1 |
| `xbar_staged-28x1x2-2x28x16` | 564 MHz | **651 MHz** | 28:1 -> 14:1 |

All three clear the 600 MHz floor they had missed, and the first came out at 0.0181 mm2 against
the 0.0278 it had measured before — smaller as well as faster. Three for three against zero for
three. The same lesson as the orchestrator's own menu, one layer down: give the model a menu, not
a blank page.

**Two other things this run of CI turned up.**

`test_arch_none_conformance.py` requires every registered backend to refuse a candidate it cannot
express by raising `NotExpressibleError`, and checks the raised type BY NAME. Both interconnect
evaluators called theirs `NotAnInterconnectError` and so failed a contract every other evaluator
honours — for as long as they had been registered, in a nightly job nobody read. The class is now
named for the ABI, with the old name kept as an alias because it is exported.

And the more embarrassing one. Rewriting the repair action replaced a span of `demo.py` between
two anchors by index, and the span contained four module-level functions that had been inserted
there earlier: `_toolchain_path`, `check_toolchain_drift`, `_calibration_path` and
`calibration_bucket`. Three were still called, `_calibration_path` from four sites. After that
edit the only check run was `import demo`, which succeeds with any of them missing. The full suite
was not re-run under the shell CI actually uses, so nothing said anything.

This is the SECOND time an index-slice edit deleted live functions — the first took `_anneal` and
`_population` out with `perturb` (D317) — and the check written then covered only the action
registry. There is no linter in this repo and none in CI, so an undefined name has nothing at all
standing between it and a runtime crash. There is now a check that every bare-name call in
`demo.py` resolves; it was confirmed by deleting `_calibration_path` again and watching it fail.

**A working habit this cost.** Everything this session was verified under `nix develop .#physical`
because the interconnect work needs those tools. CI's fast job runs `nix develop` — the default
shell — on every push. Nine tests passed under one and failed under the other for a whole session
before anyone looked.

---

## D322: A correction that was recorded but never read

D318 conditioned the calibration pool on depth, measured the gain by leave-one-out (62 MHz of mean
error down to 51), added a `bucket` column, wrote buckets from the demo, and tested all of it.
Nothing read them back. `records_for(..., bucket=...)` existed and no caller in the repo ever
passed a bucket, so the correction the record claims was not in effect anywhere: the demo went on
using the pooled number, and the 18% was real only in the offline analysis that measured it.

Half a capability, shipped with a decision record describing the whole one. The same shape as
D312's never-run harnesses and D317's never-run repair edge, and the third time this session.

**Where it now applies, which is the part that matters.** The frontier's `fmax_mhz` is the COMPOSED
estimate, and the line that reads it is:

    qualifying = {k: v for k, v in measured.items() if v["fmax_mhz"] >= TARGET_MHZ}

That filter decides which fabrics are placed for real. Applying the correction only to the printed
report would make the demo honest; applying it here changes which designs get the tool time, which
is what D316 found was going wrong — 25 of 45 fabrics reported as meeting 600 MHz did not meet it
when placed. Demoted fabrics are now named and shown with both numbers rather than silently
dropped.

**It predicts silicon.** Backfilled with the 45 real paired measurements, the depth-2 pool
(n=17, mean residual +0.186) turns a composed 879 MHz into 741. `xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8` is a
depth-2 fabric whose composed estimate is 879 and whose whole-fabric placement measured **738**.
Three megahertz, on a design the pool contains — not an independent test, but the arithmetic does
what it claims. Depth-1 takes the same 882 MHz to 654; depth-3 has four records, below the trust
floor, and falls back to pooled.

**Two bugs found by wiring it up, both mine.**

`residual_stats` never gained the `bucket` parameter — only `records_for` did — so every bucketed
lookup raised `TypeError`. It was invisible because `corrected_fmax` wrapped the call in a blanket
`except Exception` and returned the uncorrected value, which is exactly what a store with no
calibration data looks like. A defensive catch around a call whose signature I had got wrong turned
a loud error into a silent no-op. The catch is now narrow: `OSError`, `ValueError`, `ImportError`,
and nothing else.

**Still not wired.** `calibrate_result` — the generic path the campaign runner uses on every
screening result — remains pooled. Threading a bucket through it means teaching a generic ABI,
used from five call sites, about a key only the application can compute, and that is a design
change rather than a parameter. What is corrected today is the demo's own decision about who gets
placed, which is where the cost of being wrong is highest.

---

## D323: The resume printed a claim it did not act on

Running the demo end to end with every change from this session in place — the first time that had
happened — the first line was:

    resuming: 5 of 5 families already enumerated in this store

and two steps later it enumerated butterfly, then clos. The feature announced itself and did
nothing.

`already_enumerated` returned keys shaped `"enumerated:butterfly"`. The `enumerate` action's
`variant_key` is `lambda p: p["family"]`, which returns `"butterfly"`. The two never matched, so
seeding `_done` had no effect at all.

**The unit test passed because it tested a fabrication.** Its fixture built its own Action with
`variant_key=lambda p: f"enumerated:{p['family']}"` — the shape the helper produced rather than the
shape the demo registers. Both halves of a contract written by the same hand, agreeing with each
other and with nothing else. The fixture now uses the demo's own key function, which is the only
version of this test worth having.

**A second thing the same run exposed.** `COVERAGE: 0 of 5 families enumerated. NOT explored:
annealed:population:16x1200:0, annealed:population:32x2000:1, hybrid, router, staged` — after a
run whose store contained every family. `report.unexplored` carries every unrun variant of every
action, and the coverage line subtracted its length from the family count. It had been correct
until `anneal` gained declared variants (D317), at which point a change to one action silently
corrupted another action's report. The line now counts only keys that are families.

**And a third.** The orchestrator chose `repair`, and the run printed nothing whatsoever before
moving on. The action had declined — the label it picked was not a near-miss — and put its reason
in the step record, which nothing prints. A refusal that explains itself only to a data structure
is indistinguishable from a step that ran and found nothing. Declined steps now say why. Writing
that check also caught the shape of `Outcome.progressed`: it is tri-state, `None` meaning "derive
from `gained`", so testing it directly reported every successful step as declined. `was_productive`
is the resolved property and the one to read.

**What this cost, and the pattern.** Three defects, all shipped earlier in this same session, none
caught by 1,579 passing tests, all three visible in the first thirty lines of one real run. Two of
them were announced in the output as working. The tests were green because they tested the pieces
against each other rather than against the assembled thing — and the assembled thing had not been
run since before any of the pieces changed.

The end-to-end run is not a formality after a session of unit-tested changes. It is the only check
that sees the seams.

---

## D324: A gate on the entrance does nothing about what is already inside

D319 put the routability check in the screening evaluator, so no new unroutable fabric can enter
the space. The next full run still reported this as its answer:

    SMALLEST that meets timing: xbar_staged-7x4x4-7x4x4-28x1x2 — 0.0138 mm2

and, one screen later, failed to place it: `client 4 cannot reach banks [8,...`.

Rows written BEFORE the gate say capacity 28, and the frontier reads stored rows rather than
re-screening them. D319's own record noted this as open and it was left; a wrong headline is not
made right by a check that would have prevented it, and 0.5% of a 3,500-row store is enough to
own the top of a frontier when the objective rewards the defect.

The frontier now re-checks routability against each row's stored spec before ranking anything —
178 microseconds per row against a table of about fifty — and names what it drops. Three of five
finalists in the observed run were unroutable; the same three, and only those three, are removed.

---

## D325: The throughput rung answered for a fabric it could not simulate

An unroutable fabric did not merely survive the screen. It carried a healthy `8.4 words/cycle`,
which is what put it at the top of the frontier in the first place.

`_measure_throughput` already had the right instinct, one exception too narrow:

    except FabricIncorrectError:
        # NOT caught into a model fallback: a fabric that delivers words to the wrong bank
        # is not a slow candidate, it is a broken one, and substituting a modelled number
        # would keep it in the running with a clean-looking score (D268).
        raise
    except Exception as exc:      # simulator absent or fabric not buildable
        got = (modelled, f"analytic model — RTL measurement unavailable: {exc!s:.120}")

`UnroutableFabricError` is not a `FabricIncorrectError`. It fell to the generic handler, was read
as "the simulator is missing", and was answered with `expected_served_per_cycle()` — the Patel
stage-load model, which computes from switch counts and never consults a routing table, and so
returns a perfectly plausible number for a fabric where client 4 reaches no bank above 7.

D268 anticipated a fabric that delivers to the wrong bank and not one that cannot deliver at all,
which is the more complete failure of the two. Both now re-raise.

**Why nothing caught it.** The Verilator run is the strongest check in the ladder: 20,000 cycles of
uniform-random traffic, with misroute and corruption counters and a per-client delivery ratio. It
never ran. `measure_throughput` calls `routing_tables` first, which refused the fabric, and the
handler quietly replaced the refusal with an estimate. A verification layer that falls back to a
model when it cannot verify is not a verification layer — it reports its most confident number
exactly when it knows least.

The fallback itself is still right for its intended case: a machine with no Verilator should get a
modelled number and a provenance string that says so. What was wrong is that "I cannot simulate
this fabric because it is broken" and "I cannot simulate anything because the simulator is absent"
were the same branch.

---

## D326: Ports wired to nothing, and why they are shown rather than banned

Two of five finalists in a clean run were `xbar_staged-8x4x4-4x8x8` and `xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x9`.
For 28 clients into 32 banks, the first admits 32 ports where there are 28 clients and the second
drives 36 where there are 32 banks. Four wires to nothing in each. They sat beside
`xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8`, which fits exactly.

The obvious response is to refuse them, and the measurement says not to. Of 1,184 feasible fabrics
in this problem, **717 carry at least one dead port**, and the cheapest routable fabric in the
entire space has four dead inputs: 81,920 mux bits against 86,016 for the best exact fit. A switch
count that divides evenly downstream can more than pay for unused ports upstream — eight
first-stage switches waste four inputs and hand the second stage a factor it can use. Banning dead
ports would delete the cheapest design available, and it would do so on an aesthetic judgement
that the numbers contradict.

**What was actually wrong is that the waste was invisible.** Synthesis optimises a dead port away,
so all three of those fabrics placed within 0.0002 mm2 of each other and within 0.2 words/cycle.
Three of five real placements — minutes of Yosys and OpenROAD each — went to what is, in silicon,
one design point. The screen had priced the difference correctly at 8-14% more mux bits; the
placer erased it; and nothing in the output said either of those things had happened.

So the waste is MARKED, everywhere a fabric appears. The measured-results table and the decision
rung both carry a `dead` column, each with a header line saying these are neither refused nor
free: the screen charges for them and the silicon does not. And wherever a fabric is NAMED as an
answer — the two headline lines, the decision itself — it carries the count in words, because
someone reading "SMALLEST that meets timing: xbar_staged-8x4x4-4x8x8" and acting on it should not
have to cross-reference a column to learn that four of its client ports go nowhere. An exact fit
is annotated with nothing, since a marking that appears on everything marks nothing.

**Not fixed.** Finalist selection still has no diversity term, so near-duplicates can still take
three of five placements — they are merely legible now. Choosing finalists that span the trade-off
rather than clustering at one point is the change that would actually buy back the tool time, and
it is not made here.

---

## D327: Five placements, one point of the trade-off

The decision rung places the top N fabrics whole, at minutes of real Yosys and OpenROAD each. It
already refused to place the same silicon twice — a radix-4 hybrid over 28 clients IS 7x(4x4), and
the shortlist once placed it under both names. That rule compares STRUCTURE, and structure is not
what was being wasted.

In a clean run, `xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8`, `-8x4x4-4x8x8` and `-7x4x4-4x7x9` took three of five
placements. They are three different fabrics — different switch counts, different boundary
waste (D326) — and they placed within **0.0002 mm2 and 0.2 words/cycle** of each other. Three real
placements bought one number.

The screen had already said so. It separated them by 8-14% on `mux_bits`, and the placer put them
within 1.3%, because the difference between them is dead ports and synthesis optimises those away.
So the information needed to skip two of the three was available before any of them was placed.

The shortlist now runs two passes: the first skips a candidate the screen puts on the same point
as one already chosen (within 2% on area and 3% on throughput — just above what a placement can
resolve); the second drops that rule to fill any shortfall. The second pass matters as much as the
first — a front with three distinct points should still spend five placements if five were
budgeted, and a diversity rule that quietly buys fewer measurements is a worse trade than the
clustering it prevents.

On the observed cluster it now places the cheapest of the three, the throughput end, and the point
between them: three placements covering three points instead of one.

**And it was extracted from `main` to do it.** Every defect this demo shipped in a single session
lived in a function nested inside `main()` — `_anneal` and `_population` deleted by a slice edit
(D321), the enumerate key that never matched (D323), four module-level helpers cut out by another
slice (D321) — and nothing could import any of them, so the tests were green every time.
`choose_finalists` is module level and has nine tests, including the real cluster as a fixture.
That is the cheaper half of the lesson: the code that decides something expensive should be
callable without running the expensive thing.

---

## D328: Eight of thirteen decisions spent discovering there was nothing to do

A run with everything else working: five families resumed rather than re-enumerated, no failed
placements, seven unroutable rows dropped, thirteen fabrics demoted by the measured correction.
2,086 seconds against 6,394 for the same work before (D317/D323/D324/D325). And of its thirteen
orchestrator decisions, **five did work**:

    repair 8x4x4-8x4x4-32x1x2   declined: not a near-miss
    repair 8x4x4-8x4x4-32x1x2   already done
    measure 7x4x4-4x7x8         already done          (three times)
    repair 7x4x4-7x4x4-28x1x2   declined, then already done
    repair 7x4x4-4x7x8          declined: not a near-miss

`xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8` is the smallest fabric that meets timing. The model asked to repair it —
a fabric with nothing wrong — and asked three times to place one it had already placed in step 4.

**The cause is not the model's judgement.** `repair` and `measure` declare no variants, and only an
action with declared variants appears under `NOT YET DONE`. The model was shown a menu naming an
action and no legal values for it, so it guessed labels from the frontier — where the fabrics are
the good ones, which are exactly the ones that are neither near-misses nor unplaced.

The repeat grace (D317) refunded the STEP. It could not refund the model call, and at roughly a
minute each that is where the time went: the local model was 35.8% of the run, and most of its
work was deciding to do nothing.

`repair` now declares its actual near-misses, read from the store before the menu is built — six of
the seventeen this store holds, named in the prompt with their measured frequencies. An empty tuple
when nothing is repairable, which correctly removes the action from the outstanding list rather
than inviting a step that can only decline.

**Left alone deliberately.** `measure` still declares nothing, because its legal set is every
fabric in a 3,500-row store and a menu cannot carry that. Its repeats cost model calls and the
right fix is a different one — a shortlist of what is worth placing, which is what
`choose_finalists` computes at the end of a run and nothing computes during it.

**The general shape, for the third time.** D317 found the same defect for `anneal`: an action the
orchestrator never chose because the line listing outstanding work could not mention it. The rule
is now clear enough to state — an action whose legal values are knowable should declare them, and
one whose values cannot be enumerated needs a different mechanism than a menu.

---

## D329: The orchestrator was briefed with the four oldest things anyone had ever concluded

Asked whether the model might be missing context, the honest way to answer was to print the prompt
it actually receives. The context was not missing. It was wrong, and it opened like this:

    WHAT EARLIER WORK ALREADY SETTLED
    - ... the highest throughput observed is 21 words/cycle ... no configuration in either
      campaign reached the 28 minimum
    - ... the maximum observed max_throughput_words_per_cycle is 16.0 ... unsatisfied by all
    - The design space consistently fails to meet the minimum throughput requirement of 28.0

About fifty fabrics in that same store reach exactly 28. The orchestrator was told, as settled
fact and at the top of every decision, that its goal was unreachable — and then judged what to do
next against that.

**The cause is one line.** `FactStore.facts()` returns `ORDER BY mined_at, id`, oldest first, and
`lessons_digest` took `[:max_conclusions]`. The brief has always been the four OLDEST inferences in
the store. Those were drawn from two campaigns; the store now holds thirty-three. Every accurate
conclusion the mentor has produced since — the radix-2-to-8 trade-off with its four measured
numbers, the dominance finding, the latency comparison — was in the store and had never once been
shown to anyone.

Reversing that ordering replaced every line of the brief with a true and actionable one.

**What was tried first, and why it kept failing.** Before finding the ordering, three successive
guards were added against the false statements themselves: a check that a claimed maximum is not
exceeded by the store, a check for universal non-achievement, and a widening of that check as new
phrasings appeared. Each caught the case in front of it and the next paraphrase walked past —
"no configuration reached", then "consistently fails", then "without any candidate reaching".
Pattern-matching a model's prose to decide whether it is lying is a losing position, and three
rounds of it should have been the signal that the problem was upstream.

The guards are kept, because they are cheap and a RECENT conclusion can be overtaken too: a claim
about a metric's maximum is checked against the maximum the store now holds. That check earns its
place on the arithmetic, not on the phrasing. A restatement check sits beside it, comparing the
measured values and campaign ids two conclusions cite rather than their words — the pair that
motivated it overlapped 39% by vocabulary while citing exactly the same evidence.

**Also fixed, from the same prompt dump.** `repair` declared no variants, so the model guessed
labels from the frontier — where every fabric is a good one, and therefore not a near-miss. It now
declares the store's actual near-misses with their measured frequencies (D328).

**Still wrong in that prompt, and not fixed here.** `MEASURED SO FAR` shows six of fifty-seven
fabrics and leads with three that cannot route. The frontier digest does not apply the routability
re-check the results table now does, so the model's picture of what the study has is dominated by
broken designs.

**The lesson worth keeping.** A guard that filters output is worth having; an ordering that decides
which output is ever seen is worth checking first. The prompt is the whole interface to the model,
and nobody had read one.

---

## D330: The model's view of the study was six broken rows out of fifty-seven

Printing the orchestrator's prompt (D329) exposed a second defect in the same screen. Under
`MEASURED SO FAR` the model was shown this, on every decision:

    xbar_staged-7x4x4-7x4x4-28x1x2   area_mm2=0.01378  fmax_mhz=1162  throughput=8.439
    xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8          area_mm2=0.01528  fmax_mhz=878.8 throughput=14.89
    hybrid-radixradix4-xbarswitches4 area_mm2=0.01528  fmax_mhz=878.8 throughput=14.89
    xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8-first    area_mm2=0.01528  fmax_mhz=878.8 throughput=14.89
    xbar_staged-8x4x4-8x4x4-32x1x2   area_mm2=0.01575  fmax_mhz=1162  throughput=7.915
    ...

Six rows of fifty-seven. Three of them cannot route. Three more are the same fabric under three
names. Every frequency is the composed estimate, ~20% optimistic. Nothing says how much is not
shown.

**Each fault has the same shape as one already fixed elsewhere, and the prompt was missed each
time.** The shared digest sorts by the first metric and takes the top few, which here means the
cheapest — and the cheapest fabrics are the unroutable ones, because a fabric missing connections
is missing the muxes that would have cost area (D319). The results table stopped ranking them; the
prompt did not. D311 collapsed labels naming one fabric everywhere except here. D322 applied the
composed-to-placed correction to the constraint; the digest still showed the raw number.

The digest now filters to fabrics that route and carry every client, reports the corrected
frequency, deduplicates by structure, shows both ends of the trade-off rather than the cheapest
corner, and states how many of how many it is showing:

    37 of 50 measured fabrics clear 600 MHz and carry all 28 clients:
      xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8    area_mm2=0.01528  fmax_mhz=740  served=14.9
      xbar_staged-7x4x8-8x7x4    area_mm2=0.02117  fmax_mhz=740  served=17.1
      ...

**Two bugs found while writing it, both familiar.** `frontier_digest` referenced `CampaignStore`,
which `main` imports into its own scope — a `NameError` that a blanket `except Exception` reported
as "(nothing measured yet)" against a store holding fifty-seven fabrics. And the deduplication used
`_structural_key(label)`, which reads a lookup `main` fills only when it builds the results table,
after the search: during a run every key came back None and the dedup silently did nothing. Both
were caught only by running the function on the real store and disbelieving the answer.

**And the tests had to be rewritten twice.** The first fixture hand-wrote a `CREATE TABLE` that did
not match the real schema; the second hand-wrote result JSON the ABI rejects. Building the fixture
through `CampaignStore` and `Result` is the only version that tests anything — the same lesson
D323 recorded, arrived at again by the same route.

**What this is for.** The prompt is the model's entire evidence. Asked to leverage the model more,
the first move is not a new capability but to stop showing it a picture in which the study has
found six things, three of which are broken.

## D331: The proposer was told how much had been tried, never what

Asked to raise proposal quality, the store answers first. Of 123 generative trials, 26 fell back,
and the reasons are not evenly spread:

    12x  structurally identical to a fabric already proposed
     8x  expected a JSON object with a `kind`, got list
     5x  fabric reaches only N of 32 banks per client

The largest bucket is repetition, and the prompt explains it. `_coverage_note` tells the model
`xbar_staged x900, butterfly x40`, which says where the space is thick and nothing about what to
avoid. The dedup check then refuses the proposal it invites. Each refusal is a real model call and
a screening slot spent re-proposing something the store already held.

The shapes are now listed alongside the counts. Fourteen of them, since naming three thousand
would drown a prompt charged on every call — which is exactly why only counts were shown, and the
reason the omission survived.

**Which fourteen took four attempts, and three of them were guesses.** Shallowest-first surfaced
meshes and rings, which the proposal format does not even offer and the model therefore never
duplicates. Filtering to the offered kinds surfaced `butterfly-radix2..32` — plausible, but it
still omitted `xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8`, the shape this prompt's own worked example spells out and
so the likeliest thing of all to be repeated. Spreading across depths sorted by name length and
picked `clos-n2-m2` over it for being shorter.

Each ranking was a theory about what a model finds tempting, with nothing behind it. The version
kept uses the one real signal available: `_visited` is built in store order, so its tail is what
this study has been working on lately. That is evidence rather than taste. It is still a heuristic
and does not solve the worked-example case; what it guarantees is that the fabrics the search just
tried are named.

**Not addressed here.** The eight format failures — a model returning a list where one object was
asked for — are a parser that could accept both, and the reachability failures are a rule the
prompt states in prose and could state as arithmetic the model can check before answering. Both
are cheaper than the duplicate bucket and neither is done.

**And the wider answer to "leverage the model more".** Twenty-one of this repo's thirty-nine CHIA
nodes call a model, in five roles: AUTHOR (natural language to a validated Objective or
DesignSpec), GENERATE (RTL and SystemC, verified by a deterministic harness), CROSS-EXAMINE
(`check_faithfulness`, a SECOND model examining an authored artifact against the prose that asked
for it), EXPLAIN (`explain_candidate`, which backends can express a design and why the others
cannot), and SEARCH. The interconnect loop uses orchestrating, proposing, repairing and
concluding — and none of authoring, cross-examination, or explaining. Cross-examination is the
one with an obvious home here: every conclusion this demo stores is written and checked by the
same model, which is the arrangement `check_faithfulness` exists because nobody trusts.

---

## D332: A second model, because three rounds of regular expressions were not enough

Of the five roles this repo gives an LLM — author, generate, cross-examine, explain, search
(D331) — the interconnect loop used none of the middle three. Cross-examination is the one with an
obvious home: every conclusion the demo stores has been written and checked by the same model,
which is the arrangement `check_faithfulness` (D249) exists because nobody trusts.

The case for it is a session's worth of evidence. Three mechanical guards were added against false
conclusions: numbers that are not in the cited evidence (D314), words that overreach from a sample
(D314), claims overtaken by later measurement (D329). Each caught the phrasing in front of it and
the next paraphrase walked past — "no configuration reached", then "consistently fails", then
"without any candidate reaching". Pattern-matching a model's prose to decide whether it is lying is
a losing position, and the losing was measurable: three rounds, three escapes.

A judge reads what a claim MEANS. Given the same evidence and the four conclusions this store
actually held — two false, two true — a real qwen3.8 examiner separated all four:

    [FALSE] REJECTED  — The measurements show a maximum throughput of 17.3496 words/cycle
                        (in F7), not 21
    [FALSE] REJECTED  — The measurements in F14 explicitly show three candidates achieving
                        max_throughput_words_per_cycle ...
    [TRUE ] SUPPORTED — The refusal patterns in F12, F15, F18, F6 and F9 explicitly record ...
    [TRUE ] SUPPORTED — F1 (and F4, F8, F17) shows butterfly-radix2 has interstage_link_bits ...

It cited fact ids for every verdict, which no regular expression was ever going to do.

**Design, following D249 where it applies and departing where it does not.** Independent pass,
verdict per claim, never a silent approval: an unparseable reply, a judge that cannot run, or a
claim the judge skipped all come back as "not examined" rather than approved, and that string is
distinguishable from a real verdict. Verdicts are applied by claim NUMBER, not reply order, because
a model answering out of order would otherwise swap the verdicts on a true and a false claim.

Two departures. D249 uses majority-of-N because a lone 7B judge lands at 75-85%; here it is ONE
call for all claims, because judging is a read of the same evidence and the local model costs about
a minute per call — a conclusions step that took four calls instead of one would be turned off, and
a check that is turned off catches nothing. And the check is ADVISORY in the other direction too: a
judge that fails must not delete a study's findings, so failure means keep.

**What it does not do.** It cannot catch a claim that is wrong in a way the evidence does not show
— the evidence is a sample, and a judge reading the same sample inherits its blind spots. It is a
second opinion on the same facts, not an independent measurement, and the mechanical guards are
kept underneath it precisely because they check something different: arithmetic, not meaning.

**Still unused.** AUTHOR (natural language to a validated objective — this demo's problem is
hard-coded at 28 clients, 32 banks, 600 MHz) and EXPLAIN (`explain_candidate`'s "which backends can
express this, and why the others cannot") remain outside the loop.

---

## D333: The study's question came from a sentence

The interconnect demo answered one question — 28 clients, 128 bits, 32 banks, 600 MHz — because
those five numbers were constants at the top of a file. The AUTHOR role (D331) is the one that
changes that: `--problem "16 masters into 8 banks, 64-bit wide, must run at 1 GHz"` and the study
runs against what was asked for.

`flux_author_objective` authors a whole Objective IR from prose. This is smaller and differently
shaped: the interconnect study is five numbers and builds its own document, so what needs authoring
is the problem, not the document.

**Validated by construction, which is the half that matters.** Every field must be a whole number
in a range the constructor can build — booleans are excluded explicitly, being ints in Python and
otherwise sailing through — and then the space it describes is ENUMERATED. A request can parse
perfectly and describe nothing, and no amount of type-checking five numbers sees that. A rejected
reply is repaired with the real error fed back, and a request that never validates raises rather
than quietly running the default study under someone else's question.

Against the real local model:

    > "16 masters into 8 banks, 64-bit wide, must run at 1 GHz"
      -> clients=16 banks=8 width_bits=64 target_mhz=1000 bank_rows=512
    > "I need a fabric for 12 CPUs reaching 16 memory banks"
      -> clients=12 banks=16 width_bits=128 target_mhz=600 bank_rows=512   (defaults applied)
    > "make it fast"
      REFUSED: the request does not say how many clients or banks

The defaults live in the PROMPT, where the model applies them knowingly and says so, rather than
being filled in afterwards — a silent omission becoming a study nobody asked for is the failure
this arrangement avoids.

**A trap worth recording.** `near_misses` had `floor: float = TARGET_MHZ` in its signature. A
default argument binds at import, so a study authored to run at 1 GHz would have gone on screening
near-misses against 600 MHz. It is resolved at call time now. Any constant that can be set at run
time cannot appear in a default argument, and this file had exactly one.

**And a check that was not built, twice.** Both bugs found while wiring this were
use-before-assignment in `main`: `repairable` computed after the action registry that read it
(D328), `ask` initialised after the `--problem` block that needed it. Both crash the demo on
startup with every test green, because nothing runs `main` — it places silicon.

A static check for it was written twice and was wrong both times. The first only flagged names it
had already seen, so a name assigned LATER was absent and the bug walked through when it was
re-introduced to verify. The second collected every binding first and compared against the
enclosing statement's line, flagging every read inside an `if` block of a name assigned in that
same block — fifty false positives on correct code. Getting it right needs control-flow analysis,
which is a linter, and this repo has none: pyflakes, flake8, pylint and mypy are all absent from
the dev shell. `pyflakes demo.py` would catch this class in one line. That is the fix; two failed
attempts at approximating it in a test file are enough evidence that hand-rolling it is not.

**Still unused.** EXPLAIN — `explain_candidate`'s "which backends can express this design, and why
the others cannot" — is the last of the five roles the interconnect loop does not have.

---

## D334: One linter, one check, three crashes it would have caught

This repo had no linter. Not a lenient one — none: pyflakes, flake8, pylint and mypy were all
absent from the dev shell, and nothing in CI looked at a name before running it.

Three defects in a single session were the same thing. `_anneal` and `_population`, deleted by an
index-slice edit while still called (D321). `repairable`, computed after the action registry that
reads it (D328). `ask`, initialised after the `--problem` block that needs it (D333). Each crashed
the demo on its first real step. Each passed the entire suite, because all three lived inside
`main()` — which nothing imports and no test calls, since calling it places silicon.

A static check was hand-rolled twice and was wrong both times: the first only flagged names it had
already seen, so a name assigned LATER was simply absent and the bug walked through when it was
re-introduced to verify; the second compared reads against the enclosing statement's line and
produced fifty false positives on correct code. Control-flow analysis is what a linter is, and
two failed approximations is enough evidence to stop writing one.

`pyflakes` is a pure-Python package, added to the dev shell at no build cost, and it is right:
with the `ask` bug re-introduced it reports `undefined name 'ask'` at the correct line, and reports
nothing about that file once it is fixed. The gate takes F821 ONLY and ignores the rest of its
output — thirty-one unused imports and ten f-strings without placeholders are style, and a gate
that fails on style is a gate someone turns off. Confirmed by re-introducing two of the three real
bugs and watching it fail, then pass on the restored file.

**Four latent defects fell out of turning it on.** Four `undefined name` findings existed across
the repo, all the same shape: a string annotation naming a type nobody imported —
`budget: "BudgetGrant"` in `flux_store.campaign`, and three in tests. String annotations are not
evaluated, so none crashed; every one breaks any tool that resolves type hints.

**And fixing them created a new hazard, immediately.** A `TYPE_CHECKING` block never executes, so
a wrong import inside one is invisible: Python does not run it and pyflakes considers the name
bound. `BudgetGrant` was guessed at `flux_store.budget` and actually lives in
`flux_search_campaign.objective` — the fix silenced the warning and introduced a lie in its place,
which is strictly worse than the defect it replaced. Every `TYPE_CHECKING` import in the repo is
now executed by a test, where the failure is loud and free.

**What this does not do.** It checks one thing. Unused imports, shadowed names and the rest of
pyflakes' findings are reported and not gated, and a name bound only on some paths through a
function is beyond it. It catches the class that cost three crashes in a day, which is the case
it was bought for.

---

## D335: A path that was wrong and a directory that still existed

CI failed building the native crate:

    error: could not find `Cargo.toml` in `/home/runner/work/flux/flux/flux/core`
           or any parent directory

That message points at a parent-index mistake, and the first diagnosis followed it — proposing
`parents[3]` instead of `parents[4]`. `parents[3]` is `flux/evaluator`, which has no `core/` at
all. The arithmetic was right the whole time.

What moved was the crate. The reorganisation around the four module types (D296) turned `core/`
from the crate root into a directory OF module directories — `core/ir`, `core/llm`, `core/stores`,
`core/rust` — and `_CORE_DIR` was never given the `rust` segment. It is `parents[4] / "core" /
"rust"` now.

**Why it produced cargo's error instead of its own.** The function guards with
`if not _CORE_DIR.exists()` and raises a clear "expected the flux-core crate at X, found nothing".
`core/` still existed after the crate moved out of it, so the guard passed and cargo was run in a
directory with no manifest. A guard on a directory cannot tell "the thing I need is here" from
"something is here"; it checks for `Cargo.toml` now, which is what cargo needs and what actually
moved.

**A second instance, found by sweeping for the pattern.**
`core/rust/benches/profile_exhaustive_search.py` had `FLUX_ROOT = parents[2]`, which is `core`, and
then built `FLUX_ROOT / "core/ir/workload/..."` — resolving to `flux/core/core/ir/...`. Same cause,
same shape, and it survived the first check written for it: a test that the computed ROOT exists
passes, because `flux/core` is a real directory. Only the COMPOSED paths are wrong. The test
therefore checks what is built from the root, not the root.

**The general shape, and it is D320's with the operands swapped.** There, paths written inside data
files went stale because a rename is checked by the compiler for code and by nothing for data.
Here, paths computed in code went stale because `parents[N]` encodes a distance that a
reorganisation silently changes, and both wrong answers happened to name directories that exist. A
path check is only worth anything if it asks for the file it actually needs.

---

## D336: Declaring the legal values told the model; it did not constrain it

D328 gave `repair` declared variants so the menu would list the fabrics that can actually be
repaired, instead of leaving the model to guess labels off the frontier. The very next end-to-end
run produced this:

    --- orchestrator: repair label=xbar_staged-7x4x4-7x4x4-14x2x3 (the model chose it)
        declined: xbar_staged-7x4x4-7x4x4-14x2x3 is not a near-miss in this store

The menu had said `label: one of <six near-misses>` and that fabric was not among them; it meets
timing. Declaring legal values populates the prompt and the "NOT YET DONE" line. It does not
constrain the reply, and `_valid_repair` accepted any string it was handed.

So the validator checks now, and reads the near-miss list FRESH rather than trusting the menu's
snapshot: a fabric repaired earlier in the same run is no longer a near-miss, and the declared
list was built before any step ran. An unusable choice costs a re-plan instead of a step and a
model call, which is the difference between the loop correcting the model and the loop obeying it.

**The rest of that run is the point of recording it.** Four changes had landed since the last full
run — the conclusion ordering fix (D329), the frontier digest rewrite (D330), cross-examination
(D332) and the author role (D333) — none of them seen in situ, and every previous full run this
session found something. This one found one defect and otherwise came out clean:

    7 stored fabric(s) DROPPED: screened before routability was checked
    14 fabric(s) meet 600 MHz on the composed estimate but not after the measured correction
    LESSONS RECORDED: 2 conclusion(s)
    DECISION RUNG: 5 finalists placed WHOLE ... 0 failed placements
      xbar_staged-8x4x4-4x8x8         0.0154  799 MHz  ...  4i/0o
      xbar_staged-7x4x4-7x4x4-14x2x3  0.0151  868 MHz  ... 0i/10o
    DECISION: xbar_staged-4x7x8-8x4x4 — 15.5 words/cycle at 0.0158 mm2 and 629 MHz

The `dead` column carries its counts (D326), the finalists span the trade-off rather than
clustering at 14.9 words/cycle (D327), and the conclusions that survived both the mechanical
guards and the second model are about the shape of the front rather than about what cannot be
done.

**Where the time goes now.** The local model is 75.7% of the run — five calls, 857 seconds. Real
EDA tools are 4%. That is the shape of an AI-directed loop whose search is cheap and whose thinking
is not, and it is the number to attack next if the demo is to get faster: the tools stopped being
the bottleneck several fixes ago.

---

## D337: A hosted model, and what it costs to use one

The local model is 75.7% of a run — five calls, 857 seconds — against 4% for real Yosys, OpenROAD
and Verilator combined (D336). The tools stopped being the bottleneck several fixes ago, and the
thinking did not. A hosted model answers in seconds.

**What it costs is not money.** Every other proposer in this repo runs on the machine you are
sitting at, and `local_proposer`'s first line says so: nothing leaves. In this application the
prompt carries the problem being solved, every fabric already tried, and their measured area,
frequency and throughput. A design-space exploration is exactly the sort of thing an organisation
may not send anywhere, and the demo has claimed the local property in its own output since D269.

So the trade is made explicit rather than absorbed:

  - OPT-IN by a switch, `FLUX_LLM_REMOTE`, and never by a key being present. A key can be in the
    environment for unrelated reasons; that is not consent to send a study's measurements out.
  - ANNOUNCED on the first prompt that actually goes out — not at construction, because building a
    proposer and never using it sends nothing, and a warning printed then is noise that teaches
    people to ignore warnings.
  - LOCAL IS THE FALLBACK, never the reverse. No key, a rate limit, a network that is not there:
    the run continues on the local model rather than ending, and says which one it used.

The default model is a free one, since the point was speed at no cost and a default that bills
quietly is a different feature. OpenRouter speaks the OpenAI protocol, so this is the `openai`
client — already in the dev shell — pointed at another base URL; nothing here is specific to that
vendor beyond the default.

**What does not change, and it is the reason this is safe to offer at all.** The model proposes and
directs; it does not decide anything. Every fabric it names is still built by the real constructor,
screened by the real screen, and placed by real Yosys and OpenROAD on this machine. A worse model
costs evaluations and a better one saves them, and neither can produce a wrong answer — which is
the property that makes the model swappable in the first place.

**Not measured.** Whether a hosted model is BETTER at this, rather than faster, is untested. The
comparison worth running is the same shape as D289's: the same store, the same rounds, one model
each, and the frontier compared. Speed is the claim made here; quality is not.

---

## D338: A reply carrying six fabrics is five calls that need not happen

A model asked for one fabric often returns a list of them. The proposer unwrapped a
single-element list and refused anything longer as ambiguous — "which one was proposed?" — which
was 8 of 26 fallbacks in a measured run (D331). Each refusal spent an evaluation on a punctuation
habit and threw away work the model had already done.

That second cost is the larger one now. The local model is about three quarters of a run's wall
clock — 857 seconds of 1,132, against 4% for real Yosys, OpenROAD and Verilator combined (D336) —
so the expensive thing in this loop is asking, not building. A reply carrying six fabrics is five
calls that do not have to happen.

The extras are queued. `propose()` serves what is already in hand before paying for another call,
and only asks again when the queue is empty. An extra that does not validate is dropped rather
than repaired: it was never the model's headline answer, and repairing it would spend effort on a
fabric nobody asked for.

**Provenance survives the queue.** A queued proposal carries the prompt and response hashes of the
call that produced it, so a trial still points at the exchange it came from, and it is not marked
as a fallback — it is the model's own work, merely served later. Both paths now build their
Proposal through one function, because two copies of that construction is exactly how the dedup
signature and the stored one drifted apart before (D302).

**Not measured.** The saving is arithmetic — one call instead of N — and it depends entirely on how
often this model volunteers a list. Eight times in one run is the only evidence there is, and a
run where it never does is a run where this changes nothing.

---

## D339: Six repairs, three problems

A full run chose `repair` six times, each on a real near-miss, each naming the right critical path.
The reasons it gave are the finding:

    xbar_staged-14x2x3-2x21x16        595 MHz -> widest 18:1 — selector_21x128b
    xbar_staged-16x2x6-4x24x8         571 MHz -> widest 12:1 — selector_24x128b
    xbar_staged-28x1x2-2x28x16        564 MHz -> widest 14:1 — selector_28x128b
    xbar_staged-28x1x4-4x28x8         564 MHz -> widest 14:1 — selector_28x128b
    xbar_staged-28x1x1-28x1x2-2x28x16 564 MHz -> widest 14:1 — selector_28x128b
    xbar_staged-28x1x4-4x28x8-32x1x1  564 MHz -> widest 14:1 — selector_28x128b

Four of the six are one problem. Same 28:1 selector, same 564 MHz, same fix chosen four times, at
roughly 160 seconds a call. Repair was 22.2% of a 73-minute run and the model was 80% of it.

**Because a repair attacks the critical path, the critical path is what a repair IS.** Two fabrics
whose clock is set by the same selector are one repair problem however differently they are
spelled — and this store spells that one six ways out of eight near-misses. Deduplicated by widest
selector, seventeen near-misses become four distinct problems: 21:1, 24:1, 28:1, 32:1.

Only what is OFFERED is deduplicated. The menu lists one fabric per bottleneck; validation still
accepts any genuine near-miss, so a model naming a sibling is not refused for naming it. The
closest miss represents its group, because the nearest one is likeliest to be fixable and whatever
fixes it is the change its siblings need.

**This is the third time the same shape has appeared.** Finalists clustered on one point of the
trade-off and spent three placements learning one number (D327). Conclusions restated one
observation and filled three of four slots in a brief (D329). Now repairs. Each time the cost was
real work spent on a distinction that does not exist, and each time the fix was to ask what makes
two things the SAME — the point on the front, the evidence cited, the selector that sets the clock
— rather than trusting that different names mean different things.

**Not fixed.** `measure` still declares no variants, so the model can re-pick a fabric already
placed and pay a model call to be told so; it happened once in this run. Its legal set is every
fabric in the store, which is why it was left, and the answer is the same as everywhere else here:
offer the few that are worth the tool time rather than all of them.

---

## D340: The decision rung re-placed what it had already placed

A whole-fabric placement is real Yosys and OpenROAD over the complete design — measured at 320
seconds for a two-stage fabric. Nothing cached them. In one run the `measure` action placed
`xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8`, and the decision rung placed the SAME fabric again minutes later as a
finalist. Every subsequent run re-placed all five finalists from scratch, and on a warm store
almost none of them are new.

Measured after: 320.3 seconds, then 0.0, identical numbers.

**Keyed by (toolchain, fabric).** The fabric half is `structural_key` — the one definition of
identity (D311) — so two labels naming one design share an entry, which is not hypothetical here:
`hybrid-radixradix4-xbarswitches4` IS `xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8`.

The toolchain half is D316's fingerprint, and this is the first thing in the repo that can ACT on
it. D316 could only warn: it recorded which binaries a store's numbers came from and printed a
notice when they changed, leaving a human to decide what was still true. A cache keyed by that
fingerprint simply stops serving stale placements — bump OpenROAD and the entries from the old one
are unreachable rather than served with a caveat. The check that was advisory became structural by
being used for something.

**A cache that cannot be read is a miss, never an error.** This is an optimisation: a corrupt or
unwritable sidecar costs time and must not stop a study. It lives beside the store like the
calibration residuals, the mined lessons and the toolchain baseline.

**What this does not speed up.** The composed rung — 109 OpenROAD and 109 Yosys invocations in
that run, at 334 and 128 seconds total — is already memoised per selector arity and was never the
problem. The five whole-fabric placements were, and they were the least visible cost because they
happen at the end, after the interesting output has already scrolled past.

---

## D341: The last action that offered everything

`measure` was the only action left declaring no variants, and the cost was visible in every run:
the model asked to place `xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8` four times across two runs AFTER it had been
placed, paying a model call each time to be told so. `repair` and `anneal` had been fixed the same
way (D328, D317); `measure` was left because its legal set is every fabric in a 3,500-row store.

That was the wrong reading. Its legal set is the whole store; the set worth OFFERING never was. It
is the handful the decision would turn on: fabrics that route (D319), that clear the constraint
once the measured correction is applied (D322), and that have not already been placed under these
tools (D340).

The last filter is what made this possible at all. Before the placement cache there was no cheap
way to ask what had been placed — the answer lived in whatever scrolled past. A cache added for
speed turned out to be the missing piece of a different problem.

**And the pattern appeared a fourth time.** The first version of this offered
`hybrid-radixradix4-xbarswitches4`, `xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8` and `xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8-first`
as its top three candidates. One fabric, three names, three placements. D311 collapsed labels for
the frontier, D327 for the finalists, D339 for repairs, and this file wrote a fourth loop over
labels without asking what made two of them the same. The structural key was already being computed
in the loop for the cache lookup; using it cost one line.

Four occurrences is no longer a series of mistakes, it is a missing default. Anywhere this
application iterates over labels and spends something per label — a placement, a repair, a model
call, a row in a prompt — the question to ask first is what makes two of them one thing.

---

## D342: The model stopped being the bottleneck

Four changes landed together — the proposal queue (D338), one repair per critical path (D339), the
placement cache (D340), and `measure` offering only what is unplaced (D341). The first run with all
four:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| wall clock | 4,392 s | **1,168 s** |
| model calls | 25 (19 directing, 6 repairing) | **5** |
| model share | 80% | **34%** |
| failed placements | 0 | 0 |

Not one of those changes made the model faster. Every one removed work it should never have been
asked to do: fabrics it had already proposed in a reply that was thrown away, one bottleneck
offered as six problems, a fabric placed twice in a run and re-placed every run after, and a
`measure` action whose legal set was the whole store so the model kept picking something already
placed.

**Where the time goes now.** Monte-Carlo annealing is 32.5% and real tools 44% — Verilator builds,
OpenROAD, Yosys, and one whole-fabric placement. That is the shape a hardware DSE loop should have,
and it is the first run in this session where it does. The remaining model calls are five decisions
that each did something.

**The number that did not move.** `xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8` at 0.0155 mm2 and 738 MHz is the same
answer this study has been giving since the routability and correction fixes landed. Nothing here
changed what the search finds; it changed how much it costs to find it, which is the honest claim.

**An operational note.** A run leaves its tool scratch behind — Yosys liberty caches, ABC temp,
Ray session data — under a per-shell directory nothing cleans. One accumulated to 4.2 GB and the
root filesystem reached 97%, at which point Ray warns that object spilling will fail. `rm -rf
/tmp/nix-shell.*` with no live shells reclaimed 8.7 GB. Worth knowing before a long sweep, because
the failure arrives late and looks like something else.

## D343: Scratch on a disk with room, and a test that passed for the wrong reason

A run leaves its tool scratch behind — Yosys liberty caches, ABC temp files, Ray session data —
under a per-shell directory that nothing cleans. One reached 4.2 GB. The root filesystem, where
/tmp lives, reached 97%, and Ray began warning that object spilling would fail: a failure that
arrives late in a long run and looks like something else entirely.

Moving /tmp itself is a root-level change on a machine with another user on it, so the fix is
scoped to this shell instead. `FLUX_TMPDIR`, when set, becomes `TMPDIR` for everything the dev
shell runs; unset, nothing changes. It is not given a default here because this file is checked in
and the right disk differs per host — on this machine `/dev/sda2` is a local 3.2 TB volume with
3.0 TB free, while `/` has 78 GB. A network filesystem is the wrong answer however much room it
has: this is OpenROAD and Yosys scratch, and they are I/O-heavy.

**What checking it found, which was not what I was looking for.** Running a subset of tests under
the new TMPDIR produced ten failures. They failed without it too, so the redirect was innocent —
`test_screen_routability.py` imports `demo` and never put `applications/interconnect` on
`sys.path`. It passed because some other test file was collected first and did it. Run alone, nine
of its nineteen tests fail with `ModuleNotFoundError`.

That is a test passing for a reason unrelated to what it checks, and the suite could not see it
because it runs as a directory. The nightly integration sweep runs FILE BY FILE, which is where
this shape surfaces — and the nine other unit files that import `demo` all set the path themselves,
so this was one omission rather than a convention nobody followed. There is now a check that no
unit test relies on another having set the path.

---

## D344: Three things that were never about interconnects

`demo.py` had grown to 2,029 lines, and the question was which of them are about fabrics. Three
were not, and each had been invented there because that is where the need first appeared:

  * SIDECAR PATHS. Calibration residuals, mined lessons, a toolchain baseline and a placement
    cache each had their own `Path(db).with_suffix(...)`, written out four times and agreeing only
    by luck. A sidecar that lands somewhere else is a study quietly keeping two sets of books.
  * THE TOOLCHAIN BASELINE (D316). Which binaries produced a store's numbers is a property of the
    environment, not of any single result — which is exactly why it is one file rather than a
    column on several hundred rows.
  * THE MEASUREMENT CACHE (D340). Anything a real tool computes is worth keeping and is only valid
    for the tools that computed it.

`flux_study` holds all three and knows nothing about fabrics, candidates or metrics. An
application hands it an identity string and gets memoisation that survives the process and
invalidates itself when the tools move. Any study with a store and an expensive evaluator needs
the same three things; the interconnect demo simply got there first.

**What stayed in the application, and why.** The drift WARNING is still written here. What a
toolchain change means is a judgement — for this study it means cached placements are not
comparable, and how much that matters depends on how far the tools moved. The mechanism is shared;
the sentence is not.

**One duplication removed on the way.** `worth_placing` built the cache's key itself, in a second
copy of the format, to ask what had already been placed. The two spellings agreed only by
coincidence — which is precisely how the dedup signature and the stored one drifted apart in D302
and stopped catching anything at all. It asks the cache now.

**Not done, and it is the larger half.** `main()` is 751 of these 2,009 lines, and every action the
orchestrator can take is a closure defined inside it. Nothing imports them, no test calls them, and
every defect this demo shipped in a single session lived there: functions deleted by a slice edit
while still called, names read above the line that assigns them, an action registry referring to a
variable computed later. Extracting those into something importable is the change that would
actually make this reusable, and it is a larger and riskier edit than moving three utilities out.

---

## D345: The study became something another orchestrator can call

A larger design has an interconnect in it, and the orchestrator responsible for that design should
be able to ask for one and get an answer — not run a script and parse its stdout. That was not
possible: the whole study lived in `main()`, took a command line, and returned `0`.

It is now `run_study(request) -> InterconnectResult`, with `main` a command line on top of it.
Demonstrated end to end from a caller that never touches a terminal:

    met_requirement : True
    summary         : xbar_staged-7x4x4-4x7x8: 0.0155 mm2 at 738 MHz, 14.9 words/cycle
    finalists       : 2 placed on silicon
    refused         : 19
    provenance      : {steps: 2, stopped_because: ..., fabrics_screened: 3512, ...}

**What a result carries, which is the part worth arguing about.** This study's answer is not a
number. It is a fabric placed on real silicon, the evidence behind it, and an account of what was
NOT established. A caller handed only `area_mm2` has been told less than the study knows, and the
missing parts are exactly the ones this repo spent its history learning to report: that the screen
runs optimistic (D316), that a fabric can pass every check and still not route (D319), that a
model's conclusions are inferences (D314). So `not_established` is a field, `refused` carries its
reasons for a caller planning a fallback, and `met_requirement` is deliberately separate from
`decision` — a study that searched hard and found nothing clearing the constraint has a best-effort
answer and no decision, and collapsing those into one field a caller reads as success is how a
sub-flow lies to its parent.

**The request duck-types the old command line.** Its attribute names match the argparse namespace
exactly, so the forty-three `args.x` references inside the study did not move — the edit was a
rename and a split rather than a rewrite. The CLI and a programmatic caller are two front doors to
one study, not two definitions of it.

**The pyflakes gate paid for itself within the hour.** Splitting `main` left `_phase` imported in
the half that became the command line and used in the half that became the study, and the two
result types referenced but never imported. Both are `undefined name`, both crash on the first real
step, and both were reported before a single test ran. That is the third time today this class of
break followed an edit to this file, and the first time it was caught in seconds rather than by a
run.

**Still to do, and it is what "preset flows" really needs.** `run_study` is callable but lives in
`demo.py`, which is a script reached by a `sys.path` insert rather than an importable package. A
parent orchestrator can call it, but only by knowing where the file is. Moving it into
`flux_interconnect` alongside its request and result types is the next step, and the actions it
registers — still closures inside the function — are what make that move larger than a `git mv`.

---

## D346: The study is a package; the command line is 74 lines

D345 made the study callable but left it in `demo.py`, a script reached by a `sys.path` insert. A
parent orchestrator could call it only by knowing where the file was, which is not a preset flow —
it is a script with a nicer signature.

`flux_interconnect.flow` now holds it, beside the request and result types it exchanges. A caller
writes:

    from flux_interconnect.flow import run_study
    from flux_interconnect import InterconnectRequest

`demo.py` is 74 lines and contains nothing but argument parsing. That is the whole of what a
command line was ever adding.

**The move exposed how much had accumulated around a script.** Ten test files reached the study by
