inserting `applications/interconnect` on the path and importing `demo`; both experiment harnesses
did the same; two tests read `demo.__file__` to walk its AST. All of them now name the package, and
the path inserts are gone because a package on PYTHONPATH does not need one. The harness check
written in D312 caught both harnesses within a second of the move, which is exactly the job it was
given.

**FLUX_ROOT changed depth, and was verified rather than counted.** `parents[2]` from
`applications/interconnect/demo.py` is `parents[5]` from
`applications/interconnect/lib/src/flux_interconnect/flow.py`. That number has been wrong twice in
this repo's history — pointing at `applications/` after D296 and at `flux/core` after D335 — both
times because a file changed depth and nobody re-derived it. It was checked by resolving it and
asking whether `core/ir` is there, and `tests/unit/test_computed_paths.py` asks the same question
on every run.

**Two checks caught their own regressions during the edit.** pyflakes reported `FLUX_ROOT` and
`LLM_MODEL` undefined in the new command line the moment the split left its help strings behind
them. And the test asserting that no unit test relies on another having set `sys.path` flagged
ITSELF, because its own message names the pattern it searches for — a true positive about the
check rather than the code, and worth the one-line exclusion rather than a looser rule.

**What is still inside `run_study`.** The five actions are closures defined in it, so the loop is
callable but its parts are not. That is what makes a second application harder than it should be:
another study wanting the same orchestrate/propose/repair shape would take the DirectedSearch
machinery (already shared) and write its actions from scratch. Whether that is worth extracting
depends on the second application actually existing, and it does not yet.

---

## D347: Two ways to wrap a tool, and the rule that decides which

`evaluator/` looked inconsistent: twenty backends with code, and only two of them —`cacti` and
`gem5` — import CHIA at all. Read as an accident it is untidy. It is not an accident.

**CHIA ships integrations for exactly four tools**: `chia.vlsi.hammer`, `chia.vlsi.sram_cacti`,
`chia.simulators.champsim`, `chia.simulators.gem5`. Every evaluator whose tool is one of those goes
through CHIA; every evaluator whose tool is not wraps it directly. Two of twenty use CHIA, and
they are exactly the two whose tools CHIA ships. There is no third case.

**What going through CHIA buys, which is the part worth knowing.** `run_cacti` is a real
`@ChiaFunction`: the same call runs locally, as it does here, or dispatches to a cluster through
`.chia_remote()`. A from-scratch subprocess wrapper would have to reimplement that to get it back.
That is the reason to prefer CHIA's node where one exists — not consistency for its own sake.

**And why the other eighteen do not.** CHIA has no NoC simulator, no synthesis flow, no
Timeloop or ZigZag node. Booksim, Noxim, Yosys, OpenROAD, Verilator, DRAMsim3, 3D-ICE and the rest
are wrapped here because there is nothing to adapt through. That is not a gap waiting to be closed.

What does not vary is the outside: every evaluator implements the same `flux_evaluator_abi`
protocol and returns the same `Result`. That is what makes them interchangeable at a rung, and it
is the only thing a new evaluator must satisfy however its tool is reached.

**The rule was true and undocumented.** It was stated three times, in `evaluator/cacti/README.md`,
`evaluator/gem5/README.md` and `evaluator/hammer/README.md`, and nowhere a reader looks first. It
is in `evaluator/README.md` now, and `tests/unit/test_evaluator_conventions.py` checks it rather
than restating it: nothing imports `chia` for a tool CHIA does not ship, and the CHIA-backed set is
still exactly those two.

**Three empty directories, two of which said nothing.** `cimloop/`, `hammer/` and `sparseloop/`
hold no code. `hammer/` had a README explaining what it would be and why it is not there;
`cimloop/` and `sparseloop/` held a bare `.gitkeep`, and the only statement that they were
deliberate lived in the docstring of `test_backend_registry_parity.py`. A directory whose intent is
recorded only in a test is a directory the next reader deletes, so both now carry a README, and the
placeholder check asks for one.

---

## D348: A directory that nothing imported, and a README that said it could not move

`flux/build/` held six Nix derivations — Timeloop, Accelergy and its two plug-ins, timeloopfe,
barvinok — and one README for Dockerfiles that were never written. It is gone. Nothing imported
those six: zero references from `flake.nix`, zero from CI, zero from any other `.nix` file. The
flake takes all six from the `nixchip` input instead (`chipPkgs.timeloop`, `chipPkgs.accelergy`,
`chipPkgs.accelergy-library-plug-in`, `chipPkgs.accelergy-cacti-plug-in`, `chipPkgs.timeloopfe`),
and that is not just a naming coincidence: in the `timeloop` shell `timeloop-model` resolves to
`/nix/store/wc994d3p...-timeloop-4.0-unstable-2025-06-09/bin/` and `accelergy` to a nixchip python
env. `barvinok.nix` died the same way, as a Timeloop dependency `chipPkgs.timeloop` now brings
itself. They were load-bearing when the flake built them; moving to `chipPkgs.*` orphaned them,
and nothing since noticed.

**What kept them alive was a true sentence.** D344's `build/` note read: "`build/nix/` cannot move
outside `flux/`: the flake is `flux/flake.nix` and Nix can only reference paths inside the flake
directory." Every word of that is correct, and it is the reason the directory was never questioned
— it reads as a constraint pinning the files in place, which is an argument for leaving them alone.
The constraint was real. It stopped being *about anything* the moment the flake stopped referencing
the files, and a note about where a directory may live outlasted the fact that anything needed it.
A justification for a location is not a justification for existence, and the first survives the
death of the second without looking stale.

The README now states the fact that outlives the directory — this repository builds no third-party
tool itself, and adding one means adding it to nixchip — rather than explaining a path constraint on
files that are not there. `interfaces/chia_nodes/README.md` pointed a reader at `build/containers/`
for a feature it correctly called "not implemented"; it points at gap-analysis G11 instead.

---

## D349: A second application, and the seven-second rebuild that reframed it

`applications/prefetcher/` is the second problem domain, and the first test of whether
`applications/<name>/{lib, demo.py}` survives contact with a domain it was not designed around. It
does. What did not survive was my cost model for it.

THE PROBLEM. A project arrived as a directory of scripts: a ChampSim fork (Pythia's MICRO'21
artifact), three 5G baseband traces, pre-generated no-prefetcher baselines, and a two-stage ask —
maximise geomean IPC speedup of the Bingo L2 prefetcher, then minimise its hardware storage while
holding 90% of that speedup. Eleven knobs, read from an `.ini` at run time.

**The rebuild costs seven seconds.** Measured, in the dev shell, from a clean `obj/`: a full
`./build_champsim.sh no multi no 1` produces a binary that simulates identically to the shipped one
(0.70959 both, on the same trace and configuration). One evaluation is three simulations of about
six minutes. So recompiling the simulator is 0.6% of measuring it once, and the assumption that
config-space is the affordable search and code-space is the expensive one is simply false here.
Both cost the same. The difference is risk, not time: generated C++ may not compile or may be
subtly wrong, where a validated configuration cannot be. This study searches the knobs, and it
records that the source is reachable at essentially the same price, which is what makes CHIA's
`build_champsim(champsim_root, prefetcher_src, module_name)` the natural next rung rather than an
ambition.

**The evaluator is standalone, and D347's rule is why.** CHIA ships `chia.simulators.champsim`,
which by D347 should settle it. It does not fit: `run_champsim(binary, trace, *, warmup, sim,
timeout)` has no passthrough for `--config=` or `--l2c_prefetcher_types=`, and it parses `--json`
output that this fork never emits (no `json` anywhere in `src/*.cc` or `inc/*.h`; the binary
silently ignores the flag). CHIA's node targets upstream ChampSim with source-BUILT prefetchers.
This project tunes a runtime `.ini` on a prebuilt fork. The rule survives with its answer sharpened:
use CHIA when CHIA ships an integration for the tool you are driving, not merely for a tool of the
same name.

**One trace per evaluator call, not one configuration.** The objective is a geomean over three
traces, which makes the configuration the tempting unit. It caps a 64-core machine at 21 concurrent
configurations instead of 64 concurrent simulations, and it puts the baseline — a property of the
STUDY, not of the tool — inside the evaluator. `flux_prefetcher.objective` owns what a measurement
means; the evaluator reports what ChampSim said.

**The storage model is checked against the simulator's own header.** `score_memory.py` shipped with
the project and computes the same quantity, so testing one against the other would only prove they
were copied from each other. `inc/bingo.h` documents each table's formula AND a worked byte count
beside it — 488, 1472 and 1904 bytes for the shipped sizes — and those four sum to exactly the
35,096 bytes the model reports. That is ground truth this repository did not produce.

**An illegal configuration aborts the simulator.** `bingo.cc` opens with
`assert((region_size >> 6) == pattern_len)`. So screening is not an optimisation here, it is a
correctness gate: an illegal candidate does not score badly, it destroys a six-minute run. Every
constraint is enforced before ChampSim is invoked and stated verbatim in the proposer's prompt,
because a model given the goal but not the rules proposes mostly-illegal candidates (D313, D319).

---

## D350: Two applications, two front doors, one of them an accident

D349 gave the prefetcher study a CHIA node. The interconnect study did not have one, and the
difference was not a decision — it was the order the two were built in. D345 made
`flux_interconnect.flow.run_study` importable before "callable as a CHIA node" was a goal, and
nothing went back. `flux_prefetcher_dse_loop` shipped as a node because that is how it was asked
for. The result was one repository claiming that the next problem domain gets the same shape while
offering two different doors to two domains.

`flux_interconnect_dse_loop` closes it. It is thin on purpose: `run_study` is unchanged, and the
node maps its result to JSON so a parent orchestrator can read an answer without importing
`flux_interconnect`. Both studies are now a `@ChiaFunction`, an MCP tool, and a typed Python
function — the "one definition, three surfaces" convention `docs/agent-surface.md` states, which
`test_mcp_surface_parity.py` enforces and which caught all three new nodes the moment they were
exported without their registrations.

**What this deliberately did NOT do** is move the interconnect's placements onto Ray. The
prefetcher's expensive unit is one simulation — six minutes, independent, sixty-four fit on this
machine — so remote fan-out is its entire performance story. The interconnect's is a whole-fabric
placement, and `flux_interconnect.flow` already spreads those across a local pool via
`escalation_parallelism`. Dispatching them remotely would buy OTHER MACHINES, which is a real gain
and a separate decision that should be made against a measurement rather than for symmetry with a
node that needed it for different reasons.

---

## D351: The instruction count is not a flag, and the screen was lying

`demo.py` had `--warmup-instructions` and `--simulation-instructions`. They are gone. How long to
simulate is a FIDELITY decision, not a preference: it decides whether a number is a ranking hint
or an answer, and no caller should have to know that 2M+3M is one and 100M+150M is the other. The
flags pushed that judgement onto whoever typed the command and were wrong in both directions --
full length everywhere is fifty times more than the search needs, short length everywhere quotes a
hint as a result.

The study now owns it: search on SCREEN (2M+3M, about 7 seconds a run), then re-measure the best
`decide_on_finalists` at DECIDE (100M+150M, about six minutes) before deciding anything. The
finalist set is the top N by speedup PLUS whatever the stages actually chose, because stage 2
optimises storage and its answer is deliberately not the fastest -- it would otherwise never be
confirmed.

**What the first run found.** The screen is optimistic, uniformly, and the gap GROWS with how
tuned the configuration is:

    default bingo          screened 1.0607   confirmed 1.0440   +0.0167
    tuned bingo            screened 1.0746   confirmed 1.0542   +0.0204
    tuned + sms            screened 1.0823   confirmed 1.0586   +0.0237
    tuned + sms + stride   screened 1.0852   confirmed 1.0587   +0.0265

That growth is the signature of fitting a proxy: the harder the search climbs the cheap rung, the
more the cheap rung over-promises. The ORDER held exactly, which is what a screen is for and what
`experiments/screen_fidelity.py` measured at Spearman +0.776. The values are not quotable, and
every combination figure recorded before this rung existed was a screen number.

Confirmed, the real gains are smaller than the screen advertised and still real: tuning is worth
+1.02 points over the shipped configuration, adding `sms` a further +0.44, and `stride` on top of
that +0.01 -- nothing. A composition the screen ranked as the best available is, at full length,
indistinguishable from the same stack without its third member.

**Rank is not the only way a screen lies.** The first version of this rung reported a mis-ranking
only when the confirmed winner differed from the screen's leader. A screen that preserves its
ordering while halving every number passes that check and is still unusable, so the study now
reports the magnitude of the gap as well, and names what it means: the search climbs the screen,
so a large gap means the answer was fitted to the cheap rung.

**Two reporting defects the same run exposed.** The toolchain-drift check ran against the screen
baseline and its note survived into a report whose baseline came from the confirmation rung --
announcing "not comparable, different instruction counts" about numbers measured at exactly the
reference's own counts. It is checked last now, against whatever baseline the report quotes. And
the per-stage blocks printed screen numbers under a full-length baseline with nothing marking
them; they carry their rung.

---

## D352: Two denominators, and the partners nobody had tuned

Three things the prefetcher study could not previously say, and one it was saying wrongly.

**COMPOSITION IS AN AXIS.** The `multi` L2 slot runs several prefetchers at once, and the study
searched only Bingo's knobs. Measured alone, Bingo is the best of the sixteen (1.0607 against
`next_line` 1.0378 and `scooby` — Pythia's own RL prefetcher — 1.0366), so the study was tuning
the right one; it was also leaving the slot half empty. `bingo+sms` confirmed 1.0586 against
`bingo`'s 1.0542 at full length. A greedy phase now adds partners while each earns its place,
stopping on diminishing returns rather than a fixed count, because the third partner measured
+0.0001. Two exclusions keep it affordable: `bop` and `dspatch` are SLOWER than no prefetcher at
all and are never offered, and pairs measured to crash this build (`bingo+scooby` aborts,
`next_line+sms` segfaults) are skipped by name — a crash is still handled as a refusal at run
time, the list only avoids paying for it twice.

**THE PARTNERS HAD NEVER BEEN TUNED.** `sms` has eight knobs, `sandbox` seven, `ampm` five —
twenty-six across eight prefetchers — and every composition result until now ran them at their
shipped defaults. So every one of those numbers was a lower bound on what the pair can do rather
than a measurement of it. `partners.py` records each space with its shipped default, and
`test_partner_knobs.py` checks those defaults against the `.ini` files while `proj/` still exists:
a copy that drifted would measure every "improvement" against a value the simulator never used.

**TWO DENOMINATORS, NOT ONE.** "Did prefetching help" and "did TUNING help" are different
questions and were sharing an answer. Against the no-prefetcher baseline a composed stack reaches
1.0822; against the same stack AT ITS SHIPPED DEFAULTS (1.0693) the search is worth +0.0129. Only
the second says whether the search earned its wall clock — quoting the first as a tuning result
credits the search with having switched a second prefetcher on. Both references are measured on
the rung the report quotes, which is not a detail: a screened reference against a confirmed
decision reported tuning as NEGATIVE (-0.0170) when the entire gap was the screen's optimism.

**`met_requirement` WAS ASKING THE WRONG QUESTION.** Its docstring said "did the search beat the
configuration the project ships"; its code said `geomean_speedup > 1.0` — beat NO PREFETCHER,
which Bingo clears in almost any legal configuration. A run that searched hard, returned the
shipped `bingo.ini` unchanged, and labelled its own winner `proposed by incumbent` still reported
"met requirement: yes". It compares against the incumbent now, on the same rung, and a run that
found nothing says so: "tuning did NOT improve on the shipped configuration ... keeping the
default is the honest answer for this budget."

**AND `--db PATH` NOW CREATES PATH.** It never had. Measurements were cached in a sidecar BESIDE
the named file, so resume worked and the flag was a lie — what was tried, what was refused and
why, and which rung produced each number all vanished when the process exited. A `CampaignStore`
records every trial with its phase and its rung, which is what makes D351's screen-versus-confirmed
story auditable after the run rather than only in its stdout.

---

## D353: The screen was ranking noise

The prefetcher study screens candidates at 2M warmup + 3M simulated instructions and confirms
finalists at 100M + 150M (D351). The screen was known to run optimistic and that was thought to be
handled — the confirmation rung exists precisely because a screened number cannot be quoted. It was
not handled, because the wrong property was being watched.

**WHAT MATTERS IS SPREAD, NOT OFFSET.** A rung that reports every design as 0.02 too fast is
perfectly usable for a search: the offset cancels in every comparison. A rung whose error VARIES
between designs is not, and the variation is what decides whether a ranking survives. Measured
against confirmed full-length numbers for four stacks:

    screen      mean optimism    spread     cost per simulation
    2M+3M          +0.0226       0.0191            ~7 s
    10M+15M        +0.0049       0.0018           ~35 s
    25M+40M        +0.0016       0.0008           ~80 s

The gain the search exists to find — composition, confirmed — is +0.0075. At 2M+3M the spread was
**two and a half times the effect**. Every decision the search made beyond "composition helps" was
noise dressed as a measurement, and three separate results died on this:

  * `+L1D ipcp` screened FIRST at 1.0785 and confirmed LAST at 1.0426 — actively worse than Bingo.
    An entire search axis was nearly built on it.
  * Partner-knob tuning was worth +0.0008 confirmed, indistinguishable from nothing.
  * Every generated prefetcher that "beat Bingo" lost at full length, one of them by being
    HARMFUL: 0.99368 alone, and it cost Bingo 0.0049 as a partner.

`SCREEN` is 10M+15M now: five times the cost per simulation, one tenth the comparison error. The
measurements sit beside the constant, because the obvious optimisation is to shorten it again for
speed and the reason not to is not obvious at all.

**WHAT IT BOUGHT, IMMEDIATELY.** The same demo, same search, same budget, on the corrected screen:
confirmed geomean went from 1.0523 to **1.0640** — +0.0200 over the shipped `bingo.ini`'s 1.0439.
Nothing about the search changed. The clearest evidence is the tuning contribution, which went from
+0.0008 to +0.0125: tuning did not improve, the search became able to tell configurations apart.

A cheap rung is not a cheap answer, and "it ranks well enough" is a claim with a number attached.
Spearman +0.776 was measured for this screen (D351) and read as reassuring; it is not, when the
effects being resolved are smaller than the disagreement it permits.

---

## D354: A model writes a prefetcher, and the compiler is cheap

`flux_invent_prefetcher` designs new L2 prefetchers in C++, compiles them against a real ChampSim,
and measures them. The economics are what make it possible: a rebuild is about a minute while one
full-length evaluation is three simulations of six, so the compiler is nearly free feedback.

**WHAT IS GENERATED AND WHAT IS NOT.** A model writes ONE header holding the whole class. The `.cc`
that gives the vtable a home, the dispatch branch in `multi.l2c_pref`, the knob declarations in
`knobs.cc`, and the standard `#include`s are all mechanical. That is D48's rule for RTL applied
unchanged, and each mechanical piece was added because a live round was lost to it:

  * A missing `#include <algorithm>` for `std::find` — and the repair attempt reproduced it. Now
    scanned for and inserted; the fix says nothing about whether the DESIGN is good.
  * `invalid new-expression of abstract class type`, a pure virtual left unimplemented. Now
    rejected before building, naming the missing method, which the compiler's message does not.
  * Truncation. `DEFAULT_NUM_PREDICT` is 1200 tokens, sized for this repository's JSON proposals
    and about a third of what a C++ header needs; the first run reported "no header" three times
    for replies that each held a good one, stopped mid-statement. Raising the budget alone was the
    wrong fix — the local model generates at a few tokens a second, so 4000 tokens is seventeen
    minutes for one design. The prompt asks for under 70 lines instead.

**TWO WAYS TO WIN, AND THE SECOND IS EASIER.** The loop first measured inventions ALONE, which made
a good partner invisible: composition is worth +0.0075 confirmed against +0.0008 for tuning, and a
hand-written prefetcher scoring 1.0069 solo added +0.0026 to Bingo. Inventions are now measured both
ways and the brief says so — "catch what Bingo misses" is a far easier target than "beat a published
HPCA'19 spatial prefetcher", and it is the one the measurements reward.

**AND IT CONFIRMS.** The first version stopped at the screen and declared a winner that was harmful
at full length. It now re-measures its champion at 100M+150M before saying anything. On the
corrected screen (D353) that produced a real result: `bingo+invented1` at **1.04739** against Bingo's
1.04395 — +0.0034, confirmed. Small, and genuinely the first invented design to survive.

**STILL OPEN**: the loop targets Bingo alone, while the study's best is a tuned three-prefetcher
stack at 1.0640. "Beat Bingo" is the wrong question once composition is understood; "add to the best
stack" is the right one, and it is a change of reference rather than of machinery.

---

## D355: One loop, not four, and the traces in the prompt

Two things the prefetcher study lacked, found by reading its own code once it had grown.

**THE FOUR LOOPS WERE ONE LOOP.** `flow.py` reached 1,139 lines with a 320-line `run_study`, and
carried four hand-written local searches — climb Bingo's knobs, compose partners in, tune the
partners' knobs, shrink storage — each with its own wave, patience counter and stopping rule,
written days apart and agreeing with each other by accident. Every bug that one of them found
had to be found again in the others: marking candidates seen before measuring them (the search
that reported "no unexplored neighbours" after touching 4% of the space), taking the head of an
enumeration instead of a spread (the stage that measured six region-size variants and called the
other ten knobs settled), giving up on the first flat round.

They differ only in the NEIGHBOURHOOD and in what BETTER means. `search.climb` is the loop; each
phase is a move generator plus an ordering — `bingo_moves` with `faster`, `compose_moves` with
`faster_by(0.002)`, `partner_moves` with `faster`, `shrink_spread` with `smaller` under
`holds_floor`. A `Design` (Bingo's knobs, the stack, the partners' knobs) is the unit throughout,
and `seen` is keyed on all three, so a configuration measured in one stack is not mistaken for
the same configuration in another. The fixes above now exist in one place and cannot drift.

`run_study` is ten named phases over one `Study` context, readable in a screen: setup, baseline
and evidence, search, refine, compose and tune, reference, shrink, confirm, report. Measurement
— batching, rungs, the cache, the campaign record — moved to `measure.py`, by responsibility
rather than by size. The same demo produces the same numbers before and after; the diff is
net -1,065 lines against +3,247, most of the additions being the invention loop and the profiler.

The invention node had grown its own two thread pools and a third copy of the profiler; it
measures through the library now, and where it used to spend two waves per candidate ("alone",
then "with the stack") it spends one. The interconnect study's twelve closures inside its own
`run_study` — the debt D346 recorded and deferred for want of a second application to design
against — are module-level actions over an explicit `StudyContext`, extracted mechanically:
every captured name became an attribute read and nothing else changed.

**THE MODEL HAD NEVER SEEN THE TRACES.** Every prompt in this study described the workload in one
sentence written from a folder name. The traces are 380 MB of actual accesses and the simulator
reports exactly what each prefetcher misses; neither reached a model. `profile.py` turns both into
a page: parsed from the 64-byte trace records, ~20,000 distinct PCs with the busiest eight covering
5% (a per-PC table of hundreds of entries thrashes — which is what every invented design had been),
constant strides only 21-24% of accesses and two-thirds of those cross-page, and 84-89% of accesses
repeating a (previous delta, delta) pair; from the simulator's counters, the best stack leaving a
third of would-be L2 misses uncovered at 85% accuracy. The proposer is also consulted a second
time, with the top measured configurations in hand — it used to be asked once, before anything
was measured, and never saw an outcome.

The evidence changed what the model wrote. Its first design afterwards cited the profile directly
— "84-89% of accesses repeat the (previous_delta, current_delta) pair" — and was a delta-pair
predictor rather than another stride tracker. It was also inert: it compared a line number
against a delta and never armed. So an inert design is now diagnosed from the counters rather
than reported as 1.0000 — zero prefetches ISSUED means the emit path never runs; issued but none
USEFUL means the addresses are wrong — and the next round is told which. With the profile in the
prompt, the AI-proposed knob configuration was the study's stage-1 winner, and the confirmed
decision was +0.0172 over the shipped `bingo.ini` from tuning alone.

---

## D356: A third application, and a proof that costs microseconds

`applications/bankmap/` finds address-to-bank mappings that are conflict-free for N concurrent
accesses at each of a set of strides — for EVERY start address, which is the whole difficulty.
It is the third problem domain and the first whose "real tool" is a solver rather than a
simulator: the fidelity ladder here is baseline, pigeonhole proof, z3, feasibility, model.

**THE CHECKER IS THE AUTHORITY.** Every candidate — the modulo baseline, what z3 returns, what a
model proposes — is judged by one exhaustive checker that walks every start address in the space,
vectorised: 2^20 starts, one stride, N=8 is a few milliseconds. So there is no reason to accept a
sample, and z3 is not trusted either: it proposes under constraints seeded from a window of
starts, the checker tries them all, and a counter-example's differences become the next round's
constraints. Counter-example-guided synthesis with the checker as oracle — the same shape as the
other studies' loops, a cheap proposer and an authority that decides.

**WHAT MAKES THE LINEAR FAMILY TRACTABLE.** An XOR-fold is a linear map over GF(2), so two
addresses share a bank iff their XOR lies in the map's kernel. Conflict-freeness is a constraint
on window DIFFERENCES, not on addresses: one clause per difference, over the Booleans "address
bit j feeds bank bit i". z3 answers in milliseconds, minimising the XOR count, and its `unsat` is
a proof that no fold exists — which the study then turns into what IS feasible: the largest N
the strides admit, and the largest stride subset the requested N admits.

**A PROOF BEFORE ANY SEARCH.** The first live run, strides {1, 8, 16, 17} at N = B = 8, spent 216 s:
z3 proved the fold family insufficient in half a second, then a model proposed eight non-linear
mappings and the checker refused every one. None could have worked. A stride-1 window needs
a..a+7 in eight distinct banks; stride 8 needs a+8 to differ from a; and a+8 then differs from
a+1..a+7 by 7..1, all inside stride-1 windows. Nine addresses that must pairwise occupy distinct
banks, eight banks. The request fixes a difference set D = {k*s}, any set of addresses whose
pairwise differences lie in D is pairwise distinct in bank, and a clique of size B+1 in that
graph is an impossibility proof for every mapping there is. It costs microseconds, runs before
the solver, and the model is never asked.

**WHERE THE MODEL IS WORTH ITS COST** is the gap the proof leaves: the pigeonhole bound for those
strides is 7 concurrent accesses; the linear family reaches 3. N in 4..7 is where a non-linear
mapping might exist and a solver cannot say. The study stops at the proof today; searching that
gap is the next thing to build.

Three details paid for by the first run: a model proposed eight bank bits for a three-bit request
and the extra rows were silently ignored, so folds of the wrong shape are refused visibly now and
the prompt states the shape; an expression family (`+ - * % ^ & | << >>` over the address, evaluated
vectorised, refused otherwise) gives the model somewhere to go that folds cannot, priced so that a
modulo by a prime reads as the divider it is; and the demo's exit code is the verdict.

---

## D357: A confirmed number divides by a confirmed baseline

A demo run reported a confirmed decision of 1.0706 against a shipped default of 1.0574, and said
the screen had run PESSIMISTIC on the design. Every earlier confirmation had the shipped
`bingo.ini` at 1.04395. The measurement cache told the story: the decision's full-length IPCs
were there, and they divide to 1.05697; the default's divide to 1.04395; both reported figures
were high by the same factor, 1.0129 — the geomean of the ratio between the full-length and
screen-rung no-prefetcher baselines.

D355's refactor introduced it. `run_study` had passed `full_baseline` explicitly to the
confirmation scorer; the phase-based version reached for `Study.scorer()`, which bound whatever
baseline the context held — still the screen's, because the phase set `s.baseline = full_baseline`
AFTER scoring. Deltas survived (both sides inflated alike), absolutes were fiction, and the
"pessimistic screen" was the artefact. The scorer takes its baseline as an explicit argument
now, and a test pins that a scorer handed one uses it rather than the context's.

Two lessons beyond the fix. The refactor was verified with the same screen-only demo before and
after, and the outputs matched — because screen-only never runs the phase that broke. Behaviour-
preservation checks must exercise every phase, and the cheap path exercises fewest. And the
number was caught only because a second measurement existed to disagree with it: three builds
of the simulator, checked because 1.0574 for the default looked wrong, all said 1.04395. A
result nothing else can be compared with is a result nothing can catch.

**INVENTIONS ON THE COMPOSE MENU.** The invention loop's kept designs were a record a human could
read and nothing could run. `invented.py` builds one simulator with every kept design installed
(about a minute, cached by the headers' hash; the measurement cache keys on the binary's
fingerprint so builds never collide), registers each design's knobs so the partner phases treat
an invention like `sms`, and offers them FIRST — appended after twelve stock partners with six
offered a round, the first run listed them on the menu and never reached one. A design that
beat the stack by +0.0014 confirmed is now something the study can choose, tune and shrink.

---

## D358: A stage is a resource keyed by bank bits, with a capacity

The bank-mapping study (D356) asked one question: do N accesses land in N distinct banks. A
memory behind a staged crossbar has more places to collide. Stage 1 routes on some bank-index
bits into a group and the links into that group carry only so many requests a cycle; two accesses
bound for different banks still stall if they share a group whose links are full.

**THE MODEL.** A `Stage` is which bank-index bits identify its resource and how many concurrent
accesses one resource carries. Bank-level conflict-freeness is `Stage(bits=all, capacity=1)` and
is always checked; stages add constraints, never replace one. A `GxH` layout derives stages from
the top bank bits down (`4x2` over eight banks: stage 1 on bits {1,2} into four groups); explicit
`bits:capacity` covers what a layout cannot. Nothing about the mapping families changed: a fold
or an expression still produces a bank index, and the stages read bits of it.

**EVERY RUNG UNDERSTANDS IT**, which is the test of whether the abstraction was the right one:
  * the checker counts each resource's load per window and reports the loaded stage, the load
    and the capacity, not just "conflict";
  * z3 encodes a capacity-1 stage as the pairwise-difference clause restricted to the stage's
    rows, and a capacity-c stage as "among any c+1 accesses of a window, at least one pair
    differs on those bits" -- per window rather than per difference, so the counter-example
    loop refines it like everything else;
  * the pigeonhole proof uses the tightest capacity-1 resource, because a stage with fewer
    resources than banks bites sooner;
  * the model's prompt states the stages as conflict points in their own right.

**WHAT THE FIRST RUNS FOUND.** The fold z3 returns for the bank alone -- `{a1^a4, a3, a0^a5}` for
strides {1,8,16} at N=4 -- puts two accesses of every stride-1 window in one group of a `4x2`
crossbar: a bank-only answer is wrong the moment a crossbar is in front of the banks. With
single links per group the request is IMPOSSIBLE for any mapping: five addresses that pairwise
differ by multiples of 8 must occupy four groups, proved in half a second before any search.
With two links per group z3 finds a stage-aware two-XOR fold in 3.4 s that the exhaustive
checker accepts at both the bank and the stage.

---

## D359: The proposer asked for twenty and got none

A run with `--llm-round 20` reported, twice, "the model returned no parsable configuration", and
searched on without the lever that had won stage 1 in every run it reached. The model had not
failed. Twenty configurations at eleven knobs each is about 2,400 tokens of JSON; the local
model's default output budget is 1,200; the array truncated mid-object and the parser, correctly,
found no complete configuration in it. Nothing in "no parsable configuration" pointed at a budget.

Two fixes, because raising a budget alone only moves the cliff (D354 learned that with the
invention loop): the knob proposer's budget is 5,000 tokens, and no single call asks for more
than twelve — larger requests are chunked, and later chunks see earlier proposals as "proposed,
not yet measured" so they do not restate them. A truncated reply is now reported as truncated,
with "fewer configurations per call" in the message. Checked against the real model: asked
twenty, got twenty, all legal, all distinct, in two calls.

**THE RUN AFTER** is the best confirmed result this study has produced, and every lever it has
contributed to it:

    shipped bingo.ini                     1.0439      35,096 B
    bingo + sms + invented2, tuned        1.0671     206,496 B     +0.0232

The model proposed a Bingo configuration with a 64K-entry pattern table -- 800 KB, a size no
neighbourhood walk from the shipped 4K would have reached in budget -- and it led stage 1.
Compose chose `invented2`, the delta-pair predictor a model wrote from the trace evidence (D355),
as the second partner over `stride`. Stage 2 then cut the pattern table four-fold, to 206 KB, at
no confirmed cost. Against the same stack at its shipped defaults, tuning is worth +0.0154 at
full length; against the shipped default, the whole search is worth +0.0232. The screen ran
0.0023 pessimistic on the decision, which is the ladder behaving: the ordering held and the
absolute was confirmed rather than assumed.

---

## D360: Two inventions in the run, neither earned a slot

The first run to invent prefetchers *inside* the study (`--invent 2`, D355's loop called from
`_setup`) answered the question it was run for: no, a design invented in that run did not make
the decision. Compose chose `sms` beside the stage-1 Bingo and nothing else; the run confirmed
bingo+sms at 1.0578 on a budget of ten, below the standing 1.0671 (D359, budget twenty), which
stays the best confirmed result.

What the invention phase did produce is the record. `invented5` (a high-degree long-stride
predictor keyed on the line index within a page) is harmful: 0.9921 alone and 1.0494 beside
bingo+sms+stride, which reaches 1.0554 without it. `invented6` issued zero prefetches -- the
emit path never executes -- and the diagnosis from `L2C_prefetch_issued` said so at the screen.
Both were kept, as every attempt is; that is what the library is for. Two defects followed from
keeping them, and both are fixed:

- **The loop confirmed the inert design.** "Best of the round" was the design with the highest
  with-stack geomean, and an inert design ties the stack exactly, so it won a six-minute full-
  length confirmation of nothing against nothing. Confirmation now requires a contender that
  beat the reference on the screen and is not inert; otherwise the loop says so and moves on.
- **The menu admitted designs that had lost.** `library()` filtered on solo performance only
  (>= 0.99), so the harmful design and the inert one both went into the five-design simulator
  and onto the compose menu, where they cost a wave each to be refused. A design now needs a
  with-stack gain over its own recorded reference to be offered; older records with no
  reference (`invented4`) stay on the solo rule. `invented1` drops off with them -- 1.05531
  against a 1.05538 reference is a tie, not a gain.

Six inventions across D355 and this run, one of which (`invented2`) earns a place beside Bingo
and now sits in the best confirmed design. That is the honest rate: roughly one in six, at
about five minutes of build-and-screen per attempt, plus the wave compose spends on each one
that reaches the menu. Two things the record points at, neither done here. The loop's reference
is still the stock `bingo+sms+stride` (1.0554 on the screen) while the study's best stack is
`bingo+sms+invented2` (1.0567): inventions are asked to beat a stack the study has already
moved past, and a design that would complement `invented2` is scored against `stride` instead.
And the inert design's diagnosis was printed, not acted on -- repair attempts cover build
errors, not a compiled design that never emits, though the diagnosis is exactly the prompt a
repair round would need.

---

## D361: A number depends on the code it ran, not the binary it ran in

A resumed campaign reported `0 served from cache` on every wave, the 30-second no-prefetcher
baseline included. Nothing was wrong with the cache. D360's library filter had dropped three
designs from the compose menu, the simulator was rebuilt with two inventions instead of five,
and the measurement cache is namespaced by the binary's hash (D340), so every measurement from
every earlier run was unreachable. By design: a changed toolchain must not serve stale numbers.

The campaign's own sidecar says the design was stricter than the numbers are. Twelve identities
had been measured on more than one binary -- the stock `pythia` from nixchip and two rebuilds
with different invention libraries installed -- and all twelve agreed to the last digit. A
stack's IPC depends on the sources of the prefetchers it ENABLES; what else is compiled into
the binary does not reach the number. The cache is now namespaced by the STOCK binary's hash,
which still changes when the nixchip pin does, and each invented prefetcher in a design's stack
enters that design's identity by the digest of its header. A rewritten `invented2` is a
different prefetcher and misses; a library that gained or lost a design beside it hits. The
trial record still names the binary that actually ran. Three tests pin the key and one pins the
namespace through `_setup`.

**THE INVENTION LOOP'S REFERENCE**, the other thing D360 named. The loop asked every new design
to beat `bingo+sms+stride` while the study's best confirmed stack was `bingo+sms+invented2`, so
a design that would have complemented `invented2` was scored beside `stride`. The reference is
now measured, not assumed: the stock stack and, for each kept design that earned its place, the
stack it was measured beside with the design in it -- every claim the library's records make --
are run in one wave on a simulator carrying the whole library, and the tallest is the number to
beat. Candidates are built beside that library too, so a design is measured next to the stack
it was asked to add to. `reference_stack` still overrides all of it.

And the inert design is handed back. `invented6` compiled, ran, and issued zero prefetches; the
counters said so, the diagnosis was printed, and the loop asked for a fresh idea. The
diagnosis distinguishes the two common bugs -- an emit path that never executes, and addresses
that are wrong -- and either is a few lines' fix, cheaper than a new design and far cheaper
than measuring one. A design that runs but changes nothing now gets one repair round
(`inert_repairs`, default 1) with the counters' words in the prompt, is rebuilt and screened
again, and only then is written off. The loop is exercised end to end against a fake model,
compiler and simulator that agree on one story; the assertions are about what it asks for and
what it measures, in what order, not about any number.

---

## D362: Storage is the second axis, not a tie-breaker

Two consecutive runs confirmed two answers: bingo+sms+invented2 at 1.0671 for 206,496 B, and
bingo+invented2 at 1.0626 for 97,208 B. The study's own decision rule chose each one (the
smallest design holding 90% of its run's best gain) and both are correct under it. Asked which
to build, the answer was "half the storage for 0.0045 less" -- a judgement about what 109 KB
of SRAM is worth, which is not the study's to make. The study had treated storage as what
happens after speedup is maximised: stage 1 climbs into whatever tables it likes (an 800 KB
pattern table led one run), stage 2 shrinks back on a floor, the finalists are the top few by
speedup, and the report quotes one point. "We don't want to increase storage that much" is not
a request for a different rule; it is a statement that the problem has two coordinates.

Three things change, none of them the search's shape:

- **The report lays out the frontier.** Every design on the report's rung that is faster than
  everything smaller, smallest first, each row saying what its extra storage bought over the
  row above. `PrefetcherResult.frontier` carries it; the demo prints it under the decision. A
  reader who values SRAM differently picks another point with the same evidence behind it.
- **Confirmation spends its budget along the frontier**, not at its corner. The top-N by speedup
  confirmed one end of the trade-off and left every other point a screened number that D351
  says must not be quoted. `decide_on_finalists` now picks both ends of the screened frontier,
  then the widest gaps in log storage, always including stage 2's pick; short frontiers fill
  with the next fastest. The incumbent and the references are confirmed as before and no
  longer count against those slots.
- **A budget, when there is one, is applied where it is free.** `max_storage_bytes` refuses a
  configuration at the validity gate -- storage is the analytic model, microseconds -- before
  the seed slice is taken and before a climb move is measured, so the search spends its whole
  budget inside the region that could be built. The proposer is told the number in its prompt,
  because a model that discovers a budget from twenty refusals has spent its round learning
  it. The decision is then the best confirmed design that fits; the incumbent and references
  are still measured as denominators even when they do not.

Not a Pareto search: stage 1 still maximises speedup and stage 2 still shrinks on the floor,
because on this problem those two walks are what populate the frontier's ends, and the
shrink's spread across the storage range (D353) is what populates its middle. What changed is
that the study now says what it found in two dimensions and spends its expensive rung
accordingly. The `--max-storage` demo flag takes `64k`, `1.5M` or a byte count; with none, the
standings table in the prefetcher README is itself the frontier, and the 97 KB row is the one
this project prefers.

---

## D363: A first stage of small crossbars sees lanes, not windows

The first real bank-mapping request: 32 banks behind seven 4x4 crossbars feeding four 7x8s;
4, 8 or 16 accesses at once at strides {1, 2, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256}; every 4x4 must send its
four accesses to four different 7x8s. The stage model of D358 could not say it. A `Stage` was
"these bank bits, this capacity, over the window": sixteen accesses through four groups is
refused up front, and capacity 4 would allow all four accesses of one 4x4 into one 7x8. The
constraint is per INPUT crossbar: lanes 0..3 share one 4x4, lanes 4..7 the next, and a
capacity binds within each chunk of `lanes` consecutive accesses. `Stage.lanes` says so;
`--crossbar 4x8 --lanes 4` builds it; the checker counts load per chunk, z3 relates only the
pairs inside a chunk, and the validation asks whether a CHUNK fits, not the window.

**THE ANSWER IS A PROOF.** With the request expressed, the pigeonhole rung refused it in
microseconds: through 4-lane crossbars into 4 groups, a stride-1 chunk (a..a+3 in four
distinct groups, for every a) makes the group a 4-periodic function of the address, and a
stride-2 chunk then carries a and a+4 -- the same group -- through one 4x4. As a clique: a
laned stage's must-differ set is D = {k*s : k < min(N, lanes)}, here {1, 2, 3} u {2, 4, 6}, and
0..4 are five addresses that must pairwise differ in group with four groups to put them in.
That needed two generalisations of D356's proof. The must-differ set is now PER RESOURCE (the
bank's is k < N; a laned stage's stops at the chunk), so a laned stage carries its own clique
search instead of being excluded from it. And a clique is not the only proof: the pair 1+16
has no five-clique (a stride-16 chunk relates addresses 16 apart, which 0..3 do not reach) and
is impossible all the same, because the 4-periodicity forces a, a+16, a+32, a+48 into one
group -- a chromatic-number argument. So when no clique is large enough, a bounded SAT
colouring is tried: if no assignment of R resources to the addresses 0..W respects every
must-differ pair, no mapping exists, since a mapping restricted to 0..W would be one. Windows
grow geometrically to a cap; an unsat anywhere is a proof, a sat at the cap is silence.

Then the partial answers had to be worth reading. The greedy stride walk said "strides [1]
admit 16; adding any other does not", which is true and hides the real shape: EVERY pair of
these strides is impossible together, because for powers of two 2s always divides t, and each
stride alone is fine. `_stride_compatibility` proves that pairwise (28 proofs, seconds) and
says "each alone, never two". The descent by N said "at most 3", which is the clique bound
under the lanes -- four accesses at strides 1 and 2 already collide. And the first partial
answer came back as `b1 = b2 = a10`, sixteen banks wearing thirty-two names: z3 forbade a
constant bank bit but not two identical ones. It forbids both now.

What this establishes for the hardware, on the stated assumption that consecutive accesses
share a 4x4: no address-to-bank function serves two of these strides conflict-free through
that first stage, at any concurrency of four or more. The lever is not the mapping; it is
which accesses share a crossbar (an interleaved lane assignment changes every chunk), a second
link per 4x4 output (capacity 2), or one stride per kernel. That question is the user's, and
the study now hands it over with the proof rather than with six refused model proposals.

---

## D364: Every interconnect is a list of stages, plus what it assumes

"The demo should also support other topologies: a full crossbar, multiple stages, Clos,
Benes." The temptation is a topology object per network with its own checker. The bank-mapping
study has one question, asked by the checker, the solver and the pigeonhole alike: which
accesses of a window can meet at one resource, and how many that resource carries. D358's
`Stage` answered it with the bank bits that key a resource and a capacity; D363 added which
lanes share it. One more degree of freedom makes it general: HOW lanes group. A split first
stage groups consecutive lanes (`lane // lanes`); the perfect shuffle between the stages of an
omega network groups lanes that agree modulo a power of two (`lane % lanes`). `Stage.lane_key`
is "chunk" or "mod", `groups(n)` is the one place either is interpreted, and the checker, z3's
pair generation and the pigeonhole's must-differ set all read it from there.

`topology.py` then writes each network as stages and a note on what it assumes:

- **crossbar**: no stage. **staged GxH[xK]**: D358 and D363.
- **omega N**: after stage j, a packet from source s to bank d rides the link labelled (low n-j
  bits of s, top j bits of d), so two packets collide there iff their sources agree modulo
  2^(n-j) and their banks on the top j bits -- one "mod" stage per j on the top bank bits. A
  bit-reversal over 8 banks is a permutation at the banks and collides at stage 1; the identity
  passes; z3 finds a fold the network accepts and the checker agrees.
- **butterfly N**: the mirror, low bank bits and chunked lanes -- the LSB-first delta network.
- **clos n,m,r**: under per-cycle (rearrangeable) routing an ingress switch passes at most m of
  its n lanes -- a stage keyed by NO bank bits, a pure load bound -- and an egress switch takes
  at most m; the middle assignment then exists by Konig's theorem. With m >= n both are vacuous
  and the note says so. **benes**: a Clos of 2x2s, non-blocking; no stage, just the note.

The notes are the honest part. The blocking networks assume self-routing, where the path is a
function of the destination and the stage is a real conflict point; the non-blocking ones
assume a route computation every cycle, and with greedy routing they block like a butterfly.
That is a different request, and the report carries the assumption beside the verdict so the
reader can reject it. Two small things on the way: the colouring proof of D363 timed out on the
pair 1+256 (257 nodes as z3 integers) and answers in well under a second as 2-bit words, so all
21 stride pairs of the 32-bank request are now proved impossible; and a stage keyed by no bank
bits has one resource, which `resources()` and the validation already handled once `bits=()`
was allowed.

---

## D365: The MAC-array study searches inside the PE and lets the tools judge

The fourth application. "MAC array optimisation" could have meant three studies; asked, the
user chose the microarchitecture of the processing element itself, with the array's shape
given by the workload (`lanes` products per cycle at the Workload IR's precision, int8 x int8
from `mlp-gemm0.yaml` by default, another document by `--workload`). What is searched is how a
product is formed (the `*` operator, a sign-magnitude shift-and-add array, radix-4 Booth, a
Wallace carry-save tree), how the products and the accumulator input are reduced (a ripple
chain, a balanced tree, a carry-save tree with one final adder), and how deep the pipeline is
(none; products registered; plus the output; plus a cut through the reduction). Forty-eight
points, every one generated by code from a `PeConfig` and a `Shape`.

**The ladder is the interconnect study's, one rung deeper.** Every generated design is first
run by real Verilator against golden vectors seeded from the workload -- the sign corners
first, then random -- with the harness's measured latency checked against the number of
stages the configuration claims (D118's discipline; the harness counts edges after the one
that consumed `start`, so a design of n stages must measure n-1, and the first run of the
pipelined PEs was refused until that convention was read from the harness rather than
assumed). Then a new rung, `run_synthesis_flow` in the OpenROAD evaluator: Yosys maps to ASAP7
exactly as the placement flow does, and OpenSTA times the mapped netlist with no floorplan and
no wires -- a second or two per design, optimistic by what the wires would cost, identical in
method across candidates, so it ORDERS the space. Finalists spread along the screened
fmax-vs-area frontier (D362's rule, `flux_study.pareto` now shared by both studies), plus the
incumbent, are placed by OpenROAD with timing repair, and that is the rung the report quotes.
The decision is the smallest PE that makes the target clock, the interconnect study's own rule;
the frontier is printed whole.

**THE FIRST RUN**, 8 lanes, int8, 1 GHz target, 83 seconds end to end (48 verifications in
67 s, 48 syntheses in 12 s, 5 placements in 4 s):

    incumbent   behavioral-tree-p0     857 MHz   421 um2    (the D225 datapath, placed)
    decision    booth4-csa-p1         1285 MHz   431 um2    1.50x the clock, 1.02x the area
    frontier    378 um2 815 MHz (booth4-csa-p0) -> 390 um2 933 MHz (behavioral-csa-p0)
                -> 431 um2 1285 MHz (booth4-csa-p1) -> 466 um2 1536 MHz (behavioral-csa-p3)

Two things the numbers say. The multipliers alone barely differ (behavioral 961, Booth 904,
array 751, Wallace 740 MHz at the screen, all within 10% of area): ABC's own mapping of `*`
is already a good multiplier, and hand-written structure buys little at this width. The
REDUCTION and the REGISTERS are where the frequency is: a carry-save reduction with one
register stage between the multipliers and the tree is what took the clock from 857 to 1285
MHz, at 2% more area and one cycle of latency. And the screen mis-ranked: it led with
behavioral-csa-p0 at 1007 MHz, which placed at 933; the synthesis rung is optimistic by up to
200 MHz here, and the report says so beside the decision it did not make.

**What the model does.** Nothing, by default -- a 48-point space needs a judge, not a
proposer. `--invent N` asks the local model for multiplier structures the enumeration does not
contain, under the prefetcher loop's split (D355): one combinational module with a fixed
interface, refused before any tool runs if it is sequential, uses a SystemVerilog cast, or is
the `a * w` already in the space; then Verilator at the sign corners with compile errors and
failing vectors fed back, bounded; every multiplier that passes is kept under `invented/` and
joins the menu of every later run. The CHIA node is `flux_macarray_dse_loop`, the MCP tool the
same; the demo refuses to start without the three tools and names the shell that carries them.

---

## D366: Area is the objective and the incumbent's clock the floor

"Area is also a target of improvement: reduce area while preserving fmax." The decision rule
already minimised area under a clock, but the clock was a number typed on the command line,
and "preserve" names a different floor: whatever the incumbent actually makes on the rung
being quoted. `--preserve-fmax` sets the target to the incumbent's own measured fmax -- on the
screen for the screen's ordering, on placement for the decision -- so the question the study
answers is "how much area can go while the clock stays", and the answer is measured against
the same design on the same rung rather than against a round number.

The second change is a lever the space did not have. Every silicon number this repo pinned
came from ABC given the clock period to map against (D278), because a mapper with no timing
goal optimises for area and that is not what a frequency measurement asks. It IS what an area
objective asks. `mapping` is now a knob of the PE configuration -- "delay" or "area" -- and
reaches both flows as `map_for`; the RTL is identical, the netlist is not, and the cache key
carries the mapping so the two are never confused. The space doubles to 96; designs that differ
only in the mapping share one Verilator verdict, since Verilator judges the source. The report
adds one lesson: the average area saved and frequency lost by mapping for area, over the pairs
that differ in nothing else, so the reader knows how much of the frontier is a netlist choice
rather than a design one.

**MEASURED**, 8 lanes, int8, the incumbent's clock preserved (857 MHz placed):

    incumbent   behavioral-tree-p0     857 MHz   421 um2
    decision    behavioral-csa-p0      933 MHz   390 um2    0.93x the area, 1.09x the clock, no latency
    mapping     area vs delay, 48 pairs on the screen: area +1%, fmax +3% -- noise, not a lever

So the area came from the design, not the netlist: replacing the adder tree with a carry-save
reduction is 7% less area AND 9% more clock than the incumbent, combinational both. At 16
lanes the same design is 6% less area at the same clock (781 against 831 um2, both 805 MHz
placed) -- and the first run of it chose the incumbent, because the incumbent placed at 805.4
MHz and the smaller design at 805.1, and an exact "holds the clock" is a coin toss on
placement noise. A MEASURED floor is now held to within 1%; a REQUESTED target still gets no
slack, since that one is a requirement. The frontier compares frequencies to the megahertz for
the same reason: a point 0.3 MHz "faster" and 50 um2 bigger is not a frontier point. The mapper
knob stays in the space because it costs nothing (the RTL is verified once and synthesis is
seconds) and because it is exactly the kind of lever that is worth nothing at 8 bits with the
fast mapping and may be worth something at 16 -- which the report will say when it is run.

---

## D367: Resumed means the record, read back

Three runs of one campaign, one day, each printing `campaign 1fd5f337f5f5 (resumed)`, and each
starting stage 1 from the shipped default with a proposer that had never seen a result: the
first wave found 1.0632 one morning and 1.0496 the next afternoon, because the model's twenty
blind proposals happened to include a 64K-entry pattern table once and not the other time.
"Resumed" meant the measurement cache and nothing else. The campaign store had every number
the earlier runs produced, and nothing read it.

`Recorder.known()` reads it: this campaign's screen-rung trials for the stack in question, one
entry per configuration with its best number, best first. A resumed run puts the top eight
into the seed pool right after the incumbent, tagged `known`, and hands them to the first
proposer call as "already measured" -- the same argument the second call has always had, so
the model reasons from evidence on its first proposal rather than from priors. With the cache
keyed on the code that ran (D361) re-measuring those eight costs nothing, and a storage budget
(D362) filters them like everything else. The store is read through the same `trials()` the
knowledge miner uses; a refused trial, a composed stack and a confirmed number are not seeds,
and the test says which is which. New campaigns are unchanged: the pool is the incumbent, the
proposals, the neighbours, the random points, in that order (D349).

---

## D368: A tree policy for a two-objective budget

MicroEvo (Xiong et al., ICCAD'26, arXiv:2608.06183) couples an LLM with Monte-Carlo Tree
Search for microarchitecture DSE: LLM operators expand tree nodes, a Pareto-aware UCT rule
selects which node earns the next expansion, insights extracted from measured deltas feed the
prompts, and a state controller switches the model between exploit and explore. Read against
Flux, most of it is convergent evolution with different names. The proposer already reasons
from measured evidence and refusals (D349, D355, D359); typed knowledge mined from the stores
already feeds prompts under a budget with provenance (D243-D245); the frontier is already a
first-class object confirmed along its length (D362); flat-round patience is a crude fixed
cousin of their state directive; and D367 made the campaign record itself a seed. What Flux
genuinely lacked is the paper's core: a SEARCH POLICY that allocates the measurement budget
across the frontier. Every stage-1 walk kept one best and expanded it -- single-objective by
construction, with storage recovered afterwards by walking back down (stage 2).

`flux_study.pareto_uct` is that policy, generic over candidates: a tree whose selection score
is the branch's normalised hypervolume improvement against the global front, plus a crowding
term that pulls waves toward the frontier's gaps, plus a decaying exploration bonus (their
Eq. 2/5/6, two objectives exactly). Measurement stays the caller's; the module owns only
"where next" and "what the front is". The prefetcher wires it as `--strategy pareto-uct`, an
opt-in alternative for stage 1 over the same seeds, the same move generator, the same wave
size, budget and gates -- only the allocation differs. Three findings from building it, all
now pinned by tests: a leaf whose moves are spent must carry its exhaustion IN the selection
score or the caller loops on it forever (the first live test hung); `diverse_neighbours`
round-robins knobs but lists each knob's whole range ascending, which a climb survives by
re-drawing from one node and a node-switching tree does not -- the tree's moves are ordered
adjacent-first; and on the up/down tie of a log-2 knob the larger value goes first, because
taking the ascending-order tiebreak sent every node's first wave downward and the tree
declared the quality axis converged at the seed.

What was deliberately NOT taken: the LLM as the expansion operator (our move generators are
deterministic and free; the model stays in the proposer and inventor roles it has), and the
utility-scored insight memory (the mentor's mined facts already cover it with provenance,
which theirs lacks; a per-run reflection pass remains possible future work). The synthetic
landscape test shows the policy tracing a known frontier end to end within budget; whether it
beats the climb on ChampSim's real landscape is an empirical question the demo can now ask
with one flag, and nothing in the default path changed.

**MEASURED, one paired run each** (budget 20, 20 model proposals, fresh campaigns, full-length
confirmation; the proposals are sampled, so this is one sample, not a verdict):

    climb        confirmed 1.0563 at 176 KB, bingo alone; 4 confirmed frontier points
    pareto-uct   confirmed 1.0635 at 183 KB, bingo+invented2; 5 confirmed points, including
                 23.5 KB at 1.0379 and 35 KB at 1.0470 -- the compact region the climb only
                 reaches by shrinking back from its single winner

The tree's run also spent more simulations (279 against 189): not stage 1, which both cap at
the same budget, but downstream -- its stage-1 frontier led compose to keep `invented2`,
which made the tune phase and a second reference worth running. Same request, different path,
and the extra spend bought the better answer on this sample. The climb stays the default
until more samples say otherwise.

**THE SECOND PAIR** (seed 1, fresh campaigns) reversed the picture enough to settle it: climb
confirmed 1.0638 at 113 KB against pareto-uct's 1.0649 at 182 KB -- a toss-up that the
project's own area-lean preference (D362) hands to the climb -- and the climb's confirmed
frontier reached 1.0703 at 408 KB, the best full-length number this study has produced. Two
samples, one win each, differences within the proposal-sampling variance: the climb REMAINS
the default, the tree stays the opt-in for runs that want the frontier populated directly,
and the real lesson is that both strategies now route through the same compose/tune/shrink
machinery well enough that the proposer's draw matters more than the allocation policy at
this budget.

The fourth MCTS phase followed. In a game, simulation is a cheap random playout because a
partial position has no value of its own; in DSE every node is a complete design, so the
phase collapses to a value ESTIMATE, and the only honest use of one is deciding what to
measure next. `_rollout_speedup` is that estimate: the distance-weighted vote of the three
nearest measured configurations (knob distance in log-2 steps, so a PHT doubling and a
filter-table doubling are the same move), silent below five measurements. Each wave, the
affordable moves are ranked by the frontier gain their estimated speedup would buy
(`ParetoUCT.predicted_gain`); half the wave follows that ranking and half keeps the
adjacent-first order, because a rollout built from this run's own points is confidently
wrong about directions nothing has measured yet. Estimates order; only measurements are
recorded -- a test drives the whole stage against a planted landscape and checks every
scored number came from the backend. The ladder now reads: predict (free) -> screen
(~35 s) -> confirm (~6 min).

---

## D369: The record reflects in arithmetic, not prose

The last piece of MicroEvo (arXiv:2608.06183) left unadopted was Active Knowledge
Accumulation: after each expansion an LLM reflects on the measured deltas, writes a prose
insight, and a utility-scored memory retrieves the best ones into later prompts. The analysis
underneath it is right and this repo already believes it -- their "pairwise analysis" is a
controlled experiment somebody already paid for: two configurations differing in exactly one
knob, and the delta between their measured numbers. The memory on top of it is where the
designs part ways. A second store of model-authored prose drifts from the record it summarises
and carries no provenance; this repo's rule is typed facts computed FROM the stores (D243).

`flux_prefetcher.reflect` is the adoption under that rule. `pairwise_insights` reads what
`Recorder.known()` already returns and finds every pair differing in one knob (region size and
pattern length counted as the one knob they are), aggregates per knob into a direction, a mean
geomean delta and a pair count, withholds anything with fewer than two pairs (one pair is an
anecdote), and returns the strongest few. Computed fresh on every call: the store IS the
memory, there is no second one to fall out of step. On a resumed run the directions go into
the first proposer prompt as "WHAT THE RECORD SHOWS ... directions, not instructions" --
completing D367: the first call now gets the record's configurations AND what they taught --
and the strongest direction goes into the report's lessons tagged [record], so the reader
sees what the model was told. No LLM writes an insight, no utility score ranks a memory;
the magnitude and the pair count are the utility score, and they come with provenance for
free because they are arithmetic over recorded trials.

---

## D370: The inventor is told the screen's numbers

The MAC-array invention prompt asked the model to beat "the four built-in multipliers on area
and delay" -- a slogan, because invention ran before anything was measured. D359's rule
(told, not discovered) applied to the proposer's budget; it applies to the inventor's target
too: a model asked to beat a number it is never shown can only guess what fast or small
means on this library at this clock.

Invention now runs AFTER the screen. The prompt carries each built-in multiplier's measured
worst path and area from THIS run, in the same combinational tree-reduction PE the invention
will be judged in, shortest path first, with the win condition stated ("a shorter path at
comparable area, or less area at a comparable path"). Anything the model gets past the rules
and the vectors is then generated into PEs, verified once per distinct RTL, and screened
incrementally, so it reaches the same frontier the finalists are drawn from in the same run.
On a cached campaign the reordering costs nothing: the built-ins' screen is served from the
cache and the invention phase starts with the numbers in hand.

---

## D371: The nightly failed by construction

Every scheduled CI run this repository has ever had -- eighteen nightlies across three weeks,
six commits -- failed at the integration sweep, while every push run stayed green. The logs
need authentication this machine does not have, but reproducing the sweep locally in its own
shape found the cause in its first thirty seconds: the loop globs `tests/integration/*.py`,
which includes `conftest.py` and `_helpers.py`; pytest collects no tests from either and
exits 5; `|| fail=1` counts that as a failure. The job was red before any real test ran, on
its very first night, and stayed red identically ever since -- which is precisely why nobody
could name the failing test: there wasn't one.

The glob is now `test_*.py`. Two lessons worth the entry. A job that has NEVER been green is
its own diagnosis: the failure predating every code change means the job, not the code --
checked here by listing the full schedule history before reading a line of test code. And
D129's own rationale for the per-file shape ("an unknown reads as a pass") cuts both ways: a
failure that names no test reads as a mystery, and sat unexamined for eighteen runs because
the summary looked like flakiness rather than arithmetic. Whether any real integration file
also fails on CI is now answerable the ordinary way; a local sweep of the whole directory is
running to establish the baseline.

---

## D372: The wiring is a decision variable

"The lane assignment is free." That answer (the user's, to D363's standing question) turns
the bank-mapping study's hardest input into a search axis: which of the N concurrent accesses
share one of the seven 4-input crossbars is the designer's choice, and D363/D364 showed the
choice dominates -- consecutive wiring is proved impossible for any two of the seven strides,
interleaved reaches 7 of 16, and nothing said either was the best wiring.

`Stage(lane_key="free", lanes=4, blocks=7)` says so, and the solver searches the assignment
JOINTLY with the XOR-fold. The encoding that keeps it tractable: booleans y[k][b] (window
position k rides crossbar b, exactly one b, at most `lanes` per b, symmetry-broken so
position k rides a crossbar numbered at most k); a literal same_{kl} forced true when any
crossbar carries both; and the observation that a same-crossbar pair at window offset j and
stride s must be group-distinct for EVERY start address, which depends only on the product
j*s -- so one shared literal ok_o per offset product, defined by implications
(ok_o -> differs-on-stage-bits(d)) over that offset's difference set, extended incrementally
by the same counter-example loop that refines the bank clauses. The chosen partition is read
back from the model, written into the stage as its concrete `partition`, and from then on it
is the hardware: the exhaustive checker verifies the fold against it, the report prints the
wiring beside the mapping, and the model round (when it runs) is judged on it. Before an
assignment exists a free stage constrains NO pair -- a checker must not invent a wiring --
and the pigeonhole stays silent about free stages for the same reason, so "impossible" can
never be claimed against a wiring nobody chose. Unsolved assignment also skips the model
round, with the reason stated: a proposal cannot be judged against a wiring that does not
exist yet.

First result: strides {1, 2} at N=8 through the 4x4s -- proved impossible for the consecutive
wiring (D363) -- solves with the wiring free: the solver picks a partition and a fold
together and the checker confirms both.

**MEASURED, the full seven-stride request** (`--stage 3,4:1:4:free7`, 600 s budget):

    N=4    SOLVED: a 4-XOR fold, each access on its own crossbar -- the solver spread the
           window so stage 1 constrains nothing, and won at the banks. Checker-verified.
    N=8    unsat for the linear family over EVERY wiring: seven crossbars force one
           co-located pair, and no choice of it admits a fold. Best: 6 concurrent on all
           strides, or strides {1,2,16} at all 8.
    N=16   unsat likewise; 7 concurrent on all strides -- the interleaved ceiling, so
           freeing the wiring does not move N=16 within linear folds.

The joint unsat is a stronger statement than D363's fixed-wiring proofs: not "this wiring
fails" but "no wiring rescues the family". What remains beyond it is non-linear mappings on
a chosen wiring, so on joint-unsat the flow fixes the interleave BY RULE (fewest co-located
pairs, the best wiring measured) and the model round runs against that concrete target, the
report stating the wiring was chosen by rule, not found by the solver. Building that closed
a correctness hole the first test found: an UNSOLVED free stage constrains no pair, so the
baseline was being judged against hardware that did not exist -- plain modulo came back
conflict-free. Every verdict on an unsolved free stage now goes through the same rule-fixed
wiring, stated; and a partition may name positions beyond the current window (a wiring
chosen for N=8 still describes the hardware when the descent asks about N=7; the checker
trims).

---

## D373: A run you can see

"We want to draw some graph of the DSE progress -- what it explored, a trend line, what was
achieved -- as it's usually done." The record already holds everything such a figure needs
(the campaign store keeps every trial in order with its metrics, rung and refusals), so this
is a renderer, not new bookkeeping: `flux_study.progress` draws the standard pair of DSE
figures into one self-contained SVG, no plotting dependency, native `<title>` tooltips,
the validated reference palette on an explicit surface.

Top panel: measurement order against quality -- every explored point, screened as small blue
dots and confirmed ringed in orange so the rungs stay visually distinct, the running best as
a step line, refusals counted in the corner rather than plotted (a refusal has no number to
plot). Bottom panel: the objective space -- cost against quality (log cost where storage
spans decades), the frontier stepped through the non-dominated points on the report's rung,
the decision starred and labelled, the baseline as a dashed rule. The prefetcher demo writes
`<db>.progress.svg` from its campaign record (`--plot` overrides, `--plot none` skips) and
the run's campaign id now travels in the result's provenance so the plot reads the right
campaign; the MAC-array demo renders the same figure from its result payload. The bankmap
study's objective is a proof, not a numeric trade-off, so it deliberately has no such plot.

The first version showed dots, not the story ("not super useful yet" -- correct). The story
of a DSE run is where the budget went, how fast it converged, and what the cheap rung's
optimism did, so the figure grew to three panels: the convergence panel gained the run's
PHASES as labelled bands (seed, climb, compose, tune, shrink, confirm -- the store records
each trial's phase) and a direct label on the final best; a hypervolume-growth panel joined
it -- the screened frontier's normalised (quality x cost) volume after each evaluation, the
standard two-objective convergence curve, drawn only when both axes were explored; and the
results panel gained screened-to-confirmed connector lines per finalist (the screen's error,
visible as a line), the storage-budget rule when one was set, and the decision's numbers
beside its star. Dense runs draw their cloud faint so the trend stays legible.

Two corrections from use. An area-optimal study's trend is "cheapest yet", not "fastest
yet": `trend_axis="cost"` makes the convergence panel track the cost axis with a running
MINIMUM, and the interconnect figure now reads that way. And "bankmap has no numeric
trade-off" was a cop-out: every checked mapping has an XOR cost and a CLEAN FRACTION (the
worst resource's share of conflict-free start addresses, 1.0 = solved), the z3 CEGIS rounds
are a convergence curve, and the phases (baseline, z3, feasible, model) are bands like any
other run's. `MappingResult.progress` records every checked mapping -- including each solver
probe -- and the bankmap demo writes the same `<db>.progress.svg` as the rest; a search that
ends in a proof still leaves a graph of how it got there. Further polish from the same
review: the hypervolume axis is fixed at 0..1 (the volume is of the normalised unit square,
so 1.0 has an absolute reading) with the final value labelled; the incumbent appears as a
labelled diamond (every demo's headline is "beat the default"); a study's target -- the MAC
clock, bankmap's conflict-free line -- is its own labelled rule, distinct from the baseline;
the trend panel stars the evaluation where the decision was found; and the frontier's
achieved region is lightly shaded so "what was had" reads at a glance.
