## D374: The first honest nightly, line by line

D371's fixed glob made the integration sweep's verdict meaningful for the first time, so the
whole directory was run locally to establish the baseline: 109 files, 94 passing, and every
failure classified rather than shrugged at.

- `conftest.py`, `_helpers.py`: the by-construction exit-5 failures; excluded by the glob.
- `test_knowledge_riscv_corpus.py`: PATH ROT -- its root still pointed at `flux/knowledge`,
  gone since the mentor restructure, and two assertions assumed the corpus held only RISC-V
  when it now shares the store with other standards. Fixed; the RISC-V claims filter to
  `riscv-unpriv`. Every failure here predates D371's fix and was invisible behind it.
- `test_interconnect_demo_live.py`: a REAL crash -- a model-less run (`--llm-round 0`) hit
  `UnboundLocalError: drawn` at the last line of `run_study`, because the conclusions list
  was only bound inside the `if ask is not None` branch. The same defect class as the
  `ranked` bug the closure-extraction refactor found; initialised now.
- `test_gem5_adapter_live.py` and `test_leaderboard_cross_evaluator_live.py`: PIN DRIFT, not
  flakiness -- 565226 (was 550513) and 908 (was 1148), each reproduced bit-identically across
  two independent runs. The nixchip pin bump that brought Pythia (D361) also rebuilt gem5 and
  Stream, and a pinned value belongs to a toolchain. Re-pinned with the bump named at the pin,
  so the next drift is a one-line diff pointing at its cause.
- The eight live-LLM files (the agentic loops and searches, the MCP surface, generation):
  every failure was a timeout or a coverage miss recorded while the machine ran eighteen
  ChampSim slots and a 27B model; quiet reruns classify them, and the first has already
  passed idle. The claim "these do not run on CI" turned out to be only PARTLY true, which
  is the next bullet.
- SEVEN live-LLM files had no `requires_ollama` guard -- exactly the D246 bug, which was
  fixed in `test_chia_flux_agentic_search_live.py` alone and then re-introduced by every
  later file that copied a different template: the two chia agentic DSE files, both
  `*_generate_dse` files, and the three RTL demo composites. On the GitHub runner (no
  Ollama) each would have failed unguarded and turned the first honest nightly red for a
  reason that is deployment, not code. All seven now carry the module-level
  `pytestmark = _helpers.requires_ollama`; `test_systemc_accumulator_alu_demo_live.py`
  looked identical by name but compiles captured generator output and never calls the
  model, so it stays unguarded on purpose -- over-guarding would silently delete real CI
  coverage. The detector that found these was transitive (files importing
  `flux_agentic_*`/`flux_generate_*` without the marker), because a plain grep for
  "ollama" misses every caller that reaches the model through a wrapper.
- One rerun verdict is structural, not flaky: `test_concurrent_dispatch_is_really_faster_
  than_the_same_three_searches_run_sequentially` measured 0.95x under load AND 0.93x on a
  fully idle machine (362 s concurrent vs 336 s sequential) against its 1.25x requirement.
  All three searches are LLM-bound against ONE local Ollama that serialises requests, so
  the wall-clock speedup the test demanded lives in the model server's parallelism --
  deployment, not CHIA/Ray. Rewritten as
  `test_concurrent_dispatch_really_overlaps_the_three_searches`: each sub-report's
  `wall_clock_s` is measured inside its own Ray task, so genuinely overlapped execution
  sums the three spans to ~3x the dispatch window (a sequential fallback gives ~1x);
  the assertion is `overlap > 1.5`, robust to both load and backend serialisation, and the
  test no longer runs the 6-minute sequential baseline at all. The sibling
  `*_generate_dse` tests keep their softer `< sequential * 1.15` bound, which serialisation
  cannot break. `test_chia_flux_agentic_search_live.py` passed 6/6 idle in 40:28 -- pure
  contention, no code issue; note its honest solo runtime already exceeds the sweep's old
  2400 s per-file timeout, which is a second, independent way a healthy file can look red.

The meta-lesson repeats D371's: a suite that has never produced a meaningful verdict
accumulates rot silently and all at once -- four genuinely different defects (a dead glob,
a moved directory, an unbound name, a toolchain bump) surfaced on the same day because the
one signal that would have caught each of them separately had been red for other reasons
since the day it existed.

## D375: The 8B that never was

**Date:** 2026-09-02. **Trigger:** chasing the reproducible `mapping_axis` failure (D374),
the solo probe showed each LLM proposal round costing 3-10 minutes against instant zigzag
evaluations, with client-side timeouts and retries -- far too slow for the "local qwen-8B,
a few tokens/s" this repo's timing lore (D354/D359) describes.

**The fact:** `ollama list` shows `qwen3.8:latest` and `qwen3.8:27b` sharing one digest
(`22130167c4c2`, 17 GB, parameter_size 27.3B). The `latest` tag has pointed at that blob
since **Aug 20**; the `:27b` tag added on Sep 1 was a second name for a model already
serving. There is no 8B installed. The GPU is a Quadro P620 with 2 GB VRAM, so 0.5 GB of
the 18 GB model sits in VRAM and inference is ~97% CPU -- the ~5 min/round measured in the
mapping-axis probe is this machine's honest pace for the model every loop has actually
been using.

**What this invalidates:**
- Sep 1's "8B vs 27B" invention comparison (prefetcher invented7/8 compiling "at 27b"
  where "8b" output didn't; the multiplier failing "at both sizes") compared the blob with
  itself. Observed differences were run-to-run variance. The multiplier corner-case
  failure still stands as evidence about THIS model; it says nothing about a real 8B.
- Every live-LLM test-time budget was set for a model ~3x smaller than what runs. The
  D374 sweep's per-file 2400 s timeout is arithmetically impossible for several files at
  27B pace (`search_live` needs 40:28 solo when healthy), so part of what D374 filed under
  "contention" is really "wrong model, honest speed".
- The Sep 1 decision "separate stronger model eventually; for now point invention at the
  same qwen3.8:27b" was made on the false premise that two models existed.

**Action taken:** pulled `qwen3:4b` (a genuinely small Qwen3) for fast diagnosis runs
only, via `FLUX_LLM_MODEL` -- `default_local_model()`'s tag is untouched, because which
model should be the default (and whether nightly-adjacent budgets should assume 27B pace)
is Cedric's call, not a triage step. Any measurement that names its model tag remains
honest either way -- the tag just meant more than it appeared to.

## D376: The five-minute proposal that should have been five seconds

**Date:** 2026-09-02. **Trigger:** even with D375's 4B diagnosis model, mapping-axis proposal
rounds still cost minutes. A one-line answer from the 4B took 354 s through the loops' code
path; the same question answered in seconds when reasoning was actually off.

**The mechanism, measured step by step:**
- `chia.models.ollama.OllamaLLM` speaks Ollama's `/v1` OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which has
  NO field for disabling reasoning. Prompt-level `/no_think` is ignored by newer qwen3-family
  builds (measured: "Say OK." still generated 360 hidden reasoning tokens through the chat
  template, 596 raw). So every proposal from every chia-dispatched loop bought a
  multi-thousand-token hidden trace at CPU speed -- with the 27B at ~2.7 tok/s, that IS the
  5-10 minute round, and it multiplies D375's model-size problem rather than adding to it.
- Ollama's NATIVE endpoint accepts `think:false`, and the 27B honors it perfectly: "Say OK."
  became 3 eval tokens in 1.1 s.
- The repo already knew all of this: `flux_llm.NativeOllamaProposer` (D354/D359) was built for
  exactly this failure, docstring-documented with measurements -- but only the interconnect
  demo path adopted it. The chia_nodes package (nine `OllamaLLM` call sites) never did.

**Change:** `agentic.py`'s and `dse_loop.py`'s `_OllamaProposer` adapters now wrap
`flux_llm.NativeOllamaProposer` (think off by default, `FLUX_LLM_THINK=1` still the A/B arm
that restores it). These two adapters drive all five agentic-search axes and the whole
`flux_agentic_dse_loop` -- the paths that were timing out. The remaining `OllamaLLM` sites
(generate_rtl, generate_systemc, author_*, check_faithfulness, campaign) still speak `/v1`
and still pay the trace; converting them needs a per-site look at tools/metadata use, left
open. `CostTrackingProposer` is unaffected (stub-tested, wired to no real node).

**Consequence for D374/D375's ledger:** the live-LLM files' timeouts were three stacked
causes, now separable: machine contention (real, D374), a 27B where an 8B was assumed
(D375), and unsuppressed reasoning (this entry) -- the largest of the three. Their honest
runtimes need re-measuring after this change before any timeout budget means anything.

**Confirmed, both ways:** `test_chia_flux_agentic_dse_loop_live.py`, which could not finish
inside 75 minutes solo before this change, passes 13/13 in 29:53 after it. And the
"reproducible mapping-axis failure" that started this whole chase dissolved under it: a
direct run of the same loop shows EVERY pinned assertion value still true (winner 1554.0,
baseline 1666.0 spatial C, Timeloop reference exactly 512.0, replay matched, cost $0.00 --
no fourth pin drift). The F was the old `/v1` client timing out mid-round under unsuppressed
27B reasoning and surfacing as a test failure at a deterministic position -- a slowness bug
wearing a correctness bug's costume, which is why it "reproduced" so convincingly.

## D377: omni, the loop that picks loops

**Date:** 2026-09-02. **Ask (Cedric):** a fifth, "one-to-rule-them-all" demo -- give it a
prompt, the agent sees all the tools and options Flux offers (or a subset to make choices
easier), selects tools, generates inputs/files as needed: a general solver/runner/DSE.
Name and default scope chosen by Cedric: `applications/omni`, full catalog by default.

**Shape (`flux_omni`):**
- **Catalog by introspection, never by hand (D95/D96's lesson).** `FluxTool.setup()` is
  replayed against a recorder (`object.__new__` bypasses the ChiaTool server bring-up),
  yielding every registered MCP method as a `ToolSpec` -- signature from `inspect`,
  summary and per-arg docs parsed from the Google-style docstrings that surface already
  maintains. The MCP surface's parity guard therefore guards omni's menu too, for free.
- **Typed plans, refused before run.** Model replies are JSON steps
  `{tool, args, bind}`; later args reference earlier results as `"$bind.field[0]"`.
  Validation (unknown tool/arg, missing required, forward or malformed reference,
  path escapes) happens before execution and produces `Refusal`s with the exact reason,
  fed back verbatim next round -- the `InvalidLLMProposal` posture applied to plans. A
  canned plan with one typo runs zero steps, not half of itself.
- **The model plans; tools measure (D297 applied to orchestration).** Results reach the
  model as budgeted summaries; full results go to provenance. Budget stops (rounds,
  calls, wall clock) report `done=False` with whatever conclusion text exists -- never a
  fabricated success.
- **Replay is the same executor.** Every run writes `omni_run.json` (prompt, offered
  catalog, raw replies, executed plan, full outcomes); that file IS a loadable `--plan`,
  so the without-a-model demo contract holds by construction: two canned plans ship, and
  any model run replays deterministically.
- **Three meta-tools** beyond the catalog: `write_file` (workdir-sandboxed), `load_ir`
  (bundled examples), `note` -- the "generates input/files as needed" half of the ask.

**Guards:** 19 unit tests, including one that validates every canned plan against the
LIVE introspected catalog -- a drifted tool signature fails at unit speed, not in a demo
(the D374 rot class, pre-empted). Verified by running: the canned validity plan replays
5/5 steps model-free (zigzag 1554.0 cycles on the bundled GEMM -- the same number D24
pinned).

**Live verification (fourth attempt, and the first three each bought a design fix).**
Run 1: the naive 21k-token catalog crashed the Ollama runner (fix below). Run 2: the
model dithered -- described the same tool four times, never searched, budget-stopped
with no conclusion -- which bought the duplicate-step refusal, the "Round k of N" header
with a last-round-must-conclude rule, and the agentic_*/generate_*-are-slow warning.
Run 3: a real Ray-parallel sweep ran but the 40-min wrapper killed the run before the
conclusion; that bought the loop-owned wall-clock budget plus a conclude-only final
round when it expires (done stays False -- a conclusion under duress is labeled as one).
Run 4 (27B, 19 min, 6 rounds): described three tools once each, had its one repeat
refused and adapted, loaded both IR examples, AUTHORED four complete inline
Architecture-IR documents, evaluated them, and concluded "width 32, 263 cycles" --
measured, and consistent with D13's known width-32 latency optimum. One instructive
flaw: the provenance shows the four arches were X=4, X=4 again, X=16, X=32 -- the model
duplicated width 4 and labeled it width 8 in the conclusion. The winner is real; the
width-8 line is a mislabel only the recorded plan exposes. That is the provenance
contract earning its keep on day one, and it names the next guard: verifying conclusion
claims against executed outcomes (open).

**The first live run crashed the model server, and the fix is part of the design.** The
naive catalog render (every tool, every param, every doc line) measured 63 KB / ~21k
tokens; the first request dropped the connection with no response and left Ollama with no
runner. Fix, in two halves: (a) the menu is now one signature line per tool with
optionals folded into a count (`evaluate(backend, workload, +7 optional) -- ...`), and a
`describe(tool)` meta-tool expands full parameter docs on demand -- the deferred-schema
pattern, which also means the round prompt stays ~3k tokens however large the surface
grows (a unit test pins the budget); (b) `NativeOllamaProposer` grew an explicit
`num_ctx` and omni requests 16k, because a prompt silently truncated to the server's 4k
default is D354's failure shape on the input side.

## D378: interconnect_conflict -- bank hashes vs tensor tiles, with receipts

**Date:** 2026-09-02. **Ask (Cedric):** a new demo for a specified problem: a 32-bank
single-ported L1 (128-bit rows) under 28R+24W ports across MU (16/8/4 operand split,
16W), VU, and DMA; RxCxL tensors in 12 storage modes with runtime dims, written with
one tile shape and read with another; three conflict categories (intra-operand,
intra-unit, system); Pareto over area / padding / latency / throughput with fmax>600
post-synthesis; the hash must be injective on (bank, line); proofs of feasibility
boundaries; evaluation with operation-shaped inputs and an anti-overfitting guard.

**Shape (`applications/interconnect_conflict`, package `flux_iconflict`):**
- **model.py is the correctness heart**: all 12 storage modes as one vectorised
  linearization (plain orders, 2x2/4x4 H/V blocks, vectors), tile -> bank-row sets
  with edge clipping (compute padding touches no memory). A unit test proves every
  mode is a bijection onto 0..N-1; hand-computed golden addresses pin the block modes.
- **Injectivity decided exactly, not sampled**: for the GF(2)-linear hash family
  (reusing `flux_bankmap.mapping` -- Modulo/XorFold with `verilog()`), (bank,
  line=row>>m) is injective iff the m x m low-bit submatrix is invertible; a GF(2)
  elimination decides it, brute force confirms it in tests, and every solution and
  every proposal passes this gate or is refused. Read/write tile consistency holds by
  construction: `hash_of` sees the layout only, never the tile (test-pinned).
- **Six curated solutions**, each with targets/metadata/assumptions as data: modulo
  baseline, global XOR, metadata swizzle (per-tensor pitch bits -- needs a descriptor
  reaching the hash unit), bank-group partition (space separation), unit time-slots
  with fetch buffers (time separation; latency and buffer area PAID in the numbers),
  pitch-pad skew (Cost B measured exactly as stored/true-1). Plus S6 from an
  injectivity-gated XOR hill-climb and optional S7* from LLM proposal rounds.
- **Anti-overfitting is structural**: seeded GEMM/VU/DMA workloads (operation info
  included: A walks horizontally, B vertically) split into disjoint train/holdout
  seed ranges; searches tune on train, verdicts and the Pareto use holdout, both
  print side by side.
- **Proofs both ways**: certificates by exhaustion over all tile origins with dims
  <= 64 (finite domain -- exhaustion IS proof), refutations as concrete
  counterexamples, pigeonhole floors (64 rows / 16 ports >= 4 cycles under any
  design) printed beside measured latencies.

**First run's honest findings (seed 0, model-free, ~15 s):** the 4-cost front is
{S2-swizzle-meta, S5-pad-skew}; S5 buys the best holdout latency (1.004 cycles/access,
9.19 rows/cycle) for 9.1% storage padding, S2 matches it (1.017) for zero padding but
a per-tensor descriptor requirement. The certificates answered the universality
question the problem statement poses: an 8x4 tile family is PROVED conflict-free for
both, and a 4x16 tile REFUTES both at difference 17 (one row-step plus one col-step
lands on one bank) -- no static per-tensor-metadata hash in this family is universal
across tile shapes, so tile-shape metadata or scheduling must close the gap.
Time-slotting and bank-grouping are Pareto-dominated under this traffic mix; their
regime (heavier cross-unit contention) is a sensitivity the demo's knobs can reach.

**Open:** physical upgrade of frontier rows through the interconnect app's
whole-fabric OpenROAD flow (D272) for real um2 and the fmax>600 check; a chia-node +
MCP wrapper (parity discipline) so omni can drive this loop; group-capacity
fragmentation as a measured part of Cost B for S3.

---

## D379: Topology is a player, not a constant

**Date:** 2026-09-02. **Trigger (Cedric):** "shouldn't the demo design/evaluate
interconnect topologies as they impact area/fmax and conflicts... when reporting
results I want interconnect + map function." Both objections were correct: D378's
first cut fixed a 52x32 crossbar, which made Cost A a constant (the Pareto could never
trade area) and hid the conflicts a blocking fabric adds on its own.

**Change (`fabric.py` + rework):**
- A `FabricModel` is a capacity tree over bank-id prefixes -- (bits, cap) meaning "at
  most cap concurrent requests into each 2^bits bank subtree" (the staged-crossbar
  shape bankmap's stage model uses). The cycle law gains a third term:
  cycles = max(port bound, bank load, fabric load), so a report can say WHICH bound
  limited a request, and refutation counterexamples now name the culprit.
- Four topologies: xbar-full (non-blocking reference), fly-r2 (log2 stages, full
  bisection), fly-r2-slim2 (half bisection, ~half area), unit-split (three per-unit
  crossbars, 3:1 bank merge). Area rule stays structural and uniform (a link crosses
  one radix-2 element per stage); OpenROAD remains the um2/fmax upgrade path.
- A design point is now the PAIR map-policy x fabric, and is reported, plotted,
  certified, and serialized under its pair name. The study scores the full cross
  product (7 policies x 4 fabrics = 28 points); searches still tune hashes on the
  ideal fabric, then the winner is scored across every topology like everything else.

**What the pair study immediately showed (seed 0, holdout):** the full crossbar is
DOMINATED everywhere -- with any decent hash the traffic never stresses fly-r2's full
bisection, so the log fabric delivers identical latency at a third the area (73,728 vs
212,992 gate-units for S5-pad-skew). The new front is {S5+fly-r2 1.004 cy,
S5+fly-r2-slim2 1.007 cy at 38,400 units, S2-swizzle+fly-r2-slim2 1.017 cy, zero
padding}. And the certificates gained a second failure mode worth naming: on
Loop_4x4_H 4x16 tiles the swizzle keeps every BANK clean (bank load 1) yet
fly-r2-slim2 still refuses the request -- "fabric load 2 > port floor 1" -- a conflict
no hash can fix and only bisection (area) or scheduling can. 15 unit tests, demo
verified before/after.

---

## D380: An evaluation that nothing fails is not an evaluation

**Date:** 2026-09-02. **Trigger (Cedric, after running the demo):** "the result isn't
good yet." Correct: the table was flat -- every latency within 1.0-1.3 cycles, every
fabric identical on latency, area doing all the Pareto work. Three causes, all real:

1. **Latency was under-charged.** avg_latency divided a step's cycles across the
   step's requests; honestly, under a shared schedule EVERY access in a step completes
   when the step's slowest bank does, and under time-slots access i also waits for the
   slots before it. `TrafficMetrics.latency_sum` now charges per access; time-slot
   serialization is charged cumulatively instead of by a flat constant.
2. **The traffic was too easy.** Tiny tiles and truncated walks left most requests
   port-bound at ~1 cycle -- nothing to discriminate. The generator now issues peak
   pressure: tiles to 16x16 (64 rows, above the 4-cycle port floor BY DESIGN), 8-step
   walks, DMA as a streaming walk, VU/DMA join probabilities 0.7/0.6, dims 8-64.
3. **No fabric genuinely blocked.** fly-r2-slim4 (bisection 1/4, 24,064 gate-units)
   joins the spectrum; accesses carry their unit tag; and `category_breakdown()`
   measures latency at three scopes -- operand-only, +intra-unit, +system -- so each
   frontier pair's report answers "which conflict category hurts" with numbers.

**The table after (seed 0, holdout):** latencies span 12.9 to 54.6 cycles/access and
every axis now discriminates. Hash quality ranks: pad-skew 12.87 < searched XOR 13.26
< global XOR 13.33 < metadata swizzle 13.77 < modulo 16.21 -- the swizzle, best in
the easy-traffic cut, drops behind global XOR under heavy cross-tensor interference.
The front spans the real area/latency trade: {S5+fly-r2 73.7k units at 12.87 cy,
S5+slim2 38.4k at 12.88, S6+slim2, S5+slim4 24.1k at 16.45, S6+slim4} -- slim4's
~3.5-cycle premium is finally a measured price, not a free lunch. The searched hash
shows a visible train->holdout gap (12.05 -> 13.26), exactly what the split exists to
expose. Bank-group partitioning collapses under mixed traffic (43-55 cy/access): space
separation costs each tensor 3 of its 5 bank bits, and the breakdown shows it. Scope
accounting for the winners: ~4.8 cycles operand-only -> ~12.9 with intra-unit sharing
-> ~13 system: INTRA-UNIT is where this memory system actually hurts, which redirects
the next design effort (operand-aware MU scheduling, not better hashes).

15 unit tests, full suite green, demo verified before/after; the artifact's Figure 6
carries the corrected numbers.

## D381: Twelve fabrics, and pipeline depth stops being free

**Date:** 2026-09-02. **Trigger (Cedric):** "there are more interconnect options too."
Two things were missing: breadth (five fabrics is a thin spectrum) and a cost the
problem statement names explicitly -- Cost C includes "deep pipeline latency", and the
model was crediting a 5-stage butterfly with a crossbar's latency.

**Change:** `FabricModel.pipe_latency` (pipeline depth in cycles, stated per family,
added into Cost C), and seven new families joining the five: benes (rearrangeably
non-blocking at 2log2N-1 stages -- crossbar permutation capability at a fraction of
the gates, priced with the deepest pipe plus a stated global-routing assumption),
fly-r4 and fly-r4-slim2 (half the stages of radix-2, wider elements), cx-24/cx-16
(concentrator then slim crossbar -- the bet that peak concurrency sizes the fabric),
hier-4x8 (two-level crossbar), ring-8 (the cheap extreme: near-zero gates, root
capacity 8, half-ring hop latency). 84 design points per study.

**What the honest pipeline term changed (seed 0, holdout):** the full crossbar is BACK
on the front -- its 1-cycle pipe beats the butterfly's 5 stages now that stages cost
what they cost (S5+xbar 13.87 cy vs S5+fly-r2 17.87, throughput identical). The new
sweet spot is hier-4x8: 86k gate-units at 14.87 cy, one pipeline stage over the
crossbar at 40% of its area. Radix-4 beats radix-2 across the board (3 stages vs 5,
same bisection). cx-24 rides the front's neighbourhood; cx-16 pays measurable
throughput (11.8 vs 12.8 rows/cy) for its root cap. The front is now 13 pairs from
38.4k to 213k gate-units -- an actual area/latency/throughput surface, not a line.
The D379 conclusion ("crossbar dominated everywhere") was an artifact of unpriced
pipeline depth; this entry corrects it, which is what happens when a cost the problem
statement names is finally charged.

15 unit tests (benes/ring behaviors pinned), full suite green, demo verified, Figure
6/6b refreshed.

---

## D382: The demo tests its own advice, and refutes the cheap version of it

**Date:** 2026-09-02. **Trigger (Cedric):** "can we improve the demo further?" The
highest-value improvement was the one D380's scope breakdown itself demanded: it
concluded "the next lever is MU operand scheduling" -- so that recommendation became a
candidate. `schedule="stagger"` (S7-rw-stagger) issues all reads in one phase and all
writes the next: per-phase bank pressure drops from 52 ports to 28R then 24W, writes
pay one phase of latency and a priced hold buffer. Also added: `--vu-prob`/`--dma-prob`
regime knobs on the demo (the S3/S4 "their regime is heavier contention" claim is now
checkable, not just asserted), threaded through `run_study`.

**The measured verdict refutes the cheap version:** S7 lands at 14.87 cy/access with
throughput DOWN to 9.78 rows/cy (S5 shared: 13.87 cy, 12.84 rows/cy). Staggering
serializes two phases whose conflicts were largely independent -- with a good hash the
shared schedule already served reads and writes together at max-of-phases cost, while
stagger pays their SUM. The refutation sharpens D380's conclusion instead of merely
failing: the 8-cycle intra-unit term is read-read interference (A vs B tiles) plus
irreducible port arithmetic, not read-write interference -- so only operand-aware
scheduling (staggering A against B, which needs operand-level issue control in the MU)
can attack what remains, and the cheap hardware-friendly split cannot. A loop that can
refute its own recommendation is worth more than one that only confirms it.

96 design points per study now (8 policies x 12 fabrics); 15 unit tests, suite green.

---

## D383: Silicon vetoes the crossbar, and the refuted schedule's sibling wins

**Date:** 2026-09-02. Two additions closed the loop Cedric opened with "what now":

**1. The physical rung exists (`phys.py`, `--phys`).** Real Yosys+STA on ASAP7 at the
problem statement's 600 MHz: each frontier hash block (from `flux_bankmap`'s own
Verilog) and each fabric family's switching element, ~2 s per block through the same
screen macarray uses. Composed um2 = element um2 x structural ratio, always labeled
COMPOSED with the D272 caveat; the whole-fabric OpenROAD flow stays the confirm rung.
Measured verdicts: every hash is sub-1.5 um2 with >1.5 ns slack (the "hashes are free"
claim is now silicon, not assertion; Modulo is wires and is reported as such);
elements r2/r4/8:1 pass with margin -- and the 52:1 crossbar selector FAILS by
-3616 ps, over three clock periods deep. The "one-cycle crossbar" that anchored
D381's front is physically infeasible at 600 MHz: `xbar-full.pipe_latency` is now 4.0
with the measurement cited at the constant. The fmax restriction did exactly what a
restriction is for: it eliminated the paper winner.

**2. S9-ab-stagger confirms D382's sharpened hypothesis.** Phase 1 issues A (and
everything else), phase 2 issues B+C -- read-read separation, where S7's read-write
split failed. Verdict: best latency in the whole study, 12.65 cy/access on the (now
vetoed) xbar and 13.65 on hier-4x8, zero padding, zero metadata, at a throughput cost
(9.53 rows/cy) that puts it on the front as the latency-optimal corner. The D382
refutation was also regime-scoped by the field itself: rw-stagger EARNS a frontier
spot on ring-8 (26.95 vs 29.59 cy) -- phase-splitting helps exactly when the fabric's
root capacity, not the banks, is the bottleneck.

**The corrected recommendation, three iterations of honesty later:** hier-4x8 is the
fabric (on nearly every frontier row; its 8:1 element passes 600 MHz with 783 ps
margin; ~13.2k um2 composed); S5-pad-skew rides it for throughput (14.87 cy, 12.84
rows/cy, 7.8% padding), S9-ab-stagger for latency (13.65 cy, zero padding, needs
B-operand pipelining in the MU); every hash upgrade is free in area and the searched
XOR needs no metadata at all. 108 design points, 15 unit tests, suite green.

## D385: The demo states its conclusion, and derives it

**Date:** 2026-09-02. **Trigger (Cedric):** "the run of the DSE demo doesn't show these
details" -- the recommended-design synthesis lived in conversation and the decision
log, not in the report the demo prints. Decision-first is the house style; the demo
now ends with a Conclusion section, and the chia node returns the same dict.

Everything in it is DERIVED from the run's own measurements, never hard-coded, so a
different seed or regime knob can flip it honestly: the front's three corners (with
deterministic tie-breaks -- equal throughput goes to lower latency; the first cut
picked ties arbitrarily), a knee-point balanced pick (minimal equal-weight normalized
distance to the ideal over all four costs -- counting frontier rows instead favoured
whichever extreme collected ties, and measurably crowned the ring), the consensus
fabric among the best-knee third, every policy and fabric that made no frontier row
with its best measured showing attached as the reason, and the balanced pick's PROVED
tile families printed as the software contract with the refuted count beside it.

Seed-0 verdict as printed: latency corner S9-ab-stagger+hier-4x8 (13.65 cy),
throughput corner S5-pad-skew+hier-4x8 (12.84 rows/cy), knee
S6-xor-searched+fly-r4-slim2 (16.22 cy, 12.49 rows/cy, zero padding, no metadata,
47k gate-units, three proved families).

## D386: interconnect_mapping -- two little loops, one big loop

**Date:** 2026-09-03. **Ask (Cedric):** rename interconnect_conflict to
interconnect_mapping, and restructure it after the interconnect and bankmap loops:
little loops composed into a big one, because "mapping can reduce conflicts or change
the experience" -- the two halves of a design point shape each other and should be
searched that way.

**Shape:**
- **Mapping little loop** (bankmap-style): `mapping_loop(fabric, ...)` climbs the
  injective XOR space against ONE fabric's own capacity tree. The old climb only ever
  tuned on the ideal crossbar, so no hash had ever felt a subtree capacity; pairs are
  named `S6-xor@<fabric>` so the report attributes them.
- **Interconnect little loop** (interconnect-app-style): `fit_fabric(policy, ...)`
  measures per-level peak subtree loads under one mapping's residual traffic and sets
  capacities to the measured need -- zero blocking added on train by construction,
  area shrunk by the removed links, holdout judging whether it held out of sample.
  Under saturating traffic nothing is over-provisioned and it returns None; the test
  suite pins that as the honest outcome, not a failure.
- **Big loop**: `coordinate()` runs block-coordinate descent from the current front
  (tune mappings for the front's fabrics, fit fabrics for the front's mappings),
  every new pair scored and holdout-judged identically to the curated field;
  `run_study(coordination_rounds=N)` iterates until the front stops moving.

**Measured effect (seed 0):** three coordinated pairs created, all three reached the
front, and the knee-point balanced pick is now `S6-xor@fly-r4-slim2 + fly-r4-slim2`
(16.14 cy vs 16.26 for the ideal-tuned hash on the same fabric) -- the composition
demonstrably beats searching either half alone. Rename executed across package
(flux_imapping), tests, chia node (`flux_interconnect_mapping_dse_loop`), MCP tool,
agent-surface row, flake, READMEs; parity and flake guards held throughout. 18 unit
tests.

## D387: A public documentation site, generated where it would rot, hand-written where it would not

**Date:** 2026-09-03. **Ask (Cedric):** GitHub Pages documentation with three parts -- the
demo loops, "how to build your own loop", and a catalog of the modules/components that compose
into a loop. Chosen with Cedric: MkDocs Material, catalog generated from code, external-visitor
tone.

**Decisions:**
- **Site sources live under a new top-level `website/`** (`mkdocs.yml`, `docs/` inside it),
  because repo-root `docs/` is the internal record -- this file alone is 1.4 MB and must not be
  published raw. MkDocs' default output dir collides with its own conventions
  (`website/site/`), so that path is gitignored.
- **The catalog pages are generated, committed, and guarded -- not built in CI.**
  `website/generate_catalog.py` reuses `flux_omni.catalog.build_catalog()` (the omni loop's own
  introspection of the 59-tool MCP surface, D377) and renders `ToolSpec.render()` verbatim into
  six grouped pages. Importing `flux_mcp` needs the dev shell, so the Pages workflow generating
  them would mean a cold nixchip bootstrap in a docs job; instead the output is committed and
  `tests/unit/test_site_catalog_freshness.py` regenerates and diffs it in the unit suite --
  the D119/D95 pattern (`test_mcp_surface_parity.py`), one artifact further out. Grouping does
  not exist in `ToolSpec`, so the script carries an explicit name-to-page dict and refuses to
  run when it and the live catalog disagree in either direction: a new tool forces a conscious
  grouping choice.
- **`pages.yml` is a separate, nix-free workflow**: pip-installed `mkdocs-material==9.6.*`,
  `mkdocs build --strict` (broken links fail the deploy), `configure-pages` with
  `enablement: true` so the first run itself enables Pages (has_pages was false), deploy via
  the official Pages actions. `test_ci_workflow.py` pins `ci.yml` only, so no guard changes.
- **Hand-written pages adapt, not mirror, the READMEs**: the landing page carries the root
  README's thesis, the six demo pages keep problem statement, run command, and confirmed
  standings while dropping bare D-references and exhaustive flag inventories; the guide pages
  lift "the shape every loop shares" and the 7-step guide from `flux/README.md`.
- **Local preview is a throwaway venv** (`~/.venvs/mkdocs`, same pin as CI), not a flake
  addition: the canonical build environment is the pip-based CI runner, and the dev shell
  should not carry a docs tool.

**Verified:** generator run in the dev shell (GROUPS matched the live 59-tool catalog on first
run), `mkdocs build --strict` clean, freshness + parity + ci-workflow guards all green
(12 tests).

**Future work:** publishing the four self-authored
`mentor/knowledge/corpus/design-guidance/*.adoc` docs (needs asciidoc-to-markdown conversion
or an mkdocs plugin); a Pages link check against the live site.

## D388: The operator can speak while the loop runs

**Date:** 2026-09-03. **Ask (Cedric):** a component in the mentor/knowledge category:
'feedback' -- the human can give while-running feedback or redirect/guidance to the loop.
Scoped with Cedric: v1 is free-text guidance only (no hard constraints, no pause/stop verbs),
delivered by typing into the running demo's terminal, wired first into the prefetcher loop.

**Decisions:**
- **A fourth provenance class, labelled as such.** The mentor layer keeps curated text,
  measured facts, and inferred conclusions under separate honest headings; operator guidance
  is a fourth kind. `flux_feedback.render_guidance` is the only place its heading is written
  ("HUMAN GUIDANCE ... advisory directions, not measurements; every candidate still passes the
  same gates"), so no consumer can splice a note into a prompt without the label. Advisory
  means advisory: a note cannot change a constraint, skip a rung, or stop the run.
- **New package `mentor/knowledge/feedback/` (`flux-feedback`), stdlib-only.**
  `FeedbackChannel` is a daemon thread on stdin, active only when stdin `isatty()` -- under
  CI, pipes, or redirection it prints no hint and reads nothing, so a scripted run is
  byte-identical with the channel on (verified: a piped demo run shows zero feedback lines).
  Each non-blank line is acknowledged immediately from the reader thread, because a note that
  vanishes for six minutes of ChampSim feels dropped even when it is not.
- **Delivery follows the D369 pattern**: `flow._drain_human` drains at phase boundaries and
  before each proposer call, and the block threads into `build_prompt(..., human=...)` as a
  conditional kwarg beside `learned=`, spliced above the RULES. Truncation is newest-kept and
  announced ("(N earlier note(s) omitted to fit)") -- `fit_to_budget` was considered and not
  used: it is shaped for guidance-vs-facts shares, not a single note list.
- **On the record, and read back.** Every note is a `human_note` event in the existing
  `campaign_events` table (no schema change) via `Recorder.note/notes`, echoed into lessons
  tagged `[human]` -- on a model-free run the lesson says the note was recorded but reached no
  prompt, because a typed line must never vanish silently. A resumed campaign reloads earlier
  notes marked `[earlier run]`, the same read-back rule as D367's seed pool. `[human]` lines
  are excluded from the report's `[screen rung]` retag: they quote no measurement.
- **Entry points**: `flux_prefetcher_dse_loop(interactive_feedback=True)` constructs the
  channel (the node's arguments stay JSON-safe); `demo.py` passes it by default with
  `--no-feedback` to opt out. The TTY gate makes the default safe everywhere.
- **No MCP/CHIA surface in v1** -- the channel is the terminal. Named future work: a
  `flux_feedback_post` tool so an agent (or a second terminal via MCP) can post guidance into
  a running campaign's db, which WAL already makes safe; and wiring the drain into the other
  loops (interconnect's `DirectedSearch` `lessons` callable is the natural slot).

**Verified:** 11 unit tests (`tests/unit/test_human_feedback.py`: collected-once drains, inert
without a TTY, label always present, newest-kept truncation announced, persistence + resume
reload, prompt splice, model-free acknowledgment) plus the flake-packages guard; live under a
pty (`script`): hint, immediate ack, `human_note` rows in the db, and on a resumed run
"1 operator note(s) from an earlier run rejoin the proposer prompt" with the `[human]` lesson
in the report; a piped run stays inert.

## D389: The catalog page renders for readers, not models

**Date:** 2026-09-03. **Ask (Cedric):** improve the GitHub Pages tool catalog -- the pages
(e.g. /catalog/loops/) are bloated, "a mess of text".

**The diagnosis:** D387 rendered `ToolSpec.render()` verbatim onto the pages. That form is
deliberately what the omni `describe` meta-tool returns -- the flat shape a MODEL copies
arguments out of -- and on a page it reads as a wall: every tool a run of 15-20 dense bullets,
optionals indistinguishable from requireds, and the catalog's first-sentence arg-doc
truncation leaving dangling ", e.g." stubs.

**Decisions:**
- **The site gets its own renderer** in `website/generate_catalog.py`; `ToolSpec.render()`
  stays untouched as the agent surface. Per tool: an `##` heading (so Material's page TOC
  lists every tool), the summary, required parameters as a small table (name / type / what it
  is), and the optional ones -- which dominate; several tools take 15+ -- folded into a
  `??? note` collapsible table that adds the default column. Table cells escape pipes,
  flatten newlines, and drop the truncation's dangling "(e.g." fragments.
- **Same provenance, same guard.** The content is still the introspected surface verbatim
  (summaries and per-arg first sentences unedited), and
  `tests/unit/test_site_catalog_freshness.py` regenerates and diffs unchanged -- the renderer
  lives inside the generator the test calls, so a formatting drift fails CI like a content
  drift.

**Verified:** regenerated in the dev shell; `mkdocs build --strict` clean; freshness test
green; the built loops page carries 8 collapsible blocks and 13 tables where it carried one
unbroken bullet run.

## D390: A btop for the loops

**Date:** 2026-09-03. **Ask (Cedric):** a curses CLI-UI for Flux -- panels/tabs on
number keys like btop (current task, timing, output/results/measurements) and a prompt
field for feedback where enabled.

**Shape (`core/tui`, package `flux_tui`, stdlib curses only -- no new dependency):**
- **Thin shell, pure core.** The curses file owns the terminal and nothing else; panel
  content (`panels.build`) and the line editor are pure functions, unit-tested with no
  tty (8 tests). Panels: 1 task, 2 timing (flux_profile.report_lines), 3 results +
  measurements, 4 log, 5 feedback, 6 help; arrows/PgUp scroll; q quits (twice to
  abandon a live run).
- **The loop keeps not knowing about UIs.** An `EventBus` (bounded deques, never
  blocks the worker) carries task/measure/result events; the loop's ordinary print
  output lands in the log panel via a stdout redirect, so an unmodified loop already
  shows its reporting. Demos opt in with `--tui`; without a tty the TUI refuses and
  the plain path runs -- a UI that silently eats output under redirection would be
  worse than none.
- **The TUI IS the feedback channel.** Inside curses the raw-stdin reader (D388)
  cannot exist, so `TuiFeedback` implements the same duck-typed contract
  (`drain() -> list[Note]`, start/close/active) fed by the prompt line, and
  `flux_prefetcher_dse_loop` gained an injectable `feedback_channel` so the TUI's
  channel replaces -- never duplicates -- the stdin one. Notes reach the same drain
  points with the same D388 advisory label; the imapping demo mounts the TUI with the
  field disabled, honestly, until that loop consumes guidance.
- **Verified in a real pty** (script(1)): the interconnect_mapping demo ran under the
  TUI end to end, q quit cleanly, and the post-run report printed on the real stdout.

## D391: The task tab shows the work, not just its name

**Date:** 2026-09-03. **Trigger (Cedric):** "only the log tab shows data really" -- the
TUI's task panel was a flat list of stage names, and the loops never even fed it (the
prefetcher's `--tui` run left it at "no task reported yet").

**Design: one tool call = one task, and the instrument the loops already have feeds
it.** `flux_profile.phase()` was already wrapped around every expensive thing a loop
does -- ChampSim, Yosys, OpenROAD, OpenSTA, Verilator, model generation. It grew an
optional observer seam (`set_listener`; callbacks wrapped so a broken listener can
never fail a run -- test-pinned) plus `why=`/`**params` kwargs that go ONLY to the
observer (aggregation stays keyed by name, so no timing bucket ever splits). `phase()`
also gained `mark()` for instantaneous stage headlines. The TUI attaches a listener
around the whole worker, so EVERY phased block in ANY loop becomes a live task row --
no loop changed a line to get coverage.

The bus's task model is now structured (`task_start`/`task_end`: name, kind, why,
params, t0/t1, ok, note; `task()` stays as a headline marker), and the tabs divide
the story (Cedric's split): **tab 1 is the CURRENT task in depth** -- status, live
duration, why, every parameter on its own line, and long text rendered as an indented
block, so an LLM task shows its ACTUAL prompt (bounded at the bus edge, 4k chars per
value, so a chatty caller cannot grow the ring); between tasks it shows the last
finished one the same way. **Tab 2 (timing) carries the aggregate phase table plus
the call-by-call history** (when, duration, ok/FAIL, why, params-in-brief, stage
headlines threaded through).
Enriched call sites so the rows say something: ChampSim (prefetcher set + trace +
instruction counts), model calls (model tag, num_predict, think, prompt size),
OpenROAD/OpenSTA (the flow's own `what`), Verilator (topology). The prefetcher's
stage transitions mark headlines through its existing `Study.phase` seam.

**The first live report ("no task reported yet" at 0:16, Cedric) closed the gap the
seam could not see:** the prefetcher's setup -- binary resolution, trace staging to
scratch, cache/measurer build -- ran before any phased block, and no stage mark fired
until "stage1". Now the TUI marks "starting" at t=0 on its own, `_setup` phases its
real steps and marks `setup`, `_baseline_and_evidence` marks `baseline`. Re-verified
against the real loop headlessly: at t=3 the panel shows the starting stage; at t=12
two concurrent ChampSim sims render as CURRENT 1/2 with live durations, the prefetcher
stack as why, and trace/instruction parameters.

**Finishing must not lose the report (Cedric's third report):** the results tab was
empty because no loop fed it, so the only readable output appeared after quitting,
printed into terminal scrollback. `run_tui` grew `on_result(result)` -- the worker
renders the returned report into the results tab the moment the loop completes, the
view auto-switches there once (keys then navigate as usual), and the header reads
"done · q quits". The prefetcher demo passes its own `_print_report` through a
capture, so the same decision-first report is readable inside the TUI and still
printed to the real stdout after quit. A renderer that raises is logged, never fatal.

**The session's fourth report bundle (broken terminal, rerun, bloat):** (a) the tty
attributes are saved with termios at entry and force-restored after curses ends, so
echo can never stay off whatever curses, a worker thread, or a grandchild did -- the
"typed input invisible after quit" failure is closed at the layer beneath curses.
(b) `r` after completion RERUNS the loop on the same bus: history, results and
feedback notes stay on screen, the pass is marked `rerun #N`, and for loops that
resume from their own store (the prefetcher campaign, D367) a rerun literally
continues the study -- the operator can keep a loop alive from inside the TUI
instead of restarting the demo. (c) The results tab tidies captured reports
(blank-run collapse, compact 12-row measurements block) and the header gained a
spinner and elapsed clock; scrolling clamps at the top and shows ↑/↓ position
markers.

**Layout modernised (fifth report: "the db in the top is not super useful"):** the
header is now two lines -- the loop's name in bold with the live state on the right
(spinner + elapsed while running, green done / red failed where the terminal has
color) and a tab bar whose active segment is highlighted; the db path moved to a
bottom status bar as a right-aligned subtitle next to contextual key hints, and the
feedback prompt sits above that bar. run_tui grew `subtitle=` for exactly this kind
of detail that identifies a run without deserving the title.

**Every demo now has `--tui`** through one helper (`flux_tui.demo_tui`): run under
the panels when there is a tty, plain otherwise, with each demo's own report captured
into the results tab (bankmap/macarray reuse their `_print`, interconnect renders
`result.summary()`, omni and interconnect_mapping had their inline report blocks
extracted into closures for the purpose). Feedback stays enabled only where a loop
consumes it (the prefetcher); everywhere else the feedback tab says so honestly. One
archaeology note: interconnect_mapping's demo already carried an inert `--tui` flag
from the D390 session -- it now does what it promised.

**Sixth report ("(between tasks)" during a solver run): the compute is phased too.**
The proposers were already instrumented; the dead air was z3 and pure-python work.
Now bankmap's z3 XOR search is a task (strides, concurrency, budget as params),
interconnect_mapping phases its coarse stages (per-policy scoring, the hill-climb,
each coordination round, the certificate exhaustion with its size as why), and every
omni tool execution is a task named `omni: <tool>` carrying its compact arguments --
so the current-task panel always has something true to say about where the wall
clock is.

Rerun hygiene from the seventh report: "starting" marks once (it lived inside the
worker and re-marked on every rerun), rerun reports get a `── run #N ──` separator in
the results tab, and the timing tab drops its "(no timing recorded)" line when the
task history below it says more. The imapping phases verified headlessly: a 10 s run
aggregates to score 54% / certify 25% / coordinate 13% / climb 5% with the same calls
as task rows.

Verified live headlessly: a real Yosys+OpenSTA screen produced two task rows with
durations, ok status, and the flow's own why ("yosys synthesis", "opensta on the
synthesized netlist"). The curses shell itself stays hand-verified (`--tui`), the
honest boundary D390 drew. 7 TUI unit tests.

## D392: Find the interconnects first, prove the mappings where provable

**Date:** 2026-09-03. **Ask (Cedric):** restructure interconnect_mapping's big loop --
find interconnects, then combine with mapping functions, testing throughput on the
storage-mode access patterns; reuse the interconnect and mapping-function loops as
little loops, with their inner tasks visible in the TUI.

**Shape:**
- **Little loop A (interconnect-app style), `interconnect_loop`**: generates ~30
  fabric candidates over parameter grids (butterfly radix x slimming, hierarchical
  groups x uplinks, concentrator actives, ring slots, anchors), screens each under a
  reference mapping on the storage-mode traffic, keeps the screen-front. Each screen
  is a TUI task. First run: 25 candidates -> 6 kept, two of them (hier-8x4, hier-4x4)
  grid points the old fixed dozen never contained -- the search finds what a catalog
  cannot.
- **Little loop B (bankmap style), `z3_mapping_policy`**: the traffic's dominant
  strides (each tensor's row pitch in bank-rows -- the reduction that lets bankmap's
  solver speak to storage modes) go to bankmap's z3 `solve()`; a solved fold is a
  PROVEN-conflict-free policy `S10-z3-proven` (bankmap's XorFold IS this study's hash
  class, so it drops straight in). First run's verdict was honest refusal: no fold
  exists for strides {1,3,4,8,11,12,13,16} with 16 concurrent -- reported as the
  solver's verdict, not a timeout excuse. The climb gained improvement marks; the
  coordinate step's little-loop calls are now their own tasks ("mapping little-loop:
  tune hash for fabric", "interconnect little-loop: fit fabric to mapping").
- **The big loop is staged and marked**: find fabrics -> build the policy field
  (climb + z3 + optional model) -> combined evaluation on the FOUND fabrics ->
  coordination -> certificates -> conclusion. A live timing tab now attributes ~95%
  of the wall clock (Cedric's own run: coordinate 57%, scoring 19%, climb 8.5%,
  scope report 5.3%, certificates 1.9%).

**The clock counts run time, not reading time (eighth report):** pressing r after
studying results added the whole idle gap to elapsed. The bus now banks active
seconds at done() and resumes the count at restart(), and both the header and the
task panel read that `elapsed_s` -- frozen when finished, idle between reruns never
counted, task-history "when" still on the session timeline so old rows do not shift.

**Two operator keys (same session):** `f` enters MODAL feedback input -- every key
belongs to the line until Enter submits or Esc cancels, so digits, r, q and t are
typeable without fighting the keybinds (the old always-live editor made 0-9 ambiguous)
-- and `t` cycles the model's reasoning for FUTURE calls (default -> think:on ->
think:off), through a `set_think_override` seam in the native client; the status bar
shows the active state and the current call keeps its mode. The cursor appears only
in input mode.

18 unit tests; demo verified end to end (57 design points over the found fabrics;
balanced pick unchanged -- the found fabrics confirm rather than overturn D383's
answer, which is itself evidence the fixed catalog was well chosen).

## D393: The report leads with the answer

**Date:** 2026-09-03. **Trigger (Cedric):** "that result is way too bloated... I don't
understand what is the best? what is the pareto front? what are top candidates? what
is the mapping function for what interconnect?" -- four questions the report should
answer in its first screen, and instead buried under a 57-row field table, 100
certificate lines and 17 scope breakdowns (each section added by an iteration for a
reason, none of them removed for the reader).

**The default report is now the answer, in order of the questions:** a THE ANSWER
block (best overall knee pick plus the three corners, with the MAPPING and the
INTERCONNECT as separate labeled columns and the pick's proved tile families right
under it); the Pareto front alone as a compact mapping|interconnect table with
star/corner markers; a best-mapping-per-interconnect table showing BOTH the fastest
and the highest-throughput mapping per fabric (a single by-latency winner hid the
trade -- S9 swept a column it only half-deserves); guarantees as one
proved/refuted count per frontier pair; scope breakdowns for the three top picks
only. `--full` prints everything the old report did. The 20-minute exhaustive dump
is now opt-in; the 30-line answer is the default.

**Tab 6 stopped being a help page (same report):** the status bar already teaches
the keys, so 6 is now INFO -- the run's identity: the demo's own config (db, seed,

condensed, not lost.

Also this session: the timing tab's percentages divide by the TUI's ACTIVE run
clock (flux_profile's own window kept running while the operator read results --

prints as an explicit "unattributed (no phase yet)" line instead of hiding in the

## D394: A second model, so the first one can be wrong out loud

**Date:** 2026-09-03. **Trigger (Cedric):** "are the area numbers correct? is the
throughput estimation correct? can we simulate throughput? can we build
high-confidence in the model/design/results?" The honest answers, and the rung built
in response:

- **Area**: a structural RANKING, not um2. The --phys element screen is real ASAP7;
  composed-from-elements carries D272's measured both-directions gap; whole-fabric
  OpenROAD P&R for the 2-4 picks is the truth rung and worth its minutes -- for the
  field of 57 it is not.
- **Throughput/latency**: the analytic cycle law is an OPTIMISTIC bound (perfect
  intra-step scheduling, zero arbitration loss). Nothing measured that gap -- now
  something does.

**`simulate.py`: an independent discrete-event model.** Greedy arrival-ordered
arbiter, per-bank single-port grants, per-level fabric capacity, per-access port
budgets, cycle by cycle -- sharing none of the analytic arithmetic. Contract tests
pin the ladder's logic: exact agreement where a scheduler cannot help, and
sim >= analytic elsewhere. The first cut FAILED its own contract by being more
optimistic than the bound -- latency definition drift (it credited early finishers
their own cycle where D380's law charges the step barrier) -- which is precisely the
class of error a second model exists to catch, and it caught it on day one.

**Measured verdict (seed 0, holdout, top picks):** real arbitration costs
+2.0% (S9+hier-8x4) to +5.9% (S5+hier-8x4) over the analytic bound -- the estimates
are honest to within ~6%, the ranking is unchanged, and the report now prints the
gap beside THE ANSWER so "estimated" is never mistaken for "simulated". The
confidence ladder stands: analytic bound -> discrete-event sim (every pick) ->
element STA (--phys) -> whole-fabric P&R and Verilator RTL as the named next rungs.

## D408: The NLU study: the model designs the unit, the rig owns the truth

**Date:** 2026-09-04. **Cedric's ask:** a demo whose loop designs an FP16
non-linear unit (exp, log, sigmoid, tanh, gelu, recip, rsqrt), does P&R and
testing for PPA, fmax and error rate under a <=1 ULP mantissa gate, builds its own
unit tests, and works from scratch or from previous runs -- with Claude building
ONLY the runner/framework/loop, plus some seeded knowledge. `applications/nlu` is
that split, held strictly.

**What the rig owns (because a judge must):** the interface contract (one `nlu`
top with a 3-bit op port; per-op designs get a framework-generated mux wrapper so
both styles pay for selection and compare honestly); the FP16 reference
(float64 -> round-to-half, stated and versioned) with ULP distance on the monotone
key and CLASS rules for specials -- NaN by class, infinities exactly, saturation
counted as the error it is; a test-vector floor no author can lower (every
exponent bucket, both signs, subnormals, boundary values); and the discovery that
makes the gate a PROOF: FP16 has 65536 inputs, so every operator is checked
exhaustively in a purpose-built Verilator sweep (bits in, bits out, numpy judges)
-- the bankmap posture, found again where the truth is cheap. Latency is defined
as the design's register count, and the harness test that caught the off-by-one
edge is the reason that sentence exists.

**What the model owns:** the method per operator (the seeded cheat sheet in
`knowledge.py` teaches LUT, interpolation, piecewise/minimax polynomials,
Newton-Raphson, CORDIC, bit products, parabolic synthesis, and the range
reductions the exponent gives for free -- directions, not instructions), shared
vs per-op hardware, combinational vs pipeline depth -- and the TESTS: a
test-author round proposes adversarial vectors per operator, validated and merged
over the floor, persisted as campaign events so the suite accumulates across
runs. The designer prompt also reads the operator's own paper library (D407)
through the local index; Cedric had already stocked it with the PACE and CORDIC
papers among others, and the excerpts ride in cite-labelled.

**The ladder and the rim, all reused:** exhaustive prove -> yosys/STA screen ->
flux_frontier over area/fmax (error is a gate, never a trade) -> OpenROAD
placement on spread finalists for the quoted PPA -> flux_decide (target-and-floor
under --target-mhz, the knee of area/fmax/power otherwise) -> flux_report.
Records from day one: sources ride in the candidate dicts so a resumed run
re-judges earlier designs with no model attached (--llm-round 0), and the
read-back carries conclusions, style/method/latency duels (D400) and past
refusals with their counterexamples. Feedback, reload_notes, demo_run, the TUI
and the rim-conformance guard all apply -- the seventh loop is the first born
with the whole rim.

**Pinned by the framework's own tests** (13, no NLU design among them): the
reference's known values and special classes, ULP adjacency across an exponent
boundary, the floor's coverage, authored-vector validation, the parse gates, the
sweep harness against real Verilator (a bit-flipper and a register pipe -- not a
design), and the end-to-end refusal: a scripted "designer" handing in y=x as exp
is refused by exhaustion with the failing input attached, the record keeps it,
and the next run's prompt says so.

## D407: The library: your papers, indexed beside the corpus, never committed

**Date:** 2026-09-04. **Cedric's ask:** a folder under mentor/knowledge for papers
and documents the model can use the way it uses the protocols -- and gitignored,
because those documents must not be pushed.

`mentor/knowledge/library/` is that folder, and the distinction from its siblings
is the point: `corpus/` is licensed standards WITH provenance, committed on
purpose; `protocols/` is this project's own curated method documents; the library
is OTHER PEOPLE'S WORKS -- downloaded papers, vendor docs -- so it ships holding
only a README and a `.gitignore` that ignores everything else, and each machine
fills its own. The test asks git itself (`git check-ignore`) rather than parsing
the ignore file: a paper anywhere under the folder is ignored, the README and the
ignore file are tracked.

**Ingestion** is a new text connector beside the AsciiDoc one, same `Chunk`
contract: `.md`/`.txt` split per paragraph with the nearest Markdown heading
attached, `.adoc` delegating to the corpus connector, and `.pdf` extracted through
`pdftotext` at index time (papers ARE PDFs; a machine without poppler skips them
with a note, never indexes bytes as text, never crashes). Chunk ids are
library-relative so two notes.md in different subfolders cannot collide;
`build_default_index` folds the library in under standard_id "library", which
means `knowledge_lookup(query, standard_id="library")` serves it on all three
agent surfaces with no new tool. Verified live: a dropped paper was retrieved by
its own words with its heading attached and never appeared in git status.

## D406: A TUI frame is disposable; a resize must not exit the run

**Date:** 2026-09-04. **Observed (Cedric):** the prefetcher TUI sometimes exited
without anyone pressing q, mid-run. **Cause:** every draw call in the frame loop
was unguarded, and curses raises `curses.error` whenever a write lands past the
current edge -- which a resize mid-frame (a tmux pane change, a window drag) or a
terminal squeezed below the layout's rows produces reliably. The exception unwound
`curses.wrapper`; `run_tui`, seeing an unfinished run and no worker error, raised
"run abandoned from the TUI" -- blaming the user for an exit the UI caused.

**Fix, two layers.** Draw calls (`addnstr`, `hline`, `erase`, `refresh`, `move`)
now go through a `_Screen` proxy that swallows `curses.error`: a frame is
DISPOSABLE -- skip the failed write, draw the next frame against the new geometry.
Input (`getch`) and geometry (`getmaxyx`) pass through untouched, so nothing that
carries state is ever swallowed. And a panel builder that raises now renders as a
visible "panel error: ..." body instead of killing the UI -- a bug should be seen,
not converted into a phantom abandonment. The worker thread's own failures keep
their D390 path: shown in the panel, re-raised after quit.

## D405: The test files stop re-declaring the import path

**Date:** 2026-09-04. Twenty unit-test files each carried their own
`sys.path.insert` block naming the src dirs that file happened to import -- each a
hand-maintained subset of `flake.nix`'s `localSrcDirs`, and each a copy that could
go stale: the D401 flux_study split had to touch four of them, and several files
were carrying dead `sys`/`Path` imports from inserts already removed in earlier
eras.

`tests/unit/conftest.py` now parses `localSrcDirs` out of the flake itself -- the
same regex the flake guard test uses, so there is still exactly one authoritative
list -- and puts every entry on `sys.path` once, before any test module loads.
Inside the dev shell the paths are already on PYTHONPATH and the inserts are
harmless; outside it, this is what lets every test file import at all, which is
what the per-file blocks were for. Nineteen files dropped their insert blocks
(`test_experiment_harnesses` keeps its own: it inserts non-package harness paths
the flake does not list), and a pyflakes sweep removed the orphaned `sys` and
`pathlib.Path` imports from thirty. Under this regime the next package move
touches the flake and nothing under tests/.

**Date:** 2026-09-04. The smell audit's honest finding was that the D397-D403 arc

`flux_tui.demo_run(run, tui=, title=, ...)` is now a demo's whole run path: the
TUI with the f key armed when asked, the plain terminal with the stdin channel
otherwise, `run(channel)` receiving whichever is live. KeyboardInterrupt
propagates on purpose -- the demo owns its exit code and its partial-state
message. The five demos (interconnect_mapping, macarray, interconnect, omni,

`flux_feedback.scripted_channel(*texts)` is the reference fake for the drain()
contract the loops consume; the three test copies now call it. Kept as copies, on

honest no-model tail -- differ in where the echo lands (lessons, log, print), and
a parameterized helper would be as long as the variation it hides.

it duplicated the bottom bar's `f feedback` hint and cost a content row; the prompt

PeConfig, Invention, sys, the module-level local_proposer my D403 delegate left
behind) and two dead locals an earlier phase-split left in imapping. What remains
flagged is interconnect's own pre-existing residue (dead function-local imports,

And the rim itself is now GUARDED: `test_rim_conformance` pins that every loop
entry accepts the operator channel, every request names its campaign record, and
every demo (the prefetcher's richer flow excepted, by name) runs through the

## D402: Bankmap's --db was a lie; now it is the record that seeds the model round

**Date:** 2026-09-04. The follow-up audit found one substantive gap left: bankmap.
Its `--db` flag flowed through the chia node into the request and DIED UNREAD --
the exact bug class D367 named ("--db PATH created no PATH... which made the flag a
lie") -- and bankmap was the last loop with a model role (llm_round, default 6)
consuming no operator feedback, a hole in D398's "every loop" claim.

Both closed with the same rim every other loop wears, shaped to what bankmap IS.
`request.db` now opens a campaign keyed by the problem (strides, concurrency,
banks, address bits, topology, stages). Every checked mapping lands as a trial
through the existing `track()` seam -- conflict-free ones with clean fraction and
hardware cost, refused ones carrying the checker's verdict as the error, because in
this loop the refusal IS the finding. Every exit passes one `_finish()`: the last
typed note is drained (recorded even when it reached no prompt) and the decision
lands as an INFERENCE conclusion, including the best-partial and proved-impossible
exits.

The read-back is bankmap-shaped: counterexamples are this loop's teaching signal,
so `flux_records` grew `refusals()` -- what a campaign refused, with reasons, read
back -- and a RESUMED run seeds the model round's ALREADY TRIED list from its own
past refusals before the first proposal is asked for. The operator's notes lead
`build_prompt` under HUMAN GUIDANCE, `demo_tui(feedback=True)` arms the f key, the
plain path opens the stdin channel, and unit-test requests default to no record so
the suite stops littering the working directory. The test pins the whole loop:
refused proposal -> recorded with verdict -> resumed run's prompt carries both the
old refusal and the typed note.

Noted and left alone, again deliberately: interconnect's private `a_proposer`
beside flux_llm's entry points -- consolidation touches the oldest loop for
cosmetic gain.

## D400: Where the knobs are names, the laws are duels

**Date:** 2026-09-04. D397 left an honest scope note: pairwise laws land where knobs
are scalar, and macarray was the next candidate. Its knobs are mostly NAMES (booth4
vs wallace, tree vs chain vs csa) -- but two configs differing in exactly one name
are still a controlled experiment somebody paid for; what they yield is not a
direction but a winner. `flux_extract.head_to_head` is that arithmetic: value pairs
compared by equality so categorical knobs work, A-vs-B and B-vs-A orderings pooled
under one canonical matchup, anecdotes (fewer than two pairs) withheld, strongest
|effect| weighted by evidence first -- the same posture as D369, one abstraction
over. `duels_text` renders the WHAT THE RECORD SHOWS block with "verdicts, not
instructions".

**macarray gains the flywheel:** its `db` is now also its campaign record -- every
screened design (rung screen, analytic) and every placed finalist (rung confirm,
simulated) recorded with fmax and area, the decision stored as an INFERENCE
conclusion, and on resume the inventor's prompt leads with the record's duels
(confirm rung preferred, screen honestly labelled "synthesis, no wires" otherwise),
after the operator's notes and beside _beat_text's same-run numbers. Verified live
on real yosys/opensta screens, twice: same campaign (new) then (resumed), 48 trials,
both conclusions, and the read-back said things this repo already knew the expensive
way -- pipeline 1 beats 0 by +618 MHz over 12 controlled pairs, behavioral beats
booth4 by +89 MHz, and the mapper knob measured at +2 MHz, i.e. the noise D-record
already called it.

**interconnect_mapping's read-back joins in:** the pair's two REAL knobs are the
policy and the fabric's NAME -- pipe depth and area are consequences of the name and
are dropped before pairing, or no pair would ever count as controlled -- so a
resumed proposer now also sees policy-vs-policy and fabric-vs-fabric verdicts on
holdout throughput.

## D399: Deciding stays per loop; the arithmetic and the closing grammar are shared

**Date:** 2026-09-04. Phases 3 and 4 of the D397 plan, scoped the way Cedric called
it: decide is per flow -- every loop has its own metrics and its own wording -- but
under the wording the loops kept re-deriving the same three moves, each carrying a
lesson somebody paid for. `orchestrator/decide` (flux_decide) now holds them once:
`corner` (an extreme with DETERMINISTIC tie-breaks -- a tie must not pick
arbitrarily, interconnect_mapping's rule), `knee_ranked` (the balanced pick as
minimal equal-weight normalized distance to the ideal; counting frontier rows
favours whichever extreme collects ties -- measured, it crowned the ring), and
`cheapest_meeting` (the target-and-floor rule with the measured-floor tolerance,
macarray's D366, returning a RULE TAG so each report keeps its own sentence).
interconnect_mapping's `conclude()` and macarray's `decide()` now delegate, their
tests passing unchanged.

`core/report` (flux_report) is the closing grammar's single home: the demos had
already converged on `══ THE ANSWER ══`, WHAT THIS RUN ESTABLISHED, NOT
ESTABLISHED and REFUSED (N), so the module writes those headers once, returns
lines rather than printing (a TUI captures them the same way), and adds the D398
OPERATOR GUIDANCE section. Adopted by interconnect_mapping, macarray and the
prefetcher with wording unchanged -- and one honest improvement: the prefetcher's
refusal list used to stop silently at six; the shared section counts its tail
("... and N more") because a capped list that does not say so is a small lie.

What stays per loop, on purpose: the answer itself, the front table, the
per-domain columns -- the loop's own voice. And bankmap keeps its exact-truth
shape untouched, as decided.

## D398: Every loop with a model role consumes operator feedback

**Date:** 2026-09-04. D388 built the channel and the prefetcher consumed it; the
other three model-role loops showed the f-key hint without listening. Phase 2 of the
D397 plan closes that gap with one shared move, `flux_feedback.drain_guidance`:
drain what was typed since the last boundary, hand each fresh note to the loop's
own persistence (swallowing its failures -- acknowledgement must not kill a run),
fold it into the run's accumulated notes, and return the labelled HUMAN GUIDANCE
block over all of them. `demo_tui` grew `feedback=True` -- the run callable then
receives the TUI's channel (None on the plain fallback) -- and every demo's plain
path opens the stdin channel, which stays inert without a terminal so scripted runs
are byte-identical.

Per loop, at the boundary where a note can still act: **interconnect_mapping**
drains at every proposer round (the block leads the prompt, ahead of WHAT THE
RECORD SHOWS), persists each note as a campaign human_note event, echoes them on
`study.notes`, in the report and in the provenance JSON, and drains once more at
the end so a model-free run still records the line. **macarray** drains before
invention -- the block leads `build_prompt`, notes land in the lessons tagged
[human] with the honest no-model tail -- and again after confirm. **interconnect**
takes the channel through a module-level `set_feedback` seam (the same posture its
problem numbers use, D333) and folds the block into each LLM round's knowledge
text. Advisory everywhere: injectivity gates, golden vectors and holdout scoring
judge a guided proposal exactly like an unguided one -- the tests pin a note
reaching the prompt while the malformed proposal it decorates is still refused.

## D397: Records hold results and conclusions; extract builds laws

**Date:** 2026-09-04. **Plan (Cedric's refinement of the loop-shape audit):** solver
is an evaluator, not a node (removed from the crafter); calibrate joined the
evaluator row (slow-rung residuals widening the fast rung's intervals); records and
extract are TWO steps over the store -- records hold results and conclusions,
extract builds rules/laws/principles -- with code moved where it makes most sense;
decide stays per-flow over a shared base; bankmap stays the exact-truth variant;
omni's middle stays model-directed by design. This entry is phase 1.

**`mentor/records` (flux_records):** the prefetcher Recorder's pattern made
domain-neutral as SEMANTICS over `core/stores` (which stays put as the engine):
trials with rungs and refusals, `conclude()` storing INFERENCE-labelled events
beside the data (D297), `known()` reading measurements back best-first (D367),
`note()` persisting human lines, the same swallow-everything discipline -- a study
must not die because its logbook is unwritable (test-pinned).

**`mentor/extract` (flux_extract):** D369's pairwise arithmetic generalised --
knob dicts in, typed Laws out, a `coupled` hook for knobs wearing two names, the
same anecdote-withholding and evidence weighting. The prefetcher's reflect.py is now
a thin Bingo adapter over it with its public API preserved, and D369's tests passing
unchanged is the proof the generalisation lost nothing.

**interconnect_mapping closes its flywheel gap** (the newest loop was the least
aligned): `--db` (default demo-imapping.db), every scored pair recorded with holdout
metrics, refusals recorded with reasons, the run's `conclude()` stored as INFERENCE,
and on resume the LLM proposer's prompt opens with WHAT THE RECORD SHOWS -- earlier
runs' balanced picks and best measured pairs. Verified: same campaign id (new) then
(resumed) across two demo runs; an end-to-end test runs the study, reopens the
record, and asserts the read-back prompt content. One honest scope call: imapping's
candidates are not scalar-knobbed, so it feeds conclusions and best-pairs rather
than forced pairwise laws -- the laws land where knobs are scalar (prefetcher now;
macarray is phase 2's candidate).

Remaining phases as planned: feedback consumers for macarray/interconnect/imapping;
`orchestrator/decide` base; shared `core/report` scaffold.

## Still open — not resolved by this record

Resolved entries are removed rather than kept struck through: the log above is the permanent
record of *what happened*, so this section only needs to carry what is still live. Four items
that had been resolved (the first Booksim validation target, the knowledge-corpus licensing scope,
the agentic-strategy consolidation, and the hermetic-Timeloop port) were cut for that reason —
see D25, D31, D57 and D204–D206 respectively.

- **Scope-proportionality of the D26–D29 investment.** Four decisions and ~3,000 lines went into
  deepening one axis family (numeric architecture-parameter DSE, 5 agentic strategies), all
  validated against one flagship workload/architecture pair, while `docs/roadmap.md`'s own ranked
  "Immediate next actions" (knowledge-corpus licensing, an independent `noc_topology` evaluator, a
  native core, a synthesis rung) sat untouched. Not a code defect — a real question about whether
  that was the right next allocation of effort relative to D1's stated "full SoC-level DSE"
  objective, raised by D30's review and left for a deliberate choice, not resolved here.
- **The scientific-notation guard (D181) now has a live instance.** D225 reproduced the class
  for real: yosys `stat -liberty` switches to `1.93E+03` past ~1e3 um^2 and a fixed-point pattern
  failed on it. The booksim/noxim guards D181 added remain unexercised by those simulators, but
  the defect class itself is no longer hypothetical.
- **`protocols/` semantics are partial: OBI handshakes only.** D212/D213 made OBI's handshake and
  unconditional address-stability rules machine-checkable (Verilator-proven SVA from a rule-citing
  `handshakes` block), but conditional stability (`we`-gated `wdata`), ordering (R-10 aid/rid
  mirroring) and everything on other protocols stay prose-only. Every vendored quote is now
  machine-diffed against its vendored primary-document text on each test run (D214). The AXI
  documents remain structural — they are read from permissively-licensed *implementations*, not
  from Arm's specification, which cannot be redistributed (D31, D174). Setup/hold, CDC and
  metastability are deliberately absent — IEEE 1800 is not redistributable and no open substitute
  was found (D174's `definitions-clocking` coverage_note).
- **Authored artifacts are validated, not faithfulness-checked.** D232 (objectives) and D235
  (design specs) both validate structure with the real parsers and, for specs, execute the
  reference — but nothing machine-checks that the authored artifact matches the PROSE'S INTENT.
  The live tests probe intent with an independent lambda per behavior; production callers have
  no such probe. A faithfulness checker (e.g. a second model cross-examining the reference
  against the prose, or property extraction) is real, named future work on both paths.
- **Timeloop equivalence is calibration, not proof.** D206/D207/D215 measured exact agreement
  between the Docker and hermetic runners across five architectures (including one 2-D array),
  checked nightly. The workload family is still narrow (degenerate-GEMM MLPs), nothing establishes
  agreement across the input space, and `area_mm2` is 0.0 on both paths — area is untested by
  construction, not merely untested here.
- **CI cannot cover LLM-driven generation.** D155 added GitHub Actions (unit + conformance per
  push, nightly per-file integration sweep), which closes the "nothing runs the integration suite"
  gap — except for the generation tests, which need a local Ollama and skip themselves without
  one. A green nightly therefore does not mean generation works, and those are the tests that
  caught D153. Closing this needs a self-hosted runner with a model on it.
